en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll One.
Translated by Imperial Decree by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao-san Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of Fan Propagation, and the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Fahu, et al.
Chapter One: The Householder Bhadrapāla, Part One. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Blessed One, having completed the three-month summer retreat in Śrāvastī, set out to visit those who had prepared and finished his robes, accompanied by a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Together with the assembly of people— including other bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings,
ministers, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, elders, and various non-Buddhists, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas,
gandharvas, asuras, and garuḍas— [he arrived].
The kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, out of respect, reverence, and sincere faith, made offerings to the Blessed One—
the World-Honored One who accepts the world’s offerings and benefits, and who is the field of merit for the world—
namely: food and drink, clothing, bedding and seating, medicines for the treatment of illness, and other various extensive articles of use.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses the ten titles: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān; his name, fame, and renown are supreme, exalted, and transcendent, surpassing all the world.

Among the great assembly of the world—including devas, humans, asuras, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, and Brahmās—he has realized the fruits of sainthood through his own supernormal powers. Wherever he dwells, he proclaims the True Dharma, which is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its words and meaning are profound and far-reaching, pure and unadulterated, the perfect and stainless manifestation of the holy life (brahmacarya).

At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded slowly toward the kingdom of Magadha; traveling by stages, he arrived at the great city of Rājagṛha and, having reached it, stayed on Vulture Peak Mountain.

At that time, there was a householder in the city of Rājagṛha named Bhadrapāla. Having planted roots of merit in the past and performed extensive Buddhist services under former Buddhas, he possessed great wealth and vast resources for enjoyment. His storehouses were filled with gold, silver, grain, and treasures; he accumulated mani-jewels, pearls, conch shells, coral, lapis lazuli, and so forth, as well as elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, slaves, servants, attendants, and laborers.

At that time, the householder Bhadrapāla heard that the śramaṇa Gautama had left the royal palace out of pure faith to renounce the world, and was traveling through the kingdom of Magadha together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, eventually arriving in the great city of Rājagṛha and staying on Vulture Peak Mountain.

Furthermore, that śramaṇa Gautama is fully endowed with vast physical marks and meritorious qualities; his fame and renown transcend the world. He has realized the fruit of perfect enlightenment as a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān. According to what is appropriate for each, he proclaims the True Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; its words and meaning are profound and far-reaching, pure and unadulterated, possessing the characteristics of the perfectly pure and stainless Brahma-faring.
The elder then thought to himself:
"I should now go to that śramaṇa Gautama to approach, behold, and pay him homage.
That Buddha, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—his physical marks and meritorious qualities are most excellent."
When the elder Bhadrapāla had formed this thought, he immediately set out from the great city of Rājagṛha together with five hundred elders to go and pay homage to the Buddha.

At that time, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the great city of Rājagṛha for alms in due order, surrounded by a community of bhikṣus who were full of reverence and faith.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, was solemn and dignified in his deportment; his gait was tranquil and composed. His pure radiance illuminated the world, and his every movement—whether advancing or halting, bending or stretching—was upright and pristine.

At that time, Bhadrapāla and the five hundred elders saw from afar the World-Honored One approaching slowly, his majestic appearance and marks of excellence pure and dignified; his faculties were harmonious and supple, his mind was tranquil, and he was as perfectly tamed as a great nāga king, resembling a spring of water—pure and untainted.
He was surrounded by a retinue of countless devas and humans; his physical form was majestic like the color of purple gold, fully adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics.

The heavens rained down a vast and exquisite array of flowers; these falling blossoms were so dense as to completely cover the ground, and there were also seven-jeweled lotuses with billions of petals that rose up for him to tread upon with his feet.
The World-Honored One, endowed with hundreds of thousands of countless marks of majestic deportment and meritorious virtues, approached from afar.

When the elders saw him thus on the left side of the road, they conceived deep and pure faith in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and with minds of purity, they proceeded forward to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and with bodies upright and minds full of reverence and faith, they stood before the Buddha.
Then, the five hundred elders, including Bhadrapāla, addressed the Buddha together, saying:
“World-Honored One Gautama, among this great assembly, your physical marks and signs are most preeminent!”
The Blessed One Gautama’s majestic virtue excels within this great assembly!
The Blessed One Gautama’s renown excels within this great assembly!
The Blessed One Gautama’s radiance excels within this great assembly!
The World-Honored One Gautama possesses the mark of true golden color, most supreme and preeminent!
The physical marks of the World-Honored One are like those of the ancient Golden Immortals!
The physical marks of the World-Honored One are wondrous, peerless, and beyond compare!
"Blessed One, you possess all the marks and rare qualities!
Blessed One Gautama, there is no one equal to you in all the world!
Having seen that the Blessed One is endowed with such majestic marks and meritorious virtues, for what reason did you renounce the home life to become a monastic?"
At that time, the elder Bhadrapāla praised him with these verses:
“As I have previously heard of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Regarding his auspicious renown and majestic virtue,
I now behold his most supreme and wondrous marks, Possessing such extraordinary radiance.”
With the appearance of pure, exquisite, and genuine gold, His golden hue is sublime and beheld by all;
Untouched by dust and undefiled, he stands amidst the assembly Like the wondrous moon appearing among the stars.
In the past, I took refuge in the Honored One among Men, who is as exceedingly lofty and supreme as Mount Sumeru;
his crown-mark is adorned like a wondrous celestial canopy, covering all things everywhere and in succession.
The crown bone and the hair on his head are soft and smooth, possessing a wondrous color like that of the sapphire;
his neck resembles that of the peacock king, curling to the right with exquisite suppleness;
his forehead is broad, even, and pure white; and his two eyebrows are like the bow of Śakra.
The tuft of hair between the brows is pure and radiant, Like the king of stars, it shines with exquisite brilliance.
Your two eyes possess the wondrous and delightful marks; All who behold them give rise to a heart of joy.
Gazing intently, one never tires of looking; I prostrate to the World-Honored One’s pure eyes.
I behold the mark of the nose of the Honored One among Men: It is lofty, long, and straight, like a mountain of gold;
The lips are like amber and resemble the *bimba* fruit; Pure and radiant, they are like precious jewels.
The marks of the teeth are bright, pure, and brilliantly white, Like milk, like lotus roots, and like the bill of a duck.
Firm, pure, closely set, and even; moving and turning with grace and charm;
the large and small teeth are dense yet not thick;
the four fangs are sharp and stainless, like a king of swans amidst his flock—lustrous, pure, the whitest among the white.
Your face is like the pure radiance of the rising sun, with the color of a red utpala lotus or copper;
your tongue is pure, wondrous, broad, and long, completely covering your mouth and entirely pristine.
Within the realms of devas, humans, and Brahmā, I have never before seen such sublime marks and signs of a Buddha.
The lobes of your ears are like those of a lion king; possessing the marks of a lion, you are virtuous and fearless.
I observe that your throat possesses majestic power, beautifully receiving all flavors with pure radiance.
His neck is upright and free from curvature or crookedness; he always obtains the supreme flavor among all flavors.
His countenance and deportment are grave, dignified, and exquisite; the seven parts of his body are flat and full, as is renowned throughout the world.
The most supreme and auspicious Honored One among men, like the radiance of the sun appearing upon a mountain peak, possesses what are called the seven places that are level and full:
the palms of both hands, the soles of both feet, the two shoulders, and the single nape of the neck;
these seven places are equally full, perfectly complete, pure, and brilliantly radiant.
His two arms are long, straight, and furthermore supple and round, Like those of a nāga king, wondrous and pure;
Neither high nor low, his two arms are equal, Hanging down, they extend past the knees.
His upper body is like that of a lion king; his form is as perfectly rounded as a nyagrodha tree;
like Nārāyaṇa, his body is indestructible; he is fully endowed with great strength and the power of patience.
The hairs on his body point upward and are soft and supple; each hair curls to the right.
His pure and wondrous body is unstained by dust or grime, like a lotus flower that remains unsullied by water.
His private organ is concealed and hidden, as secret as that of a well-trained and noble horse-king;
his two thighs are like soft grass, and his two calves are positioned in perfect symmetry.
The heels are level and full, with feet in perfect proportion; both hands and feet possess the webbed membrane between the toes;
furthermore, like those of a king of geese, the fingers and toes are slender and long, numbering twenty in total.
The fingers are long and slender with copper-colored nails; the soft hairs on all the digits grow downward.
Beneath the soles of the feet are the complete thousand-spoked wheels, and the ankle bones are neither coarse nor prominent.
His tread is level and even, without high or low; as he walks, his feet remain four finger-widths above the ground.
His most supreme and wondrous marks in the world are perfect; as he steps, precious lotuses appear beneath his feet.
The World-Honored One’s gait is one of great fearlessness; like a lion king, he is without high or low.
Neither slow nor fast, he moves with balanced composure, sporting with sovereign ease and free from all dread.
The devas rain down a multitude of exquisite flowers, In the sky they vyingly play sublime music;
Non-humans offer worship with reverent devotion— Such are the rare signs of this Buddha’s supernormal powers.
His physical form surpasses Vaiśravaṇa; his majestic radiance exceeds that of a hundred thousand suns.
Among all the multitudes of devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās, none possess such supreme merit.
Now a doubt has arisen within my mind: The Buddha possesses the most supreme power of supernatural faculties;
what further gateway of merit did he behold, that the Buddha left the household life to achieve the fruit of sainthood?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the elder Kṣemaṃkara and the other elders, saying: "Elders!
I see ten kinds of afflictive dharmas that gather in the world; this suffering is exceedingly great."
What are the ten? First, birth is a disturbance;

second, aging is a disturbance; third, illness is a disturbance; fourth, death is a disturbance; fifth, sorrow is a disturbance; sixth, lamentation is a disturbance; seventh, suffering is a disturbance; eighth, affliction is a disturbance; ninth, grief and wailing are disturbances; tenth, saṃsāra is a disturbance.
Having seen these ten kinds of afflictive phenomena gathered together in the world, I therefore left the home life with pure faith in order to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Foolish worldlings, bound by the snares of saṃsāra, give rise to agitation, grief, and lamentation;
old age and sickness swiftly pursue them.”
Because of sorrow and lamentation, there is suffering and affliction; the law of death comes to devour one.
If one is rescued and escapes, one is liberated from the net of the three realms of existence.
"Furthermore, householder!
The single dharma of anger causes mutual harm as beings gather in the world; this suffering is exceedingly great.
There are ten forms of such harm. What are these ten?
First, because of my own mind, I have already committed various harmful acts in the past.
Second, giving rise to such thoughts, I am currently committing various harmful acts in the present.
Third, one gives rise to the thought: "In the future, I shall commit various harmful acts.
Fourth, one gives rise to the thought regarding those dear to me: "They have not yet committed various harmful acts [against me]."
Fifth, regarding those whom I love, thoughts arise that they do not currently inflict any harm.
Sixth, regarding those whom I love, thoughts arise that they shall not inflict any harm in the future.
Seventh, one gives rise to the thought that those who are not dear to me have already committed various harmful acts in the past.
Eighth, one gives rise to the thought that those who are not dear to me are currently committing various harmful acts in the present.
Ninth, one gives rise to the thought that those who are not dear to oneself will cause various harmful acts in the future.
Tenth, one gives rise to the thought of performing acts that are unbeneficial, harmful, and faulty.

Having seen these ten kinds of harmful matters gathered together in the world, and in order to cause others to be free from those harms, I have therefore left the household life with pure faith to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Among sentient beings, hatred is greatest; Each and every one harms another.
In the past, present, and future, they inflict harm, Accomplishing ten kinds of harmful deeds."
One who loves does not harbor malice—whether toward what has been done, what is yet to be done, or what is being done now;
nor do they establish a nature of harm.
Even if one acts with hostility toward me, they do not act in a way that causes me injury.
As it was in the past, so shall it be in the future;
having produced harmful karmic deeds along with meaningless faults and the ten afflictions of harm,
I beheld these dharmas of harm and thus left the home life out of pure faith.
"Furthermore, householder!
Among the various views, the collection of worldly, perilous, and evil views constitutes a suffering that is exceedingly great.
There are ten kinds of such perilous and evil views.

What are the ten? First, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding the view of a self; second, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding the view of a sentient being; third, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding the view of a life-span; fourth, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding the view of a person; fifth, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding the view of annihilationism; sixth, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding the view of eternalism; seventh, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding the view of non-action; eighth, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding the view of causelessness; ninth, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding the view of inequality; tenth, giving rise to dangerous and evil views regarding wrong views.

Having seen these ten kinds of perilous and evil views, and desiring to cause all beings universally to shatter them, I have therefore left the household life with pure faith to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The view of a self, a person, and a sentient being, And likewise the view of a life-span—
All such foolish worldlings Are shrouded by perilous and evil views."
To sever the views of eternalism and nihilism, as well as non-action,
And to establish [beings] in right view— amidst the false, the causeless, and the uneven—
I have therefore gone forth. Throughout incalculable, nayuta-hundreds-of-thousands of eons,
Throughout kalpas numbering in the koṭis, he acts for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
"Furthermore, householder, there is a great arrow of illness that gathers in the world; this suffering is exceedingly great."
There are ten kinds of great arrows of illness. What are these ten? First, the arrow of craving; second, the arrow of ignorance;

third, the arrow of desire; fourth, the arrow of greed; fifth, the arrow of hatred; sixth, the arrow of delusion; seventh, the arrow of pride; eighth, the arrow of views; ninth, the arrow of formation; and tenth, the arrow of destruction.

Regarding these ten kinds of great disease-arrows, I desire to cause them all to be completely extracted; for this reason, I have left the home life with pure faith to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Because of the arrow of craving, one accumulates through greed; Because of a lack of wisdom, one is shrouded in darkness.
Enveloped by the dark ignorance of delusion, One wanders on toward other aggregates."
The arrow of desire pierces as it is shot; the arrow of craving causes one to swallow [the bait];
the arrow of hatred gives rise to delusion; the arrow of ignorance completely shrouds all.
The arrow of views gives rise to opposition; likewise, the arrow of pride brings about ruin.
All foolish worldlings, however, slander one another,
claiming "this is false" and "that is real," thus giving rise to mutual conflict and dispute.
To shatter the arrow of the world’s disease, there is only the Buddha’s dharma of non-arising.
All sentient beings in the world are constantly pierced by arrows;
to rescue and protect them, he pulls them out and causes them all to be free from every suffering.

The First Chapter of the Section on the Elder Bhadrapāla, Part Two:
"Furthermore, Elder, the fundamental basis upon which all phenomena such as craving are established is the aggregation of the world; this suffering is exceedingly great."
There are ten kinds of fundamental dharmas of craving. What are these ten?

First, because of craving as a condition, one gives rise to seeking; second, because of seeking as a condition, attachment arises; third, because of attachment as a condition, the view of self arises; fourth, because of the view of self as a condition, one reckons things as fixed; fifth, because of such fixation as a condition, sensual desire arises; sixth, because of sensual desire as a condition, one gives rise to clinging; seventh, because of clinging as a condition, stinginess arises; eighth, because of stinginess as a condition, one engages in grasping; ninth, because of grasping as a condition, one fails to exercise restraint; tenth, because of failing to exercise restraint as a condition, manifold sufferings arise. Because of this lack of restraint, one wields swords and staves, engaging in combat and litigation; due to these causes, one gives rise to various unwholesome dharmas of sinful karma, such as double-tongued speech and the like.

Having seen these ten kinds of dharmas rooted in craving that are gathered together in the world, I desired to establish them in the dharma that is rootless; for this reason, I went forth with pure faith and proceeded to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Swallowed by craving, sentient beings pursue this and that;
Gaining profit, they cling to the view of self, And take what they receive as definitive."
"This is something I must do"—thus desire and greed increase;
once desire and greed have increased, attachment gives rise to stinginess.
Regarding the faults of worldly stinginess, one becomes firm and deeply attached to them.
Because of grasping, one fails to guard oneself, giving rise to a continuous succession of faults and transgressions.
Through such lack of restraint, the fool seizes swords and staves to inflict harm;
he extensively commits various karmic deeds of evil, whereby suffering increases thereafter.
Once craving has increased through its conditions, all manner of sufferings arise;
having realized supreme enlightenment, I cause them to abide in that which is rootless.
"Furthermore, householder!"
The collection of dharmas of the group of those fixed in error is a worldly assembly; this suffering is exceedingly great.
There are ten types of false dharmas. What are these ten?

First is wrong view, second is wrong intention, third is wrong speech, fourth is wrong action, fifth is wrong livelihood, sixth is wrong effort, seventh is wrong mindfulness, eighth is wrong concentration, ninth is wrong liberation, and tenth is wrong knowledge.

These ten kinds of factors of the wrongly fixed class (mithyā-niyata-rāśi) are gathered together in the world, and this suffering is exceedingly great. Having seen this, I have caused all beings to transcend every wrong dharma; for this reason, I have left the home life with pure faith to realize the fruit of unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Held within by false views, The domain of false reflection,
Speaking false words, One gives rise to and performs all manner of false deeds.”
Wrong livelihood and wrong effort, Wrong mindfulness and wrong concentration,
Give rise to that wrong liberation, And invariably produce wrong knowledge.
These various groups of the wrongly fixed (mithyā-niyata-rāśi) Are established by the foolish.
To cause them to turn from the heterodox and enter the orthodox, for this reason I have left the household life.

Furthermore, householder, the evil realms are deep and perilous, and the world is gathered therein; these sufferings are exceedingly great. One gradually moves toward the evil destinies, increases the evil destinies, and opens wide the gates to the evil destinies—namely, there are ten kinds of unwholesome karma.
What are the ten? First is killing;

second is stealing; third is sexual misconduct; fourth is false speech; fifth is frivolous speech; sixth is divisive speech; seventh is harsh speech; eighth is covetousness; ninth is malice; and tenth is wrong view.

"These ten kinds of unwholesome courses of action lead gradually toward the evil realms, increase the evil realms, and extensively open the gates to the evil realms. Having seen this, in order to bring about deliverance from all perilous and evil paths, I have therefore left the household life with pure faith to seek the realization of the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Sentient beings who take life, who seize the wealth and property of others,
and who engage extensively in sexual misconduct— they shall swiftly fall into hell.”
Divisive speech and harsh words, Falsehoods lacking in certainty, And the flowery, deceptive talk of fools— These are the fetters of affliction for ordinary beings.
With greedy minds, they delight in the wealth of others; From anger, all manner of faults arise.
Those with much destruction through wrong views shall fall into the evil destinies.
One should know that there are three kinds of physical transgressions, four kinds of verbal ones, and likewise three kinds of mental ones;
the one who commits them falls into the evil destinies.
If one commits various transgressions, one will certainly fall into the evil realms;
if one is free from these three transgressions, one will certainly not fall into the evil realms.
"Furthermore, householder!
The afflictions (*kleśa*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and the various stains of defilement that gather in the world constitute a suffering of great magnitude.
There are ten types of such defilement. What are these ten?

First is the defilement of the stain of stinginess; second, the defilement of the stain of violating the precepts; third, the defilement of the stain of anger; fourth, the defilement of the stain of laziness; fifth, the defilement of the stain of distraction; sixth, the defilement of the stain of wrong wisdom; seventh, the defilement of the stain of lack of learning; eighth, the defilement of the stain of doubt; ninth, the defilement of the stain of lack of faith and understanding; tenth, the defilement of the stain of lack of respect.

Having seen these ten kinds of defiled phenomena gathered together in the world, I have caused all beings to dwell securely in the undefiled Dharma; for this reason, I have gone forth with pure faith to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The phenomena of the world’s continuity, Oppressed by the ten types of affliction,
Are attached to the defilements of the conditioned, Without weariness for even a moment.”
Ordinary, foolish worldlings, defiled by the stain of stinginess, destroy and fail to fulfill the training in ethical discipline that gathers in sentient beings.
The foolish turn their backs on patience; they are indolent and deficient in vigor.
Unable to stabilize the mind, possessed of evil wisdom and dull-witted,
they abandon their parents, elders, teachers, and preceptors;
seeing no light of the world, those of evil wisdom give rise to doubt.
When the Buddha teaches the profound Dharma, some give rise to slander;
shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, they do not respect the noble Dharma.
Having seen the phenomena of defilement, they do not cling to the conditioned.
Unconditioned and undefiled, it brings sentient beings to tranquility.
"Furthermore, householder!
Birth, death, fear, and the gathering of the world—this suffering is exceedingly great."
This consists of ten kinds. What are these ten?

First, the suffering that is exceedingly great when stinginess and envy cover and form fetters; second, the suffering that is exceedingly great when the factors of ignorance constantly entangle one; third, the suffering that is exceedingly great when the ocean of desire overflows; fourth, the suffering that is exceedingly great when the limbs and joints are crushed by the hardships within desire; fifth, the suffering that is exceedingly great when one is bound by affection and pierced by the arrows of desire; sixth, the suffering that is exceedingly great when the smoke and dust of anger and resentment billow and fill the air, erupting into blazing flames; seventh, the suffering that is exceedingly great when the fire of greed burns; eighth, the suffering that is exceedingly great when the poison of hatred lies hidden and concealed; ninth, the suffering that is exceedingly great when the obstruction of delusion is like a thorn; tenth, the suffering that is exceedingly great when one is pursued and bound by the vast wilderness of birth and death, its perils and terrors.
Having seen these ten kinds of phenomena, I desired to eliminate and sever them; for this reason, I left the household life with pure faith to realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One restated the preceding meaning in verse:
"Birth, youth, and old age devour all; The marks of physical beauty are destroyed and become unattractive.
Lacking mindfulness and wisdom, it is a gateway to decline; This dharma can destroy the characteristics of the world."
Sickness can swallow up one's physical strength and complexion;
it utterly destroys one's power and diligence, while further diminishing the sensory faculties, leaving one with inferior strength and no refuge.
The fear of death is like the roar of a rākṣasa; it constantly pursues all classes of living beings.
When its time comes and life is exhausted, it is devoid of compassion, destroying all lifespans in the world.
The phenomena of old age, sickness, and death are extremely fierce and evil, Afflicting all sentient beings in the world;
For the sake of diligently seeking the gate of peace and bliss—free from aging and death— I have gone forth into homelessness.
Three fires burn within this world, and no protector of the world is seen;
I have resolved to protect the world, and pray that sweet rain may fall to extinguish all these fires.

The right paths of the world are all destroyed; Blind, obscured, and further shrouded in delusion, I pray you open the pure eyes for all sentient beings, And leave the home-life to reveal the Right Path.
Sentient beings give rise to doubt and confusion, And are thus obstructed and shrouded by various hindrances;
I vow to eliminate their minds of regretful wrongdoing, Therefore, having gone forth, I proclaim the True Dharma.
Sentient beings give rise to mutual opposition, Seeking out faults to destroy one another;
Therefore, I have left the home life to benefit the world, Universally wishing that all beings may cease their anger.
In this world, parents are most deeply beloved, yet sentient beings, with minds of pride, do not honor them;
wishing to break down the banner of their own conceit, he therefore left the home life to provide protection.
I see sentient beings shrouded by craving, falling into ruin because of wealth and possessions;
if they could obtain the seven noble riches, they would cause the world to be free from the suffering of poverty.
Sentient beings mutually give rise to conflict and harm, sustaining themselves through that which is meaningless and unbeneficial;
they will certainly bring destruction upon their own bodies. Therefore, I cause them to leave the three realms of existence.
Fools do not understand what is beneficial; thus they pervade the three realms.
Out of a desire to benefit them, I have gone forth from home; I shall now demonstrate the true Dharma to the world.
Sentient beings are immersed in hell; seeing them undergoing extreme suffering and various boundless evils, I have left the household life so that they may be liberated.
Sentient beings inflict harm upon one another, And quickly return to the various realms of animals;
Out of the arising of compassionate vows, I have left the home life, To act as a refuge for those who are without refuge.
I see sentient beings in the realm of hungry ghosts, Suffering the extreme torments of hunger and thirst;
Having realized unsurpassed, great Bodhi, I universally bestow upon them the supreme food of nectar.
In the human realm, the pursuit [of desires] is a great suffering; in the heavenly realms, the suffering of decline and extinction increases to the extreme.
Having realized that the sufferings throughout the three realms are profound, I have left the household life for the sake of deliverance.
In this world there are those devoid of shame, who, deluded by desire, bring confusion to evil beings;
making no distinction between their retinue or honored kin, they swallow them up with lust like swine or dogs.
Attached to desire and bound to women, I see sentient beings fettered by them;
they give rise to minds of pride and intoxication that lead to what is meaningless and harmful, and therefore I have gone forth to provide rescue and protection.
Sentient beings are ruined by their lack of mastery; though terror reaches unto death, they find no liberation.
Having left the home-life and attained Bodhi, I cause all to awaken and attain universal mastery.
Within the dwellings of laypeople there is no spiritual benefit; I have seen hundreds of thousands of such faults.
Now I shall travel through these various regions, leading all beings to transcend the limits of birth and death.
At that time, when Bhadrapāla and the five hundred elders heard what the Buddha had said, they conceived a sense of rare wonder and all spoke these words:
"The Bodhi of the Buddha is truly vast; it is only now that we know the Buddha to be the Truly Awakened One."
Then the elders, with one voice and in unison, spoke these verses:
“We five hundred elders have come to take refuge in the Buddha out of fear of old age.
We pray that you will teach the unsurpassed, supreme Dharma-gate, so that we may transcend the limits of suffering caused by aging and death.”
The World-Honored One’s perfect and pure marks are utterly stainless; having transcended the three realms of existence, he has attained liberation.
He rescues those within the gates of arising and ceasing in the three realms, leading them from the house of the three realms to attain sovereign mastery.
Liberated from craving, free from fear, with a stainless and pure mind cleansed of dust,
the unsurpassed Great Teacher, perfectly disciplined, has revealed the supreme Dharma of ambrosia.
The Unsurpassed Hero abides in the supreme marks; among gods and men in this world, none are his equal.
This Peerless One, Honored by the World, proclaims the supreme, middle, and great Dharma of Great Compassion.
Having exhausted all faults and severed the three impurities, possessing the pure eye and free from darkness,
with the dust, obscurity, and net of delusion entirely removed, you proclaim the boundless Dharma that is free from defilement.
Out of compassion for the world that lacks a refuge, you rescue those within the currents of the three realms of existence;
from a heart of pity, you give rise to great loving-kindness, swiftly causing them to emerge and dwell securely in well-being.

In the ocean of birth and death, filled with pride, delusion, and evil, where the suffering of illness and adversity surge like the tide, all sentient beings sink without rescue; out of compassion, the Buddha brings them deliverance.
The Buddha’s body is pure like a mountain of gold, Perfectly endowed with a hundred kinds of supreme majestic radiance;
With the most sublime and sweet Brahma-voice, He proclaims the supreme Dharma through wondrous jewel-like speech.
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is pure; Primordially luminous, its purity is likewise so.
Though there is no agent, the experience of action does not perish; Thus it is well-expounded for those who have not heard.

His conduct is virtuous and his fame is boundless; with the ten powers, fearlessness, and spontaneous wisdom, his mind is equal to space and his knowledge is infinite. He skillfully expounds the Dharma of the Śramaṇa’s vows.
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:

"The roots of goodness of these five hundred householders have matured; I should now preach the True Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for them, so as to transform these lay dwellings into the appearance of renunciation, exhausting all outflows and realizing the ultimate limit."
At that time, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged in mid-air.

Then, the five hundred elders conceived deep affection, pure faith, and reverence for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and performed various acts of offering and approached him with virtuous and sublime devotion.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five hundred elders, saying: "O elders!

Regarding all that exists in the world—birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, affliction, grief, and the cycle of rebirth—are you each desirous of seeking liberation from these ten kinds of disturbing phenomena?"

"Furthermore, regarding these ten kinds of harmful matters—the unbeneficial things arising from the past, present, and future within the realm of the pleasant and the unpleasant—do you each desire to seek liberation from them?"

"Furthermore, among the various views in the world, there are many perilous and evil views, namely: the view of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span; the views of annihilationism and eternalism; the views of non-action, causelessness, and inequality; and those various false views. Do you each wish to seek liberation from these ten kinds of perilous and evil views?"

"Furthermore, there are ten great arrows of disease in the world, namely: craving, ignorance, desire, greed, hatred, delusion, pride, views, as well as formation and destruction. Do you each wish to seek liberation from these ten kinds of great arrows of disease?"

"Furthermore, there are ten dharmas that are the roots of worldly craving: namely, because of craving, one pursues; because of pursuing, one craves; because of craving, one holds the view of self; because of the view of self, one becomes fixed in opinion; because of being fixed in opinion, one develops sensual desire; because of sensual desire, one becomes attached; because of attachment, one becomes stingy; because of stinginess, one grasps; because of grasping, one fails to guard oneself; and because of failing to guard oneself, suffering arises. Do you each wish to seek liberation from these ten dharmas that are the roots of craving?"

"Furthermore, there are the dharmas of the world’s group of those fixed in error: namely, wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, wrong liberation, and wrong knowledge. Regarding these ten kinds of dharmas of the group fixed in error, do you each desire to seek liberation from them?"

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Court Chaplain for the Transmission of the Dharma, Great Master of the Bureau of the Imperial Sacrifices, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmarakṣa, and others. Chapter One: The Honorable Guardian of the World (Bhadrapāla), Part Three. "Furthermore, Householder!..."

Furthermore, regarding the ten unwholesome courses of action in the world—namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong view—do you each desire to seek liberation from these ten kinds of unwholesome courses of action?

Furthermore, there are ten types of defiled phenomena in the world, namely: the defilement of stinginess, the defilement of violating the precepts, the defilement of malice, the defilement of laziness, the defilement of distraction, the defilement of faulty wisdom, the defilement of lack of learning, the defilement of doubt and confusion, the defilement of lack of faith and resolve, and the defilement of disrespect. Do you each wish to seek liberation from these ten kinds of defiled phenomena?

Furthermore, there are ten kinds of fear regarding birth and death in the world, namely: being shrouded by stinginess and envy; being entangled by ignorance; the surging waves of the ocean of desire; the hardships within desire; being pierced by the arrows of desire; being stifled by the smoke of resentment and hatred; being scorched by the fire of greed; being concealed by the poison of anger; being obstructed by delusion like thorns; and the fearsome perils of the wilderness of birth and death. Do you each wish to seek liberation from these ten kinds of fear regarding birth and death?
At that time, five hundred elders spoke with one voice before the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

We each desire to be liberated from ten kinds of afflictive dharmas. To speak briefly, we each desire to seek complete liberation from those ten dharmas, including the ten kinds of fears regarding birth and death."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the five hundred elders, saying:
"If you each desire to seek liberation, from what source should that liberation be sought?"
O householders!
The eye does not desire liberation. Why is this?
The eye is fundamentally without transition and likewise without action; the eye has no thoughts and no cognition. Therefore, one should know that the eye is fundamentally not established by a self.
"O householders!
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind do not desire liberation. Why is this?"

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are fundamentally without transition and likewise without activity; the mind has nothing to which it can direct thought and nothing that it can cognize. Therefore, one should know that the mind is fundamentally not established by a self.
O householders!
Form does not desire liberation. Why is this?
Form does not undergo transformation nor is it produced; form is without thought and without cognition. Therefore, one should know that form is fundamentally not established by a self.
One does not seek liberation from sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena (*dharmas*). Why is this?

Because *dharmas* do not undergo transformation nor are they produced; *dharmas* have no thoughts and no cognition. Therefore, one should know that *dharmas* are fundamentally not established by a self.
"Furthermore, householder!
One does not desire liberation from the aggregate of form. Why is that?

The aggregate of form is without transition and without activity; the aggregate of form is without volition and without cognition. Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of form is not established by a self.
One does not desire liberation from the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, or the aggregate of consciousness. Why is this?

Because the aggregate of consciousness neither transforms nor acts; the aggregate of consciousness neither intends nor cognizes. Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of consciousness is not established by a self.
"Furthermore, householder!
The earth element does not desire liberation. Why is this?

The earth element does not undergo transformation nor does it perform any action; the earth element has no volition and no cognition. Therefore, one should know that the earth element is not established by a self.
The elements of water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness do not desire liberation. Why is this?

Because the element of consciousness has no transformation and nothing to be done; the element of consciousness has no thought and no cognition. Therefore, one should know that the element of consciousness is not established by a self.
“O householders!
You should know that all phenomena arise from false conceptualization; they are dependent on conditions, lacking power and being weak, turning in accordance with conditions.”
If there are conditions for phenomena, then those phenomena can be designated;
if conditions do not exist, then phenomena likewise cannot be designated.

Yet, within all that is designated among phenomena, there is not the slightest phenomenon that can be apprehended, nor is there the slightest phenomenon that arises or ceases, originates or perishes, nor is there any distinct phenomenon that is either annihilated or eternal.
"O you elders!
For this reason, you should know thus: all those phenomena arise from false conceptualization; they are bound to conditions, lacking power and being weak, turning in accordance with conditions."
If there are conditions, those phenomena can be designated;
if the conditions for phenomena do not exist, then phenomena likewise cannot be designated.

Yet, within all these designated phenomena, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be apprehended, nor is there any phenomenon that arises or ceases, originates or perishes, nor is there any distinct phenomenon that is either annihilated or eternal.
You should know this: if there is false conceptualization and improper mental attention, then designation can be established;
if there is no false conceptualization, no improper mental attention, there is nothing to be designated.
If there is improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), then that ignorance (*avidyā*) can be designated;
if there is no improper mental attention, ignorance likewise cannot be designated.
Because ignorance exists, formations are designated; because ignorance does not exist, formations are not designated.
Because formations exist, consciousness is designated; because formations do not exist, consciousness is not designated.
Because the phenomenon of consciousness exists, name-and-form can be designated; because the phenomenon of consciousness does not exist, name-and-form likewise cannot be designated.
Because name-and-form exists, the six sense bases can be designated; because name-and-form does not exist, the six sense bases likewise cannot be designated.
Because the six sense bases exist, contact can be designated; because the six sense bases do not exist, the phenomenon of contact likewise cannot be designated.
Because contact exists, feeling can be designated; because contact does not exist, the phenomenon of feeling likewise cannot be designated.
Because the phenomenon of sensation exists, craving can be designated; because the phenomenon of sensation does not exist, the phenomenon of craving likewise cannot be designated.
Because the phenomenon of craving exists, grasping can be designated; because the phenomenon of craving does not exist, the phenomenon of grasping likewise cannot be designated.
Because the phenomenon of grasping exists, becoming can be designated; because the phenomenon of grasping does not exist, the phenomenon of becoming likewise cannot be designated.
Because the phenomenon of existence exists, birth can be designated; because the phenomenon of existence does not exist, the phenomenon of birth likewise cannot be designated.
Because the phenomenon of birth exists, old age and death can be designated; because the phenomenon of birth does not exist, old age and death likewise cannot be designated.
"In this context, one should understand what is meant by 'old age.

It refers to the deterioration and transformation of physical appearance; labored breathing and groaning; walking with the aid of a staff; the maturation and alteration of the sense faculties; the depletion and exhaustion of the life span; and the decay of one's functional characteristics. Because it is described in such terms, it is called old age."
What is called death?

It refers to the arrival of the time of final passing, the characteristic of cessation that is extinguished, the dispersal of the aggregates, the body falling to the ground, and the destruction, dissolution, and transformation of that homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*); because it is described in this way, it is called death.
"This is the mark of aging; this is the mark of death. Taken together, they are termed 'aging and death.
Because the phenomenon of birth exists, aging and death can be established; because the phenomenon of birth does not exist, aging and death likewise cannot be established."
What is called "birth"?

It refers to the arising, the universal emergence, the exit from the womb, and the establishment [of the body]; it is the gathering of the five aggregates, the completion of the six sense bases, and the successive aggregation of those factors of commonality (*nikāya-sabhāga*). Because it is described in this way, it is called "birth."
“Because the phenomenon of existence exists, birth can be designated; because the phenomenon of existence does not exist, the phenomenon of birth likewise cannot be designated.
What is called ‘existence’?
It refers to existence in the realm of desire, existence in the realm of form, and existence in the formless realm; these are called existence.”
"Because the phenomena of grasping exist, existence can be designated; because the phenomena of grasping do not exist, the phenomenon of existence likewise cannot be designated.
What is called 'grasping'?

It refers to the grasping of sensual desire, the grasping of views, the grasping of precepts and observances, and the grasping of the discourse on self; that which is spoken of in this way is called grasping."
“Because craving for phenomena exists, grasping can be designated; because craving for phenomena does not exist, the phenomenon of grasping likewise cannot be designated.
What is called ‘craving’?

It refers to craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena. Because it is described in this way, it is called ‘craving.’”
"Because the phenomenon of feeling exists, craving can be designated; because the phenomenon of feeling does not exist, the phenomenon of craving likewise cannot be designated.
What is called 'feeling'?

It refers to all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition, all feelings produced with ear-contact as condition, all feelings produced with nose-contact as condition, all feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition, all feelings produced with body-contact as condition, and all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition. Because it is described in this way, it is called 'feeling'."
“Because the phenomenon of contact exists, feeling can be designated; because the phenomenon of contact does not exist, the phenomenon of feeling likewise cannot be designated.
What is called ‘contact’?
It refers to eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact. It is because of what has been thus described that it is called ‘contact.’”
“Because the six sense bases exist, contact can be designated; because the six sense bases do not exist, the phenomenon of contact likewise cannot be designated.
What are called the six sense bases?
They are the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base. These, as thus described, are called the six sense bases.”
"Because name-and-form exists, those six sense bases can be designated; because name-and-form does not exist, the six sense bases likewise cannot be designated.
What is meant by 'name-and-form'?"

That is to say, feeling, perception, and mental formations are designated as "name" (nāma); feeling, contact, attention, the four great elements, and that which is derived from the four great elements are designated as "form" (rūpa). Taken together, these are called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa).
“Because the phenomenon of consciousness exists, name-and-form can be designated; because the phenomenon of consciousness does not exist, name-and-form likewise cannot be designated.
What is called consciousness?”

That is to say, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness; because they are described in this way, they are called "consciousness.
Because the phenomena of formations exist, consciousness can be designated; because the phenomena of formations do not exist, the phenomenon of consciousness likewise cannot be designated.
What is called "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*)?

It refers to pervasive reflection on forms, pervasive reflection on sounds, pervasive reflection on odors, pervasive reflection on tastes, pervasive reflection on tangibles, and pervasive reflection on mental phenomena (*dharma*); because it is described in this way, it is called volitional formations.
"Because ignorance exists, formations can be designated; because ignorance does not exist, formations likewise cannot be designated. What is called ignorance?

It refers to not knowing the past limit, not knowing the future limit, not knowing both the past and future limits; not knowing the internal, not knowing the external, and not knowing that which is between; not knowing the Four Noble Truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; not knowing conditions; not knowing within dependently arisen phenomena what is dark and what is bright; not knowing what is a condition and what is not a condition; not knowing what is obstructive and what is non-obstructive; not knowing what is faulty and what is faultless; not knowing what should be approached and what should not be approached; and regarding all phenomena, not knowing and not seeing, being unable to awaken to the samādhi of the present—what is thus described is called ignorance."
Because improper mental attention exists, that ignorance can be designated; because improper mental attention does not exist, ignorance likewise cannot be designated.
What is called improper mental attention?
It is: "Did I exist in past lives, or did I not exist?
Did I pass away in past lives, or did I not pass away?"
What kind of being was I in previous lives?
What shall I become in future lives—will it be existent or non-existent?
And in those future lives, where shall I abide?
In future ages, what kind of being shall I become?
Regarding internal phenomena, how can there be doubt as to whether a self exists or does not exist, and whether it is present or absent?
"What is that which arises and what is that which does not arise? If there is something that arises, of what kind is it?

Because they give rise to such improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), among the six views and other views, there arises the view of a self (*ātman*) and the view of no-self (*anātman*); they are unable to observe "self" and "what belongs to self" (*ātmiya*) with equanimity and according to reality.
Because of such improper contemplation of inequality, various views arise; thus, there is a self and a world, which are precisely the dharmas that serve as conditions.
Regarding those phenomena that are conditioned: they are impermanent, lacking strength, powerless, and unsubstantial; they are non-final and subject to transformation and decay.
To reckon these non-final phenomena as being truly established and truly situated—once such a view has arisen—is therefore called improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*).
"Because false discrimination exists, improper mental attention can be established; because false discrimination does not exist, improper mental attention cannot be established."
What is called "false conceptualization"?

It refers to [the notions of] self, person, sentient being, life-span, individual (pudgala), youth, mind-born, agent, and experiencer. This is what is termed "conceptualization," which refers to the pervasive imagination produced by foolish, ordinary, and unlearned persons regarding the self, person, sentient being, life-span, and so forth. This is called conceptualization.
In brief, it is therefore called "unreal imagination" (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
Because this unreal imagination exists, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) can be established;
because unreal imagination does not exist, improper mental attention cannot be established.
"Because this false discrimination and improper mental attention exist, ignorance can be designated; because these two factors do not exist, ignorance likewise cannot be designated."
Because ignorance exists, those formations can be designated; because ignorance does not exist, formations likewise cannot be designated. To state it briefly:
as long as the phenomenon of birth exists, old age and death can be designated; because the phenomenon of birth does not exist, old age and death likewise cannot be designated.
"O householders!
You should know that all phenomena arise from false conceptualization and are dependent upon conditions.
As for these conditioned phenomena, they are impermanent and lack power; they are weak and lack solidity, evolving only in accordance with conditions."
Because dependent phenomena exist, those various phenomena can be designated; because dependent phenomena do not exist, those phenomena likewise cannot be designated.

Yet, within all that is designated among phenomena, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be cognized, nor is there the slightest phenomenon that arises or ceases, originates or perishes, nor is there any distinct phenomenon that is either annihilated or eternal.
"O householders!
It is as if there were a great stream of water flowing into a pond, and various insects and fish were dwelling within it.
What do you think?"
"And by what power do those fish rely?
The elder addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"It relies on water as its power.
The Buddha said to the householder,
"What do you think?"
“Does water truly possess power?
The householder replied to the Buddha, “No.”
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Sugata!"
The Buddha said, "Householder!
Water is fundamentally without thought; how could it possess power?"
The householder said to the Buddha,
“I have no power,
World-Honored One!”
"It is powerless,
Sugata," the Buddha said.
“Householder! All phenomena arising from false conceptualization are likewise thus: they are powerless and lack solidity, revolving according to conditions.

Because the causal conditions exist, those phenomena can be designated; because the causal conditions do not exist, phenomena likewise cannot be designated. Yet, within all these designations of phenomena, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that can be apprehended, nor is there the slightest phenomenon that arises or ceases, originates or perishes. Furthermore, there is no separate phenomenon that is either annihilated or eternal.”
"O householders!
When one examines that causal dharma through correct reasoning, it is truly not to be trusted.
Because it is not to be trusted, fear arises; because of that fear, one flees in the four directions."
Furthermore, by examining with sincerity and according to the principle of reality, one considers:
"What is this dharma? What is that dharma?
Through such examination, one no longer perceives any cause for alarm, fear, or flight.
Furthermore, when one investigates according to reality, there is no dharma whatsoever; since there is no dharma, how could one run about?
Why is this so? O Householders!
Because all phenomena are unattainable, all mental states and intentions are likewise unattainable.
Furthermore, O householders!
All phenomena are selfless, for they are free from defilement and dust.
All phenomena are devoid of a sentient being, because they are free from a self.
All phenomena are devoid of a life-principle, because they transcend all dharmas such as birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair.
All phenomena are devoid of a person, for the three periods of time have been severed.
All phenomena are without words or letters, for they are detached from all sounds and speech.
All phenomena are originally without dust, for there is nothing upon which they depend.
All phenomena are quiescent, because they possess the characteristic of proximate tranquility.
All phenomena penetrate all places, because their intrinsic nature is like space.
All phenomena rely upon emptiness, because there is no fixed manifestation.
All phenomena are immovable, for they have no basis of reliance.
All phenomena abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), for they correspond to non-abiding and immovability.
All phenomena are beyond verbal expression, for they are free from the waves of language.
All phenomena are without the mark of form, because they are free from shape, manifest color, and the sphere of resistance.
All phenomena are without equality, because they are free from the mark of self.
All phenomena are without that which is cognized, because they are free from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
All phenomena are without containment, for they transcend the path of the sensory domain of the eye.
All phenomena are not to be relied upon, for they transcend the paths of the sensory domains of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Three. 4.
