Translated by the Imperial Preceptor Guangfan, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Weijing, and others, by imperial decree.
Chapter One, Part Four: The Chapter on the Elder Bhadrapāla. Furthermore, the Buddha addressed the elders, saying:
"All dharmas are neither observed nor unobserved."
Why is this? Because they are free from arising, abiding, and ceasing.
All phenomena are without transition and without activity, for they are free from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
"All dharmas are bound to conditions, for their intrinsic nature lacks power.
Furthermore, O householders!

The eye is a product of the four great elements; it is impermanent, lacks strength, and is not ultimate. It is a dharma that is without solidity, without power, and subject to rapid decay; it is not to be trusted."
It is a collection of much suffering, much affliction, and many diseases; therefore, O householders!
The eye has no basis and no agency, and the same is true for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"Composed of the four great elements, it is impermanent, lacks strength, and is not ultimate; it is without solidity, lacks power, and is a phenomenon that quickly decays—this is not to be trusted.
It is full of suffering and affliction, a gathering place for manifold diseases. Therefore, O householders!"
The mind has no basis and is without fabrication.
O householders!
These dharmas should be studied in this way: this eye is like a mass of foam, which cannot be grasped or rubbed;
The eye is like a floating bubble, unable to endure for long;
the eye is like a mirage, produced from the thirst of karma and afflictions;
the eye is like a plantain tree, lacking any substantial core within its own nature.
The eye is like a magical illusion, arising from inversion;
the eye is like a dream, consisting of false perceptions;
the eye is like an echo, dependent upon conditions.
The eye is like a reflected image, appearing through the confrontation of karma;
the eye is like a floating cloud, momentarily devoid of characteristics;
the eye is like a flash of lightning, vanishing and ceasing in an instant.

This eye has no master, being like the earth; this eye has no self, being like water; this eye has no sentient being, being like fire; this eye has no life-span, being like wind; this eye has no person, being like space.
This eye is unreal, having the four great elements as its abode;
this eye is empty by nature, being devoid of "I" and "mine."
This eye is devoid of cognition, like grass, wood, tiles, or pebbles;
this eye is devoid of agency, being turned by the power of the wind;
this eye is empty, filled with impurities.
This eye is deceptive; though it may be treated and polished, it ultimately ends in dispersal and destruction.
This eye is like a well in a mound, pressed by old age.
This eye has no ultimate limit or boundary; in the end, it must return to death.
"O householders!
You should know that as it is with the eye, so it is with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; in brief, you should understand all phenomena in this same way."

All foolish ordinary beings give rise to craving and attachment toward all those desired phenomena, namely: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.

"Furthermore, regarding those aggregates of form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness; the eye-element, form-element, and eye-consciousness-element, up to the mind-element, phenomena-element, and mind-consciousness-element; the earth-element, water-element, fire-element, wind-element, space-element, and consciousness-element—within these phenomena there is desire and attachment, even unto all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena characterized by names and signs."
Therefore, O householders!

You should not give rise to attachment toward those things you desire—namely, wives, children, houses, wealth, and treasures—and you should not harbor greedy grasping for such things. Instead, you should develop pure faith and leave the home life to go forth into homelessness.

Having gone forth, he does not give rise to worldly desires; because he is free from desire, he is fully endowed with pure precepts, cultivates the practice of the pure Prātimokṣa, and perfects the stainless forms and rituals of the Dharma, feeling great dread even toward minor transgressions.
"O householders!
If you train in this way, you will attain the perfection of the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*).
Because ethical discipline is perfected, the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, as well as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, are not grasped."

"The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness are without grasping; the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element, up to the mind element, the phenomena element, and the mind-consciousness element, are without grasping."
"The earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element are without anything to be grasped.
To speak briefly, all those phenomena are entirely without anything to be grasped."
Because there is no grasping, there is no diminution or loss.
What phenomena are without diminution or loss?
They are: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; and forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects are without diminution or loss.
“The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness do not diminish or perish.
The eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element, up to the mind element, the phenomena element, and the mind-consciousness element, do not diminish or perish.”
"The earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element do not diminish or perish.
Since these phenomena do not diminish or perish, they are without defilement."
Because it is free from defilement, one swiftly attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
What is the dharma of pliancy?
It is the state of non-seeing (*adarśana*).
If there is nothing seen, then in all directions there will be not the slightest dharma that acts as an obstruction.
If there is no obstruction, then one is not harmed by oneself, nor harmed by others; thus, neither self nor others are harmed.
Because they are free from harm, their minds are not impaired, and they are thus able to enter that pure nirvāṇa without remainder.
Furthermore, O householders,
as for what is called "entering," what is it that enters?
That is to say, it is not that which enters through the eye, nor that which enters through the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind.
Furthermore, O householders!
If one clings to the idea that the eye is produced from conditions, this is attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self," and is thus far removed from nirvāṇa.
What is separation from nirvāṇa?
It means being separated from nirvāṇa because of greed, separated from nirvāṇa because of hatred, separated from nirvāṇa because of delusion, and separated from nirvāṇa because of lack of wisdom.
O householders!

One who lacks wisdom does not depart from the past, does not depart from the future, and does not depart from the present; such a person is definitively without wisdom and is produced apart from wisdom.
What is called wisdom?
It is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
What is called the knowledge of exhaustion?
This refers to the inexhaustible wisdom of the past, the inexhaustible wisdom of the future, and the inexhaustible wisdom of the present.
It arises from the wisdom that is free from the cognition of phenomena.
That wisdom which is free from cognition is the eye itself, arising from conditions through the wisdom that is free from cognition.
The eye is without self; if there is no self, there is no grasping; if there is no grasping, there is no abandoning; if there is no abandoning, there is liberation.
What is liberation?

That is to say: liberation from the grasping at a self, liberation from the grasping at a sentient being, liberation from the grasping at a life-span, liberation from the grasping at a person, liberation from the grasping at annihilationism and eternalism, liberation from all grasping, and liberation from the grasping at conceptual discrimination.
Once that non-conceptualization has occurred, there is neither a conceptualizer nor an object of conceptualization.
Phenomena are without conceptualization, yet they are not separate from conceptualization.
What is meant by "without conceptualization"?
This means that there is no conceptual differentiation between "self" and "what belongs to self.
If there is no conceptual differentiation regarding the self, then there is neither grasping nor rejecting; if there is neither grasping nor rejecting, that is the liberation one enters.
Whether a phenomenon is dissociated from fetters or not dissociated from fetters, in both cases one attains transcendence.
From what is one liberated?
It is said: from all suffering.
O Householders!
One should seek such a dharma of renunciation;
yet, within this, there is no dharma that can be grasped. Why is this?
"If there is anything grasped, fear arises.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate and clarify these meanings, spoke in verse:
"Because of grasping at phenomena, fear arises; Due to that fear, one shall fall into the evil realms."
If one sees such causes for fear arising, it is because consciousness perceives phenomena as existing and thus gives rise to grasping.
If one can contemplate the right path according to reality, the light of wisdom will shatter all darkness;
through this vision, one immediately attains the clarity of supreme wisdom, and should know that no distinct nature can be apprehended.
One should carefully contemplate all empty places; they are shifting, false, and unreal.
Do not make them a gateway to peace and happiness, for the world is deluded by craving.
Knowing emptiness as it truly is, and knowing that all phenomena are empty and devoid of reality,
I have attained the gate of peace and joy free from sorrow, and have also attained the supreme bliss of immovability.
If one can thus correctly understand, one knows that all phenomena are empty;
through this, one is liberated from the causes of all suffering, and therefore no ground for dispute can be established.
From various desires arises attachment; from attachment arise all afflictions.
Attachment is another name for grasping (*upādāna*); because of grasping, one is born into the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*).
Because existence exists, there is birth and thus cyclic wandering; when the three realms of existence cease, there is no further birth.
The phenomena of old age, sickness, and death likewise follow into non-existence, and one ultimately does not undergo the suffering of impermanence.
Know that when there is no desire, there is no grasping; because there is no grasping, there are no three realms of existence.
When existence ceases, there is no birth, and the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death are no longer experienced.
Therefore, you elders, together resolve to abandon the mind of grasping;
casting off all kinsmen and the causes of attachment, you shall quickly perfect the marks of a bhikṣu.
Regarding knowledge, wealth, benefit, and all desired things, one should cultivate mutual contentment;
wherever one goes, let there be humility and a humble mind, so that for others everywhere, virtuous benefit may increase.
Do not give rise to the thought that you alone maintain the precepts; do not regard others as those who break them.
Amidst the characteristics of upholding or violating the precepts, do not disparage others as transgressors.
Just as a wild deer that falls into a snare brings about its own destruction, so too does the binding of the mind by the snares of Māra;
likewise, harming others brings about harm for oneself.
The fool conceives thoughts of harm, praising himself and disparaging others—a profound fault.
One should even cease such slander toward those who break the precepts, let alone toward those who practice the holy life and uphold the discipline.
Those wise ones among the assembly of learned rishis, who constantly cultivate the practice of seclusion and tranquility,
renounce body and life without attachment, and diligently seek the dharma of liberation and peace.
Having completely abandoned all non-Buddhist schools and their scriptures—which lack the root of benefit—one should delight in the gateway of the profound True Dharma;
that Dharma proclaims the principle of ultimate emptiness.
One should know that the fundamental locus of the mind consists of what are called the twelve internal and external bases (*āyatana*).
From these arise the causes of various karmas; the locus where karma long endures is said to be the phenomenon of volition (*cetanā*).
The eye-faculty and the form-object are two conditions; together with the eye-consciousness, they constitute three factors as the conditions for its arising.
When these do not harmonize and are dispersed, it is like the principle of fire without fuel.
All phenomena thus produced arise through mutual conjunction;
there is neither an agent nor an experiencer, and the true path is ever manifest in all actions.
The body is composed of internal and external phenomena; herein one should know that the self and dharmas are empty.
Fools possess inverted and attached minds because they do not understand the self and what belongs to the self.
Within the eye there is no dharma that exists, nor can anything be found externally;
there is no self, no agent, and no life-principle—know that all dharmas are likewise thus.
The eye does not universally conceive the desire for liberation; the same is true for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Since form and the other sense objects possess no turning and no active gate, one should contemplate all phenomena as being likewise.
Just as when the waters of the great ocean surge, foam momentarily arises yet lacks substance;
so too, when one observes the eye and other faculties with discernment, they are found to be without solidity or power, like foam.
The five aggregates are by nature a provisional combination, Like that mass of foam, lacking solidity or strength;
They are the gateway to liberation from all afflictions, As well as from the sorrows of birth, old age, and the like.
Having gone forth within my teaching, you have thoroughly understood that all phenomena are like illusions;
thus, you do not receive the offerings of the faithful in vain, and are further able to universally make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
At that time, having heard the Buddha proclaim the profound True Dharma, the five hundred elders, while still on the road, became free from dust and defilement and attained the pure Dharma-eye.

Just as white cloth, untainted by dust or blackness, easily takes on dye, so too it was with these five hundred householders: in this very place, their Dharma-eye became pure, far removed from dust and defilement.
At that time, the World-Honored One further proclaimed the essentials of the Dharma for the five hundred elders, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them.
The Buddha said: "Elders!..."
The eye is intensely aflame.

How so? It is because the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion are aflame; the fires of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction are aflame. I say that this phenomenon brings suffering and affliction upon oneself.
The same applies to the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind being ablaze.
What constitutes this blazing?

It refers to the blazing fires of greed, hatred, and delusion; the blazing fires of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction. I declare that these phenomena bring suffering and affliction upon oneself.
The sensory objects of form are ablaze.
How are they ablaze?
It means that the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion are ablaze; likewise, the various fires of the sensory objects of sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are ablaze as well.
"Furthermore, householders!
The aggregate of form is ablaze.
How is it ablaze?
That is to say, the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion blaze fiercely;
likewise, the fires of the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness blaze fiercely as well.
The principle regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) is likewise.
Furthermore, O householders!
The earth element blazes with fire.
That is to say, the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion blaze fiercely.
It is likewise with the blazing of the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.

That is to say, the flames of greed, the flames of hatred, and the flames of delusion blaze intensely; likewise, the flames of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction blaze intensely. I declare that these phenomena cause one to experience suffering and affliction for oneself.
"Furthermore, householder! One should train thus:
'The eye is without grasping'; likewise for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, they too are without grasping.
Form is without grasping; likewise for sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena, they too are without grasping. One should train thus."
"Furthermore, householders!

The aggregate of form is without grasping; the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the eighteen elements, are all without grasping. You should train yourselves in this way."
Furthermore, householders!

The earth element is without anything to be grasped; the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element are likewise without anything to be grasped. You should train yourselves in this way.
"Furthermore, householders!
One should train thus: 'In this realm there is nothing to be grasped; in other realms there is nothing to be grasped.
Furthermore, householders!"
Because the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are without grasping, they are without dependence.
Because forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena are without grasping, one attains non-dependence within all sense bases.
"Furthermore, householders!

Because the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, the aggregate of consciousness, and the eighteen elements are without anything to be grasped, one attains non-reliance within these aggregates and elements."
"Furthermore, householders!
Because the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, space element, and consciousness element are not grasped, one attains non-reliance within these six elements."
Furthermore, O householders!
Because there is nothing to be grasped in this world or other worlds, one attains non-reliance within all worlds.
Furthermore, O householders!
If all dharmas are without anything to be grasped, then one attains non-reliance regarding all dharmas.
O Householders!

All dharmas are neither obtainable nor unobtainable; if one can thoroughly understand that there is neither obtaining nor non-obtaining, one is then able to be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. I declare this to be liberation from all sufferings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to further clarify these meanings, spoke in verse:
“This entire world is ablaze with intense flames; The two fires of birth and death perpetually burn.
Without rescue, all foolish beings are tormented; Only the Dharma of the Noble Path remains eternally undying.”
What phenomenon brings light to the world?
A Buddha, a Tathāgata, has now appeared; in a single instant, he skillfully contemplates the gateway to the True Path, and gives rise to a diligence that is ever firm and steadfast.
One should contemplate that all phenomena have no basis; through the light of wisdom, one sees and destroys all darkness.
By seeing, one immediately attains the clarity of supreme wisdom; one should know that in their distinct natures, nothing can be apprehended.
If one can observe that there is no basis for reliance and understand that all phenomena are empty,
then through such understanding of the dharma-gate of emptiness, the bodhicitta is empty and non-existent.
One should know that the dharmas of greed, hatred, and delusion— these three blazing fires, most fierce and evil—
universally incinerate the life-span of the world, yet beings remain long in sleep, ignorant and unawakened.
All that is born, aged, sick, and dying, constantly oppressed by sorrow,
lamentation, pain, and affliction— know that these which harass the world are all phenomena without any basis.
At that time, having heard this True Dharma spoken by the Buddha, the hearts of the five hundred elders were opened and their minds were liberated; they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
We have now truly gained a great and wholesome benefit!
Having developed pure faith in the Buddha’s Dharma, we have gone forth as monastics;
furthermore, in the presence of the Buddha, we have fully received the pure precepts.
At that time, the Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣus!
Immediately, the hair and beards of those elders fell away of their own accord, and the saṃghāṭī robes were donned upon their bodies; they thus attained the appearance of bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"You have received and maintained the kashaya robes; Your hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and you are all pure.
Holding the alms-bowl with perfect and auspicious marks, All of you have become Arhats."
Having realized the fruit and relying on the Dharma of their teachers,
they each uttered pure udānas before the great assembly of devas and humans, perfecting the appearance of pure bhikṣus.
In the past, in the presence of various Buddhas, He practiced the vast conduct of giving in all its forms;
At the single call of "Welcome," joy arose within him, And he extensively cultivated all wholesome dharmas everywhere.
Now that you have seen me appear in the world, Your pure mind has been further increased and refined;
By virtue of that superior and purified mind, Listen to the most supreme and pure Dharma.
Having heard the Buddha’s words, they realized the fruit of sainthood;

Far removed from the view of self and all attachments, they directly awakened to the perfected nature of the dharma of emptiness; Birth has been exhausted for them, and they have all attained liberation.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Four.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Five.

Chapter Two: The Yakṣa Abhaya At that time, after the World-Honored One had converted five hundred elders along the way, he paused at that spot with calm composure and careful deliberation, intending to enter the great city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, among the various worthies and sages in the great city of Rājagṛha, there was a great yakṣa named Abhaya who thought to himself:
"To encounter a Buddha, the World-Honored One, is extremely difficult to obtain; I should now present the World-Honored One with superior and wondrous food and drink."
Then the yakṣa Abhaya immediately offered to the World-Honored One excellent food and drink, pure and perfect in color, fragrance, flavor, and texture.
At that time, out of compassion for the yakṣa Abhaya, the World-Honored One accepted the offered food.
When the Buddha had finished receiving the food, immediately there were sixty-eight thousand yakṣas in the air who uttered these words of praise:
"Excellent, excellent!
The sound of their voices of sympathetic joy resounded throughout the entire realm of space.
Then the yakṣa Abhaya addressed the assembly of yakṣas gathered before him, saying:
"I have already offered pure and exquisite food and drink to the Tathāgata.
You all, members of this assembly, should likewise offer pure food and drink to the community of bhikṣus; this shall bring you benefit and peace for a long night."
Then all the yakṣas immediately offered the most excellent food and drink to the assembly of bhikṣus; out of compassion, the assembly of bhikṣus accepted all that food.
At that time, after the World-Honored One and the assembly of bhikṣus had accepted the food, they proceeded gradually toward the great city of Rājagṛha.

At that moment, there were countless thousands of hosts of devas, countless thousands of hosts of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as countless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings, all surrounding and following the World-Honored One.

At that time, before arriving at the great city of Rājagṛha, the World-Honored One first proceeded to a vast and open location; having arrived, he prepared an excellent and sublime seat and sat upon it.

Then the yakṣa Abhaya immediately scattered divine, exquisite māndārava flowers, utpala flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers, as well as celestial, exquisite sandalwood powder, over the Buddha as an offering. He scattered them everywhere, spreading them widely and profusely; having finished scattering them, he stood before the Buddha with palms joined.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the yakṣa Abhaya and the assembly of yakṣas had attained profound purity of mind, immediately emitted a great and most wondrous radiance.

It is the natural law for the light emitted by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, to consist of countless colors and various hues as it issues from the gateway of their mouths—namely blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, and green. This radiance universally illumines boundless worlds, eclipsing the majestic brilliance of the sun and moon so that they no longer appear; its light shines forth, reaching downward to the hells and upward to the Brahma world.
The light returned to the place where the Buddha was, circumambulated him seven times to the right, and then vanished into the crown of the Buddha’s head, or from his shoulders, or from his knees.

It is the natural law that, since time immemorial, when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestow a prophecy upon beings in the hells, the light vanishes from between the Buddha’s feet; if they bestow a prophecy upon animals, the light vanishes from his back;
if they bestow a prophecy upon hungry ghost beings, the light vanishes from his front;
and if they bestow a prophecy upon those in the human realm, the light vanishes from his left side.
If he were to bestow a prediction of enlightenment for the heavenly realms, the light would vanish into his right side;
if he were to bestow a prediction for a śrāvaka, the light would vanish into his knees;
if he were to bestow a prediction for a pratyekabuddha, the light would vanish into his shoulders.
When the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestow the prophecy of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon the bodhisattvas, the light retracts into the crown of their heads.

At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having seen the vast and pure radiance emitted by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke these verses:
“For what cause today, O World-Honored One, Do you emit this great radiance that shines everywhere?”
Extensively bringing benefit to all worlds, for what purpose do you manifest this radiance?
Who today has planted the seeds of the noble ones, and heard the vast causes of the Buddha’s Bodhi?
Who has received the prediction in this present age?
Who dwells securely in the fruit of liberation?
This emission of light by the One of Great Wisdom is not without cause; he manifests these radiant signs for the sake of taming beings.
"The signs of the light you have emitted bring forth illumination; O Muni, the Holy Honored One, how has this light appeared?
Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"There is a yakṣa named Abhaya; because he has faith in the Buddha, he offered food and drink."
Because he has generated a most supreme and pure mind, I now manifest this sign of light.
This yakṣa shall pass away from this world and immediately be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven;
when his life there comes to an end, he shall subsequently be born in the Yāma Heaven.
When the Yāma heaven has ceased and he is born in Tuṣita, he creates defiled karma because of sensual desires;
returning once more, he falls into birth among humans, where he shall become a king endowed with supernatural powers.
He becomes a Wheel-Turning King, a lord among men, ruling over the four great continents with sovereign ease;
when his life in the human realm has ended, he is reborn and receives sublime retribution in that Brahma world.
After twenty koṭis of kalpas have passed, they shall always be honored and trusted by all;
in those celestial realms and among humans, they will repeatedly come and go, experiencing every joy.
Thereafter, having renounced his royal throne and with pure faith left the household life to become a monk,
he shall ultimately attain that sublime enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Throughout thirty thousand births, he repeatedly extinguished that yakṣa body;
subsequently, he was reborn again in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he reverently performed the work of a Buddha for the Buddha.
Once he has beheld the Honored Buddha Maitreya,
that yakṣa will immediately attain the realization of the fruit of arhatship and, following the Great Teacher, extend his offerings.
After a full thousand births as yakṣas, they shall establish themselves in unsurpassed, great bodhi;
through those various roots of goodness cultivated in each birth, they shall never again fall into the evil realms.
Or again, they may encounter a thousand Buddhas, honoring and revering those Most Honored among Men,
for the sake of seeking unsurpassed, great Bodhi and for the benefit of all sentient beings.
Or for two or three thousand births as yakṣas, they made offerings with flower garlands and the like;

this becomes the supreme cause for the Buddha’s bodhi. For a thousand koṭis of births they made offerings to the Buddhas, and thereafter they purified their own bodies and subsequently revered the Buddha’s bodhi.
The yakṣa had a son named Mahāśaila; having received a yakṣa body, he possessed supernatural powers.
The yakṣa Mahāśaila gave rise to a pure mind and made this vow: "May I attain the fruit of Buddhahood."
In the future, you shall always revere the Buddha, the World-Honored One; in all places, you shall make great vows.
Having now seen me and extended offerings, you have given rise to the most supreme bodhicitta.
By means of these very roots of goodness, may they forever leave behind the various evil realms of the three miserable paths;
having beheld the Honored Buddha Maitreya, may they offer him ten million exquisite jeweled parasols.
Having offered precious parasols and with a purified mind, he further offered tens of millions of exquisite garments to the Buddha;
after making such vast offerings and gifts, he then resolved to seek renunciation.
For five hundred years, they exerted themselves with diligence, purely practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) for the sake of seeking unsurpassed,
great bodhi and for the benefit of all sentient beings.
By means of such supreme conditions, he universally practiced the deeds of generosity and ethical discipline;
for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, he engaged in extensive cultivation.
The number of kalpas that I know, I shall proclaim according to what I have known and seen;
but as for the subsequent practice throughout kalpas, it is beyond my knowledge and cannot be described.
As previously stated in the parables, they have seen as many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River,
and they have rendered respectful homage to each and every one of those Buddhas.
How wondrous is this supreme wisdom, the mind of great knowledge! This very great mind is unsurpassed;
it extensively offers worship to all Buddhas and brings universal benefit to sentient beings beyond measure.
In the future, you shall become a Great Holy Honored One, unsurpassed by anyone in all the worlds;
the Yakṣa Mahāgiri shall attain Buddhahood, with the name Bhaiṣajyarāja as his Buddha-title.
Throughout seventy koṭis of years, he extensively proclaimed the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
within the assembly of the Buddha named King of Physicians, there was a great congregation of twenty koṭis.
And as for the resolve generated by that assembly, they shall all practice the perfection of giving;
thereafter, the community of bhikṣus will further increase until their number reaches twenty-one koṭis.
Within that vast assembly, there were immeasurable hosts of śrāvakas;
all the śrāvakas present in that gathering were intent upon great bodhi.
That Buddha benefits all sentient beings; when his work of transformation is complete, he shall enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the True Dharma shall abide in the world for a full hundred thousand years;
throughout five hundred kalpas, it will remain perfect and complete, with Buddhas and their assemblies of bhikṣus present.
Thereafter, whether after the passing of one kalpa or even a thousand such kalpas,
the Wise One appears to transform the world, causing beings to draw near to the Buddha-dharma.
It is said that one whose mind possesses excellent aspiration, who is profoundly firm and richly learned, is supreme;
one must utterly eliminate all lack of firmness and always maintain profound stability through skillful observation.
It is proclaimed that those who possess great learning can increase their sublime wisdom;
these four fundamental dharmas, the gateway to the true meaning, are the refuge for all bodhisattvas.
That which is called generosity, ethical discipline, learning, and renunciation, and so forth, is exceedingly virtuous on the path of the bodhisattva;
it proclaims the gateway to the true path of enlightenment and is unsurpassed within the most excellent vehicle.
For those who proclaim the path of the śrāvakas, who sever the net of doubt and are further virtuous,
and who extensively benefit all sentient beings— I emit light that shines everywhere upon them.
The Buddha’s appearance in the world is a great radiance; know that this supreme state is most difficult to encounter.
He proclaims the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate for the universal benefit of all the world.
At that time, the yakṣa Mahāparvata thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One is now proceeding toward the Great City of Rājagṛha, to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; I should now plant a small root of merit before the World-Honored One."
He immediately addressed the assembly of yakṣas within his own retinue, saying:
"O virtuous ones!
You should know that the World-Honored One is about to proceed to the Great City of Rājagṛha, to Vulture Peak Mountain."
“You all should rouse yourselves with diligent vigor and each, according to your own capacity, perform acts of offering for the Buddha, the World-Honored One.

When the yakṣa Mahāparvata had finished speaking, he immediately joined his own assembly and retinue, and from the great city of Rājagṛha to Vulture Peak Mountain, they cleared away all earth, stones, sand, and gravel along the path until it was like a pure, round mirror. They sprinkled pure, fragrant water everywhere along the road, and further spread exquisite garments continuously across the way. Along the path, they placed various wonderful flowers at intervals, each as large as a man’s height, and adorned them with banners, pennants, and jeweled canopies. They also set out exquisite ointments in precious vases and various fine incenses, interlacing them with jeweled cords and hanging flower garlands as ornaments.
Furthermore, exquisite music resounded in the air,
and moreover, blue lotuses (utpala), white lotuses (kumuda), and punnāga flowers were strewn across the entire range of an arrow-shot.
Furthermore, various other birds flew and sang along the path; it was interlaced with golden cords and covered above by nets of the seven treasures as well as golden nets.
At that time, having extensively adorned the path, the Great Mountain Yakṣa transformed his own body, together with his assembly;
their bodies were joyful, their minds were joyful, pure and pleasing, and they gave rise to a heart of supreme joy.
A purely wholesome mind, a supple mind, a pure mind, an unobstructed mind, a joyful mind,
a mind directed toward the Buddha, a mind directed toward the Dharma, a mind directed toward the Saṅgha, an immovable mind toward enlightenment,
a fearless mind, an incomparable mind, a mind most supreme throughout the entire triple world, and a mind of loving-kindness and compassion.
The mind of compassion for all sentient beings; the mind of sympathetic joy; the mind of equanimity;
the mind that constitutes a great vessel for the accomplishment of all Buddha-dharmas; the true mind and the firm mind; the indestructible mind and the ever-increasing mind;
the mind of renunciation toward the stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; and the mind of accomplishment toward the stages of the bodhisattvas.
Having generated such pure thoughts, they approached the place where the Buddha was.

Upon arrival, they prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and stood to one side. Joining their palms toward the Buddha, they spoke these verses:
“I now prepare for the Buddha a vast array of offerings, The most supreme and most excellent of all.”
May I attain the holy fruit of Buddhahood And proclaim the most supreme and subtle Dharma.
May I perfect the ten powers And joyfully abide in the four fearlessnesses,
Bringing vast benefit to all sentient beings, Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, acts in all his deeds.
Endowed with the thirty-two supreme and wondrous marks, Adorned by the eighty secondary characteristics,
You shall become a great light for the world, Shining everywhere like the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
He turns that pure and wondrous wheel of Dharma, supreme with its twelve aspects;
he proclaims the gateway of the nectar-like True Dharma, universally bringing benefit to all sentient beings.
He extensively manifests miraculous transformations, just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifested them;
he skillfully brings benefit to all sentient beings, even unto countless koṭis of beings.
The World-Honored One manifests a great radiance, Like a mighty dragon king, free from all fear;
Thus he widely proclaims the True Path, Awakening to unsurpassed Bodhi.
May I become a shelter, a refuge, and a protector; may I become a destination for the gathering and transformation of all sentient beings.
May I likewise attain this state, and may all deeds that benefit sentient beings be brought to full completion.
May I become the sovereign lord of all classes of beings born within the five destinies,
causing them all to be liberated from the causes of suffering, just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has been liberated.
Making offerings to the Honored One among bipeds, whose boundless majesty and radiant light shine forth;
the Lord of Devas, the Nāgas, and the Asuras all universally offer worship to this peerless one in the world.
I perform this most supreme and excellent deed; may I become like a Great Dharma Lord, perfected with the thirty-two marks of excellence, the highest being among gods and humans.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the yakṣa Mahāparvata:

"According to the teachings spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, If one cultivates the causes of the unsurpassed True Dharma, Sentient beings shall attain the supreme Dharma-gate; Unsurpassed Bodhi will not be difficult to obtain."
The Great Holy Lord, the Light of the World, having received these offerings, radiates the light of the Buddha;
amidst the assembly of devas, nāgas, spirits, and humans, he is the one worthy of receiving all such offerings.
Having realized the unsurpassed Great Bodhi, you sit serenely beneath the king of trees amidst the great assembly;
having vanquished the hosts of great and evil Māras, you extensively proclaim the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

At that time, the World-Honored One was respectfully surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and other beings numbering in the hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with great majesty and virtue, possessed of great supernormal powers, manifested great transformations, extensively performed deeds, and emitted great rays of light; he caused the buddha-fields to tremble and rained down great lotuses, while hundreds of thousands of kinds of exquisite music resounded, and wonderful lotuses as large as chariot wheels appeared for him to tread upon with his feet.
The Blessed One proceeded from that great mountain along a road beautifully fashioned and adorned by the yakṣa Citra, and went to Vulture Peak Mountain.
Having arrived there, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"You should prepare for the Buddha a sublime seat—a Dharma seat, a supreme seat, a preeminent seat in the three realms, and a seat of exquisite jewels."

Once the Tathāgata had ascended his seat, he gathered in all sentient beings and proclaimed and expounded that profound, true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; he brought to fulfillment all the supreme practices of bodhisattvas, removed all doubts and uncertainties of sentient beings, and illuminated right wisdom to sever the web of all doubts.
"The Tathāgata has preached this profound sūtra extensively out of compassion, for the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings in the world of devas and humans.
At that time, having received the Buddha’s command, the Venerable Ānanda prepared an excellent seat for the Tathāgata.
At that time, there were sixty-eight koṭis of celestial hosts, each of whom prepared and offered a precious throne for the Buddha.
Having invited the Tathāgata to ascend these seats, they spoke a verse in unison before the Buddha:
"We now extensively arrange for the Buddha A most excellent precious throne and exquisite robes."
May the Buddha, out of compassion for all devas and humans, ascend the precious throne as is appropriate.
Once the Buddha-Tathāgata has ascended the throne and proclaimed the True Dharma that leads to the further shore,
the world shall tremble in six ways, and all beings will give rise to great joy.
The Buddha’s light shines universally upon the great assembly, brilliantly illuminating the buddha-fields and the king of mountains;
all beings behold the Great Holy Honored One, and their pure desire for the various dharmas is awakened.
All the devas, nāgas, and human multitudes, along with all the various classes of the eight divisions of beings, are able to see one another’s bodies; herein, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
All the hundreds of thousands of koṭis and nayutas of the great assemblies of devas and humans each beheld the Buddha,
the Great Holy Honored One, as he proclaimed the rare and wondrous phrases of the Dharma.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, together with his ministers, officials, and retinue,
arrived at the Buddha’s assembly in an instant, approaching the Holy One to listen to the Dharma.
The Buddha, knowing that the assembly was fully settled, surveyed the four directions thoroughly;
for the sake of all the gathered multitude, including devas and humans, he brought vast benefit to sentient beings.
The World-Honored One addressed the entire assembly:

"Those who have doubts should question the Honored One among Two-Legged Beings; according to whatever you ask, I shall provide clarification, universally causing all doubts and delusions to be severed."
At that time, all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm, as well as the entire assembly of devas and humans in the world, paid their respects and gazed up at the World-Honored One;
with pure minds, they stilled all external distractions and listened with single-minded concentration to the Tathāgata’s proclamation of the profound and true Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
"Do not take your seat.

You should observe those among the assembly of bhikṣus who have not yet arrived for this gathering; go now to where Mahākāśyapa is on the southern slope of the Snowy Mountains and summon them to attend the assembly."

Then, having received the Buddha’s command, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately exercised his supernormal powers and went to where Mahākāśyapa was on the southern slope of the Snowy Mountains.
Upon arrival, he said to him:

“Venerable One, you should know that the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, is currently at Vulture Peak Mountain, gathered with a great assembly of śramaṇas, brahmins, humans, and devas, preaching the Dharma.”
The Buddha has sent me here to summon you, Venerable One.
I pray that you will follow the Buddha’s command and attend the assembly;
do not allow us to incur the offense of concealing the Dharma from one another.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa said to the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"You should go on ahead; I shall follow you immediately to the place where the Buddha is."

At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, while seated amidst the assembly, exercised his own supernormal powers and transformations; surrounded by the fourfold assembly, he arrived in an instant at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, where the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, was staying.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side, not far from the Buddha.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, traveling by means of his supernormal powers, reached the Buddha’s presence and saw that the Venerable Mahākāśyapa had already arrived at the assembly and was seated to one side.
Having seen this, he said:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa, you are endowed with supernormal powers; how is it that you have arrived at the Buddha's assembly so swiftly?
Venerable Mahākāśyapa then addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana, saying:
“As the Buddha has declared that you are foremost in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), why is it that at this time you are so slow?
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha*, Fascicle Five.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Tang Dynasty, the Court-Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit and Buddhist Texts, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, His Majesty’s Subject Weijing, et al., by Imperial Decree.

Chapter Three: The Bodhisattva’s Contemplation, Part One. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I have a slight doubt that I wish to inquire about; I only pray that the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha will graciously explain it for me.”
"If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, grants permission for my request, I shall then question him.
The Buddha said,
"Śāriputra!..."
Ask whatever you wish.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha shall explain it according to your questions, so that all may have their doubts resolved.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

By accomplishing how many dharmas does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attain such that their physical actions are free from faults, their verbal actions are free from faults, and their mental actions are free from faults; such that their physical, verbal, and mental actions are pure; such that their physical, verbal, and mental actions are immovable; and such that the power of celestial Māras or external paths cannot restrain them? Only then do they deeply resolve upon the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), successively accomplish the various virtues of the stages (*bhūmi*), and become able to act as a place of refuge for all sentient beings, as a torch of light, as a great river, as a great bridge, and as a great ship or raft, ferrying all across to the other shore, serving as a shelter, a rescue, a home, and a destination, remaining unshakable and unwavering in the mind of omniscience?
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, wishing to extol this meaning, questioned the Buddha in verse:
"For what reason does the one of heroic wisdom Abide securely in great bodhi,
Proclaiming the wondrous Dharma-gate of merit, And realizing the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi?"
What is the practice of those wise and courageous ones who benefit all living beings?
Furthermore, by observing what dharma-gate can one attain the unsurpassed path of Buddhahood?
Furthermore, by what dharma do you subdue the hosts of Māra, And dwell securely at the great site of enlightenment?
How do you cause billions of world-systems to tremble, And fully realize the supreme and wondrous fruit of bodhi?
By what meaning is one called a "Bodhisattva," and what is the significance of such a term?
Please explain herein the gateway to enlightenment, which is the most supreme among all Buddha-dharmas.
What is it that you practice within all the worlds, That you are able to extensively benefit all sentient beings?
Free from all defilements and attachments like a lotus flower, You liberate tens of millions of multitudes of beings.
How should one receive the offerings of the devas, nāgas, and the wise, as well as all humans and non-humans?
I now ask about this meaning; I pray that you will explain it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying: "Śāriputra!
You should now know that if a bodhisattva can accomplish a single dharma, they will be able to universally embrace immeasurable Buddha-dharmas in one place and in many places."
What is this one dharma?
It is the arousal of the profound and firm mind of great bodhicitta.
This is precisely what it means for a bodhisattva to accomplish one dharma, whereby they are able to universally embrace immeasurable Buddha-dharmas in a single place and across many places.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
what is meant by 'profound and firm'?"
"What is called the bodhicitta?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"That which is profound and firm is so because it is true and indestructible, and because it is steadfast and immovable."
Immovability is because there is no retreat or discouragement; the absence of retreat or discouragement is because of being well-established;
being well-established is because there is no regression; the absence of regression is because of skillfully observing sentient beings;
skillfully observing sentient beings is because it is the root of great compassion; the root of great compassion is because it is the vast mind. The vast...
The great mind is the skillful knowledge of the methods for maturing sentient beings;
skillful knowledge of the methods for maturing sentient beings is sovereign sublime bliss; sovereign sublime bliss is the absence of categories;
the absence of categories is the absence of attachment; the absence of attachment is the gathering of sentient beings; and the gathering of sentient beings...
Birth is the ability to skillfully observe those sentient beings who are weak and inferior;

to skillfully observe those weak and inferior sentient beings is to act as their savior and refuge without giving rise to a mind of anger; not giving rise to a mind of anger is to observe with skillful regard;
to observe with skillful regard is to be without attainment; to be without attainment is to have a virtuous intention. Virtue...
Because intention is non-existent, it is non-existent; because it is non-existent, it is perfectly pure;
because it is perfectly pure, it is naturally immaculate; because it is naturally immaculate, it is internally stainless; because it is internally stainless, it is externally pure.
Śāriputra! These and other such dharma-gates, ranging from "reality" and "indestructibility" to "internal stainlessness" and "external purity," are called profound and firm.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
That which is called the bodhicitta is this very mind that is free from all faults and cannot be pursued by any afflictions;
it takes no pleasure in other vehicles."
That mind is firm and solid, not corrupted or disturbed by any heterodox or external speech;
that mind is indestructible, such that none of the hosts of Māra can move it;
that mind is resolute, nurturing all roots of goodness and fundamental practices.
That mind is immovable because it delights in the Buddha-dharma;
that mind is well-established because it has ascended to the bodhisattva stages;
that mind is unsurpassed because it is without antidote.
That mind is like a vajra, for it skillfully discerns all Buddha-dharmas;
that mind is equanimous, for it is without high or low;
that mind is pure in its intentions toward all sentient beings, for its intrinsic nature is undefiled.
That mind is stainless, for it is illuminated by the light of wisdom;
that mind is vast, for it accommodates all sentient beings;
that mind is untainted, for it is like space.
That mind is unobstructed, because it contemplates unimpeded wisdom;
that mind understands all places as they correspond, because its great compassion is uninterrupted;
that mind is directly realized, because it is pure and praised.
That mind accomplishes the seeds of all-knowledge, for it brings all Buddha-dharmas to perfection;
that mind abides in the universal bestowal of all matters of happiness, for its vow is most supreme;
that mind is fully endowed with pure precepts, for it is free from any transgression.
That mind cultivates patience, because it is free from all anger;
that mind is diligent, because it is not indolent;
that mind is meditative concentration, because it approaches tranquility.
That mind is free from malice because it is endowed with wise conduct.

Furthermore, that mind is the true foundation for accomplishing the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation;
that mind is the true foundation for perfecting the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The mind that is realized as awakening is called the bodhicitta. Because this sattva seeks the bodhicitta with profound stability and fullness, he is therefore named a Bodhisattva."
This is also called the "vast multitude of sentient beings," the "supreme sentient beings," and the "most excellent sentient beings of the three realms.
This refers to those whose physical actions are free from faults, whose verbal actions are free from faults, and whose mental actions are free from faults;
whose physical actions are pure, whose verbal actions are pure, and whose mental actions are pure. Their physical actions...
Immovable—immovable in verbal action and immovable in mental action—one cannot be shaken or diverted by any celestial Māras or followers of external paths.
Having deeply resolved upon the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*), one shall gradually attain all the virtues of the stages (*bhūmi*).
Unstained by any worldly phenomena (*lokadharma*), one is able to skillfully discipline all sentient beings.
Prostrate! You act as a universal subduer, a refuge, a torch of light, a great river, a vast bridge, and a great boat;
you ferry all beings across to the other shore, serving as a shelter, a rescue, a home, and a destination.
You have deeply resolved upon the mind of omniscience, and for no [other] purpose...
Unmoved by the celestial Māras or external paths, this bodhisattva possesses pure faith that is profound, firm, vast, and pure regarding the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Delighting in seeing the noble ones and delighting in hearing the profound Dharma, their mind is free from stinginess as they extensively practice giving and renunciation. They always delight in renunciation, their mind is without obstruction, and toward all sentient beings they possess no distracted mind, no regressive mind, and no scattered mind. Having conviction in karma and its retribution, they are pure in faith and free from doubt; in all their actions they are entirely free from uncertainty, and they do not deny the karmic results of wholesome or unwholesome dharmas.

Having thoroughly understood these matters as they are, one does not commit sinful karma regarding the conditions of body and life; one remains far removed from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, greed, hatred, and wrong views—thus severing all ten unwholesome courses of action;
one constantly cultivates and accumulates the ten wholesome courses of action and maintains pure faith in the truth of the principles.
Among śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, he constantly cultivates the factors of enlightenment, possesses pure ethical discipline, and extensively hears and receives all wholesome dharmas.
Having heard them, he diligently practices with profound and firm mental attention; he is well-tamed, thoroughly stilled, and closely pacified.
He is free from all disputes and never utters unloving speech; his mind is purely wholesome, devoid of any unwholesome intent.
Diligently practicing wholesome dharmas and abandoning unwholesome dharmas, being neither haughty nor humble and remaining unmoved, free from all praise and blame, abiding in right mindfulness,
with a mind of sublime meditative equipoise, severing the bonds of the three realms of existence; pulling out the poisoned arrows, casting off all heavy burdens,
delighting in dwelling in tranquility, crossing over all doubts and regrets, and not undergoing further existence— thus [he] constantly...
They approach, revere, comply with, and serve the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, śramaṇas,
and brahmins without opposition, and they never depart from virtuous spiritual friends.

To embrace the true Dharma, proclaiming the gates of the true Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden others—namely, that through giving one attains great wealth, through upholding the precepts one is reborn in heaven, and through extensive learning one attains great wisdom.
Thus it is taught in accordance with practice: "This is generosity and it yields the fruit of generosity;

this is stinginess and it yields the fruit of stinginess; this is ethical discipline and it yields the fruit of ethical discipline; this is the violation of ethical discipline and it yields the fruit of violating ethical discipline;
this is patience and it yields the fruit of patience; this is malice and it yields the fruit of malice."

The fruit of anger; this is diligence obtaining the fruit of diligence, this is laziness obtaining the fruit of laziness, this is meditative concentration obtaining the fruit of meditative concentration, this is distraction obtaining the fruit of distraction, this is wisdom obtaining the fruit of wisdom, this is delusion obtaining the fruit of delusion; this body is virtuous.
This bodily conduct results in the fruit of good bodily conduct; this bodily misconduct results in the fruit of bad bodily conduct.
This verbal conduct results in the fruit of good verbal conduct; this verbal misconduct results in the fruit of bad verbal conduct.
This mental conduct results in the fruit of good mental conduct; this mental misconduct...
Regarding the fruits of the conduct one has practiced—whether that conduct was agreeable or disagreeable—one discerns: "This is wholesome; this is unwholesome;
this is what should be done; this is what should not be done. Whatever one thus performs will bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings throughout the long night.
These actions do not bring benefit or happiness to all sentient beings throughout the long night.
Such things as these [are what] the spiritual friends proclaim, teach, benefit, and gladden through the True Dharma.

“Knowing them to be great vessels of the Dharma, one should proclaim the profound gateways to liberation—namely, the gateway of emptiness, the gateway of signlessness, and the gateway of wishlessness—as well as the state of non-creation and non-action, non-arising and non-origination, and the absence of self, person, sentient being, or life-principle. Furthermore, one should teach the profound doctrine of dependent origination: namely, because there is existence, there is birth; that is to say, conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness; conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form; conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases; conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; conditioned by contact is feeling; conditioned by feeling is craving; conditioned by craving is grasping; conditioned by grasping is becoming; conditioned by becoming is birth; and conditioned by birth arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering comes into being.”

Because they do not exist, there is nothing that arises; where there is no arising, there is cessation. That is to say: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. In this way, this entire great mass of suffering ceases.
However, within this, not even the slightest phenomenon—whether arising or ceasing—can be found as something real. Why is this?
Because all phenomena are dependently originated;

they have no master, no agent, and no experiencer, but are turned by causes and conditions. Therefore, herein there is no phenomenon that can be turned, nor is there anything that does not turn, nor anything that turns along with others.
The designations of the three realms that arise from what is unreal exist as designations because they evolve from afflictions and evolve from suffering; all of them are produced from what is unreal.

If one examines this as it truly is, there is not even the slightest phenomenon that acts as an agent; since there is no agent, there is nothing produced, and in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), nothing at all is apprehended.
As it has been taught, there is no dharma that can be turned back, nor is there any non-turning.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas hear such profound dharmas as these, they believe and understand them without giving rise to doubt or regret, thereby entering the gate of unimpeded wisdom regarding all dharmas.

Therefore, one does not cling to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one does not cling to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or phenomena; one does not cling to the eye-element, form-element, or eye-consciousness-element, up to and including the mind-element, phenomena-element, or mind-consciousness-element. Thus, one resolves with faith that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty.

“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva abides in such faith and understanding, they do not diminish or lose it; they never cease to see the Buddhas, never cease to hear the true Dharma, and never cease to serve the assembly.”
In every lifetime they are born, they shall never be separated from seeing the Buddhas, never be separated from hearing the Dharma, and never be separated from serving the pure assembly.

They shall encounter the appearance of Buddhas in the world before their very eyes; in every place where they are born, they shall give rise to great diligence to zealously seek the wholesome Dharma, and the diligence they exert shall never be for matters that are meaningless or without benefit.

That is to say, they are well able to renounce the meaningless pursuits of dwelling in houses, the meaningless pursuits of wives, children, kinsmen, wealth, enjoyments, slaves, and so forth, as well as all other faults of attachment to sensual pleasures, games, and amusements; and with pure faith, they go forth into homelessness within the true Dharma of the Buddha, the Tathāgata.

Because of that pure mind of renunciation, they draw near to spiritual friends and remain ever unbroken; reflecting upon wholesome dharmas, they attain a noble aspiration and practice the wholesome dharmas they have heard with true sincerity.

They do not cling to the superior wisdom formed by words and letters; with a profound mind, they are fully endowed with a love for the Dharma without weariness, diligently seeking out extensive learning.

They extensively expound the Dharma as they have heard it to others, free from a heart of attachment, and not for the sake of seeking fame, reputation, or gain. When teaching the Dharma to others, they do not contradict their own words; they teach the Dharma to others exactly as they have heard it and exactly as it abides, explaining it extensively to others in accordance with each individual's needs.
Based on the Dharma as it has been heard, one gives rise to a mind of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and does not transgress the mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings.

For the sake of extensive learning, one does not begrudge body or life; having few desires and being content, one delights in solitary places, remains far removed from all clamor and bustle, and is well able to sustain oneself through such means.
According to the Dharma they have heard, they skillfully examine its meaning; they embrace the correct meaning without becoming attached to the literal words.

In accordance with what they have embraced, among all the assemblies of gods, humans, and asuras in the world, they do not act solely for their own benefit, but rather strive diligently for the sake of the unsurpassed Mahāyāna and for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings—namely, for the Buddha-wisdom, the unequaled wisdom, and the most supreme wisdom in all the three realms—and they remain diligent regarding the deeds performed by others.
