The Third Chapter, "The Bodhisattva’s Contemplation," Part Two: Furthermore, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"What is called the dharma of non-negligence?"
This refers to what is called "constantly restraining and guarding the sense faculties.
What is meant by "restraining and guarding the sense faculties"?

It means that after the eye has seen a form, one does not grasp at its signs, nor does one grasp at its subtle details; furthermore, one does not become attached to the various flavors of forms and so forth, but understands the Dharma of renunciation as it truly is.

In this way, when the ear hears sounds, the nose smells fragrances, the tongue perceives tastes, the body feels tactile sensations, and the mind cognizes mental phenomena, they do not grasp at their marks, nor do they grasp at their subtle secondary characteristics; nor do they become attached to the various flavors of such phenomena, but rather understand them as they truly are as the dharma of renunciation.
What has been described in this way is called heedfulness. Furthermore, Śāriputra, heedfulness means that having disciplined one’s own mind, one well protects the minds of others;

one removes the afflictions and realizes the bliss of the Dharma. One does not engage in investigation, nor does one investigate thoughts of desire, thoughts of malice, or thoughts of harm. One does not investigate the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of malice, or the unwholesome root of delusion. One does not investigate misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, or misconduct of mind. One does not investigate lack of firm attention, and in brief, one does not investigate any sinful actions or unwholesome dharmas whatsoever.
What has been thus described is called heedfulness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva who is heedful applies himself with profound and firm mental attention, corresponding to diligent practice.
If a phenomenon exists, one knows it as it truly is—existent; if a phenomenon does not exist, one knows it as it truly is—non-existent.
What is existent? What is non-existent?

That which is called the right path, when practiced with diligence, can give rise to faith and understanding, and thus exists; the wrong path, when practiced with diligence, cannot give rise to faith and understanding, and thus does not exist.
That all karmic actions have retribution exists; that all karmic actions have no retribution does not exist.
The eye exists, but the true nature of that eye does not exist.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind exist; however, the true nature of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind does not exist.

Form is impermanent, suffering, non-ultimate, unstable, and subject to disintegration—this exists; yet the reckoning of form as permanent, pleasant, ultimate, stable, and not subject to disintegration does not exist.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent, suffering, non-ultimate, unstable, and subject to disintegration—this exists; yet the reckoning of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as permanent, pleasant, ultimate, stable, and not subject to disintegration does not exist.

"Furthermore, among the various dharmas such as 'ignorance conditions volitional formations' and so forth, that which is unreal—such as ignorance conditioning volitional formations up to birth conditioning aging and death—exists; that which is definitively real—such as ignorance conditioning volitional formations up to birth conditioning aging and death—is non-existent.
That a practitioner of giving can bring about great wealth exists; that a practitioner of giving instead incurs poverty and destitution is non-existent.
That one who maintains the precepts is born in heaven exists; that one who violates the precepts is born in heaven is non-existent."
Great wisdom exists when there is extensive learning, and it is absent when there is folly;
it exists when there is correspondence with cultivation, and it is absent when there is no correspondence with cultivation;
it exists when there is correspondence with profound and firm mental attention, and it is absent when there is no correspondence with profound and firm mental attention.
For a bodhisattva who exerts diligent vigor, the attainment of the fruit of bodhi exists; for one who is indolent, it does not exist.
For one free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) who engages in worldly affairs, it exists; for one possessed of overweening pride who seeks to realize nirvāṇa, it does not exist.
To penetrate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in all places, it exists; to harbor attachment to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, it does not exist.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Therefore, you should know that a bodhisattva who is heedful is able to apply deep and firm attention and practice with diligence; such a one will be widely revealed by the wise throughout the world. However, throughout the world, those who lack wisdom are unable to reveal it. If one does not know whether things exist or do not exist according to conventional truth, how can one accord with the true meaning taught by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones?"
Śāriputra! All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, briefly encompass all phenomena by means of four dharma seals.
What are these four?
First, all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; second, all conditioned phenomena are suffering; third, all dharmas are without self; fourth, nirvana is tranquility.
Yet all sentient beings, amidst the impermanence of conditioned phenomena, conceive the notion of permanence.
If sentient beings were to sever this notion of permanence, that would indeed be what is taught by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, all sentient beings conceive the notion of pleasure within the suffering of conditioned formations;
if sentient beings were to eliminate this notion of pleasure, that would indeed be what the Tathāgata has taught.
Furthermore, all sentient beings conceive the notion of a self within all phenomena that are without self;
if sentient beings were to eliminate this notion of self, that would be precisely what the Tathāgata has taught.
Furthermore, all sentient beings give rise to a perverted mind that grasps at attainments within the principle of the tranquility of nirvāṇa;
if sentient beings were to sever this perverted mind of grasping at attainments, that would indeed be what is taught by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one can thoroughly understand that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent, one will then be able to comprehend and enter into the emptiness and impermanence of their nature.
If one can thoroughly understand that all conditioned phenomena are suffering, one will then be able to abandon all seeking and aspiration.
If one can thoroughly understand that all phenomena are without self, one is then able to contemplate the liberation gateway of the samādhi of emptiness.
If one can thoroughly understand the tranquility of nirvāṇa, one is then able to engage in cultivation amidst various signs, yet does not prematurely realize the limit of reality.
Śāriputra! If bodhisattvas practice these dharmas with diligent application, they will not lose any wholesome qualities and will swiftly fulfill all Buddha-dharmas.
Chapter Four: The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata, Part One At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:

“A bodhisattva who abides in faith, regarding the ten kinds of inconceivable dharmas of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, attains pure faith and understanding; they transcend conceptual discrimination, leave behind all doubt and regret, and subsequently give rise to physical and mental joy, a sense of rapture, and the thought of their rarity.”
What are the ten?

First, regarding the inconceivable and most supreme physical marks of the Buddha-Tathāgata, one develops a sense of wonder through pure faith and understanding, up to the point of experiencing a state of sublime joy.
Second, regarding the inconceivable, wondrous, and excellent voice of the Buddha-Tathāgata, they have pure faith and understanding, even to the point of conceiving a sense of its rarity.
Third, regarding the inconceivable, supreme, and great wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgata, they have pure faith and understanding, even to the point of conceiving a sense of its rarity.
Fourth, regarding the inconceivable, subtle, and wondrous radiance of the Buddha-Tathāgata, they have pure faith and understanding, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.
Fifth, regarding the inconceivable, perfected morality and meditative concentration of the Buddha-Tathāgata, they have pure faith and understanding, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.
Sixth, regarding the vast and inconceivable superknowledges (*ṛddhi*) of the Buddha-Tathāgata, one’s faith and understanding are pure, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.
Seventh, regarding the ten inconceivable powers of knowledge (*jñānabala*) of the Buddha-Tathāgata, one’s faith and understanding are pure, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.
Eighth, regarding the inconceivable four fearlessnesses of the Buddha Tathāgata, they have pure faith and understanding, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.
Ninth, regarding the inconceivable great compassion of the Buddha Tathāgata, they have pure faith and understanding, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.

Tenth, regarding the inconceivable unique Buddha-qualities (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*) of the Buddha Tathāgata, they maintain pure faith and understanding, even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder.

A Bodhisattva who abides in faith, diligently seeking these ten kinds of inconceivable and marvelous qualities of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, does not fear nor grow weary; their mind remains unshakable, even until their body, flesh, skin, bones, tendons, veins, blood, and marrow become withered and parched. If they have not yet attained the ten inconceivable qualities of the Tathāgata, they shall not give rise to fatigue in the interim, but will surely attain them through diligent and persistent seeking.

Śāriputra! A bodhisattva who abides in faith regarding these ten kinds of inconceivable qualities of the Buddha-Tathāgata should maintain such pure faith and understanding, and even give rise to the thought of their being truly marvelous.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The physical marks of the Tathāgata are inconceivable; One should contemplate his subtle and pure Dharma-body.
It is signless and free from the gate of obstruction; The Bodhisattva is able to give rise to faith and understanding therein.”
Even the extensive analysis of all realms of existence—these sounds are inconceivable to anyone but the Buddha;
regarding this jewel-like Dharma gate in all places, one should have faith and understanding in the Buddha’s sphere.
All classes of sentient beings, with their distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior faculties—only the Buddha’s supreme wisdom can know them all;
the power of his wisdom in faith and understanding is inconceivable.
The boundless great radiance of all Buddhas, An inconceivable net of pure light,
Shines extensively throughout the ten directions, Piercing through all the oceans of infinite lands.
The pure and wondrous precepts of the Muni appearing in the world do not rely upon worldly dharmas;
dwelling in the pure faith of a bodhisattva who abides in faith, they believe in the inconceivable spiritual powers of the Buddha.
The gateways to the supernatural powers and spheres of all Buddhas cannot be known by the bodhisattvas;
the Buddhas always abide in a state of meditative equipoise, and the gates of the Buddhas' liberation are inconceivable.
The Dharma-realm is vast and free from discrimination; Only the Buddha’s supreme power can fully know it.
The Great Sage, endowed with the power of wisdom, Is boundless and limitless, equal to space itself.
Even if all classes of sentient beings were to mutually pose questions as numerous as the ocean,
answering each inquiry exhaustively with a joyful mind— such is the Tathāgata’s inconceivable fearlessness.
To bring benefit to a single sentient being, And likewise for infinite sentient beings,
Causing them all to dwell securely in a disciplined mind— Such is the inconceivable great compassion of the Tathāgata.
The Tathāgata is fully endowed with all the marks, And is able to awaken to the understanding of all phenomena;
Through the gateway of the qualities of the unshared Buddha-dharmas, He manifests wisdom in all places.
These ten kinds of inconceivables encompass all Buddha-dharmas and enter into the nature of phenomena;
if one can universally give rise to a mind of faith and understanding, the bodhisattva dwells well in pure confidence.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how is it that a bodhisattva dwelling in faith develops pure conviction and even gives rise to a sense of wonder regarding the most supreme physical marks of the Buddha Tathāgata?
It means that the body of the Buddha-Tathāgata is pure; he is universally able to eliminate and sever all unwholesome dharmas, and is fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas.
The body of the Tathāgata is already free from all impure, foul, and evil dharmas—such as sinews, bones, blood, flesh, discharges, outflows, and various defiled states.
The body of the Tathāgata is by its very nature luminous, pure, and translucent; it is forever free from the stains of all afflictions;
it transcends the world and is not defiled by any worldly phenomena.

The body of the Tathāgata is nurtured by the accumulation of immeasurable merit, wisdom, and sublime practices for the sake of sentient beings; it is cultivated through the practice of immeasurable wholesome dharmas such as morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; it is adorned with the flowers of all supreme merits, appearing like various forms reflected in a great round mirror, and further manifesting like the moon’s reflection in pure water.
Furthermore, the body of the Tathāgata is like the realm of empty space, universally encompassing all; it is also like the dharmadhātu, most supreme and most excellent.

The Buddha’s body is without outflows, for all taints have been exhausted; the Buddha’s body is unconditioned and does not fall within the categories of numerical reckoning. It is a body like empty space, a body of unequaled equality, the most supreme body within all the three realms.
Furthermore, the body of the Tathāgata is a body that cannot be compared and a body for which there is nothing to compare it with;
it is pure and stainless, free from all defilements, and its self-nature is luminous.
It cannot be observed in the past, nor can it be observed in the future, nor can it be observed in the present; it cannot be observed by lineage, nor by form, nor by marks.
It is not to be perceived as a physical form, nor as the secondary marks of beauty;

it is not to be perceived by the mind (*citta*), nor by the intellect (*manas*), nor by consciousness (*vijñāna*); it is not to be perceived through seeing, nor through hearing, nor through recollection, nor through conceptualization;
it is not to be perceived as the aggregates (*skandha*), nor as the sense bases (*āyatana*), nor as the elements (*dhātu*).
It is to be observed as non-arising, not to be observed as abiding, not to be observed as ceasing, not to be observed as grasping,
not to be observed as relinquishing, and not to be observed as renunciation.

It cannot be observed through conduct; it cannot be observed through visible color; it cannot be observed through features; it cannot be observed through shape; it cannot be observed through coming; it cannot be observed through going; it cannot be observed through ethical discipline; it cannot be observed through meditative concentration; it cannot be observed through wisdom; it cannot be observed through liberation; it cannot be observed through the knowledge and vision of liberation; it cannot be observed through having signs; it cannot be observed through being signless; it cannot be observed through the characteristics of phenomena; it cannot be observed through the accomplishment of all marks; it cannot be observed through the fearlessnesses; it cannot be observed through the analytical knowledges; it cannot be observed through the supernormal powers; it cannot be observed through great compassion; and it cannot be observed through the accomplishment of the unique qualities of a Buddha.
The appearance of all Buddhas is like a magical illusion, like a mirage, like the moon reflected in water;
it is the wondrous body of self-nature, the body that is empty, signless, wishless, and boundless;
the body without category, the body without accumulation, the body without discrimination, the body without dependence, the body without distinction, which has already attained excellent abiding.
The self-nature body that is neither moving nor turning; the self-nature body that is neither form nor non-form;

the self-nature body that is neither feeling nor non-feeling, neither perception nor non-perception, neither formations nor non-formations, and neither consciousness nor non-consciousness; the body that is neither real nor born, and is not a body of the great elements;
the body of the unprecedented and the karma of the unprecedented; it is not produced by the eye, nor does it emerge from form.
It is not external; it does not depend on the ear and does not emerge from sound, nor is it external;
it is not what the nose smells and does not emerge from fragrance, nor is it external; it is not what the tongue discerns and does not emerge from flavor, nor is it external;
it is not what the body contacts and does not emerge from tangibility, nor is it external.
It is not turned by the mind, not turned by the intellect, and not turned by consciousness; nor is it non-turning, nor does it follow along with turning.
It attains abiding in an immovable body equal to space, wherein the supreme dharmadhātu merges into the realm of space.

Śāriputra! Regarding such dharmas as these, a bodhisattva who abides in faith is able to attain pure faith and understanding toward the inconceivable, pure, and wondrous physical marks of the Tathāgata; they transcend conceptual discrimination, leave behind all doubt and regret, and subsequently give rise to signs of physical joy, mental joy, and delight, conceiving a sense of their rarity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Throughout immeasurable koṭis and nayutas of kalpas, He has extensively cultivated the bodhisattva practices;
Amidst the three types of pure and wholesome bodily actions, He diligently sought the peerless body of the Sugata."
Giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness throughout the worlds of the ten directions, Extensively practicing generosity with one's own body and life,
Always remaining free from the defiled mind of lustful misconduct, Diligently seeking the unsurpassed, space-like body.
Adorned with pure and subtle upper garments, having practiced the perfection of giving throughout immeasurable eons, you have perfected the sublime conduct of dānapāramitā;
you extensively bestow [these gifts] upon the supreme sons of the Buddhas.
As the yak cherishes its tail, so one guards the precepts;
Able to sacrifice body and life with patience free from resentment, One seeks the Buddha-body with an untiring mind, Extensively cultivating the perfection of diligence.
Contemplating the meditative realm of all Buddhas, With a joyful inner mind, I shall give rise to wisdom and skillful means;
May I likewise attain the supreme body of the Sugata within the dharmadhātu.
Having extensively performed the virtuous deeds of all Buddhas, And attained the fruit of Bodhi, supreme among men,
One shall obtain the vast body of space, Perfectly free from defilement, pure and stainless.
Free from the marks of self and person, empty of intrinsic nature, signless, ineffable, and unattainable—
having transcended the sphere of all sensory faculties, the body of the Great Muni is thus attained.
Detached from form and sound, the mind is pure; Unborn and unconditioned, it is primordially empty.
One shall attain the unmoving body of a Tathāgata, Just as the Ten-Powered Sugata is likewise.
Just as various bodies are conjured by illusion— such as the forms of elephants, horses, and humans—
so too do the physical marks of the Buddha, the Honored One of Ten Powers, appear to those with deluded, false, and inverted minds.
The countless Sugatas of the past, and likewise all the Buddhas of the future,
possess the same peerless Dharma-nature body, which is the supreme Dharmadhātu, equal to space.

“Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva established in faith encounters such inconceivable and most supreme bodily marks of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, their faith and understanding become pure; they transcend conceptual discrimination, leave behind all doubt and regret, and subsequently give rise to signs of physical joy, mental joy, and gladness, conceiving a sense of wonder.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how is it that a bodhisattva who abides in faith develops pure conviction regarding the inconceivable, sublime voice of the Buddha-Tathāgata, and even gives rise to the thought of its rarity?

Śāriputra! All the sounds produced by the Buddha, the Tathāgata, within those various assemblies, are for the purpose of subduing and guiding all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions toward all manner of wholesome benefits; they universally accord with their inclinations and cause them all to give rise to joy.
However, the Buddha, the Tathāgata, does not form such a thought as:
"I am able to proclaim the various dharmas for this assembly of bhikṣus;
I shall preach the Dharma for this assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, brahmins, kṣatriyas, householders, laymen, and assemblies of Brahmās."

Furthermore, the Buddha-Tathāgata, in accordance with what is appropriate, proclaims such teachings as sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, udānas, nidānas, avadānas, itivṛttakas, jātakas, vaipulyas, adbhutadharmas, and upadeśas; he teaches these to all assemblies, even including the hosts of Brahmā, as is fitting for them.

All classes of sentient beings, with their various distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior faculties, hear these phrases of the Dharma; yet all those phrases issue from the gateway of the Tathāgata’s mouth, and according to their respective faculties, each attains understanding. Within this process, there is no mutual contradiction or obstruction in speech, as each clearly perceives and comprehends the Dharma.
This is the manifestation of the Tathāgata’s fruition of past merit as a wondrous voice, which causes all sentient beings to follow it, understand it, and enter into it.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the voice of the Tathāgata is subtle, smooth, pleasing, and delightful; it is pure and stainless, exquisite and a joy to hear. It is also clearly articulated, neither coarse nor harsh; those who hear it experience physical joy and their minds never grow weary.

Those who hear it feel joy in their hearts, and from that joy, delight arises; they understand it clearly and all give rise to love and pleasure. Their minds and intentions become harmonious and well-adjusted. It is like the sound of a lion, the sound of clouds and thunder, the sound of the ocean tide, the subtle and wondrous sound of the kalaviṅka bird, the pure Brahma-sound, the sound of a great drum, the auspicious sound, the soft and supple sound, the resonant sound, the pure and exquisite sound that brings satisfaction to the faculties of all sentient beings, the sound that causes all assemblies to rejoice, and the most supreme sound endowed with all excellent marks.
Whether here or there, all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are fully endowed with immeasurable merit and pure vocal qualities.

Śāriputra, such as these are the inconceivable, wondrous, and excellent vocal qualities of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas; regarding them, a bodhisattva who abides in faith develops pure conviction and even gives rise to the thought of their being truly marvelous.
At that time, the World-Honored One, to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Tathāgata possesses the mark of the sublime Brahma-voice; The sounds he utters are perfectly disciplined.
The Brahma-multitudes cannot equal the Buddha’s voice— Such qualities as these he fully possesses.”
The Buddha’s voice can be associated with loving-kindness, And his vast compassion is likewise sublime;
It is likewise associated with joy and equanimity— Such is the wondrous sound that issues from the Sage, the Holy Honored One.
Hearing this sound can extinguish the various unwholesome states of sentient beings— the fire of greed, the poison of hatred,
and the darkness of ignorance— and it possesses all such qualities of sound.
Among the various groups of people in all different regions, throughout the entire human race,
even as far as this Jambudvīpa— the Buddha perfectly understands their manifold languages.
Sentient beings, according to their hearing of the Buddha’s voice, And the hosts of devas dwelling on earth or in the sky,
Having heard the sublime voice of the Muni, Are able to understand and enter it through the power of that voice.
Whether two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed, or those without feet—whatever such beings hear the Buddha’s voice, as soon as they touch it or hear it, a tranquil mind arises;
in all those places, they turn toward the sound.
Within the trichiliocosm, they illuminate and subdue all classes of sentient beings;
universally encompassing those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties, they skillfully turn [the wheel of Dharma] in accordance with the Buddha’s voice.

Those who should be disciplined hear of liberation; Free from all conceptualization and non-conceptualization, With a mind in meditative equipoise, they are taught the gateway to the Noble Truths; Within this, there is neither grasping nor bondage.
Boundless sentient beings hear the Buddha’s voice; having heard it, they extinguish all afflictions.
With sincere devotion, they take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; having heard it, they become fully endowed with precepts and patience.
The Tathāgata’s most supreme and wondrous voice—this sound is profound, vast, and of infinite measure;
as the sound is boundless, so too is wisdom boundless. Through this wisdom, the bodhisattva’s faith is certain, free from doubt or regret.

Chapter Four, Part Two: The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

What is meant by a bodhisattva abiding in faith who, regarding the supreme and inconceivable great wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgata, possesses pure faith and understanding, transcends conceptual discrimination, and is free from all doubt and regret; and who subsequently gives rise to signs of physical and mental joy and gladness, conceiving the thought that it is something marvelous?
"Śāriputra!
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, turn all dharmas through unimpeded knowledge and vision.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

I shall now, for your sake, employ analogies to proclaim and elucidate the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom, so that those bodhisattvas who abide in faith may attain pure conviction and even conceive a sense of wonder.

Śāriputra! Suppose, for example, that in as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, one were to take all the grasses, trees, branches, leaves, stems, and trunks, and cut them into pieces the size of four fingers. Then, someone might gather them together in one place and burn them with fire; once burned, they would all become ashes, which are then scattered into the great oceans of all those worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where the ashes remain distributed within the sea for hundreds of thousands of years.

Yet the Tathāgata possesses the perfection and fullness of the power of wisdom, such that he is able to take various ashes from within those various great oceans and distribute them throughout all those worlds—namely, a certain amount of ash, for a certain number of worlds, with a certain number of foundations, a certain number of aggregates, and a certain number of branches and leaves—distributing them all across various locations without any loss or diminution.

Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have perfectly awakened to the dharma-realm; by virtue of that awakening, they are able to fully know all such vast activities throughout these various worlds.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses great majesty, great supernormal powers, and a vast reputation. If there are sons or daughters of good family in the world who possess pure faith and understanding toward the supreme, great wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgata, and are free from conceptual discrimination, they are all established by the compassionate mind of the Tathāgata. They realize the ultimate limit of all roots of goodness and further bring about the end of all suffering.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have perfectly awakened to and understood the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
If there is anyone who can give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding toward the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the merit they obtain shall never be lost or destroyed.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
I shall now again provide a parable to clarify this meaning, for there may be wise people who can understand it through my metaphorical explanation."

Suppose there were a person with a lifespan of one hundred years who, at a certain time, took a single drop of water the size of a hair-tip and divided it into a hundred parts; carrying these to the presence of the Buddha, he addressed him thus:
"World-Honored One!..."
"I now take this drop of water and entrust it to the Buddha’s care.
When I return later to retrieve it, the Buddha shall give it back to me.
The Buddha then accepted it and placed that drop of water into the Ganges River; it flowed along with the current, overflowing and gradually entering the great ocean.
At that time, after a hundred years had passed, that person came to where the Buddha was and spoke these words:
"World-Honored One!
In the past, I entrusted drops of water to you; I pray that the Buddha will now return them to me."

"Śāriputra! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, being fully endowed with the most supreme and perfect great wisdom, takes from within that great ocean a single drop of water—previously deposited there and divided into a hundred parts—and gives it to that person."
That single drop of water is not diminished, touched, destroyed, or lost by the waters of the ocean.
Śāriputra, the metaphor I have spoken is clear and distinct; how much more so for one who can perceive its meaning!
In this way, even after a long period of time, these drops of water cannot be destroyed by the power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom.
It is the same for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

If sons or daughters of good family can, regarding such great wisdom of the Tathāgata, possess pure faith and understanding free from conceptual discrimination, all this is established by the compassionate mind of the Tathāgata. Taking the Buddha’s merits as their object, they rain flowers from the midst of space, directly realizing the ultimate limit of all roots of goodness, and further bringing about the end of all suffering.
Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have perfectly awakened to and understood the dharma-realm.
If there is anyone who can give rise to even a single thought of faith and understanding toward the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the merit they obtain shall never be lost or destroyed.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Can the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, apart from the wisdom of a Tathāgata, transform all phenomena?"
The Buddha said, "No, Śāriputra."
At that time, Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is designated as 'wisdom' (jñāna)?
What is designated as 'consciousness' (vijñāna)?"
“Śāriputra! You should know that consciousness abides in four stations:
first, consciousness abides following form; it abides conditioned by form, and it is constantly approached, increased, made firm, and expanded.”
Second, consciousness abides following feeling and abides conditioned by feeling, and it is constantly approached, increased, made firm, and expanded until it is fully accomplished.
Third, consciousness abides following perception and abides conditioned by perception, and it is constantly approached, increased, made firm, and expanded until it is fully accomplished.
Fourth, consciousness follows its movement and abides; conditioned by movement, it abides, constantly drawing near to, increasing, becoming firm, and expanding that which is accomplished.
This is what is called consciousness.
What is called wisdom?
It is the aggregate of wisdom that, while abiding within the five aggregates of clinging, clearly understands them; this is termed wisdom.

Furthermore, when the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, and space element are each clearly understood as abiding within the consciousness element, this is termed consciousness.
Furthermore, if consciousness makes conceptual distinctions regarding the dharma-realm, this is called wisdom (*jñāna*).

Moreover, the designation within form as cognized by the eye, the designation within sound as cognized by the ear, the designation within odor as cognized by the nose, the designation within taste as cognized by the tongue, the designation within tangibles as cognized by the body, and the designation within phenomena as cognized by the mind—this is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Furthermore, if the internal mind is tranquil and there is no outward activity, and one gathers [the mind] through wisdom such that not even the slightest phenomenon is subject to conceptual discrimination, yet one does not depart from discrimination—this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, when consciousness arises with an object of perception, as the consciousness of mental attention, or as the consciousness of discrimination, this is called "consciousness" (vijñāna).
Moreover, when there is no grasping, no appropriation, no object of perception, and no conceptualization, this is called "wisdom" (jñāna).

Furthermore, if consciousness has a place to abide within the phenomena of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and if consciousness operates within the conditioned, this is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
If there is no consciousness that can operate within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), then the wisdom regarding the unconditioned is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
If consciousness discerns that within the phenomena of arising, abiding, and ceasing there is no arising, no ceasing, and no abiding, this is called "consciousness. Śāriputra,
regarding such phenomena as these, this is what is called "consciousness," and this is what is called "wisdom."

Therefore, you should know that the great wisdom of the Tathāgata is inconceivable. A bodhisattva who abides in faith possesses pure faith and understanding; they transcend conceptual discrimination, leave behind all doubt and regret, and subsequently give rise to signs of physical and mental joy and gladness, conceiving a sense of its rarity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Even if all the grasses and trees throughout the worlds of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were burned by someone until they were entirely reduced to ash, and those ashes were placed within the great ocean for hundreds of thousands of years; [the merit of that person would still surpass it]."
The Buddha, the Honored One of Ten Powers and Subtle Wisdom, can later take the ashes from within the ocean,
along with various roots and seeds from all directions, and distribute them all without any loss.
Holding the realms of sentient beings in the ten directions within their minds, they fully comprehend all conduct of greed, hatred, and delusion;
regarding all inclinations and actions, they realize them as neither increasing nor decreasing.

The World-Honored One of Great Wisdom and Ten Powers, throughout the ten directions and even across the entire Dharma-realm, acts as a charioteer without giving rise to a discriminating mind; all the Buddha-sons believe and understand this.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is meant by the inconceivable, subtle, and wondrous radiance of the Tathāgata? When a bodhisattva who abides in faith develops pure faith and understanding, transcends conceptual discrimination, and leaves behind all doubt and regret, they subsequently experience the arising of physical joy, mental joy, and a state of sublime bliss, giving rise to the thought that this is something marvelous."

This refers to how the Buddha, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has perfectly awakened to all the vast, subtle, and sublime radiance within the dharma-realm; this entire trichiliocosm is encompassed by it, universally illumined by a blazing and brilliant light, like the sun rising high without being shrouded by clouds.
In the same way, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha likewise manifests vast, brilliant,
and blazing light throughout this trichiliocosm, eclipsing all the stars, mountains, stones,
medicinal herbs, trees, lamps, and great masses of fire upon the earth, surpassing them with his most supreme and expansive radiance.
Subtle, wondrous, and brilliantly blazing, it surpasses the radiance of the sun and moon,
as well as the various lights from the palaces, bodily ornaments, and other regalia manifested by the gods of the Four Great Kings;
and the palaces manifested by the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa, Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, and Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens.
The various radiances of the physical ornaments and so forth, as well as the radiances of the emanated palaces, bodies,
and ornaments of the gods of the Brahma-pāriṣadya, Brahma-purohita, Brahma-kāyika, and Mahābrahmā heavens,
were surpassed by these most excellent, vast, subtle, and brilliantly blazing radiances.

Among the emanated palaces, bodily ornaments, and various radiances of the gods of Limited Light, Immeasurable Light, Luminous Sound, Limited Purity, Immeasurable Purity, Universal Purity, Cloudless, Merit-Born, Vast Fruit, Non-Perception, Free from Affliction, Free from Heat, Good to Behold, Good to See, and the Ultimate of Form, the pure radiance of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, surpasses them all as the most excellent, vast, subtle, and brilliantly blazing light.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has perfected the vast, immeasurable virtues of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. Śāriputra!

If all the light designated and manifested throughout this trichiliocosm were compared to the light possessed by the Buddha Tathāgata, it would not equal even one hundredth part; indeed, it would not equal even an *upaniṣad* part.
For example, if ordinary gold were placed among a mass of Jāmbūnada gold, that ordinary gold would have no luster; it would neither blaze nor shine.

Furthermore, whatever manifestations of light exist throughout this trichiliocosm are entirely eclipsed and lack any brilliance or radiant splendor in comparison to the supreme light of the Buddha, the Tathāgata.

The light of the Tathāgata is unsurpassed, vast, most excellent, and without limit; it manifests as the fruition of supreme wholesome karma and pervades this trichiliocosm with its great radiance, such that the illumination provided by the sun and moon, or by day and night, cannot be considered true light in comparison.
The Tathāgata, out of compassion for all sentient beings in the world, causes them all to dwell securely within the pure and perfect radiance.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, shines extensively throughout incalculable worlds.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already attained the supreme pāramitās and the prajñāpāramitā.
"Śāriputra!..."
I shall now further provide a parable to clarify this meaning.

Suppose there were a person who took all the soil from the great earth of this trichiliocosm and ground it entirely into dust. Carrying this dust with them, they traveled toward the eastern direction; having passed one world-system, they set down a single grain of dust, and having passed a second world-system, they set down another grain.
In this manner, they proceeded through the southern, western, and northern directions, setting down a grain of dust in every world-system they passed.
Śāriputra, what do you think?
Would those particles of dust reach the very limit of all worlds?
Śāriputra said:
“No, World-Honored One.”
"No, Sugata," he replied.
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! It is the same with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Within all those worlds, he illuminates them extensively with pure radiance; yet compared to the Buddha’s radiance, all other lights do not equal even one hundredth part, nor even an *upaniṣad* part.”
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already attained the supreme pāramitās and the prajñāpāramitā.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

All the grasses, trees, forests, the Iron Ring Mountains, and even Sumeru, the king of mountains, throughout the great earth—all these are sustained by the power of the Tathāgata’s great radiance, and thus they shine extensively throughout the trichiliocosm."

However, inferior sentient beings are unable to believe or understand this. Some sentient beings are unable to behold the Tathāgata’s circular halo; some sentient beings gaze extensively upon it within that circular halo; some see the Buddha’s light for the distance of one *krośa*; some see the Buddha’s light within the distance of one *yojana*; and some see the Buddha’s light within the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
As for the light of the Tathāgata, who is able to behold it throughout hundreds of thousands of worlds?
It is those Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (bhūmi) who are able to see the Buddha’s light in all boundless worlds.
The Tathāgata, out of compassion for all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the realm of space and the realm of sentient beings, universally illuminates them with pure radiance.

Upon hearing this teaching, those bodhisattvas who abide in faith develop pure faith and understanding; they transcend conceptual discrimination, become free from doubt and regret, and subsequently experience physical and mental joy, a sense of well-being, and signs of delight, giving rise to the thought that this is truly marvelous.
At that time, the World-Honored One, to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The radiance of all suns and moons, The light of Śakra and Brahmā,
And even the light of the Heaven of Ultimate Form— None of these can compare to the marks of the Buddha’s light.”
The various lights of the Akaniṣṭha Heaven and other realms, even those throughout the trichiliocosm,
when compared to the light from a single pore of the Buddha, do not equal even a sixteenth part.
The radiance of space is vast and expansive, and the vastness of sentient beings is likewise so;
if one beholds the Tathāgata’s pure radiance, it is boundless, limitless, and equal to space.
Those who are to be transformed by the Buddha’s manifestation see the Buddha’s light;
they are not like those born blind in this world, who cannot see the radiance of the sun and instead claim that sunlight does not exist.

So it is with inferior beings: though the Buddha constantly illuminates them with his radiance, they themselves cannot perceive that pure light, and instead claim that the Buddha’s light does not exist at all.
All those who behold the Buddha’s halo— whether at a distance of one krośa, or one yojana,
or even within a trichiliocosm— are able to perceive the marks of the Buddha’s radiant light.
Bodhisattvas who have already ascended the stages—the eighth, ninth, and tenth—abide securely within these great grounds;
beholding the Buddha’s radiance, they possess great wisdom.
The Bodhisattva proceeds toward the Great Wisdom of the Buddha, Relying upon the boundless wheel of radiant light;
Performing all buddha-deeds to benefit sentient beings, Throughout the inconceivable lands of all Buddhas.
The Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, are inconceivable; their inconceivable light is likewise so.
They open the gate of pure faith in an inconceivable way; the gateway to the mass of all merits is inconceivable.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is meant by the inconceivable perfection of the Tathāgata’s ethical discipline and meditative concentration? When a bodhisattva dwelling in faith develops pure conviction and understanding, transcends conceptual discrimination, and becomes free from all doubt and regret, they subsequently experience physical and mental joy and a sense of well-being, giving rise to the thought that this is truly marvelous."
Śāriputra! The Tathāgata, with words of absolute truth, speaks thus:

"All sentient beings born into the world who possess the aggregate of pure precepts—whose physical actions are pure, whose verbal actions are pure, and whose mental actions are pure—and who, though born in the world and aging in the world, are not defiled by worldly dharmas, attaining the dharma of the Brahmin’s freedom from transgression, and further attaining the śramaṇa’s dharma of the samādhi of tranquil contemplation, shall attain the supreme pāramitā."
Furthermore, the Tathāgata spoke these words of truth and reality:

"I do not see anyone in the entire world—whether Māra, Brahmā, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, humans, asuras, or others—who is able to possess a pure aggregate of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) and an aggregate of meditative concentration (samādhiskandha) equal to the immeasurable, pure aggregates of ethical discipline and meditative concentration of the Buddha, the Tathāgata."

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has already attained the supreme pāramitā, and has already attained the pāramitās of ethical discipline and meditative concentration.
“Śāriputra! I shall now further provide a parable to clarify this meaning; would you like to hear it?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time; we pray that the Buddha will explain it for us.
If the bhikṣus should hear the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s pure perfection of ethical discipline and meditative concentration, they will, upon hearing it, believe, accept, and uphold it.”
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Eight.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Nine.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Da Fu, Acting Director of the Bureau of Scholarly Promotion.

Chapter Four: The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata, Part Three. Furthermore, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"What do you think?"
"Which is greater: the realm of earth or the realm of sentient beings?
Śāriputra replied to the Buddha, "World-Honored One!
The realm of earth is not great; the realm of sentient beings is greater."
The Buddha said:
“Śāriputra! It is so, it is so;
the realm of sentient beings is vast.”

Śāriputra! Suppose all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation; whether possessing form or formless; whether possessing perception, lacking perception, or neither possessing nor lacking perception—even extending to the entire realm of sentient beings—should, in a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta, all simultaneously attain human bodies, without any before or after.
Furthermore, may all those sentient beings who have attained human form as described above realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a single kṣaṇa, a single lava, or a single muhūrta.

Furthermore, all those Buddhas and Tathāgatas thus accomplished each manifest transformations before them, with each Tathāgata having one thousand heads; each head has one thousand faces, and each face has one thousand tongues.
These Tathāgatas are fully endowed with the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered analytical knowledges, and unimpeded eloquence. Śāriputra!

Furthermore, even if those Tathāgatas were to jointly praise all the merits of the Tathāgata’s perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) and his aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), they would not reach their limit even after the passage of *koṭi-nayuta* kalpas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The merit of the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīla-skandha) of a single Buddha-Tathāgata is boundless; likewise, the merit of the aggregate of ethical discipline of all these Buddha-Tathāgatas—from their unsurpassed great wisdom, liberating eloquence, and so forth, up until their entry into Great Nirvāṇa—is entirely equal throughout that interval.
Why is this? Because within the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one gives rise to conceptualizations of intrinsic existence (*sasvabhāva*).

Therefore, the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*), his merit, his unsurpassed great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*), and his supreme eloquence (*pratibhāna*) are immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless, equal to space (*ākāśa*).
Śāriputra!

Let alone the aforementioned single trichiliocosm, even if all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions—reaching as far as the sands of the Gaṅgā River in number, extending universally to the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—were all to obtain human bodies in a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta, and were all to realize the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
To summarize and expand upon this: even regarding that which is without intrinsic nature, one gives rise to conceptualizations of it having intrinsic nature.

Therefore, the Tathāgata’s aggregate of ethical discipline, his merit, his unsurpassed great wisdom, and his most excellent eloquence are immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless, equal to the expanse of space.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata has already attained the supreme pāramitā, having perfected and purified the śīla-pāramitā.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
"I shall now further proclaim the Tathāgata’s perfection of meditative concentration by clarifying its characteristics.
Would you like to hear it?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time; we pray that the Buddha will explain it for us, so that the bhikṣus, having heard what is taught, may faithfully believe, accept, and uphold it.
The Buddha said:

“Śāriputra! In a future time, in a future age, seven suns will appear in the world. At that time, this trichiliocosm will blaze, burn fiercely, and burn most intensely everywhere, becoming a single mass of flames.”
At that time, whether the Tathāgata was walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, ten kinds of rare phenomena appeared in that location.
What are these ten?
First, the ground is as level as the palm of a hand; this is the first rare and marvelous phenomenon.

Second, at that time, within this trichiliocosm, though it is ablaze, burning intensely, and blazing everywhere until it becomes a single mass of flames, wherever the Tathāgata walks, stands, sits, or lies down, no thorns shall appear in that place, but gold and jewels shall well forth; this is the second rare and marvelous phenomenon.

Third, when this trichiliocosm is ablaze, burning all around, and intensely blazing everywhere until it becomes a single mass of flame, at that time the Tathāgata—whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—enjoys a ground as vast as he requires; this is the third rare and marvelous quality.

Fourth, at that time, within this trichiliocosm, it was blazing, intensely blazing, and utterly blazing, becoming one single mass of flame; yet wherever the Tathāgata walked, stood, sat, or lay, in those places there would naturally grow extraordinary grasses—vivid green, supple, soft, curling to the right, like *kañcanamaṇi* jewels—and possessing a wondrous fragrance. This is the fourth rare and marvelous phenomenon.

Fifth, at that time, throughout this trichiliocosm, it was blazing, universally blazing, and intensely blazing everywhere, becoming one single mass of flame. Yet, whether the Tathāgata was walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, in that very place there would naturally surge forth water endowed with eight meritorious qualities: namely, first, cool; second, light; third, soft; fourth, fragrant; fifth, delicious; sixth, clear; seventh, never tiring when drunk; and eighth, causing no harm even when drunk much. To possess such water complete with these eight meritorious qualities is the fifth rare and marvelous phenomenon.

Sixth, at that time, within this trichiliocosm, it was ablaze, burning everywhere, and blazing intensely throughout; it was entirely a single mass of flame. Yet, whether the Tathāgata was walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, in that very place a cool breeze would naturally blow and touch him.
Śāriputra! It is like this:

during the intense heat of the summer months, when a person is utterly exhausted, someone might go to the banks of the Gaṅgā River and, taking advantage of its coolness, gradually enter the river. By bathing their body, they remove their feverish distress and attain a state of lightness, ease, composure, and joy.

Emerging from the river and standing on the bank, they walk back and forth; not far away, they see a great forest, lush and verdant, with branches and leaves spreading wide. Its shadows are deep and pure, hanging down in a canopy that completely covers it. Within it, the exquisite beauty is as if adorned with an intermingling of various jewels. At that moment, the person goes to that grove and sits down calmly, while cool breezes blow in from all four directions to touch them.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata is likewise; by the radiant brilliance of the karmic fruition of his past virtuous deeds, a pure and cool breeze naturally blows and touches him. This is the sixth rare and marvelous quality.

Seventh: At that time, this trichiliocosm was ablaze, burning all around, and blazing intensely everywhere, becoming one single mass of flame. Yet, at that time, whether the Tathāgata was walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, in those very places there would naturally appear various water-born flowers—namely, utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka flowers. This is the seventh extraordinary phenomenon.

Eighth: At that time, this trichiliocosm was ablaze, burning all over, and blazing intensely everywhere until it became a single mass of flame. Yet, at that time, whether the Tathāgata was walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, in that very place there would spontaneously appear various land-growing flowers—namely, *adhimuktaka*, *campaka*, *sumana*, *vārṣika*, *aśoka*, *pāṭala*, *karaṇikāra*, *taraṇī*, and so forth. Such flowers as these were endowed with perfect color and fragrance; this is the eighth rare and marvelous phenomenon.

Ninth: At that time, within this trichiliocosm, it blazes, blazes everywhere, and blazes intensely and everywhere; it becomes a single mass of flame. Yet, whether the Tathāgata is walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, that location remains composed of diamond—firm, solid, and indestructible. This is the ninth rare and marvelous quality.

Tenth: At that time, this great trichiliocosm was ablaze, burning intensely, and blazing all over, becoming one single mass of flame. Yet, whether the Tathāgata was walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, in that very place a most exquisite jeweled stūpa appeared. All devas and humans, as well as Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, gazed upon it with reverence and made offerings. This is the tenth rare and marvelous phenomenon.
“Śāriputra! These ten kinds of rare phenomena will appear in succession in that region, because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has thoroughly awakened to the nature of the dharmadhātu.”

Entering samādhi according to their respective forms and characteristics, he dwells in a state of meditative equipoise with a single-pointed mind of pure bliss; though many eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges pass, it is to him as if a mere mealtime, for the Tathāgata suffers no impairment or loss within that samādhi.
Śāriputra!

When the Tathāgata is in meditative concentration, he remains therein for one kalpa, or a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas, a hundred thousand kalpas, one koṭi kalpas, a hundred koṭi kalpas, a thousand koṭi kalpas, a hundred thousand koṭi kalpas, or a hundred thousand koṭi nayuta kalpas, after which he arises from concentration.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has already attained the supreme pāramitā.
As for that supreme pāramitā, it possesses great supernormal powers, great majestic virtue, and great mastery; therefore, the Tathāgata is perfectly and fully endowed with them.
Śāriputra! Just as when a deva is born in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, he dwells focused upon a single object— namely, the object of consciousness—
and for eighty-four thousand kalpas that consciousness does not transition into any other consciousness, until at the exhaustion of his life-span, he passes away.

“Śāriputra! From the time the Tathāgata first realized the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi during the first watch of the night until his entry into mahāparinirvāṇa during the middle watch of the night, the dharma of samādhi remained undestroyed and unextinguished throughout that interval.”
When the Tathāgata is in meditative absorption, there is no mind that can be turned, no mind that acts, no mind that investigates, no mind that functions universally,
no mind that increases, no mind that decreases, no mind that is distracted,
no mind that is elevated, no mind that is depressed, no mind that is gathered and protected, and no mind that is concealed.
Without a mind that conforms, without a mind that opposes, without a mind that sinks, without a mind that wavers,
without a mind that rejoices, without a mind that clings with affection, without a mind that discriminates, without a mind that is free from discrimination, without a mind that calculates,
without a mind that flows along with consciousness, and without a mind that relies upon the eyes, ears, or nose.
The tongue, body, and mind do not rely upon form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or mental phenomena;
the mind does not engage in those phenomena, nor does it engage in the wisdom regarding them;
the mind does not observe them in the past, nor does it observe them in the future, nor does it observe them in the present.

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, thus abiding in samādhi, has not the slightest dharma that arises in his mind; yet, regarding all dharmas, he constantly proceeds with unimpeded knowledge and vision, without any conceptual awakening whatsoever.

The Tathāgata is free from mind, intellect, and consciousness; even within the state of meditative concentration, he does not diminish or lose [his awareness], yet he constantly performs all Buddha-activities without any deliberate arousal of thought.
At that time, the World-Honored One, to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, The Buddha cultivated the path throughout the three realms of existence;
With precepts, learning, concentration, and patience, his mind was never distracted, And he thus perfected the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.”
Such is the karmic fruit of the Buddha’s wholesome deeds: Surpassing the world with pure precepts, free from the stains of conceptual proliferation, as pure as space;
The pure precepts of the One of Ten Powers are equal to empty space.
The Buddha attained perfect enlightenment in the first watch of the night, and later entered nirvana in the middle watch;
the Buddha has no mental activity and no pervasive movement, remaining without loss or diminution in all states of tranquil concentration.
The aggregate of the ten powers is likewise undiminished, as are his supernormal powers and the factors of liberation;
for hundreds of thousands of eons he abides in a single mind, for the Buddha is without discrimination and free from conceptualization.
Within the meditative state of the Buddha that is like space, he turns the threefold meaning through his unimpeded wisdom;
though his mind and mental factors investigate without discarding anything, the Son of the Buddha gains faith and understanding in the Buddha’s ten powers.

“Śāriputra! Regarding such dharmas as these, a bodhisattva who abides in faith should maintain pure faith and understanding within the Tathāgata’s teachings on ethical discipline and meditative concentration; they should transcend conceptual discrimination and be free from all doubt and regret. Thereafter, they further give rise to signs of physical and mental joy and gladness, conceiving a sense of wonder.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

how is it that a bodhisattva who abides in faith develops pure faith and understanding regarding the Tathāgata’s power of supernormal knowledge (ṛddhividhi-jñāna), even to the point of conceiving a sense of wonder?
"Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has always proclaimed that among the assembly of śrāvaka bhikṣus, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana is the foremost in supernormal powers."

Within that assembly of bodhisattvas, if one were to compare them by means of the supernormal powers of śrāvakas, I do not see any śrāvaka whose supernormal powers are equal to those of a bodhisattva.
If one were to compare the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva with those of a Buddha, I do not see any instance where the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva are equal to those of a Tathāgata.
Those bodhisattvas constantly reflect:
"The supernatural powers of the Tathāgata are inconceivable; we shall exert diligent effort, aspiring to accomplish the spiritual power of the Tathāgata."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
I shall now speak again by way of a parable to elucidate the power of the Tathāgata’s supernormal knowledge and wisdom.
Do you wish to hear it?"
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Now is precisely the right time. We pray that the Buddha will explain it for us, so that the bhikṣus, having heard what is taught, may believe, accept, and uphold it.”
The Buddha said:
"Śāriputra, what do you think?"
“Does Mahāmaudgalyāyana possess great supernormal powers?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”
"I have personally heard the Buddha speak and have personally received his teaching: among the assembly of śrāvaka bhikṣus, Mahāmaudgalyāyana is the foremost in supernormal powers.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"

Suppose the great trichiliocosm were filled with all the śrāvakas, each possessing supernatural powers equal to those of Mahāmaudgalyāyana, as dense as a forest of rice, hemp, bamboo, reeds, or sugarcane, all identical in such power and appearance.

Whatever power, majesty, and strength of diligence possessed by all the śrāvakas, and whatever supernatural transformations they manifest according to their indications—compared to the Buddha Tathāgata, these do not equal even one hundredth part, nor one thousandth part, nor one hundred-thousandth part, nor one koṭi-th part, nor one hundred-koṭi-th part, nor one thousand-koṭi-th part, nor one hundred-thousand-koṭi-th part; they do not equal even a calculable part, a numerical part, a figurative part, or even an *upaniṣad* part.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has already attained the supreme pāramitā. Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, placed a single mustard seed within this ground; yet, through the sustaining power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddha-Tathāgata, all those śrāvakas, with all their majesty and capacity for supernormal powers, were utterly unable to lift that mustard seed, nor could they move it even by the measure of a single hair-tip.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already attained the supreme pāramitā and the pāramitā of supernormal powers (abhijñā).

Śāriputra! Let us set aside what has been said regarding this trichiliocosm; even if all sentient beings throughout the ten directions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; whether with form or without form; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—all these beings were simultaneously to attain the fruit of a śrāvaka and possess great supernormal powers just like Mahāmaudgalyāyana, yet even all those śrāvakas, through their combined power, influence, and supernormal transformations, would be unable to move a single mustard seed or even the tip of a single hair.

Why is this? Because the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has already attained the supreme pāramitā and the pāramitā of supernormal powers; he possesses great majesty and virtue, possesses great supernormal powers, and has attained great mastery.
At that time, the Blessed One again addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"Have you not heard that during the kalpa of the wind-disaster, there arises a great wind named Vilamba, which roars and blows across this trichiliocosm, striking Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains, the Great Iron Ring Mountains, and so forth, as well as the four continents up to the eighty thousand islands? Those various great oceans are blown and surged upward, scattering and spreading throughout an area of one yojana."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
In the past, I personally heard the Tathāgata proclaim such matters as these.”
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra!

During the kalpa of the wind disaster, great winds blow and strike this trichiliocosm, causing Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, as well as all other mountains and the great oceans to surge upward. They are shattered and dispersed, spreading everywhere for countless hundreds of thousands of yojanas.”
The various devas dwelling on the earth were likewise all blown about, scattered, and dispersed everywhere; even their dust could not be seen, let alone mountains and stones.
All the palaces and mansions within the Yāma Heaven were blown apart, destroyed, and scattered everywhere; even their dust could not be seen, much less the palaces themselves.

The palaces and abodes of those gods—the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Brahmakāyika Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Brahmakāyika-sabhā Heaven, the Mahābrahmā Heaven, the Parīttābha Heaven, the Apramāṇābha Heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven—were all buffeted, shattered, and dispersed in every direction; not even their dust could be seen, let alone their palaces.
Śāriputra! Even when such great winds blow, swirl, and strike with such force, not even a hair’s breadth of the Tathāgata’s exquisite robes can be moved or damaged, let alone their hem.
Why is this? Because the Buddha-Tathāgata is fully endowed with inconceivable supernormal powers, inconceivable conditions, inconceivable conduct, and inconceivable great compassion.

Śāriputra! When that great wind blows and surges, the great winds do not cease throughout the ten directions—east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, above, and below—in all worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

At that time, the Tathāgata raised the tip of his finger and pointed toward the great wind-circle; immediately, all the great winds were completely stilled. This is because the Tathāgata’s power of supernatural knowledge and wisdom is inconceivable and suffers no diminution.

Śāriputra! A bodhisattva who abides in faith should, regarding the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge of supernormal knowledges, attain pure faith and understanding; transcending conceptual discrimination and free from all doubt and regret, they subsequently give rise to the signs of physical joy, mental joy, and gladness, conceiving a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“May all sentient beings throughout the three realms Become śrāvakas endowed with wisdom,
Possessing wisdom equal to that of Mahāmaudgalyāyana, And fully perfected in the pāramitā of supernormal powers.”
If the Tathāgata were to place a single mustard seed, most minute in size, within this very spot,
all those who manifest supernatural powers would be utterly unable to move it.
Throughout all worlds in the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
when the Vilamba winds blow and strike, they swirl and roar, pervading every quarter.
When such great winds arise, the Buddha raises his exquisite robes to display them;
yet they cannot move even a single hair-tip, due to the inconceivable power of the Buddha’s spiritual majesty.
When a great wind blows with extreme ferocity, the Muni, by raising the tip of a single hair,
can through his supernormal power arrest that great wind-circle, as vast as the boundless expanse of space.

“Śāriputra! A bodhisattva who abides in faith should, regarding such supernatural powers of the Tathāgata, have pure faith and understanding, and even give rise to the thought of their being marvelous.
*The Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha*, Scroll Nine.”
The Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Imperial Court, Driven-and-Scattered Official, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
Great Master of Sanskrit, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Weijing.
Translated by Imperial Decree by [Name] The Fourth Part of Chapter Four:

The Inconceivable Powers of the Tathāgata "Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva established in faith hears of the ten inconceivable powers of knowledge of the Buddha-Tathāgata, they develop pure faith; they transcend conceptual discrimination and depart from all doubt and perplexity. Thereafter, they further experience physical and mental joy, a state of sublime bliss, and give rise to the thought of its rarity."

Because the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers of knowledge, he thoroughly understands the superior states; amidst the world of devas and humans, he can roar the lion’s roar and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel, which no deva, human, Māra, or Brahmā can ever turn, for there is none who shares the same Dharma as the Tathāgata.

What are the ten powers? First is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible; second is the power of knowing the ripening of karma; third is the power of knowing various inclinations and understandings; fourth is the power of knowing various elements; fifth is the power of knowing the superior and inferior faculties; sixth is the power of knowing the paths leading to all destinations; seventh is the power of knowing the defilement and purification of meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments; eighth is the power of realizing the recollection of past lives; ninth is the power of realizing the divine eye; and tenth is the power of realizing the exhaustion of the outflows.
Śāriputra! These are called the ten powers of knowledge of the Tathāgata.

Because the Tathāgata possesses these ten powers of knowledge, he thoroughly understands the superior states; amidst the great assembly, he can roar the lion’s roar and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel, such that there is no one in all the world who shares the same Dharma as the Tathāgata.
"What is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible?
It refers to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, who, by means of his unsurpassed and most supreme power of knowledge, understands as it truly is that which is possible and that which is impossible."
What is possible?
What is impossible? Śāriputra!

What is called "impossible" refers to that which cannot be admitted: that one who commits evil by way of body, speech, or mind could experience a pleasant, radiant, and lovely karmic fruit—such a thing is impossible.

As for that which may be admitted: it is possible that the performance of various evils by means of body, speech, and mind cannot bring about a desirable, radiant, and lovely retribution; such a thing is indeed the case.

Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible that the performance of virtuous deeds of body, speech, and mind could result in the attainment of unpleasant, lusterless, or unattractive retributive fruits.

That which is capable of being received refers to the performance of various virtues through body, speech, and mind, which can indeed bring about desirable, radiant, and lovely karmic results; such a thing is possible.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who is stingy to experience the fruit of great wealth;
however, it is possible for a person who is stingy to experience the fruit of poverty.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for one who practices generosity to experience the fruit of poverty;
however, it is possible for one who practices generosity to experience the fruit of great wealth.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who has broken the precepts to be reborn among gods or humans;
however, it is possible that such a person will fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for one who upholds the precepts to fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals;
however, it is possible for one who upholds the precepts to be reborn among gods or humans.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who harbors malice to experience the fruit of physical beauty;
however, it is possible for a person who harbors malice to experience the fruit of ugliness.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who practices patience to experience the fruit of ugliness;
however, it is possible for a person who practices patience to experience the fruit of physical beauty.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who is indolent to attain the samādhi of presence;
however, it is possible that an indolent person does not attain the samādhi of presence.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who practices with diligence not to attain the samādhi of presence;
however, it is possible for a person who practices with diligence to attain the samādhi of presence.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person with a distracted mind to attain the path of liberation;
however, it is possible that a person with a distracted mind fails to attain the path of liberation.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible that a person who is able to abide in one-pointedness of mind should fail to attain the path of deliverance;
it is possible that a person who is able to abide in one-pointedness of mind should attain the path of deliverance.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person lacking wisdom to eliminate all seeds and habitual tendencies;
however, it is possible that a person lacking wisdom cannot eliminate all seeds and habitual tendencies.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person of wisdom not to eliminate all seeds and habitual tendencies;
however, it is possible for a person of wisdom to eliminate all seeds and habitual tendencies.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who commits killing to experience the fruit of long life as a result of the causes of killing;
however, it is possible for a person who commits killing to experience the fruit of short life.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for one who abstains from taking life to experience the fruit of a short lifespan;
however, it is possible for one who abstains from taking life to experience the fruit of a long lifespan.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who commits theft to experience the fruit of great wealth;
however, it is possible for a person who commits theft to experience the fruit of poverty.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who abstains from stealing to experience the fruit of poverty;
however, it is possible for a person who abstains from stealing to experience the fruit of great wealth.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who is sexually depraved to have children and a wife;
however, it is possible that a person who is sexually depraved does not have children and a wife.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who has abandoned sexual misconduct to have no children or wife;
however, it is possible for a person who has abandoned sexual misconduct to have children and a wife.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who speaks falsehoods not to incur slander;
it is only possible for such a person to incur slander.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for one who abstains from false speech to incur slander;
it is possible, however, that such a person does not incur slander.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who engages in divisive speech to have their retinue remain undivided;
however, it is possible for their retinue to become divided.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for the members of a family to be separated from one another if that person refrains from divisive speech;
however, it is possible if their family members do not remain united.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who speaks harsh words to constantly hear pleasant speech;
however, it is possible that such a person does not hear pleasant speech.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who has abandoned harsh speech not to hear pleasant words;
if they were to hear them, that would be possible.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who engages in frivolous speech to attain decisive eloquence;
that they should not attain it is possible.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible that a person who abstains from frivolous speech should not attain decisive eloquence;
if they do attain it, that is possible.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person of great greed to attain great wealth;
however, that they do not so attain is possible. Furthermore, regarding what is impossible:
it is impossible for a person free from greed to have their great wealth interrupted; [it is only possible for them to maintain it].
