If there were no severance or continuity [of karma], such a case would be possible.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible that a person with a mind of hatred should not fall into hell;
if they do fall, such a case is possible.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible that a person free from hatred should not be reborn in the happy realms or the celestial worlds;
yet, if such a person were so reborn, that would be possible.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person of wrong views who accumulates the causes of wrong views to attain the Noble Path;
however, it is possible that a person of wrong views who accumulates the causes of wrong views does not attain the Noble Path.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible that a person of right view, having accumulated the causes of right view, should fail to attain the Noble Path;
however, it is possible that a person of right view, having accumulated the causes of right view, should attain the Noble Path.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who practices the perfection of giving not to attain the stage of a pure mind;
however, that they do attain it is entirely possible.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for one who maintains pure precepts not to attain a state of pure mind;
if they do so attain it, that is possible.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who gives rise to views of apprehending something to attain the patient acceptance that accords with reality;
it is possible, however, if they do not so apprehend.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible that a person who has realized the liberation of emptiness should not attain the patience of conformity;
it is possible that they should attain it.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person of evil conduct to attain a state of light and peaceful mind;
however, that they do not so attain is possible.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a person of evil conduct to attain mental discipline and pliancy;
however, that they do not so attain is possible.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for women to become universal monarchs;
it is possible for men to do so.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for women to become Śakra, Lord of the Devas;
it is possible for men to do so.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for women to become Brahmā kings;
it is possible for men to do so.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for women to manifest the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood;
however, it is possible for those on the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*) to attain the fruits in successive order.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) to manifest and realize the eighth stage;
however, it is possible for one to attain nirvāṇa within this very aggregate of existence.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who is a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) to manifest the transition to the third stage;
however, it is possible for such a person to attain nirvāṇa within this very aggregate of existence.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for a person who has attained the stage of Non-returner (anāgāmin) to return again to the human realm;
however, it is possible for such a person to attain nirvāṇa within this very set of aggregates.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for an Arhat to possess residual habitual tendencies;
it is possible that he possesses none.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible that noble ones should seek out teachers or masters of a different class to receive instructions on different doctrines;
if it were otherwise, that would be possible.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible for one who has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) to fall back;
however, that they shall eventually realize awakening (*bodhi*) is indeed possible.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible that a bodhisattva, having sat at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), should not realize the fruit of enlightenment;

however, it is possible that a bodhisattva, having sat at the seat of enlightenment, will certainly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi) and only then rise from his seat.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, to have any manifestation of seed-habits (*vāsanā*);
however, that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are able to completely eradicate all seed-habits is indeed possible.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for the wisdom of a Buddha-Tathāgata to encounter obstacles;
it is only possible for the wisdom of a Buddha-Tathāgata to be without obstacles.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible that one could behold the most supreme uṣṇīṣa of all the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas;
however, that one cannot see the Buddha’s uṣṇīṣa is indeed possible.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for anyone to know the mental activities of a Buddha;
however, it is possible that one cannot know the mental activities of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible for a Buddha-Tathāgata, while abiding in a state of meditative equipoise, to possess any sign of objective attainment;
however, it is possible for a Buddha-Tathāgata to remain constantly in a state of meditative equipoise.
Furthermore, regarding what is impossible: it is impossible that the speech of the Tathāgata could be false or indeterminate;
it is possible that the word of the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is not false.
Furthermore, as for what is impossible: it is impossible that the Tathāgata should have any faults;
it is possible that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are free from all faults.
“Śāriputra! Such dharmas as these are explained in detail within the [sections on] the four fearlessnesses and the eighteen unique qualities.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
It is impossible that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, should have any obstruction in what they know or see regarding the present world;
it is only possible that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have no obstruction in what they know or see regarding the present world."

Śāriputra, the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible as thus described is without limit; if one wished to know its limit, could it be known, for example, like that of space?
Just as the limits of space cannot be known, so too are the limits of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha’s power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible.

When bodhisattvas established in faith hear of this inconceivable power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible, they give rise to pure faith; they transcend conceptual discrimination and depart from all doubt. Subsequently, they experience physical and mental joy and a sense of rapture, giving rise to the thought of its rarity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The space of the ten directions is boundless and immeasurable; The power of knowledge regarding what is possible and impossible is likewise so.
This power of knowledge is truly pervasive throughout the world, As he extensively expounds the supreme, true Dharma."
If a person possesses the vessel of liberation, one knows their conduct and speaks the Dharma for them;
for those sentient beings who are complete vessels of the Dharma, one knows what is possible and impossible and dwells in the practice of equanimity.
The void and the great earth may yet be moved, But the Buddha’s teaching on karmic retribution is never false.
When the knowledge of what is possible and impossible is perfected, One possesses the ten powers of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
“Śāriputra! This is the first power of knowledge of the Tathāgata.

Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha possesses such supreme power of knowledge, he understands the superior states; amidst the great assembly, he can roar the lion’s roar and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel, such that in the world there is no one whose Dharma is equal to that of the Tathāgata.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma?

It means that the Buddha-Tathāgata, by means of unsurpassed wisdom, regarding all sentient beings of the past, future, and present, knows as they truly are the causal bases and stages of the various karmas they have performed—whether it be the causal basis of the body-faculty extending through the stage of the eye-faculty, or the causal bases and stages of such faculties as these; the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are."

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty-nature for generosity yet practice the conduct of ethical discipline, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both themselves and others, proclaims for them the Dharma of generosity.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty of ethical discipline and cultivate the practice of giving, the Tathāgata, because he fully knows the faculties of both himself and others, immediately proclaims for them the Dharma of ethical discipline.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty-nature of patience yet practice the path of diligence, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both self and others, teaches them the Dharma of patience.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty of diligence yet cultivate the practice of patience, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both themselves and others, proclaims for them the Dharma of diligence.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty of meditative concentration and cultivate the practice of superior wisdom, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both himself and others, accordingly proclaims the Dharma of meditative concentration for them.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty of superior wisdom and practice the cultivation of meditative concentration, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both themselves and others, proclaims for them the Dharma of superior wisdom.
In brief, this applies even to all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

If sentient beings possess the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) of a śrāvaka yet practice the vehicle of a pratyekabuddha, the Tathāgata, knowing the capacities of both himself and others, teaches them the Dharma of the śrāvaka vehicle.

If there are sentient beings who possess the spiritual capacity of a pratyekabuddha yet practice the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both himself and others, proclaims for them the Dharma of the pratyekabuddha vehicle.

If there are sentient beings who possess the root-nature of the Mahāyāna yet practice the paths of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both himself and others, shall proclaim the Dharma of the Mahāyāna for them.
If there are sentient beings who possess the faculties of the Supreme Vehicle and cultivate Mahāyāna practices, the Tathāgata knows them truly and knows them as they are.

If there are sentient beings who accumulate causes for happiness in the present life but experience the retribution of suffering in future lives, the Tathāgata knows this with certainty and according to reality.

If sentient beings accumulate the causes of suffering in the present life and experience their bitter retribution in future lives, the Tathāgata knows them with certainty and in accordance with reality.

If sentient beings accumulate the causes of happiness in the present life and thereby experience the retribution of happiness in future lives, the Tathāgata knows this with certainty and in accordance with reality.

Śāriputra! Regarding all sentient beings throughout the past, future, and present, the Tathāgata truly knows, without error or distinction, every one of their karmic actions—both causes and effects—exactly as they are, with absolute certainty.
Having understood according to what is known, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma to all beings as is appropriate for them.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata,

the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, knows, exactly as it is, the karmic fruits and retributions of all sentient beings in the past, future, and present, as well as the causes and bases for their accumulation.
The power of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is without limit; if one wished to know its limit, could it be known, for example, as that of space?
Since the limit of space cannot be known, so too is the limit of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha’s power of wisdom regarding the maturation of karma.

When bodhisattvas established in faith hear of the Tathāgata’s inconceivable power of knowledge regarding the retribution of karma, they give rise to pure faith; they transcend conceptual discrimination and depart from all doubt and perplexity. Subsequently, they further experience signs of physical and mental joy and gladness, conceiving a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The Buddha thoroughly understands all causes and effects; With the eye of wisdom regarding the dharma of karma, he can perceive them all.
His unimpeded wisdom pervades the three periods of time; He clearly comprehends the conduct of all sentient beings.”
The causes of suffering and pleasure, as well as all aspirations, throughout the five realms of existence for all sentient beings—
the causes of all the various sufferings of saṃsāra— the Sugata understands them all with certainty and perfect clarity.
All karmic retributions of black and white deeds, as well as their causes, effects, aspirations, and requests—
the Benevolent One truly and completely knows them all, as if beholding a wish-fulfilling gem in the palm of his hand.
If the causes cultivated for various karmic dharmas are slight, yet the future retribution obtained is immeasurable;
or if the causes are immeasurable, yet the fruit is still minute—the Sugata truly understands all such realities.
The fruits of practicing the conduct of the śrāvakas are as he wishes; the causes for the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddhas are likewise as he wishes;
and the fruit of unsurpassed wisdom is also thus as he wishes—the Sugata understands all these exactly as they truly are.
If one cultivates the causes of suffering through prior karma, one will later reap the fruit of happiness;
if one cultivates the causes of happiness through various karmas, one will later reap the fruit of suffering.
Such is the nature of the law regarding the cause and fruit of suffering; it is likewise for the cause and fruit of happiness.
The convergence of one’s own karma and its fruits— the Sugata understands them all as they truly are.
All phenomena of suffering that evolve through the three times, pervading all sentient beings within the five destinies—
truly without interruption and without alternative modes— the Buddha’s unsurpassed wisdom clearly comprehends them all.
“Śāriputra! This is the second power of knowledge of the Tathāgata.

Because the Tathāgata is endowed with this supreme power of knowledge, he thoroughly understands the superior states; amidst the great assembly, he can roar the lion’s roar and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel, which no one in the world—whether devas, humans, Māras, or Brahmās—can ever turn, and there is none who can equal the Tathāgata in his Dharma.”
"In the *Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha, Volume Ten: All karmic fruits and retributions are known exactly as they are.
How are they thoroughly understood? Śāriputra!"

It means that the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, regarding the roots of goodness accumulated through the past karma of all sentient beings and their departure from all unwholesome states, know exactly and in accordance with reality how they will receive those wholesome fruits in future lives.

If sentient beings commit unwholesome deeds, accumulate unwholesome causes, and distance themselves from wholesome dharmas, thereby obtaining unwholesome fruits in future lives, the Tathāgata knows each and every instance as it truly is.
If sentient beings accumulate karmic causes that result in an inferior state in future lives, the Tathāgata knows them with certainty and in accordance with reality.

If sentient beings accumulate karmic causes that result in a superior state in the present life and likewise result in a superior state in future lives, the Tathāgata knows them with certainty and in accordance with reality.

If sentient beings accumulate karmic causes by engaging in inferior conduct in past lives but engage in vast conduct in future lives, the Tathāgata knows this definitively and in accordance with reality.

If sentient beings accumulate karmic causes that initiate even a small portion [of an action], yet are destined to experience a vast and sublime state of existence, the Tathāgata knows this with certainty and in accordance with reality.

If sentient beings accumulate karmic causes and give rise to them on a vast scale, yet are destined to experience only a small portion of superior states, the Tathāgata knows this with certainty and in accordance with reality.
If sentient beings cultivate the practices of śrāvakas and attain the fruit of śrāvaka, the Tathāgata knows them definitively and in accordance with reality.
If sentient beings cultivate the practices of pratyekabuddhas and attain the fruit of pratyekabuddha, the Tathāgata knows them definitively and in accordance with reality.
If sentient beings cultivate the causes for the Buddha’s wisdom and thereby bring about the fruit of that Buddha-wisdom, the Tathāgata knows this with certainty and in accordance with reality.
If sentient beings accumulate the causes of suffering in the present life and yet experience the retribution of happiness in future lives, the Tathāgata knows this with certainty.
[From the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-bodhisattvapiṭaka-saddharma-sūtra*, Scroll 5]
The Fifth Part of Chapter Four: The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Great Tang Dynasty, the Dharma Teacher of Light and Brahma, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Weijing, and others, by imperial decree. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
What is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various inclinations and understandings?

It means that the Buddha-Tathāgata, regarding all the various differences in the inclinations and understandings possessed by all sentient beings and all individuals (*pudgala*), knows each one exactly as it is.
If sentient beings fundamentally abide in craving and give rise to understanding through aversion— as extensively explained in the sūtras—
and if sentient beings fundamentally abide in attachment to delusion and give rise to understanding through aversion, the Tathāgata knows each and every such case as it truly is.
If sentient beings fundamentally abide in unwholesome dharmas and give rise to understanding toward unwholesome dharmas, the Tathāgata knows each and every one of them as it truly is.
If sentient beings fundamentally abide in wholesome dharmas and give rise to understanding toward wholesome dharmas, the Tathāgata knows each and every one of them as it truly is.
If there are sentient beings who practice inferior conduct yet give rise to faith and understanding toward sublime teachings, the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are.
If there are sentient beings who practice sublime conduct yet give rise to faith and understanding toward inferior teachings, the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are.
If sentient beings practice inferior conduct yet give rise to faith and understanding toward a superior state, the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are.
If sentient beings practice superior conduct yet give rise to an inferior understanding, the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are.
If sentient beings give rise to faith and understanding toward the group of those fixed in error and grasp the dharmas of that fixed state, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If sentient beings give rise to faith and understanding toward the group of those fixed in correctness and grasp the dharmas of that fixed state, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If there are sentient beings who attain liberation within the group of those destined for correctness (samyaktva-niyāma), the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If there are sentient beings who have faith and understanding in the dharmas of the desire realm and enter from the desire realm, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If there are sentient beings who believe in and understand the dharmas of the form realm and enter from the form realm, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If there are sentient beings who believe in and understand the dharmas of the formless realm and enter from the formless realm, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If sentient beings believe in and understand the fixed laws of the three realms and enter them throughout the three realms, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If sentient beings originally abide in an inferior state yet attain a sublime dharma, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If sentient beings, while abiding in a superior state, should obtain inferior dharmas, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If sentient beings give rise to various inclinations, various physical forms, various enjoyments, and various experiences, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If there are sentient beings who, through their past karma, are destined to experience a fall, the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are.
If there are sentient beings who, through their faith and understanding, take up the dharma of liberation and attain that liberation, the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are.
Having thus known it as it truly is, the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma accordingly to each being.
"Śāriputra, this is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the inclinations and convictions of beings; it is without limit, equal to space."

If bodhisattvas established in faith, having heard of the Tathāgata’s various supreme powers of knowledge regarding diverse inclinations, develop pure faith, transcend conceptual discrimination, and become free from all doubt; thereafter, they further experience physical and mental joy, signs of delight, and give rise to the thought of their rarity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The various modes of faith and understanding in the world, Throughout the past, future, and present, are limitless;
Just as those understandings correspond to their thoughts, The Buddha, the Honored One among Men, fully comprehends them all."
If one gives rise to faith and understanding toward phenomena of desire, yet fundamentally remains attached to the state of aversion—
and the same applies to the meanings of aversion or delusion— the Buddha clearly understands all according to their faith and understanding.
The various phenomena such as abiding in greed and abiding in delusion, which are sustained by the mind and are difficult to fathom,
continue without interruption throughout all conduct— all these the Supreme Sage’s victorious wisdom clearly understands.
If sentient beings of inferior conduct Return to faith and resolve in the vast Dharma,
Or if their practice is superior while their resolve is inferior— The Buddha, the Honored Subduer, clearly understands them all.
If sentient beings take up the category of those fixed in error, the manner in which they arise and return is likewise so;
regarding all the gates of liberation within the three realms, the Buddha clearly understands them according to their respective inclinations and understandings.
The various and diverse physical forms that arise, and likewise the differences in their enjoyments,
are all clearly understood by the Supreme Honored One among bipeds, for their retributions do not differ according to prior karma.
Having understood them according to their faith and comprehension, he teaches the Dharma as is appropriate for each;
this is the third door of the power of knowledge regarding inclinations—O Son of the Buddha, you should give rise to pure faith.
“Śāriputra! Such is the Tathāgata’s third power of knowledge regarding the conviction of others’ inclinations (*adhimukti-jñāna-bala*).

Because the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is endowed with this supreme power of knowledge, he understands the superior states; amidst the great assembly, he can roar the lion’s roar and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel, which no one in the entire world—whether devas, humans, Māras, or Brahmās—can ever turn. There is none who shares the same Dharma as the Tathāgata.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various elements?
It refers to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, knowing the various elements as they truly are."
If there are sentient beings who, within the various worlds, are nurtured by various meritorious actions, the Tathāgata is able to know them all as they truly are.
If there are sentient beings who are nurtured by non-meritorious actions, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If sentient beings nurture themselves through immovable conduct, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
If sentient beings cultivate the conduct of renunciation, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element.
How does he know them?
This means that the Buddha, having realized internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness,
knows everything up to the mind-element, the phenomena-element, and the mind-consciousness-element exactly as they truly are.
How is this known?
It is because the Buddha thoroughly understands internal emptiness, external emptiness, and internal-external emptiness.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
The Tathāgata thoroughly understands the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, and the space element, knowing them all exactly as they are.
How is he able to know them?

That is to say, because it is like space, one likewise understands it as such. The Tathāgata fully knows that the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm arise from conceptual differentiation; he knows the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*) as having the characteristic of being produced through volitional effort; he knows the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*) as having the characteristic of being without volitional effort; he knows the defiled realm (*saṃkleśadhātu*) as having the characteristic of adventitious afflictions; he knows the pure realm (*viśuddhidhātu*) as having the characteristic of natural luminosity; he knows the realm of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāradhātu*) as having the characteristic of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and ignorance; and he knows the realm of nirvāṇa as having the characteristic of wisdom arising from proper mental attention (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Whether it be the reliance upon the various elements (*dhātu*), the dwelling within the various elements, the conformity to the various elements, the establishment of the various elements, the functioning of the various elements, the intentionality of the various elements, the tranquility of the various elements, or the attachment to the various elements—the Tathāgata knows each of these exactly as they truly are. Having known them accordingly, he then teaches the Dharma."
Śāriputra! This is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*); such supreme power is without limit.

If bodhisattvas who abide in faith, having heard of the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge in this way, develop pure faith, transcend conceptual discrimination, and become free from all doubt, they will subsequently experience physical and mental joy, a sense of well-being and delight, and give rise to the thought of its rarity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"All sentient beings in all worlds Take various realms as their basis;
The manner in which they follow and turn according to those realms is likewise understood By the Buddha, the Unsurpassed Honored One."
Wholesome, unwholesome, and imperturbable formations, as well as the meaning of all realms of transcendence—
according to the various realms and destinies in which the mind abides, nirvana remains unmoving and eternally quiescent.
All the realms of the eye and the realm of forms, and likewise the realm of visual consciousness,
as well as within the realms of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind— the Tathāgata understands them all exactly as they truly are.
Having fully understood that realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), the realm of mental consciousness is likewise so;
understanding all phenomena to be empty internally and externally—this is the Great Sage’s power of wisdom.
The earth element, the water element, and the fire element, and likewise the wind element as well—
when these elements are fully understood, they are seen to be no different from space itself.
All that exists in the realm of desire and the realm of form, and likewise in the formless realm—
the Tathāgata fully knows all these, as well as those things arising from conceptual discrimination.
And that space is without limit; likewise, all realms are boundless.
Although the Buddha has universal knowledge of all things, he does not give rise to a sense of self, yet is able to understand them.
Knowing that all elements are without arising, And knowing that all elements are without cessation—
Such a mind, tranquil regarding all elements, The Unsurpassed Hero fully comprehends.
Just as space is without limit, so too is the Buddha’s wisdom boundless;
through unimpeded wisdom he fully understands all various inclinations and liberates them all.
Having known the faith and understanding that arise in the mind, and having fully tamed billions of sentient beings, the Tathāgata has perfected the fourth power;
O Son of the Buddha, you should give rise to pure faith.
“Śāriputra! Such is the Tathāgata’s fourth power of knowledge, explained at length until: ‘There is no one who shares the same qualities as the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
What is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties?
It refers to the fact that the Tathāgata knows, one by one and in accordance with reality, all the various faculties of sentient beings, whether they be superior or inferior.
How does he know this?

It is said that he knows the dull faculties, the middling faculties, and the sharp faculties; furthermore, he thoroughly knows all superior faculties, even down to the nature of the faculties from which various karmas arise—whether arising from greed, arising from hatred, or arising from delusion—and the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are.
He knows, exactly as they are, all such discriminations of various karmas arising from the false imaginings of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Likewise, he knows, exactly as they are, all such discriminations of the faculties arising even in slight measure from greed, hatred, and delusion; the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are.
He also knows as it truly is that the various faculties arise from the vast proliferation of greed, hatred, and delusion;
he also knows as it truly is that the various faculties arise from the grasping of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Whether they are the nature of roots that are wholesome causes, unwholesome causes, immovable causes, or causes of renunciation, the Tathāgata knows them all as they truly are.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra! The Tathāgata thoroughly knows the eye-faculty, ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, body-faculty, and mind-faculty of all sentient beings; the female faculty, male faculty, and life-faculty; the faculty of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity; the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; and the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,' the faculty of 'knowing,' and the faculty of 'one who has known. Regarding these twenty-two faculties, the Tathāgata knows them all exactly as they are."

Furthermore, among the sense faculties, if the faculty of the eye serves as the cause for the state of the faculty of the ear, but not for the faculties of the nose, tongue, or body, the Tathāgata knows this all exactly as it is.

If the cause of the ear faculty extends to the state of the nose faculty, if the cause of the nose faculty extends to the state of the tongue faculty, if the cause of the tongue faculty extends to the state of the body faculty, or if the cause of the body faculty extends to the state of the eye faculty—the Tathāgata knows all such causes and states of the faculties exactly as they truly are.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty for generosity yet practice the conduct of ethical discipline, the Tathāgata, because he fully knows the faculties of both himself and others, proclaims for them the Dharma of generosity.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty for upholding the precepts and cultivate the practice of giving, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both self and others, accordingly proclaims the Dharma of upholding the precepts.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty-nature of patience yet practice the path of diligence, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both self and others, accordingly proclaims for them the Dharma of patience.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty of diligence and cultivate the practice of patience, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both himself and others, proclaims for them the Dharma of diligence.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty of meditative concentration and cultivate the practice of supreme wisdom, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both himself and others, then proclaims for them the Dharma of meditative concentration.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty of superior wisdom and cultivate the practice of meditative concentration, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both himself and others, proclaims for them the Dharma of superior wisdom.
In brief, this is likewise said even regarding all the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).

If there are sentient beings who possess the spiritual capacity (*indriya*) of a śrāvaka yet practice the vehicle of a pratyekabuddha, the Tathāgata, knowing the capacities of both self and others, then proclaims the Dharma of the śrāvaka vehicle for them.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculty-nature of a pratyekabuddha yet practice the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both himself and others, shall proclaim for them the dharma of the pratyekabuddha vehicle.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculties and nature of the Mahāyāna yet practice the paths of the Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha vehicles, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both himself and others, shall preach the Dharma of the Mahāyāna for them.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculties and nature of the Supreme Vehicle and cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna, the Tathāgata, knowing the faculties of both himself and others, proclaims for them the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle.

If there are sentient beings who possess the faculties of being unfit vessels for the Dharma—incapable of receiving it—the Tathāgata, having fully understood that they are incapable and not fit vessels, shall simply set them aside.
If there are sentient beings who possess the capacity and are fit vessels for the Dharma, the Tathāgata shall proclaim the True Dharma for them.
Śāriputra, among all sentient beings, the Tathāgata fully knows them whether he observes their faculties or does not observe their faculties.
If there are faculties that lead to transcendence, he fully knows them; if there are faculties that do not lead to transcendence, he also fully knows them.

According to whatever faculty-nature sentient beings possess—whether it be their modes of conduct, their underlying dispositions, their conditions, their obstacles, their ultimate destination, or their final faculties—the Tathāgata knows each and every one of them exactly as they are.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Knowing the dispositions of the faculties of those who head toward the other shore, Knowing the natures and inclinations of sentient beings,
Thoroughly understanding all the faculties of the world, The Lion among Men proclaims the True Dharma."
Universally observing the capacities of those with inferior, middling, and superior faculties, his peerless wisdom turns everywhere;
knowing which sentient beings are vessels for liberation, he proclaims the sublime Dharma through wisdom so that they may be enlightened.
Having definitively understood the origins of all afflictions, and having thoroughly comprehended the various faculties of sentient beings— whether they be few or many—
he teaches the Dharma of wisdom and practice in accordance with those faculties.
Whether sentient beings possess roots of goodness, or possess various unwholesome roots—the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
the natures of the faculties of suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity;
the faculties of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; and likewise the faculties of female, male, and life—[the Tathāgata knows them all].
Just as he has proclaimed that faculty of faith, so too is the ultimate meaning of the remaining faculties.
Regarding the nature of the faculties, their spheres of activity, and their various characteristics, they function universally according to the inclinations of sentient beings.
He proclaims the sublime Dharma-gates in accordance with their faculties, his wisdom clearly and perfectly understanding all phenomena of suffering.
The faculties of the śrāvakas are difficult to liberate; only the Buddha’s bodhi brings about true transcendence.
Since śrāvakas do not know the cause of the Buddha’s wisdom, [the Buddha] speaks of the most supreme power of bodhi for their sake.
“Śāriputra! This is the fifth power of knowledge of the Tathāgata; it is explained at length until: ‘There is no one who shares the same qualities as the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
What is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the path leading to all destinations?
It refers to the Buddha, the Tathāgata, knowing as they truly are all paths leading to every destination throughout all places.
How is this known?

One knows each and every one of them: those sentient beings who abide in the group of those fixed in the right, those who abide in the group of those not yet fixed, and those who abide in the group of those fixed in the wrong.

If there are beings dwelling within the realm of those established in the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), who possess the power of causes and their prior practices, and are fully endowed with clarified and sharp faculties— the Tathāgata,
knowing that they are capable and are vessels for liberation, teaches the Dharma to them according to the power of their past causes.

If one abides within the realm of sentient beings in the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*), because their characteristics are matured through the power of those conditions, they attain liberation upon receiving the appropriate teaching and instruction according to their needs.

If the power of their conditions has not yet matured, they do not attain liberation; the Tathāgata awaits the convergence of their causes and conditions, and as soon as they encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world, he preaches the Dharma for them.
Having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, they practice with profound and firm diligence, thereby attaining the supreme fruit.

If there are beings dwelling in the realm of those fixed in false determination, who do not cultivate right action, whose faculties and natures are dull and obscured, and who are not fit vessels for the truth, the Tathāgata does not preach the Dharma for them.
Because they lack the capacity to bear [the burden] and are not vessels for liberation, the Tathāgata, having known this, shall discard them.
For this reason, all bodhisattvas should diligently practice and don the armor of vigor.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands three kinds of bases for attachment: namely, there is a basis for attachment arising from signs of excellence; furthermore, there is a basis for attachment arising from signs of extremes; and furthermore, there is a basis for attachment arising from prior causes.

The Tathāgata thoroughly understands three types of bases for hatred: namely, there is a basis for hatred arising from the characteristic of affliction and harm; furthermore, there is a basis for hatred arising from the dissatisfaction of craving; and furthermore, there is a basis for hatred arising from past habitual tendencies.

The Tathāgata thoroughly understands three kinds of bases for delusion: namely, there is a basis for delusion arising from the cause of ignorance; furthermore, there is a basis for delusion arising from the cause of the view of a self-identity; and furthermore, there is a basis for delusion arising from the cause of doubt.
The Tathāgata knows each and every one of these as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the Tathāgata is able to know all places of suffering through his swift supernormal powers, because of his sharp faculties.
Alternatively, in states of suffering, the Tathāgata is able to comprehend through slow supernormal power because his faculties are dull;
furthermore, in states of happiness, he is able to comprehend through swift supernormal power because his faculties are sharp.
Alternatively, regarding a state of ease, one is able to comprehend it through slow supernormal power because of having supple faculties;
furthermore, regarding a state of slowness, one is able to comprehend it through slow supernormal power because of the obstruction of the path.
In regard to that which is slow, one is able to comprehend it through swift supernormal power (*abhijñā*) in order to attain pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
In regard to that which is swift, one is able to comprehend it through slow supernormal power because there is no ultimate tranquility (*atyanta-śānti*).
Regarding the state of swiftness, the Tathāgata understands it through swift supernormal power because there is no distinction between them.

Furthermore, there are cases where one attains the perfection of the power of discernment but not the power of cultivation; cases where one attains the perfection of the power of cultivation but not the power of discernment; cases where both the power of cultivation and the power of discernment are fully perfected; and cases where neither the power of cultivation nor the power of discernment is perfected—the Tathāgata knows each of these exactly as they are.

Furthermore, there are those who possess the aspiration but lack the practice; those who possess the practice but lack the aspiration; those who possess both the aspiration and the practice; and those who lack both the aspiration and the practice—the Tathāgata knows each of these exactly as they truly are.
Furthermore, there are instances where bodily action is pure while speech and mind are not;
there are instances where mental action is pure while body and speech are not;
and there are instances where bodily, verbal, and mental actions are all impure.
Furthermore, there are instances where the activities of body, speech, and mind are entirely pure;
the Tathāgata knows each of these exactly as they truly are. “Śāriputra!

Regarding all sentient beings in all places, whether their karmic actions as causes are active or quiescent, the Tathāgata, by means of unimpeded wisdom, accords with and turns along with those beings.
Śāriputra! Thus, this Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the path leading to all destinations is without limit, equal to space.

When bodhisattvas established in faith hear this, they develop pure faith; they transcend conceptual discrimination, leave behind all doubt and uncertainty, and subsequently experience physical and mental joy, a sense of rapture, and give rise to the thought of its rarity.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Eleven.
6. The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Twelve.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Court, the Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, the Great Dharma Master of Light and Sanskrit, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Weijing and others, by imperial decree.
Chapter Four: The Inconceivable Qualities of the Tathāgata, Part Six. At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha thoroughly understands the power of the knowledge of the destination; He knows the causes for those who are in the stage of right determination."
As well as those sentient beings of the indeterminate group—the signs of their maturation are all clearly understood by him.
The Buddha thoroughly understands the three bases of greed; likewise for the three types of hatred and delusion.
Regarding the various gateways of these three afflictions, the Buddha fully knows the conditions and causes thereof.
He fully understands those of sharp faculties in states of suffering, and those of dull faculties with sluggish supernormal powers;
likewise, he fully understands those of sharp faculties in states of pleasure, as well as those characterized by sluggishness. The Buddha knows them all completely.
There is sluggishness where there is sluggish power, or a sharp faculty where there is sluggishness, or a sluggish faculty where there is swiftness;
yet in swift supernormal powers, there is no difference in their characteristics.
Some possess the power of discernment but lack the power of cultivation; some possess the power of cultivation but lack discernment;
some possess both powers in full perfection; and some lack both yet are nonetheless clearly realized.
In some cases, the intention may be complete while the practice is not;
through both the dual presence and the dual absence of these two factors, the Buddha perceives all things with universal clarity.
In some cases, bodily action attains purity, while speech and mind do not;
likewise, there are times when speech and body are pure, yet the mind is not—such is the meaning.
Some may have purity in the mental karma, while the same principle applies to what is neither verbal nor physical;
or again, when both speech and mind are pure, the principle for what is not physical is likewise.
The Buddha’s physical, verbal, and mental actions are all pure; he observes them all and knows them completely.
According to the gates of tranquility thus accomplished, this is the sixth supreme power of knowledge of a Buddha.

“Śāriputra! This is the Tathāgata’s sixth power of knowledge—the knowledge of the paths leading to various destinations. Because the Tathāgata is endowed with this supreme power of knowledge, he thoroughly understands these superior destinations; indeed, there is no one in the world whose Dharma is equal to that of the Tathāgata.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge arising from the defilement and purification of dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, and samāpatti? It means that the Buddha, the Tathāgata,
knows as they truly are all the dharmas of dhyāna, vimokṣa, samādhi, samāpatti, defilement, and purification belonging to both himself and others."
How is it known?
One knows, exactly as they are, all the various defiled phenomena of all sentient beings, whether their causes or their conditions;
and one likewise knows, exactly as they are, all the purified phenomena of those sentient beings, whether their causes or their conditions.
What is the cause? What is the condition?
It is said that among all the various defilements of sentient beings, improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is the cause, and [ignorance (*avidyā*) is] the condition.
Consciousness is the condition; ignorance is the cause and volitional formations are the condition; volitional formations are the cause and consciousness is the condition;
consciousness is the cause and name-and-form is the condition; name-and-form is the cause and the six sense bases are the condition;
the six sense bases are the cause and contact is the condition; contact is the cause and feeling is the condition; feeling is the cause... [and so on].
With craving as condition, craving as cause; with grasping as condition, grasping as cause;
with existence as condition, existence as cause; with birth as condition, birth as cause; with objects of perception as condition, afflictions as cause;
with karma as condition, views as cause; with latent tendencies as cause, craving as condition.
With that which has arisen as a condition, for all the various bases of defilement of sentient beings— such causes and such conditions—
the Tathāgata knows each and every one of them exactly as they are.

Furthermore, regarding the causes and conditions: for all sentient beings, there are two causes and two conditions within the pure dharma. If sentient beings hear the speech and sounds of others that are in accordance with the truth, they are able to each form deep and firm mental attention (*manasikāra*), skillfully cultivate meditative visualization (*samādhi*), and dwell well in one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*).
Furthermore, regarding the two causes and two conditions: they refer to the wisdom already arisen and the wisdom not yet arisen.
Furthermore, regarding the two causes and two conditions: they refer to the investigative contemplation of arising phenomena without realizing nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, as for the two causes and two conditions: they are the fulfillment of knowledge and conduct to realize and attain liberation.
Furthermore, as for the two causes and two conditions: they are the cultivation of the gates of liberation and the wisdom of intrinsic liberation.
Furthermore, as for the two causes and two conditions, they refer to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Furthermore, as for the two causes and two conditions, they refer to the true awakening to reality and that which is attained through reality.
In this way, regarding all sentient beings within the pure Dharma, the Tathāgata knows each and every one of their causes and conditions exactly as they truly are.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

All sentient beings have various objects of focus for purification and objects of focus for defilement. There are those who take up objects of focus for purification because they investigate them as they truly are;
there are those who take up objects of focus for defilement because they investigate them as they truly are.
There are those who, amidst objects of perception characterized by affliction (*saṃkleśa*), grasp at objects of perception characterized by purity, because they investigate according to reality;
and there are those who, amidst objects of perception characterized by purity, grasp at objects of perception characterized by affliction, because of the grasping of overweening pride (*abhimāna*).

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s supreme wisdom is vast and boundless, capable of revolving universally through its thorough and accurate knowledge. That is to say, he enters the gate of the first dhyāna-concentration, which is free from sinful karma and discursive thought, characterized by the joy and bliss born of seclusion; he proceeds from the first dhyāna-concentration up to arising from the cessation of perception and feeling, and even from the cessation of perception and feeling back to arising from the first dhyāna-concentration.
The eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa) refer to entering in forward order, entering in reverse order, and entering in both forward and reverse order.

What are the eight? First, the liberation of one possessing form who perceives forms; second, the liberation of one with internal non-perception of form who perceives external forms; third, the liberation of the pure, which is personally realized and dwelt in fully; fourth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space; fifth, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness; sixth, the liberation of the sphere of nothingness; seventh, the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; eighth, the liberation of the cessation of feeling and perception.

Regarding these eight liberations, whether practiced in direct or reverse order, one is able to visualize them through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), and the vow (*samaya*).
However, the Buddha-Tathāgata, within samādhi, is entirely without conceptual discrimination, nor does he have any objective referent (*ālambana*) or any state of entry therein.
The Tathāgata enters all doors of samādhi within a single samādhi; when he arises from one concentration, it is the same for all concentrations.
Within the mind of meditative equipoise, the Tathāgata has no continuous succession, no mind that apprehends anything, and no mind that observes.
All the samādhis of the pratyekabuddhas surpass those of the śrāvakas;
the samādhis of the bodhisattvas surpass those of the pratyekabuddhas;
and the samādhis of the Buddhas surpass those of the bodhisattvas.
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s supreme, transcendent wisdom pervades all things.
If anyone gives rise to the mind of a śrāvaka, the Tathāgata fully knows all their speech and the teachings he provides for them.

If one generates the mind of a pratyekabuddha, or if one generates the mind of a bodhisattva, he likewise knows it as it truly is, and accordingly teaches the Dharma and provides instruction. Śāriputra!

This is the Tathāgata’s seventh power of knowledge arising from the defiled and pure states of meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi, and attainment; it is boundless, limitless, and equal to space.

When bodhisattvas abiding in faith hear this, they develop pure faith; they transcend conceptual discrimination and leave behind all doubt and uncertainty. Thereafter, they further give rise to physical and mental joy, a sense of well-being and delight, and conceive a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“The various defiled natures of all sentient beings, And the causes for the purification of all sentient beings— The Great Fearless Honored One fully understands them all;
Having understood them, he teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate.”
As for the causes of all afflictions, they arise from the condition of ignorance;
with ignorance as the cause and volitional formations as the condition, and so on until the link of existence gives rise to all forms of suffering.
The root of all afflictions arises from improper mental attention;
from these causes and conditions, the links of existence are produced. Because the Buddha thoroughly understands this, he has provided this elucidation.
The root of all karma is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), with ignorance (*avidyā*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) as its conditions;
thus, the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) leading to suffering arise, and all phenomena originate following the sounds of others.
Contemplating with profound and firm attention, one clearly discerns the two causes and the two conditions;
sentient beings thus realize the cause as it truly is, and by means of that cause, they are able to attain tranquil stillness.
If sentient beings seek the cause of liberation, they should skillfully contemplate all conditioned phenomena;
the Noble Subduer fully understands this, and thus remains deeply and firmly established in pure ethical discipline.
One should carefully and truthfully contemplate the dharma of emptiness, Skillfully practicing the gateways to liberation;
Released from the suffering and hardships of the three realms of existence, One attains true, pure, and thorough awakening.
Sentient beings believe in the Buddha’s pure Dharma— the gates of liberation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
and you skillfully proclaim the *samāpattis*, as well as the meditative concentrations of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Sentient beings are fully possessed of all afflictions; The Buddha taught the gates of meditative concentration and liberation.
Having perfected the seventh power free from defilement, The Buddha skillfully taught how to tame those who are difficult to tame.

“Śāriputra! Such is the Tathāgata’s seventh power of knowledge. Because the Tathāgata is endowed with this supreme power of knowledge, he thoroughly understands the superior states, such that there is no one who shares his Dharma.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
what is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting in the recollection of past lives?
It means that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, by means of unsurpassed wisdom, recollects and fully knows the numerous and manifold past lives of both himself and others."

Whether it be one birth, two births, three, four, or five births; ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or fifty; a hundred births, a thousand births, or even a hundred thousand births; up to and including countless koṭis, nayutas, and hundreds of thousands of births—he knows all such matters through recollection.

Whether it be during the eon of formation, the eon of destruction, or the eon of both formation and destruction—even throughout countless eons of formation and destruction—regarding all sentient beings who existed in the past in such-and-such a direction and such-and-such a place: their names, their clans, their lineages, their appearances, their complexions, their physical forms, their lifespans, their durations of stay, their experiences of suffering, and their experiences of pleasure; where they passed away and where they were reborn; and having passed away in one place, being reborn in another; whether these matters were manifest or unmanifest, pertaining to themselves or others—there are countless and manifold such instances of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).

If sentient beings possess such causes, and from whatever origins they have come by virtue of those causes, the Tathāgata knows each and every one of them as it truly is; having known them, he teaches the essential points of the Dharma for their sake.

The Tathāgata is able to sustain and fully know all the past mental activities of all sentient beings—whether it be the continuity of the mind, the objects of the mind, or the arising of the mind—and within those objects, the mind remains unimpaired and undestroyed.
Śāriputra! Because the Tathāgata knows the mental continuum of a single sentient being, he understands, in accordance with reality, the very nature of whatever mind continues in succession.
From the arising of a single thought, even if one were to speak for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, one could not exhaustively describe it.

Therefore, you should know that the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, fully understand the mental activities of all sentient beings; they are boundless, and even if one were to speak for ten million eons, one could not exhaustively describe them.
The unsurpassed, supreme wisdom of the Tathāgata is likewise without limit. Śāriputra,
such power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge in realizing the recollection of past lives is inconceivable, peerless, immeasurable, incalculable, and beyond description.
Regarding all sentient beings throughout the boundless reaches of existence, the Tathāgata is able to know them through recollection by means of his supernormal powers and wisdom.

Whatever roots of goodness sentient beings may plant as they arise—whether in the Buddha Vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle, the Śrāvaka Vehicle, or any other wholesome dharmas—the Tathāgata knows them all through recollection.

By means of great majestic power, the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to the objects of the roots of goodness of all sentient beings, causing those beings not to regress from the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, so that they may all attain liberation according to their faith and understanding—whether they have resolved upon the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, or the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Śāriputra! This is the Tathāgata’s eighth power of knowledge—the realization through the recollection of past abodes—which is boundless and equal to space.
When bodhisattvas established in faith hear this, they develop pure faith, transcend conceptual discrimination, and become free from all doubt, even giving rise to the thought of its rarity.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
“For a hundred koṭis of kalpas without end, The Buddha, the Lamp of the World, illuminates past lives;
He fully knows the five types of minds—his own and others’— As clearly as looking at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand.”
The lifespan, the number of eons, and physical appearance, as well as the causes for the birth and death of sentient beings—
all these, including the boundless and limitless past, are fully known by those who possess the vessel of the Dharma.
The mental states and mental factors of sentient beings in the world, arising in continuous succession without interruption—
the Noble One, with his great wisdom, fully knows all these past mental phenomena, infinite in number.
Once the Buddha has known the mind of a single sentient being, it is likewise for as many as the sands of the Ganges;
throughout the three realms of existence, limitless and boundless, it remains inexhaustible even unto the end of time.
Thus, the wisdom of his conduct is inexhaustible, Innumerable and likewise without limit;
The ocean of the World-Honored One’s wisdom is vast and boundless, Fully knowing the virtuous inclinations of all sentient beings.
Revered by the Muni, possessing immeasurable qualities, with supernatural powers and wisdom all vast and great,
he can recollect through his majestic spiritual power the causes of the wholesome dharmas cultivated in the past.
Thus, these immeasurable matters of great merit, Are well-considered through the three types of supernormal knowledge;
Abiding securely in the great mind of non-retrogression, One has already cultivated the supreme practices of the path to liberation.
The Sugata’s perfect wisdom is boundless; he knows the minds of all sentient beings.
The power of his eighth knowledge is vast and infinite; O Son of the Buddha, you should give rise to pure faith.

“Śāriputra! Such is the Tathāgata’s eighth power of knowledge. Because the Tathāgata is endowed with this supreme power of knowledge, he thoroughly understands the superior states; indeed, there is no one who possesses a dharma equal to that of the Tathāgata.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting in the realization through recollection of the divine eye?

It means that the Buddha, the Tathāgata, with his unsurpassed wisdom and the pure divine eye which surpasses the fleshly eye, beholds all sentient beings in the world—at the time of their birth and at the time of their death; whether they are noble or lowly; whether they possess auspicious or inauspicious marks; and whether they are heading toward a good rebirth or a bad rebirth. According to the ripening of the karmic retribution of each sentient being, the fruits they receive, the Tathāgata knows them all."

Furthermore, if sentient beings perform unwholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, reviling the noble ones and giving rise to false views, then because they have accumulated the causes of such false views, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the miserable realms among the hells, hungry ghosts, or the animal realm.

If sentient beings perform various virtuous deeds through their physical, verbal, and mental actions, do not revile the noble ones, and give rise to right view—because they have accumulated the causes of right view—they will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in the heavenly realms.

Furthermore, with his pure divine eye, the Tathāgata surveys all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions; they are as boundless as the realm of empty space and as immeasurable as the dharma-realm.
It is impossible to describe how the light of the Tathāgata’s wisdom illuminates and manifests all Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

One may see all great fires blazing fiercely; one may see all signs of formation and destruction; one may see sentient beings coming forth from within the light; one may see sentient beings at the moment of birth and at the moment of death; one may see Bodhisattvas appearing within the light; or one may see Bodhisattvas passing away from Tuṣita Heaven and descending to be born in the human world, entering the mother’s womb with divine power, and taking seven steps immediately after birth—one can perceive all such events as Bodhisattvas dwelling in the womb and entering the womb.

In some instances, they see the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appearing within their radiance; in others, they see Bodhisattvas attaining the fruit of perfect enlightenment; in others, they see the Buddhas turning the Great Wheel of Dharma; and in others, they see the Buddhas relinquishing the conditioned activities of their life-span and entering Great Parinirvāṇa.
In some instances, he saw the assembly of śrāvakas appearing within the light, and further saw the śrāvakas proceeding toward the realization of nirvāṇa.
In other instances, he saw the assembly of pratyekabuddhas appearing within the light, and further saw the pratyekabuddhas manifesting various supernatural powers to perform great purification.

There may be sentient beings who are unable to come by riding upon the Buddha’s light; these include the hosts of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and the hosts of seers possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijña*), who are not equal to the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, and for this reason cannot come by riding the light.
Nevertheless, by means of the light of the power of wisdom of the Buddha’s pure and supreme divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), they too all come riding upon the light.
Alternatively, the Tathāgata may manifest a vast radiance the size of a chariot wheel, and sentient beings may come riding upon that light.

In this manner, throughout the entire realm of sentient beings across the three thousand great thousandfold world systems—immeasurable and boundless—all devas and humans appear within the wisdom-light of the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

With the Tathāgata’s pure divine eye, he surveys all Buddha-fields and the realms of sentient beings. Regarding whichever sentient beings are to be transformed and delivered, as soon as he observes them and perceives those who may be delivered, the Buddha immediately manifests before them to transform and deliver them."
Once those sentient beings have been delivered, the remaining sentient beings likewise remain unaware of it.
Śāriputra, this is the Tathāgata’s ninth power of knowledge— the realization through the divine eye— which is without limit and equal to space.
"When bodhisattvas who abide in faith hear this, they will conceive pure faith, and so on, up to conceiving a sense of wonder.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Sugata’s divine eye is pure and stainless, The result of causes of wholesome karma accumulated over billions of eons."
The Buddha’s eye observes and illuminates throughout the ten directions; the Buddha-fields are vast and inconceivable.

Whether in the process of formation or destruction, all phenomena and their characteristics—be they masses of blazing, fiery garlands or many realms entirely empty—are all clearly illuminated by the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom.
The vast and inconceivable realms of sentient beings— whether in the form or formless realms,
or those fallen into the good or evil destinies— are all clearly illuminated by the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom.
The Buddhas of the present, numbering in the millions, as well as all the Noble Ones who have already entered nirvāṇa,
along with the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas— the Buddha’s self-arisen wisdom illuminates them all clearly.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, the Bodhisattva practices all the various deeds of enlightenment;
his awakened wisdom is clear and penetrating, without concealment, as the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom illuminates everything.
Thus the Sugata’s stainless eye can perceive even the most subtle aspects of sentient beings;
the power of his ninth eye of wisdom is inconceivable—sons of the Buddha, you should give rise to pure faith.

“Śāriputra! Such is the Tathāgata’s ninth power of knowledge. Because the Tathāgata is endowed with this supreme power of knowledge, he thoroughly understands the superior states; indeed, there is no one who possesses a dharma equal to that of the Tathāgata.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge consisting in the realization of the destruction of the outflows?

It means that by means of his unsurpassed power of knowledge, the Buddha-Tathāgata has exhausted all outflows such that no further outflows increase; his mind is well-liberated and his wisdom is well-liberated. Having realized his own direct penetration, he acts according to his practice, knowing: 'Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.'"

By means of this power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows, which is pure and luminous, the Tathāgata completely severs all seeds and habitual tendencies, such that he cannot be compared with any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha.
Those śrāvakas who have exhausted their outflows still possess limitations and have not severed their habitual tendencies.
Those pratyekabuddhas who have exhausted their outflows likewise possess limitations; they lack great compassion and are devoid of eloquence.

The Tathāgata, whose outflows are exhausted, is endowed with all the marks; he has completely severed all seeds and habitual tendencies, and through his great compassion, he embraces others with fearless eloquence and profound, skillful discernment—surpassed by none in all the worlds.
It abides in a state of mental unification, accomplished through perfect harmony. Why is this?

Because the Tathāgata is devoid of the seeds of karma and devoid of the seeds of affliction; and because he is free from transgression in his modes of conduct, he is like the empty sky—pure, limpid, and crystalline, which smoke, clouds, dust, and mist can never defile.
The Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*) is likewise; no seeds of any afflictions (*kleśa*) can defile it.

Abiding in such pure power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows, the Tathāgata has exhausted all outflows and proclaims the Dharma for the exhaustion of outflows, as well as teaching the Dharma for severing grasping and attachment, so that all sentient beings may understand that all false conceptualizations and objects of grasping do not arise, and universally cause sentient beings to investigate according to reality.

The Tathāgata, through skillful means, teaches the Dharma by means of parables, so that all sentient beings, having understood those unreal phenomena of the outflows as they truly are, shall not grasp at even the slightest phenomenon among all dharmas, and shall bring all grasping and attachment to complete cessation.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata thoroughly knows the accumulation of all outflows (āsrava) of all sentient beings, the dharma for the cessation of those outflows, and the path leading toward the cessation of those outflows.
Having known these as they truly are, the Tathāgata teaches the essentials of the Dharma to them according to what is appropriate for each.

Bodhisattvas who abide in faith, having heard of the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge that realizes the exhaustion of outflows, develop pure faith; they transcend conceptual discrimination, leave behind all doubt and perplexity, and even give rise to the thought of its being marvelous.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to further clarify this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddha is fully endowed with the power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of outflows;
Vast, immeasurable, pure, and unobstructed, he has perfected the gateway of supreme wisdom of the ten powers, And proceeds toward the realization of the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi."
Unlike the śrāvakas' knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, which is limited by residual tendencies, habitual patterns, and the fetters of obstruction,
the Supreme and Most Victorious Honored One among men has utterly eliminated all residual tendencies and limitations.
Whatever knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows belongs to the pratyekabuddhas, they have abandoned great compassion and eloquence;
the World-Honored One has fully perfected the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, and his great compassion and eloquence are both immeasurable.
The Buddha dwells securely in the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows; he fully knows that the outflows in the world are unreal.
Amidst all phenomena which are illusory, he has thoroughly understood this principle as it truly is.
Compassionately mindful of the world’s extreme suffering and affliction, he taught the Dharma of non-self, emptiness, and impermanence;
within these deceptive and unreal phenomena, one should contemplate the supreme state of tranquility.
Without self, without person, without sentient beings, And with neither agent nor experiencer—
amidst all phenomena that are illusory, The Buddha, with a heart of compassion, contemplates the path to liberation.
The Tathāgata has already transcended all weariness and fatigue; his true wisdom is likewise free from forgetfulness.
The Muni constantly abides in the gateway of meditative union, extensively benefiting the world by proclaiming the True Dharma.
The Ten Powers can crush all other doctrines; the Ten Powers are boundless, equal to space.
The Honored One who perfectly abides in the Ten Powers turns the supreme wheel, peerless and incomparable.

“Śāriputra! Such are the ten powers of knowledge of the Tathāgata. Because the Tathāgata is endowed with these ten powers of knowledge, he thoroughly understands the superior states; amidst the world of devas and humans, he can roar the lion’s roar and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel, which no deva, human, Māra, or Brahmā can ever turn. There is none who shares the same Dharma as the Tathāgata.”

Bodhisattvas who abide in faith should, regarding the inconceivable and most supreme power of wisdom of the Buddha-Tathāgata, maintain pure faith; they should transcend conceptual discrimination and be free from all doubt. Thereafter, they further give rise to signs of physical joy, mental joy, and gladness, conceiving a sense of its rarity.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Twelve;
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha,
Volume Thirteen.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Four: The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata, Part Seven. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."
What are called the four fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata that are inconceivable?
Bodhisattvas abiding in faith should give rise to pure faith, transcend conceptual discrimination, and be free from all doubt, even to the point of conceiving a sense of their rarity.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata possesses four kinds of fearlessnesses. Because the Tathāgata is endowed with these four fearlessnesses, he thoroughly understands the superior states; amidst the great assembly, he can roar the lion’s roar and turn the sublime Brahma-wheel, which no other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas can turn. Among all those in the world—gods, humans, māras, or brahmas—none possess a dharma equal to that of the Tathāgata.
Śāriputra! What are the four fearlessnesses?
The first is the fearlessness of omniscience, which means that the Buddha-Tathāgata, having already perfected the unsurpassed, supreme wisdom, speaks these words in the midst of the great assembly:

"I have attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment; this Dharma is realized and known by the Buddha alone, and no other among gods, humans, or the world can match the Buddha's discourse on this Dharma."
The Tathāgata has attained equal and perfect enlightenment by means of this Dharma. How, then, is it said that the Tathāgata has attained equal and perfect enlightenment?

It is because the Buddha-Tathāgata has attained perfect enlightenment through the equality of all dharmas; among all dharmas, there is neither high nor low. Whether they be the dharmas of ordinary beings, the dharmas of noble ones, the dharmas of Buddhas, the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa), the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, mundane dharmas, supramundane dharmas, faulty dharmas, faultless dharmas, outflowing (sāsrava) dharmas, non-outflowing (anāsrava) dharmas, conditioned (saṃskṛta) dharmas, or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas—the Tathāgata regards all such dharmas with complete equality. This is called the Tathāgata’s manifest attainment of perfect enlightenment.
In this context, what is meant by "equality"?
It refers to the equality of emptiness, because one perceives its intrinsic nature;
it refers to the equality of signlessness, because signs are [themselves] the intrinsic nature.
The equality of wishlessness, because the three realms are its intrinsic nature;
the equality of non-arising, because arising is its intrinsic nature;
the equality of non-action, because action is its intrinsic nature.
It is the equality of non-arising, because its intrinsic nature is arising;
it is the equality of non-encapsulation, because its intrinsic nature is encapsulation;
