Why is this? The mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) of the Tathāgata cannot be described; the mental faculty (*manas-dharma*) and consciousness-phenomena (*vijñāna-dharma*) of the Tathāgata cannot be fathomed by means of wisdom or eloquence.

The Tathāgata’s wisdom knows the minds of all sentient beings as they are, enters into the intentions of all sentient beings as they are, and penetrates the intellects of all sentient beings. Regarding all phenomena as determined, he has no reliance on others even regarding the dharmas of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He transcends objects of perception and is free from all dependent origination; he extinguishes the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*) and all evil destinies. He surpasses all demonic teachings and is distinct from all demons; he is liberated from all deceitful and illusory dharmas and remains entirely remote from them. Having abandoned the notions of "self" and "mine," and having removed the obscuring darkness of ignorance and delusion, he cultivates the Eightfold Noble Path and is free from all doubt. Equal to space, he is impartial within the *dharmadhātu* and without differentiation.
Śāriputra! Such dharmas as these constitute the mental karma of the Tathāgata, which is preceded by wisdom and follows the course of wisdom.
This is the fifteenth unique quality of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma) of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha-spoken Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra, Volume Fifteen.
The Buddha-spoken Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra, Volume Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Imperial Court, Dr.

[Chaosandafu], Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit and Chinese, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Weijing and others, by imperial decree. From the Remainder of Chapter Four, "The Inconceivable Nature of the Tathāgata": "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
In past ages, the Tathāgata turned that which was to be turned by means of unattached and unimpeded wisdom and vision.
How so? Śāriputra!
That is to say, regarding all matters concerning the formation and destruction of the Buddha-fields of the past, the Tathāgata is able to know them all through the skillful means of calculation.
Furthermore, they are able to know all medicinal herbs and forests within a buddha-field.
Moreover, they are able to know all sentient beings within a buddha-field, including the various categories of beings and their conventional designations.
Furthermore, all sentient beings within the Buddha-field—possessing their various dispositions, behaviors, and diverse physical forms—are known by him in their entirety, throughout the vast expanse.

Moreover, he knows all the Buddhas appearing in those Buddha-fields performing their various transformative deeds, even down to each one extensively proclaiming the True Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.

There may be sentient beings who are to be converted through the Dharma of the Śrāvakas; there may be sentient beings who are to be converted through the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas; and there may be sentient beings who are to be converted through the Mahāyāna Dharma. Furthermore, the Buddha is able to know all such characteristics of sentient beings throughout the past—whether the vastness of the Buddha-fields, the vastness of the assembly of bhikṣus, the vastness of their lifespan, or the vastness of the duration of the True Dharma remaining in the world; even the matters of food, drink, and enjoyments for sentient beings over long or short periods, down to the inhalations and exhalations of sentient beings—including whether they are born or perish, their rebirths in various realms, their diverse faculties, and their diverse inclinations—the Buddha knows them all.
With an unattached mind, the Tathāgata sustains and fully knows all those phenomena.
Regarding the infinite minds and the mental factors that arise from them, the Tathāgata is able to know them all through the skillful means of calculation.

The Tathāgata, with the wisdom of direct perception (*pratyakṣajñāna*), observes the minds of all sentient beings in the past exactly as they are; thus, the Tathāgata’s supreme and preeminent wisdom is never interrupted, and he teaches the Dharma to all sentient beings according to their needs.
Śāriputra! This is the sixteenth unique quality of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
In future ages, the Tathāgata turns that which is turned by means of unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision. How so?
It is because he fully knows all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas who shall appear in the world throughout future ages.

Even unto the future kalpas when the fires of destruction blaze forth, when great waters flood and drown all, and when fierce winds blow and rage; or again, when the various Buddha-fields remain tranquil and unmoving; down to the point where every element of the earth within those Buddha-fields is crushed like fine dust, as well as all medicinal herbs and forests, and even the appearances of all the stars and constellations; down to the appearance of Buddhas in the world, Pratyekabuddhas in the world, Śrāvakas in the world, and Bodhisattvas attaining realization throughout all the Buddha-fields; and down to the matters of sentient beings’ inhalation and exhalation, their eating and drinking, and their various enjoyments.

Whether walking or standing, even unto all sentient beings throughout the vast expanse of the universe—each and every one of them proceeding toward liberation, whether by the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna to attain liberation—all such as these are fully known by those Tathāgatas.
Furthermore, throughout all Buddha-fields, every single place where sentient beings are born, as well as every arising of their minds and mental factors—all of these the Tathāgatas know completely.

Although he knows thus, the Tathāgata does not provide any support for sentient beings in future ages; rather, in future ages, he observes as appropriate and proclaims the True Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.
"Śāriputra! This is the seventeenth unique quality of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
In the present world, the Tathāgata proceeds by means of unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision.
How so? It is said that regarding all Buddha-fields in the ten directions in the present, the Tathāgata is able to know them all through three kinds of numerical methods.
The Tathāgata fully knows all present Buddhas, all Bodhisattvas, all Pratyekabuddhas, and all Śrāvakas.
Furthermore, he universally knows the characteristics of all present constellations, and he also thoroughly understands all present medicinal herbs, trees, and forests.
Furthermore, regarding all the earth elements in the ten directions, even when crushed into atoms as fine as motes of dust, he is able to know them all through the skillful means of calculation.

Moreover, regarding all the water elements in the ten directions, such as droplets the size of a hair-tip surging upward; and all the fire elements in the ten directions, which arise and perish with extreme rapidity; and all the wind elements in the ten directions, blowing and striking with a hundred different forms and characteristics—he is able to know them all through the skillful means of calculation.
Furthermore, even if all the empty realms of the ten directions were gathered together in a mass the size of a hair-tip, they could all be known through the methods of calculation.
Moreover, he can fully know the three types of sentient beings' realms in the present.
Furthermore, he is able to know all the realms of sentient beings currently existing in the hells, as well as the causes for their birth there and the conditions from which they arise.
Moreover, he is able to know all the realms of sentient beings currently existing among animals, as well as the causes for their birth there and the conditions from which they arise.
Furthermore, he is able to fully know all present realms of hungry ghosts (*preta*), including their causes of birth and their causes of arising.
Moreover, he is able to fully know all present human realms, including their causes of birth and their causes of cessation.
Furthermore, he is able to fully know the present realms of the various devas, as well as the causes for their birth and the causes for their cessation.
Moreover, he is able to fully know all present sentient beings and that which their minds should sustain—whether they possess afflictions or are free from afflictions.

Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings in the present, whether they are those who should be transformed and delivered according to their faculties and natures or those who should not be so transformed, the Tathāgata knows them all.
Yet, the Buddha-Tathāgata does not possess two kinds of evolving consciousness that flow along with [conditions].
The Tathāgata, by means of this supreme dharma-gate of entering into the principle of non-duality, teaches it for the sake of all sentient beings.
Śāriputra! This is the eighteenth unique quality of a Buddha belonging to the Tathāgata.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Because the Tathāgata is fully endowed with these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma), he pervades all worlds throughout the ten directions, shining with radiant light amidst the great assemblies. He is perfectly possessed of all majestic splendor, renown, and the most supreme, auspicious, and rare dharmas."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The Tathāgata’s eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma) are like space, having no limit. If one could know the limit of space, one would know the limit of the Tathāgata’s unique qualities of a Buddha."

Therefore, when the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas hear these eighteen unique qualities of a Tathāgata, having heard them, they develop pure faith; they transcend conceptual discrimination and depart from all doubt and uncertainty. Thereafter, they further experience physical joy and mental joy, giving rise to the thought of their being truly marvelous.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"The Subduer, the Holy One, is free from fault; His actions of body, speech, and mind are entirely unmoving.
He teaches the Dharma as appropriate to benefit sentient beings; This is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One."
The Buddha’s mind is neither high nor low; all opposition and compliance are stilled.
Cultivating the practice of non-contention with a liberated mind—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The Buddha, the Honored One who has tamed all, is free from loss of mindfulness;
he fully understands the dharmas of liberation and conduct, and his four unhindered analytical knowledges are perfectly clear—these are the unique qualities of the Supreme Honored One.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, the Tathāgata always abides in a state of meditative equipoise;
free from the notion of a sentient being and devoid of a distracted mind—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.

The Sugata is free from all diverse perceptions; regarding the Buddha-fields and sentient beings, he gives rise to the practice of equanimity, O Greatly Renowned One—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The Buddha’s mind possesses no relinquishment that lacks discernment; it definitively observes the right path with skillful insight.
It distinguishes yet is entirely free from discrimination—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The Benevolent One does not diminish his desire for wholesome dharmas;
he constantly practices the gateways of compassion and skillful means to subdue immeasurable multitudes of sentient beings—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
His diligence has never diminished in the slightest; he has subdued all views, vast and boundless.
He likewise skillfully disciplines his body, speech, and mind—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The Tathāgata does not diminish in right mindfulness; having awakened to bodhi, he proceeds to the site of enlightenment.
Regarding all phenomena, he has realized awakening yet possesses no conceptualizing mind—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The Buddha is without discrimination and free from conceptualization;
Abiding in equanimity with a mind of meditative concentration, All phenomena are definitively without support— This is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The Buddha’s wisdom resolves all things in a single instant;
he fully knows the conduct of all sentient beings and expounds the Dharma-gates according to their inclinations—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
One who attains awakening through sound is called a Śrāvaka; one who contemplates dependently arisen phenomena is named a Pratyekabuddha.
Free from attachment and stainless as space—this great mind of equanimity is inconceivable.
Abiding from of old in a mind free of conceptualization, sustaining a mind naturally liberated,
he proclaims the Dharma of liberation as appropriate— this is the unique quality of the Supreme Victor.
Manifesting majestic deportment for the multitude to behold, he enters the cities with body erect and gaze steady;
adorned with the marks and signs and possessing a multitude of awesome radiances, all sentient beings who see him are tamed.
When sentient beings behold the Buddha’s true light, many koṭis of beings attain wondrous bliss;
touched by this light, they are tamed and brought to birth—this is the uncommon quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, And all sentient beings can hear it according to their own inclinations;
Just as sound meets its echo, this principle is consistent— This is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The mental karma of the Sugata is fundamentally non-existent, yet the deeds performed by his wisdom are never forgotten;
his noble wisdom enters the minds of sentient beings accordingly—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
Perfectly endowed with meditative concentration and equipoise, He does not engage in any conceptual proliferation;
His practice of equality is like space— This is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The Tathāgata fully knows the past ages, Turning all dharmas without obstruction;
With the wisdom of liberation, he understands all realms of existence— This is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
All future phenomena in the world—whether they shall be attained or not—sentient beings, buddha-fields, and Tathāgatas:
the Buddha knows them all with complete clarity and without weariness.

The Buddha’s mind has never known any distraction; throughout future ages he observes accordingly, knowing that sentient beings and phenomena are likewise so—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
Whatever occurs throughout the present world, the Tathāgata knows it all without attachment;
the Buddha, the Tamer of Men, is equal to space—this is the unique quality of the Supreme Honored One.
The Tathāgata’s unique qualities, eighteen kinds of inconceivable, Are revealed according to reality as being like space; Bodhisattvas should give rise to pure faith.

“Śāriputra! Because the Tathāgata is fully endowed with these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma), the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, understands the spheres of mastery and, amidst the great assembly, utters the lion’s roar and turns the sublime Brahma-wheel, which no other śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, māras, or brahmās can turn; there is none who shares the same Dharma as the Tathāgata.”

“Śāriputra! When bodhisattvas who abide in faith hear such inconceivable teachings of the Tathāgata, having heard them, they shall give rise to pure faith and delight; they shall transcend conceptual discrimination and be free from all doubt. Thereafter, they shall further experience physical joy and mental joy, conceiving a sense of wonder.”
Chapter Five: On Loving-kindness, Compassion, Joy, and Equanimity (Maitrī-karuṇā-muditā-upekṣā-varga), Part One.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, thoroughly recognize that a bodhisattva dwelling in faith is a fit vessel—one capable of upholding the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka and a vessel for the teachings of all Buddhas—they go to that person's abode and, according to what is appropriate, expound for them the Dharma of the path to enlightenment."
"Śāriputra! For this reason, you should know that a bodhisattva who abides in faith is a great vessel of the Dharma. Śāriputra!"

I recall that in the past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, and even further back through immeasurable, inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Mahāskandha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
That Buddha, within that world among the great assembly of devas, humans, asuras, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, realized the fruit of sainthood through his own supernormal powers.

For the great assembly, he proclaimed the True Dharma—good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end; profound in its words and meaning, pure and unadulterated, and possessing the characteristics of the perfectly pure and stainless holy life.

Śāriputra! Within the assemblies of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha, there were seventy-two nayutas of the great assembly of śrāvakas; all were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions, having attained mastery over their minds and reached the further shore.
At that time, there was a country named Supreme Banner, where there was a great king named Supreme Life.
He ruled according to the True Dharma; the land was vast, peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, and its population was flourishing.

That king had a son named Vīryaprabhāsa, whose physical appearance was upright and majestic, bringing joy to all who beheld him; having planted roots of goodness in the past, he had already drawn near to, honored, and made offerings to hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Tathāgatas of the past.
At that time, the Prince, together with his own retinue, was staying in a particularly exquisite and great park.

Then the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha, knowing that the Prince of diligent practice was a vessel for the Buddha-dharma and capable of bearing the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and having thus known this, immediately went to the park.
Having arrived, he then stood in mid-air and expounded the Dharma of the path to enlightenment for the Crown Prince Vīryaprabha.
That Buddha addressed him, saying:
"Crown Prince!..."
In this context, what is called the path to enlightenment?
It refers to the practice of gathering all sentient beings through the cultivation of the perfection of loving-kindness; this is precisely what is called the path to enlightenment.
"What, furthermore, is called the perfection of loving-kindness for all sentient beings? Prince,
it refers to a bodhisattva practicing vast loving-kindness within the realm of sentient beings."
That realm of sentient beings is like the realm of empty space;

just as empty space is vast, expansive, and boundless, so too is the Bodhisattva’s heart of loving-kindness. Within the realm of sentient beings and among the multitudes of beings, there is nowhere that this vast and expansive heart of loving-kindness does not pervade.
"Prince, you should know that just as the realm of sentient beings is without limit, the Bodhisattva’s compassionate contemplation is likewise immeasurable.
Furthermore, just as space is boundless, so too is the realm of sentient beings without boundary."
Because sentient beings are boundless, the mind of loving-kindness is likewise without limit.
Prince, you should know that the realm of sentient beings is vast and numerous, unlike the realms of earth, water, fire, or wind.
Now I shall speak an analogy to clarify this meaning, demonstrating that the realm of sentient beings is vast and immeasurable. Prince!

Suppose there were worlds in the eastern direction equal in number to the sands of the Ganges River, and likewise in the southern, western, and northern directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading all ten directions with worlds equal in number to the sands of the Ganges—and suppose all of these were a single great ocean, filled with water of one and the same source and flow.

Suppose all the multitudes of sentient beings in all the worlds throughout the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were each divided into a hundred parts, even down to the measure of a single hair-tip, and from those portions a single drop of water were taken; then, again as before, suppose the number of sentient beings equal to the sands of the Ganges were each divided into fifty parts, even down to the measure of a single hair-tip, and from those portions another single drop of water were taken.
Next, as before, he again reduced the number of sentient beings, equal to the sands of the Ganges, by half for fifty times, until it was as small as the tip of a single hair.
O Prince!
As previously stated, that mass of great water cannot be compared to the number of sentient beings through any method of calculation, for it is immeasurable and boundless.
Because the realm of sentient beings is immeasurable and boundless, the bodhisattva’s mind of loving-kindness is likewise so.
"Prince! What do you think?
Can you know the measure of all the roots of goodness arising from a bodhisattva’s contemplation of loving-kindness?"
The Prince replied:
"No, World-Honored One!"
"No, Sugata. The Buddha said:
“O Prince! The roots of goodness of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s contemplation of loving-kindness are likewise immeasurable and boundless.
Furthermore, O Prince!”

The Bodhisattva’s mind of loving-kindness is able to protect himself and bring benefit to others; because of this loving-kindness, he harbors no anger toward others nor does he feel weariness. Free from all resentment and ill-will, he stills all faults, perceives neither opposition nor compliance, manifests purity, and extinguishes all defilements.

May they constantly experience sublime bliss in body, speech, and mind; may they eliminate all defilements and pacify every fear; may they skillfully guard against anger and malice, giving rise to a pure intention; may they extinguish all strife and refrain from grasping at swords or staves, turning toward the gates of liberation and remaining free from all harm.

They completely distance themselves from all forms of deceitful intent, disordered speech, and false words, and instead accord with what is beneficial for others while sustaining their own bodies and lives.
Constantly revered by Śakra and Brahmā, adorned with majestic virtue, and praised by the wise;
he protects the ignorant and upholds the holy life, remaining unattached to the realm of desire.

They skillfully embrace all that arises, such as the path of liberation; yet they do not delight in meritorious conduct, nor do they accumulate any superior meritorious conduct, while constantly increasing [their practice].
Adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, all inferior and deficient faculties are entirely eliminated.
One proceeds toward the right path of the happy realms and nirvana; all evil destinies are ceased in an instant, and one finds joy and delight in the love of all dharmas.
Regarding the enjoyment of all desires, great wealth, and royal sovereignty, he is entirely free from attachment despite the increase of such pleasures.
He gives rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and practices generosity, free from all discriminatory thoughts.
One practices all the trainings in ethical discipline in accordance with the path, skillfully providing protection for those who violate the precepts.
One manifests the power of patience and remains far removed from the deeds of Māra, such as arrogance and the like.

Exerting diligent effort in the practice of renunciation, one seeks liberation from the root afflictions within the meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments by means of a resolute mind.

The pure cause of supreme wisdom gives birth to all forms of loving-kindness, learning, and dhāraṇī; it is entirely free from conflict or harm toward oneself or others, and it pacifies and eliminates all demonic and afflictive elements.
In walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, they increase all sublime joys and harmonies, and sweep away all unwholesome natures and mental engagements.
Constantly adorned with the exquisite fragrance of shame and remorse, they extinguish all obstacles, difficulties, and afflictions pertaining to the evil realms.
He constantly gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness to rescue and protect the world; with a mind of great compassion, he relinquishes his own happiness to accord others their happiness.
"Furthermore, Prince!
The loving-kindness generated by the śrāvakas serves only their own self-interest, whereas the loving-kindness of a bodhisattva constantly benefits all sentient beings."

Furthermore, it should be known that a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment practices compassion directed toward sentient beings; a bodhisattva at the stage of cultivation practices compassion directed toward phenomena; and a bodhisattva who has attained patience practices unconditioned compassion.
"O Prince!
All that has been thus explained constitutes the practice of great loving-kindness by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
If Bodhisattvas abide in a mind of loving-kindness, they are then able to practice vast loving-kindness for the sake of all sentient beings."

The Fifth Chapter: On Loving-kindness, Compassion, Sympathetic Joy, and Equanimity (Continued) Furthermore, the Tathāgata Mahāskandha addressed Prince Vīryaprabhāsa, saying:
"What is called the Bodhisattva’s mind of great compassion?"
When a bodhisattva seeks that unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they take great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as their precursor.

Just as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of a person is preceded by inhalation and exhalation, so too is the accumulation of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) by a bodhisattva preceded by great compassion.

Furthermore, just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King is able to obtain all treasures because the Jewel-Wheel serves as his precursor, so too a Bodhisattva is able to obtain all Buddha-dharmas because Great Compassion serves as his precursor.
Therefore, you should know that the great compassion of a bodhisattva never abandons any sentient being.
"Furthermore, Prince,
how does a bodhisattva direct the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings?"

It is said that a bodhisattva observes how all sentient beings in the world are firmly attached to the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); pursued by this, they give rise to various views that serve as fetters.
The Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma for severing attachment; this is how the Bodhisattva turns the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva perceives that all sentient beings in the world dwell in a state of perversion, reckoning impermanent phenomena as permanent, suffering as happiness, non-self as self, and the impure as pure.
The Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma for the purpose of severing such perversions; this is how the Bodhisattva turns the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings in the world, through their perversions, grasp at and become attached to various defiled desires, giving rise to lustful and defiled minds even toward their own mothers and sisters.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"How strange!
The sentient beings of this world, burdened by sinful karma, are attached to the realms of desire; they follow what is not practiced by the noble ones, and their conduct is filled with perversity."
Considering their origin, they dwelt within the mother’s womb and were subsequently born from her; why, then, do you now give rise to lustful thoughts?
Sisters share the same substance, having emerged from the same mother’s womb; how could you, on account of defiled conditions, conspire together for union?

They are ruined, utterly ruined, and most utterly ruined; their bodies and minds are destroyed by unrestrained greed, hatred, and delusion. Ruined by ignorance, they annihilate the True Dharma, establishing what is non-Dharma and practicing perilous and difficult dharmas, thereby entering the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

For example, when a pack of foxes enters a charnel ground during the night, they give rise to thoughts of malice and ill-will while waiting for their prey; so too it is with sentient beings who are inverted and defiled by worldly attachments.

Furthermore, just as a person born blind in this world cannot perceive various forms and colors and thus falls into dangerous and evil places, so too are sentient beings who are defiled by attachment.
Furthermore, just as a herd of pigs feeds on discarded and impure things, so too are sentient beings defiled by attachment.
Because they are corrupted by the defilements of inverted conditions, they enter the realm of Māra, are bound by Māra’s noose, and sink into the mire of desire.
The Bodhisattva teaches them the Dharma for severing and eliminating defiled craving; this is how the Bodhisattva turns the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings in the world are shrouded by the five hindrances and pierced by the arrows of desire, becoming attached to objects everywhere. Having seen forms with the eyes, they become attached to those beloved objects; having heard sounds with the ears, smelled odors with the nose, tasted flavors with the tongue, and felt tangibles with the body, they give rise to grasping and attachment according to whatever they find dear.

Alas! Sentient beings dwell in many places of conflict and harm; they associate with evil friends, mutually seeking wealth and profit. Sharing the same views and understanding as those evil friends, they obtain no meaningful benefit but instead inflict mutual injury and affliction upon one another. They abound in unwholesome states such as torpor and drowsiness; overcome by lethargy and delusion, they are pursued by a lack of wisdom, giving rise to various forms of regretful wrongdoing.

These sentient beings have their minds defiled by adventitious afflictions and give rise to various doubts; these sentient beings are unable to definitively attain the most supreme and profound Buddha-dharma.
The Bodhisattva teaches them the dharmas for severing the hindrances and obstacles; this is how the Bodhisattva directs the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings in the world give rise to various forms of pride: namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*), the pride of self (*asmimāna*), overweening pride (*adhimāna*), inferiority pride (*ūnamāna*), and false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
These seven types of pride are: first, to consider oneself superior to those who are inferior;
second, to consider oneself equal to those who are superior;
third, to consider oneself superior to those who are superior.
Fourth, relying on the self that one clings to;
fifth, calculating oneself as possessing many virtues and giving rise to pride regarding superior qualities and dharmas;
sixth, calculating oneself as being slightly inferior to others.

Seventh is to consider oneself possessed of virtue; because of such pride, one fails to praise those who deserve praise and fails to honor those who deserve honor. One does not respect elders, nor can one receive instruction from teachers and masters. Furthermore, one is unable to inquire of the wise: "What is wholesome and what is unwholesome? What should be approached and what should not be approached? What should be done and what should not be done? What is blameworthy and what is blameless? What is the right path, what is samādhi, and what is liberation?"
Regarding such matters as these, [the beings] are unable to inquire further.
The Bodhisattva then preaches for them the Dharma for severing all demonic obstacles; this is how the Bodhisattva turns the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings in the world are bound by the ropes of craving—namely, their attachment to men and women, wives and concubines, wealth, profit, and so forth."

Because of attachment, one takes pleasure in the perils of birth and death and the evil realms of the three miserable destinies; bound and fettered by the three realms of existence, body and mind lack autonomy, and due to this lack of autonomy, one creates various karmas of transgression.

The Bodhisattva, in order to cause all those beings to proceed toward the noble path to Nirvāṇa, proclaims the True Dharma; this is how the Bodhisattva directs the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva observes all sentient beings in the world who, being separated from virtuous friends and associating with evil friends, become defiled by ten kinds of unwholesome dharmas due to such association: namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong view."

When a bodhisattva desires to cause all sentient beings to be embraced by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), to extinguish and eliminate all unwholesome karma, to accumulate the pure path of the ten wholesome actions (daśakuśalakarmapatha), and to proclaim the True Dharma—this is the bodhisattva’s cultivation of great compassion (mahākaruṇā) toward all sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings in the world are shrouded and obstructed by delusion; they are constantly pursued by the darkness of ignorance and cling to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, a pudgala, an agent, an experiencer, and 'I' and 'mine.'"

In order to purify the eye of wisdom of all such sentient beings and to cause their various views to be extinguished, the bodhisattva proclaims the true Dharma; this is how the bodhisattva directs the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings in the world are submerged in birth and death and are unable to attain liberation; they are constantly being slaughtered by the slayer of the five aggregates."

In order to bring about the liberation from the five aggregates, to transcend the perilous wilderness of saṃsāra, and to emerge from the three realms, the Bodhisattva proclaims the True Dharma; this is how the Bodhisattva directs the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva observes that all sentient beings in the world perform various unwholesome deeds; just as a thorny tree, though it grows, achieves nothing, so too it is with those who create unwholesome karma—they revolve through the five destinies in this life and the next, unable to proceed toward the noble path to Nirvana."
The Bodhisattva opens for them the gate of nirvāṇa so that they may enter it, proclaiming the True Dharma; this is how the Bodhisattva directs the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.
"Furthermore, Prince!
Because a bodhisattva thus observes all sentient beings in the world, they turn toward the mind of great compassion through ten aspects.
What are these ten?
First, the transformation of a mind free from flattery and deception, because it is liberated like space.
Second, the transformation of a profound and firm mind, because it is capable of skillful liberation.
Third, the transformation of non-artificial supernormal powers, because it is liberated through the true path.
Fourth is the transformation of the mind free from crookedness, because it brings to rest all crooked minds and skillfully effects renunciation.
Fifth is the transformation of the true mind, because it effects renunciation through equality toward all sentient beings, without any sense of high or low.
Sixth is the turning that follows and protects others, because one’s own mind is pure and well-emancipated.
Seventh is the turning of the mind of firm wisdom, because one is free from the minds of movement and stillness and always dwells in well-emancipated stability.
Eighth is the transformation of relinquishing one’s own happiness, because of renunciation through the absence of attachment.
Ninth is the transformation of bestowing happiness upon others according to their needs, because of renunciation through benefiting others.
Tenth is the transformation of bearing the extremely heavy burden of sentient beings, because of excellent renunciation through firm diligence.
By means of these ten kinds of superior characteristics, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva directs the mind of great compassion toward all sentient beings.

Furthermore, if there are sentient beings who should attain liberation through the Mahāyāna Dharma, the bodhisattva gives rise to compassion and brings about their liberation; this is called the great compassion of a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, when sentient beings who ought to cultivate the dharmas of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and superior wisdom give rise to compassion and accordingly achieve liberation, this is called the great compassion of a bodhisattva."

"Furthermore, for sentient beings who should cultivate the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path; for those who should engage in the most excellent activities rooted in joy and the successive meditative concentrations, up to the vast chapters on the ten paths of wholesome action—I shall turn the wheel of Dharma accordingly. Arising from a heart of compassion, I shall employ the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom as food and drink to nourish their life of insight."
This is called the great compassion of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion from their own well-performed and excellent conduct; according to whatever actions are appropriate for sentient beings, they are able to fully fulfill the inclinations and aspirations of those beings.
This is called the great compassion of a bodhisattva.
If bodhisattvas mahāsattvas are fully endowed with such a mind of great compassion, they are able to observe sentient beings and cause them all to obtain such dharmas as these.
This is how a bodhisattva, through contemplation and compassionate concern, gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
"Furthermore, Prince,
what is the bodhisattva’s mind of joy?

That is to say, regarding all wholesome dharmas, whenever a bodhisattva contemplates them, they experience joy and delight; upon hearing these wholesome dharmas, they are neither startled nor afraid, nor do they give rise to weariness. They eliminate all divergent mental states and dwell in peaceful contentment, delighting in the bliss of all dharmas.
With a joyful mind and compliant body, his own mind becomes pure and a sense of rapture arises.
Beholding the Tathāgata’s body adorned with the primary and secondary marks, he diligently seeks them with love and joy, experiencing an ever-increasing and sublime delight.
They listen to the Dharma without weariness, practicing according to the Dharma with joy and delight.
They joyfully endure all harsh words directed at them.

Following whatever dharmas of joy arise within them, they give rise to an unimpeded mind toward all sentient beings, extensively proclaiming them to inspire superior understanding; free from any sense of secrecy or stinginess, they subdue their own avarice.

He bestows gifts with joy according to the needs of those who seek them; his face is always serene and radiant as he protects those who have violated the precepts; he honors those who uphold the precepts and constantly gives rise to purity. Having attained purity through his own practice, he transcends all fears of the evil realms and joyfully brings comfort to all sentient beings.
When malicious words or provocations arise from those who come before him, he joyfully endures them.
When giving away his eyes or parts of his body, he joyfully and willingly endures it.
His mind is uninterrupted, constantly generating delight and giving rise to a heart of joy.

He respects teachers and elders, as well as those superior to himself, never giving rise to contempt or arrogance. His face is always serene and smiling, and he is the first to speak. He is free from frowning and deceitful intentions, having completely eliminated all confused speech and worldly attachments.

With a joyful heart, one delights in all dharmas of renunciation; one looks up with reverence to the teacher as to the Bodhisattvas; one holds the True Dharma in the highest esteem, as if protecting one’s own body; one honors the Tathāgata as if cherishing one’s own life; one reverently receives the master as one does one’s parents; one loves and cares for all sentient beings as if they were one’s own children; one follows the preceptor as if guarding one’s eyes; one respects practitioners as if protecting the crown of one’s head; one accepts the various pāramitās with faith as if strengthening one’s hands and feet; one values the Dharma-preacher as if loving a wondrous jewel; one diligently seeks the True Dharma as if valuing excellent medicine; and one praises and serves the King of Physicians as if seeking a boat upon the water.
"O Prince!
What has been thus described is the bodhisattva’s mind of joy.

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this mind of joy, they shall always experience gladness at all times; they will diligently seek the true Dharma without ever becoming weary, and they will give rise to a joyful heart to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva."
"Furthermore, Prince!
What is the bodhisattva’s mind of equanimity?
This so-called 'equanimity' has three kinds.
What are the three?
First, relinquishment through afflictions; second, relinquishment through protecting oneself and others; third, relinquishment according to the proper time.
What is meant by relinquishment through afflictions?

That is to say: being neither elated by respect nor dejected by disrespect; having no sense of personal gain when receiving benefit, and no resentment or anger when suffering loss; maintaining an even mind toward those who observe the precepts and those who violate them; feeling no joy at praise and no anger at slander; remaining composed amidst insult and unshaken by flattery; being well-able to discern all phenomena of suffering and constantly examining all phenomena of happiness; following what is favorable without attachment and not severing what is adverse; dwelling with an even mind toward both virtuous and non-virtuous friends; and likewise remaining free from duality regarding both good and evil deeds.

They maintain equanimity and relinquish both pleasant and unpleasant objects; they neither accept nor reject what they have heard much or what they have not heard; they experience neither attraction nor aversion toward well-spoken or ill-spoken words; and they treat both consolation and reproach with equal impartiality.

With a mind of equanimity, they cherish themselves and all other sentient beings, not begrudging even their own bodies or lives; they illuminate all beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—with impartiality; they abide in the Dharma of equality regarding both beautiful and foul appearances; and amidst both the true and the false, they are inherently and truly pure.
"O Prince!
As has been explained, when a bodhisattva possesses a pure mind of equanimity that is free from partiality, this is called the equanimity regarding all afflictions.
What is meant by the equanimity that protects both oneself and others?"

When a bodhisattva cuts from their own body and gives away flesh as an act of giving, they abide in a mind of equanimity, seeking nothing at all. There is no activity of body, no activity of speech, and no movement within the mind. There is no mark of the eye, no mark of form, and so on, up to no mark of the intellect and no mark of phenomena. This total lack of movement is called "equanimity" (upekṣā).
Non-action that is free from harm is also called equanimity; well-performed action that is unwavering is also called equanimity; enduring both oneself and others is also called equanimity.
Abiding in a mind of equality toward all benefits and harms is also called equanimity.
The absence of all disputes and litigation is called the supreme equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The certainty of one’s own mind is also termed equanimity.
Having examined oneself and others and found no harm whatsoever, the bodhisattva dwells in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-citta*) and practices equanimity.
However, the renunciation of a bodhisattva is not the same as the dharma of renunciation practiced by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Why is this?

Because a bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding that dharma of renunciation, clearly understands what is to be constantly cultivated; they always diligently seek all wholesome dharmas and practice renunciation according to the proper time and in accordance with the occasion.
What is meant by "equanimity according to the occasion"?

It refers to the Bodhisattva observing those sentient beings who are not vessels for the Dharma and those who have not heard it, and dwelling in equanimity toward them all; furthermore, dwelling in equanimity toward all sentient beings who suffer from decline, ruin, and censure; and finally, transcending the Śrāvaka vehicle with certainty and relinquishing it.
When practicing generosity, one practices the relinquishment of ethical discipline;
when practicing patience, one practices the relinquishment of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence;
and when practicing diligence, one practices the relinquishment of ethical discipline.
When practicing meditative concentration, one practices the relinquishment of generosity;
when practicing wisdom, one practices the complete fulfillment of the relinquishment of the five perfections.
This is called relinquishment according to the appropriate time.
All things that ought to be done and those that ought not to be done—all such phenomena abide in equality, which is also called equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who abides in the practice of equanimity, even all categories of wholesome dharmas are termed "equanimity."
"O Prince!
What has been thus described is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s cultivation of the minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward all sentient beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, addressed Śāriputra, saying:
At that time, after the Tathāgata Mahāskandha had taught the Dharma of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity to Prince Vīryaprabha, he further proclaimed the six pāramitās.
What are these six?

They are the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of superior wisdom.
Thus he proclaimed the various *pāramitās*, causing the Crown Prince Vīryaprabha to exert diligent effort and practice accordingly.
Chapter Six: The Perfection of Generosity (*Dānapāramitā*)—Part One Furthermore, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"What is meant by 'exerting diligent effort in the *pāramitās*'? "
Śāriputra! If one applies diligent effort toward the six pāramitās, this is said to be the cultivation of the bodhisattva practice.

Those six pāramitās are: the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of superior wisdom.
Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas see those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, or the poor, the destitute, and the homeless who come to beg, they bestow upon them everything according to their desires.

Whether it be food, drink, clothing, ointments, flower garlands, or places of residence; or medicine for the treatment of illness, lamps, music, wives, children, slaves, servants, gardens, pavilions, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral, amber, mani-jewels, pearls, and other exquisite treasures; or elephants, horses, chariots, wealth, grain, and treasuries—even down to the sovereignty and pleasures of a wheel-turning monarch over the four continents; or even limbs such as hands, feet, ears, noses, eyes, or the flesh, blood, marrow, and bones of one’s own body—there was nothing in the world that he would not give away.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are ten dharmas which a bodhisattva, if they can fulfill with purity, should practice as giving.
What are these ten?

First, the bodhisattva’s giving does not seek difficult or arduous enjoyments; second, the bodhisattva’s giving does not oppress or afflict sentient beings; third, the bodhisattva’s giving does not cause alarm or fear in others; fourth, the bodhisattva’s giving never refuses what has been requested; fifth, the bodhisattva’s giving is free from the display of signs; sixth, the bodhisattva’s giving is without discriminatory thoughts toward any sentient being; seventh, the bodhisattva’s giving is without harm; eighth, the bodhisattva’s giving is without distinctions regarding realms or lands; ninth, the bodhisattva’s giving to sentient beings is without mental fabrication. The tenth dharma is missing from the Sanskrit original.
“Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva can purify these ten kinds of dharmas, they should practice giving.
Furthermore, there are ten other dharmas which, if a bodhisattva can fully purify, they should practice giving.”

What are the ten? First, the bodhisattva’s giving that does not contradict the ripening of karma; second, the bodhisattva’s giving with no perverse intention; third, the bodhisattva’s giving with no lack of resolute conviction; fourth, the bodhisattva’s giving without weariness; fifth, the bodhisattva’s giving that is not for the sake of seeking out [the recipient's] face; sixth, the bodhisattva’s giving without malice or harm; seventh, the bodhisattva’s giving without retreat or dejection; eighth, the bodhisattva’s giving that is not for the sake of praise for maintaining ethical discipline; ninth, the bodhisattva’s giving that is not for the sake of disparaging those who violate ethical discipline; tenth, the bodhisattva’s giving that does not seek karmic retribution.
If a bodhisattva can purify these ten kinds of dharmas, they should practice giving.
Furthermore, there are ten other dharmas; if a bodhisattva can fully purify them, they should practice giving.

What are the ten? First, the bodhisattva’s gift free from slander; second, the bodhisattva’s gift free from contrariety; third, the bodhisattva’s gift free from blemish; fourth, the bodhisattva’s gift free from anger; fifth, the bodhisattva’s gift free from malice and envy; sixth, the bodhisattva’s gift free from resentment; seventh, the bodhisattva’s gift free from lack of respect; eighth, the bodhisattva’s gift free from not giving with one's own hands; ninth, the bodhisattva’s gift that appropriately restrains an inferior mind; tenth, the bodhisattva’s gift free from expectation regarding the place of rebirth.
If a bodhisattva can purify these ten kinds of dharmas, they should practice giving.
Furthermore, there are ten other dharmas; if a bodhisattva can fully perfect and purify them, they should practice giving.

What are the ten? First, the bodhisattva’s giving is never lacking in firmness; second, the bodhisattva’s giving is boundless; third, the bodhisattva’s giving is without fragmentation; fourth, the bodhisattva’s giving does not depend on the faith of others; fifth, the bodhisattva’s giving is not attached to an inferior mind; sixth, the bodhisattva’s giving does not seek the enjoyment of physical beauty, wealth, or noble status for the sake of joy; seventh, the bodhisattva’s giving does not seek the state of Brahmā, Śakra, or the world-protecting devas; eighth, the bodhisattva’s giving does not seek the stages of the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha; ninth, the bodhisattva’s giving does not disparage the wise; tenth, the bodhisattva’s giving dedicates every virtuous benefit toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
If a bodhisattva can purify these ten kinds of dharmas, they should practice giving.

The Sixth Chapter: The Perfection of Generosity (Dānapāramitā), Part Two. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."
There are ten kinds of praiseworthy qualities; if a bodhisattva can fulfill them with purity, they should practice generosity.
These praiseworthy qualities refer to the fact that by means of renunciation from the conditioned, one attains the fruits of the conditioned.
A bodhisattva should practice giving in this manner, whereby they will attain ten kinds of praiseworthy qualities. What are these ten?
First, by giving food, one attains long life.
Second, by giving drinks, one pacifies and eliminates all afflictions of craving and thirst.
Third, by giving various vehicles and carriages, one is able to obtain all manner of beneficial and joyful matters.
Fourth, by giving excellent garments, one immediately gives rise to a sense of shame and remorse, as if obtaining a golden canopy.
Fifth, by giving various ointments, flowers, and garlands, one immediately attains the exquisite fragrance and adornment of ethical discipline, learning, and meditative concentration.
Sixth, by giving various exquisite incenses and powdered incenses, one immediately obtains limbs that are soft and supple, and a fragrant aroma that is rich and pervasive.
Seventh, by giving various delicious flavors, one immediately obtains the supreme taste among all tastes, as well as the ability to fully possess the sublime marks of a human being.
Eighth is the gift of a place of reliance, which means being able to serve as a dwelling, an island, a rescue, a refuge, and a destination for all sentient beings.
Ninth, by giving medicine and medical requisites to those who are ill, one immediately attains the perfect fulfillment of the sublime bliss of the ambrosia that is free from aging and death.

Tenth, if one gives various kinds of life-sustaining requisites, one immediately attains the perfect fulfillment of the supreme and wondrous requisites for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
These ten kinds of dharmas praised for giving are those which a bodhisattva seeking awakening shall obtain as all-encompassing praise and support.
Furthermore, there are ten other dharmas praised for giving; if a bodhisattva can purify these, they should practice giving.
What are the ten?
First, if one gives the gift of light, one immediately attains the purity of the five eyes of a Tathāgata.
Second, if one gives the gift of exquisite songs, one immediately attains the purity of the divine ear.

Third, if one gives gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral, amber, mani-jewels, pearls, and other rare treasures, one will immediately obtain the thirty-two marks of a Great Man characteristic of the Tathāgata.
Fourth, if one gives various kinds of exquisite jewels and various kinds of exquisite flowers, one will immediately attain the eighty minor marks of a Tathāgata.
Fifth, if one gives elephants, horses, and carriages, one will immediately attain a vast multitude of people surrounding and attending one in full attendance.

Sixth, if one gives excellent gardens and groves, one will obtain the perfect fulfillment of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), samādhi, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
Seventh, if one gives wealth, grain, and treasuries, one will obtain the perfect fulfillment of the treasury of all Dharma-jewels.
Eighth, if one gives slaves and laborers, one immediately attains mastery over all actions, becoming fully endowed with the spontaneous wisdom of a Buddha.
Ninth, if one gives wives, children, and kinsmen, one immediately attains the most excellent, lovely, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, becoming fully endowed with it.

Tenth, if one bestows the position of sovereign wealth and happiness over the four great continents, one immediately attains all the wholesome dharmas of a bodhisattva and achieves the complete perfection of omniscience.
These ten kinds of dharmas praised for giving are what a bodhisattva shall obtain as all-encompassing praise and support when seeking awakening.
Furthermore, there are ten other dharmas praised for giving; if a bodhisattva can purify these, they should practice giving.
What are the ten?

First, if one bestows the exquisite pleasures of the five desires, one immediately attains the purity of the aggregates of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, as well as the fulfillment of all wishes regarding matters of play, amusement, and entertainment.
Second, if one gives a pair of feet, one will immediately attain the perfection of the feet of Dharma-meaning and proceed to the site of enlightenment.
Third, if one gives two hands, one will immediately attain the perfection of the hands of Dharma that constantly bestow [teachings] upon others.
Fourth, if one gives away their ears, they will immediately attain the full perfection of all faculties, free from any deficiency or impairment.
Fifth, if one gives away their nose, they likewise attain the full perfection of all faculties.
Sixth, if one gives the various limbs of the body, one immediately attains a faultless body, pure like the body of a Buddha.
Seventh, if one gives one's eyes, one immediately attains the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Eighth, if one gives blood and flesh, one immediately attains the true body and life of all sentient beings, and through this true giving, one’s own life is well-sustained.
Ninth, if one gives marrow, one immediately attains a vajra-like body that is firm, solid, and indestructible.

Tenth, if one gives the upper part of the body, the head and crown, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva immediately attains abiding in the most supreme and unsurpassed state within the triple world, and realizes for themselves the perfect fulfillment of the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna).

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva seeks awakening, they should practice giving in this manner; through such characteristics as these, they are able to fulfill all Buddha-dharmas, which are then praised and embraced.

“Śāriputra! A wise bodhisattva, by means of his profound and superior wisdom, does not delight in the wealth and objects of pleasure cherished by the world; rather, he strives diligently to seek unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, to seek the Dharma of ambrosia, to seek the wisdom of great awakening, and to seek the tranquility of nirvāṇa.”

There is nothing among all the objects of worldly desire and all forms of sublime pleasure that a bodhisattva does not relinquish, for it is entirely for the sake of relying upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Śāriputra, it is like those in the world who cultivate the land: when they first wish to weed the fields, they first rely on sturdy wood and then prepare various implements; with oxen leading the way, they perform the work of plowing and weeding upon the soil—whether inferior, middling, or superior—and once their labor is accomplished, they thereby sustain their bodies and lives.
Because that cultivator maintains his body and life, he is able to procure gold, silver, and various treasures; indeed, he is able to procure all things such as wealth, grain, and clothing.
Why is this? Because wealth is not equal to grain; grain is the fundamental necessity.

It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: if one practices giving with worldly goods that are pleasing to people, according to the proper time and place, one is thereby able to rely upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Śāriputra! It is just as when a herd of cows first eats green grass, and subsequently drinks water that is neither too hot nor too cold.

Once the food and drink are properly balanced, they produce milk; from that, curd is produced; after that, fresh butter; and finally, refined butter. In this sequence, everything is successively accomplished.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva is also like this: first practicing generosity with worldly wealth and goods that are pleasing, they are then able to rely upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and accomplish whatever they desire. They may become a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), or they may accomplish three kinds of supreme marks: namely, the ten stages of a bodhisattva, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the four fearlessnesses.
Furthermore, by accomplishing a thousand kinds of activities, one immediately attains the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (āveṇika-buddhadharma).
Moreover, by accomplishing a thousand kinds of activities, one attains the sixty kinds of pure and wondrous vocal tones of a Buddha.
Furthermore, by accomplishing one hundred kinds of activities, one immediately attains one of the Tathāgata’s marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
Moreover, by accomplishing two hundred kinds of activities, one immediately attains the Tathāgata’s supreme, pure *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head.
Furthermore, by accomplishing one hundred kinds of excellent marks of merit, he is able to fully possess the sound of the great Dharma conch of all Tathāgatas.
Moreover, by accomplishing hundreds of thousands of koṭis of excellent marks of merit, he attains the Tathāgata’s mark of teeth that are pure white, even, and closely set.
Śāriputra! Therefore, you should know that Bodhisattvas are fully capable of accomplishing the karmic fruition of the Tathāgata’s supreme deeds.

If one can give rise to a single thought of loving-kindness and bestow gifts upon beggars as they deserve, this is no different from giving rise to as many such thoughts as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; it is precisely through this that one can accomplish the Buddha-samādhi.

It should be known that once the Buddhas have arisen from samādhi, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas are able, from each and every pore, to manifest the sovereign transformations of a hundred samādhis.

Śāriputra! All such supernatural feats and the supreme characteristics of the Buddha-dharma performed by the Tathāgata are entirely due to the bodhisattva’s prior cultivation of great practices, having offered to the Tathāgata the wealth and goods cherished by the world.
Because they are embraced [by this practice], they seek the nectar-like Dharma and seek the tranquility of nirvāṇa.
Śāriputra, for these reasons,
when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice giving with the wealth and goods cherished by the world, they are able to rely upon and achieve the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

I recall that in the past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, and even beyond immeasurable, innumerable, and inconceivable kalpas, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Puṇyaprasava Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
The lifespan of that Buddha was one thousand years.

Within his assembly were hundreds of thousands of great bhikṣus, all of whom were great arhats; their outflows were exhausted, they were free from further afflictions, their minds attained mastery, and they had reached the other shore.

At that time, there was a spinner of thread, whose physical appearance was upright and dignified, and whom all people delighted to behold; the place where he dwelt was not far from the location where the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was staying.

That person, having performed his own work within his own house and completed his labor, went out from his house at the usual time in the afternoon and proceeded to where the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Puṇyasaṃbhava, was staying.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he gave rise to a pure mind and offered a single thread to the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now offer this single thread to the World-Honored One; may the Buddha, out of compassion, accept this gift of mine."
"By these roots of goodness, may I, in future lives, obtain all the methods of gathering [disciples].
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately accepted him.

From then until his attainment of Buddhahood, the spinner followed this sequence, offering a total of five hundred strands of thread to the World-Honored One; by virtue of this, for fifteen kalpas he did not fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, by means of these roots of goodness, he became a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) for a thousand *koṭi* of lifetimes.
Again, by these roots of goodness, he became Śakra, Lord of the Devas, for a thousand *koṭi* of lifetimes.
Furthermore, by means of these roots of goodness, one shall attain the physical marks of a person with supple limbs that are lovely to behold.

Having first undertaken supreme and sublime deeds, one shall approach, serve, honor, and revere ten billion Buddhas (*koṭi*), offering them incense, flowers, lamps, ointments, food, drink, clothing, banners, pennants, precious parasols, and medicinal requisites. Finally, after the passing of further incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), one shall realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, becoming known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān, named Suvigraha.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, dwelt for a lifespan of twenty koṭis of years.

Within his assembly were twenty koṭi-nayutas of bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats; their outflows were exhausted, they were free from further afflictions, their minds attained mastery, and they had reached the further shore.

There was an assembly of fifty million great bodhisattvas, all of whom were firmly established in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they proclaimed the true Dharma, extensively delivering immeasurable and innumerable sentient beings, and having brought about their benefit and happiness, they entered great *nirvāṇa*.

After that Buddha, the World-Honored One, enters parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for a full one thousand years, extensively performing the work of a Buddha, no different from my own present entry into parinirvāṇa.

Śāriputra! You see this spinner who, having generated a pure mind, offered a single thread to the Tathāgata; in this way, he successively accomplishes the Buddha-dharma, because his pure mind is vast.
Śāriputra! Therefore, you should know that if the mind is neither expansive nor diligent, one cannot attain a sublime karmic fruition.
However, if the mind is pure, even by relying on worldly wealth and giving a small amount according to one's capacity, one will obtain all fruits that are desirable and delightful.
Furthermore, the wise Bodhisattva achieves many benefits through the power of superior wisdom (*adhiprajñā*).
Why is this? Because that power is vast and because the power of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) of what has been performed is immeasurable.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"In giving, one seeks not the marks of physical form, Nor seeks enjoyment or abundant wealth;
Seeking only the unsurpassed Bodhi of the Buddha, One obtains great benefit from even a small gift."
Seeking neither fame nor good reputation, nor even the pleasures of the world,
and having severed all longing for arising and ceasing, one seeks only the great fruit of Buddhahood, with no other dharma.
Regarding food, drink, clothing, and all requisites, they seek nothing at all from any quarter;
yet with a mind of giving as vast as even a hair-tip, they seek the gate of ambrosia, which is ever open and expansive.
In all acts of giving, there is no discrimination between high and low; nor is there any heart of flattery, crookedness, or stinginess.
Within this, all indolence is completely eliminated, as one courageously undertakes deeds that benefit the world.
Whether it be wealth or grain that sustains life, or whatever else there may be, give it all away in charity;
having given, give rise to vast and great joy, and the liberation of Bodhi will not be difficult to attain.
To parents, wives, children, and all those one loves, One gives to all who come as beggars;
In giving, there is no heart of hatred or envy— This is the practice of supreme bodhi.
In all that is seen, may there be no anger; may one always view evil friends as if they were virtuous friends;
may one grant consolation to those who are fearful, and remain without attachment to any phenomena or worldly affairs.
Seeking no royal throne, he gives rise to the desire for the Dharma; He constantly proclaims the gateway of the True Dharma of renunciation.
His gift of Dharma reaches all sentient beings, Benefiting the world without ever forsaking it.
Seeking not the various sublime pleasures among the devas, but seeking only the unsurpassed *bodhi* of a Buddha;
not desiring the great renown of giving, he abandons his own body as well as all other dharmas.
Only the Buddha’s bodhi shall never be forsaken;
it is not sought through the visual consciousness of forms, nor is birth among the various heavens sought; one seeks only the supreme bliss of nirvāṇa.
In all actions performed, there is no dependence; whether in success or failure, one seeks nothing at all.
The wise person constantly gives rise to a mind of right knowledge, clearly understanding all dharmas of the true path.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
For this reason, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas diligently practice and cultivate the perfection of giving, they are extensively cultivating the supreme conduct of a Bodhisattva."
Chapter Seven: The Perfection of Ethical Discipline (Śīlapāramitā). Part One. Furthermore, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"What is called the bodhisattva mahāsattvas’ cultivation of the perfection of ethical discipline? This is precisely the extensive cultivation of the bodhisattva’s sublime practices."
Śāriputra! There are three kinds of dharmas that a bodhisattva always practices skillfully.
What are these three?
This refers to the virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind.
What is the virtuous conduct of the body?
A bodhisattva stays far removed from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; this is called the virtuous practice of bodily action.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva remains far removed from false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech, this is called wholesome conduct of the vocal karma.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva possesses non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view, this is called wholesome conduct of the mental karma.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"How may this body, speech, and mind always engage in wholesome conduct?
If the body does not perform actions, there will be no killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct; this is called wholesome conduct of the body."
If one does not perform actions through speech, there will be no false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, or harsh words; this is called virtuous conduct of speech.
If one does not perform actions through the mind, there will be no covetousness, malice, or wrong views; this is called virtuous conduct of mind.
The Bodhisattva further examines things as they truly are: if body, speech, and mind were devoid of activity, how could they manifest or express any phenomena?
What is established regarding body, speech, and mind?

If it were blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, purple, azure, or green, by what could it be manifested? There would be no manifestation through visual consciousness, nor manifestation through auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental consciousness.
Why is this? Because there is no producer and produced, nor any agent and acted upon.
If these were non-existent, how could one establish the various categories of action?

Having reflected thus, the bodhisattva realizes that the characteristics of morality (śīla-lakṣaṇa) are manifest as being without anything to be done. If there is nothing to be done, what representation could there be?
If there is no representation, there is also no grasping. This is what is called the "skillful conduct" of a bodhisattva.

One does not observe even the characteristics of the precepts; because there is no inclination toward the characteristics of the precepts, there is nothing to be observed. When one observes in this way, the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) cannot arise.
If the view of a self-body does not arise, then one does not perceive, through correct investigation, either the upholding or the violating of precepts.
If one observes in this manner, one has no cognitive apprehension of the dharma of the precepts, nor of their rules, nor of their objective sphere.
Maintaining the precepts in this way, one finds nothing to be attained in oneself or in others, nor is there anything to be practiced.
Because there is no practice regarding self or others, there is neither violation nor grasping of the precepts.
If both self and other are unapprehendable, then the precepts are also unapprehendable.
If the precepts are unapprehendable, then there is no deficiency or transgression in the training of the precepts.

If there is no deficiency or transgression in the training of the precepts, then the precepts themselves are without deficiency or transgression; thus, the precepts are without anything to be grasped.
Why is there no grasping?
Because all phenomena are without anything to be grasped.
Therefore, all phenomena have neither self nor other; within this selflessness, how could one grasp at anything?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
“Physical action is pure, and speech is likewise; The mind is always pure as one cultivates pure conduct.
Maintaining the purity of the precepts and practicing them constantly— This is called a bodhisattva upholding the pure precepts.”
The ten paths of wholesome action are most excellent; they are well-observed by the wise Bodhisattvas.
When there is no cultivation whatsoever of body, speech, or mind, this is called the wise upholding of pure precepts.
There is no cultivation, no excellence, and no transmission; there is neither form nor visible color.
If one does not perceive the characteristics of form and visible color, how could any objects be manifested for the eye to see?
If precepts were unconditioned and devoid of cultivation or effort, the eye could not perceive the realm of forms;
the same would apply to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, such that no objects could be represented.
If the sense-faculties and consciousnesses lack any triggering characteristics, one should contemplate with a compassionate mind that even pure precepts do not exist;
within the precepts there is nothing to be attained and nothing to abide in.
Thus understanding the notion of selflessness, one guards the precepts without anything to guard;
without the notion of precepts, one practices within the precepts, remaining free from all views amidst the conduct of awakening.
If one does not observe any views, And there is neither seeing nor even understanding, Then even this state of non-seeing is absent;
Within it, there is no apprehension of either upholding or violating precepts.
If one enters the principle of the unguarded True Dharma, the conduct within the precepts is inconceivable;
being well able to understand the gateway of true protection, there is neither precept nor anything further to be attained.
Because of the perception of non-self, there is no attainment of precepts; Non-self likewise does not exist within the precepts.
To always give rise to a mind free from fear as taught— This pure precept is called the discourse on non-self.
When there is no grasping or understanding of the precepts, there is no self; the basis upon which the precepts rely likewise does not exist.
Without precepts, without seeking, and without the word "self," there is neither upholding nor violating, and nothing to be grasped.
Because precepts are without self, there is nothing that arises; being without self, one is thus able to be without the notion of precepts.
The practice of bodhi is the gateway to profound wisdom; through such characteristics of the precepts, one attains fearlessness.
Those who have transgressions likewise have nothing to attain; those who uphold [the precepts] do so through the increase of the Sage’s power.
That all dharmas are without attainment is also thus; yet for the sake of the ignorant, one speaks of upholding and transgressing.
How great is the one who well guards the pure precepts! Regarding the supreme fruit of the precepts, they are neither bound nor liberated;
Because all views are severed, no transgression arises, And they shall never fall into the three evil realms.
Precepts have nothing to be maintained and nothing to be received; when the view of self does not arise, one does not fall.
To thus fully understand the precepts therein is itself to neither maintain nor violate them.
If one cannot perceive my Dharma, there is no observation even within the three realms of existence;
how much less could there be any practice of observance or transgression? One who perceives in this way is a true upholder of the precepts.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are ten kinds of wholesome dharmas of a bodhisattva that arise from that pure mind and intention, that arise from those superior practices of diligence, and that arise from that vast karmic retribution of supreme, excellent aspiration and resolute conviction. They consist in: attending upon and serving the noble ones; not giving rise to discrimination regarding teachers or masters as being either 'noble' or 'teacher'; hearing and receiving the true Dharma while diligently seeking non-attachment; and aspiring for bodhi without begrudging body or life."

Śāriputra! These ten kinds of superior dharmas of a bodhisattva who upholds the precepts all emerge from within the bodhisattva’s own mind; if one can abide securely in these ten kinds of dharmas, one will be able to accumulate all wholesome dharmas.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Scroll 18.
The Buddha-spoken Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka,
Scroll 19.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Scattered Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, recipient of the purple robe, during the Western Heaven (India). Chapter Seven, Part Two: The Perfection of Ethical Discipline.
The Buddha said: "Śāriputra!..."
What are called wholesome dharmas?
