It should be known that there are three kinds of wholesome dharmas, namely: wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas thus abide in wholesome conduct, they are able to diligently seek and practice the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; they will then attain Bodhi, which constantly follows them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"One should always practice the deeds of body well; this is what all Buddhas have proclaimed.
By approaching a preceptor in every place, one will soon attain the state of great learning and wholesome realms."
Regarding the supreme person: they constantly give rise to a mind of loving-kindness to benefit sentient beings;
their speech is wondrous and pleasant, free from love or hatred, so that those who hear what they say develop a joyful aspiration.
Following all phenomena according to their marks, one is free from anger and malice; with an extremely noble intention, one is entirely impartial.
Cultivating the practice so that no sinful or lustful thoughts arise, one observes with a mind of loving-kindness and always maintains reverence.
Having heard the pure teaching of the Tathāgata, one should revere the True Dharma;
by reason of that reverence for the True Dharma, one will swiftly attain the fruit of awakening.

“Having thus become established in these ten kinds of wholesome dharmas, the bodhisattva diligently seeks out and practices the true Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; he draws near to and serves his ācāryas, following all their instructions, even down to the minor tasks such as providing them with water jars.”
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are ten kinds of mental arousal in a bodhisattva.
What are these ten?
First, a bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: "How painful!

The bodies of all sentient beings in the world are afflicted by disease and distress; four snakes brandish their venomous fangs and harm one another. Accumulating all manner of sufferings, they give rise to many faults—boils, carbuncles, sores, scabs, wind-disorders, bile-disorders, and phlegm-disorders. Manifesting various forms of illness such as those of the eyes and other organs, they pass through many hardships and extreme harms. Rapidly decaying and lacking any solidity, weak, frail, and withered, they quickly move toward the end of life, to be cast away in the forest without a single thing to be enjoyed."
"I shall cause all sentient beings to become weary of this unsubstantial body and to aspire to take up a firm and true body.
"Śāriputra, this is the first arousal of the bodhicitta by a bodhisattva."

Having generated the resolve, one is able to diligently seek out and practice the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, attend upon and serve various ācāryas, and follow whatever they do, ranging from general duties down to the humble service of providing water jars.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"The various elements are like snake venom, fierce and evil; The four kinds mutually serve as one another's support.
Each gives rise to much anger and harm, Producing widespread great illness and affliction within the body."
The two sense-bases of eye and ear give rise to various ailments; the same holds true for those born from the nose and tongue.
The suffering born of the lips and teeth is even more profound, as are the other maladies that arise throughout the body.
When carbuncles first appear, they produce piercing pain; when sores and scabs suddenly break out, the agony increases intensely.
Other various ailments arise through many gates, which thereby envelop and entwine the body on all sides.
Since this body has given rise to manifold sicknesses and afflictions, all manner of sufferings have accumulated within it;
devoid of meaning or benefit, it is subject to much harm, swiftly wasting away until the body perishes.
Once cast away in the forest, what remains? Impermanence is swift and lacks solidity.
Contemplate thus this foul and impure body, which serves as a gathering place for all manner of illness and suffering.
You should cultivate virtuous and noble deeds; these shall serve as the causes for attaining the Buddha-body in the future.
Having cast off such a body of manifold evils, which is swiftly broken, ruined, and decayed,
the Buddha-body is perfected, complete with all virtues— an inconceivable Great Dharma-body.
Looking back upon this body of manifold sufferings, where all outflows increase and nothing is pleasant, one should know that there is no separate dharma of outflow;
it is precisely this body that is the cause of the outflows.
Dwelling briefly in the heat, one desires coolness; Or staying amidst the freezing cold, one longs for shelter.
Alas! What joy is there in this body?
Constantly entangled by old age and death, it is beset by many harms.
Wearied by cold and terrified by heat, their minds are tormented; all who fall away are utterly ruined.
The wise should cultivate the deeds of a true man, aspiring to attain the supreme, authentic body, becoming fit to attend upon the Ācārya, and loathing this illusory physical form.
“Śāriputra! This is the first production of the thought of enlightenment by a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
Second, the Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: "Alas!
All sentient beings in the world possess bodies that are not solid or real; they are subject to annihilation, destruction, ruin, and dispersal."
"Śāriputra! It is like a skilled potter in the world who fashions various vessels according to their respective sizes; though they are successfully produced, they inevitably return to destruction."
The unsubstantial bodies of sentient beings in this world, formed of illusion, are likewise thus.
Furthermore, they are like a great tree with spreading branches, leaves, and abundant flowers and fruit; though it may be lovely and pleasing, it ultimately falls into decay.
The unsubstantial bodies of sentient beings in the world are just like fully ripened fruits;
they are also like drops of dew on the tips of blades of grass at a clear night, which vanish as soon as they are touched by the rays of the sun.
The unsubstantial bodies of sentient beings in the world are likewise impermanent, remaining for only a brief moment.
Furthermore, it is like the great oceans and rivers of the world where the flow of water never ceases; yet the bubbles that gather upon the water appear and vanish instantly.
The bodies of sentient beings in the world are like a mass of foam that cannot be grasped or rubbed; they are just like this.
Furthermore, they are like raindrops falling from the sky that form bubbles, which perish as soon as they arise and cannot remain for even a moment.
The insubstantial bodies of sentient beings in the world, whose inherent nature is weak and inferior, are likewise thus. Śāriputra,
bodhisattvas desire to cause sentient beings to grow weary of and abandon such insubstantial bodies, so that they may aspire to and attain a body that is firm and real.
"This is the second resolve of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Just as a skilled craftsman in the world fashions jars and basins, Using a staff, a wheel, clay, and other materials to complete the vessel,"
All things alike return to the gate of destruction; the life-span of sentient beings is just the same.

Furthermore, like a great tree with wide-spreading roots, its branches and leaves lush and its flowers and fruits abundant, all things alike return to the gate of falling away; the life-span of sentient beings is just the same.
Furthermore, like dewdrops resting on the tips of blades of grass, which vanish instantly when struck by the scorching rays of the sun, the objects of the eye do not remain for even a moment;
the lifespan of sentient beings is likewise.

Furthermore, just as the great ocean and the rivers’ waters contain masses of foam that are inferior and lack solidity, so too are the illusory and frail bodies of sentient beings; like those masses of foam, they are all devoid of reality.
Furthermore, just as when the rain from heaven pours down in torrents, Whirlpools form in the water and bubbles arise,
Which vanish into emptiness in an instant upon observation— So too is this unsubstantial body.
One conceives the thought of reality regarding this unsubstantial body; yet within that very reality, one gives rise to thoughts of unreality.
Such a person does not enter the gate of true reality; this is the realm of false conceptualization and delusion.

If one forms the thought of reality regarding what is real, and generates the thought of unreality regarding what is unreal, that person enters the gateway of reality; this is the true sphere of right reflection.
Once you have given rise to the thought of true reality, serve your venerable teacher and offer him a water vessel;
by transforming this illusory and unreal body, you shall attain a firm and authentic essence.
“Śāriputra! This is the second production of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
Third, the Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: "How tragic!
All sentient beings in the world are unable to reflect in this way:"

"Throughout the long night of birth and death, I have been far removed from virtuous friends and drawn near to evil associates; I have initiated indolence and inferior diligence, shrouded by false views, obscured by the darkness of delusion, and exhausted; I have practiced neither giving nor loving-kindness, nor performed any wholesome deeds, but only created evil karma whose fruit has now matured. Having brought about these unwholesome physical characteristics, my craving has intensified, leaving me emaciated and haggard."

Or they may be born among the hungry ghosts (preta), unable to sustain their lives and taking fire as food; for many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, or many hundreds of thousands of years, they do not even hear the sound of water, let alone obtain a drink.

"I now resolve to give rise to this mind: may I draw near to and practice wholesome dharmas, and associate with virtuous friends; by means of such causes and conditions, may I obtain a human body, live a righteous life, and practice various acts of giving; even to the point of sacrificing my own life to draw near to and serve my ācāryas; and regarding the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, may I diligently seek and cultivate it according to all that is required, summarily including even the service of providing a water jar."
"This is the third arousal of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"All spiritual friends existing in the world, One should go to them and constantly draw near."
Unable to repeatedly draw near to virtuous causes, they consequently fail to give rise to various wholesome deeds.
Because they associate with evil friends, they constantly distance themselves from the wise and good;
their diligence becomes inferior and slack, and they produce faults such as stinginess, malice, flattery, and deception.
Not practicing generosity and lacking joyful devotion, one cannot cultivate any wholesome dharmas;
when the fruit ripens, it will bring about a frail and emaciated body.
One shall sleep through the long night of saṃsāra, with the aggregates as retribution, shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and beset by many terrors.
With neither food nor drink, their hunger and thirst increase; They undergo a vast multitude of sufferings and afflictions.
Throughout many hundreds of thousands of years, The suffering of thirst prevents them from even hearing the sound of water.
Having failed in the path of generosity, they no longer behold it; They obtain not a single auspicious sign of the world.
I now give rise to such a mind: The human body in this world is exceedingly difficult to obtain;
I vow to draw near to the ācārya, And swiftly attain the perfection of all virtuous deeds.
One should always distance oneself from evil associates, And always draw near to those who are noble and virtuous;
Even sacrificing one’s body and life is no hardship, Wishing to establish the supreme foundation for Bodhi.
Raising up respect for the ācārya, Generating reverent faith and a pure mind,
To receive and serve him with my head bowed— May this be the supreme root of bodhi.
“Śāriputra! This is the third generation of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
Fourth, the Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: "The sentient beings of the world should reflect thus:

'Throughout the long night [of saṃsāra], we have been far removed from virtuous friends and have associated with evil friends; we have initiated indolence and inferior diligence; we have been shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, exhausted, lacking patience and love, and devoid of all wholesome signs. Our minds are distressed and our bodies weary as if struck by blows; oppressed by manifold sufferings, we afflict and disturb other sentient beings.'"
If those conditions did not exist, how could one incur such transgressions?

Because of this, one extensively creates various unwholesome karmas; when the retribution of those unwholesome karmas matures, one shall fall into the realms of cattle, oxen, camels, and donkeys, unable to sustain one's life.

In those realms of rebirth, they take grass as their food; they suffer from chewing, gnawing, and biting, as well as from being beaten, fear, and the hardship of carrying heavy loads, remaining far removed from all virtuous qualities such as generosity.

"I have now resolved to give rise to this mind: I shall draw near to virtuous friends and obtain a human body; I shall not begrudge my life or limb in practicing extensive giving and performing all manner of wholesome deeds; I shall draw near to and serve my ācāryas, diligently seeking and cultivating the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka according to all its requirements, ranging from the most general down to the humble service of providing water jars."
"This is the fourth arousal of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Sentient beings dwell for a long night in perilous evil, Lacking understanding of the various noble paths."
Born among the beasts such as camels and donkeys, one endures a vast multitude of sufferings.
If, in the future, one should obtain a human form and extensively perform virtuous deeds,
turning toward the gateway of the true path to Bodhi— this is the supreme mark of the wise.
I shall arouse respect for those who are already well-established in the Buddha-dharma;
by following the instructions of the ācārya, may this become the supreme root of bodhi.
Throughout inconceivable eons of the past, wandering in the cycle of birth and death,
one has traversed every path that is meaningless and profitless, unable to practice the giving of alms.
Unable to sustain one's own life while dwelling in the world, Lax and indolent, one distances oneself from virtuous friends;
Constantly following the instructions and teachings of evil companions, One turns back and returns to the realms of the miserable destinies.
In continuous succession among camels and donkeys, one is bound with cangues and shackles; the body is fettered, confined, and beaten.
This is the fruition of having distanced oneself from virtuous friends; even within the realms of cattle and beasts, karma does not perish.
Once born into the realms of camels and donkeys, one is bound by heavy chains in deep suffering and misery;
beaten with staves and whips while burdened with excessive loads, it is difficult at such a time to find the company of virtuous friends.
A human body is most difficult to obtain; To draw near a virtuous friend is likewise difficult.
If one draws near for even a moment, great merit is accomplished; Over time, one can overcome all hardships.
If one can well cultivate the actions of body and speech, And with diligence remain far removed from all faults,
With a peaceful mind and a livelihood that accords with the conduct of the multitude, Then I shall draw near to such a spiritual friend.
Serving the ācārya without flattery or crookedness, from this moment I have resolved upon bodhicitta;
I shall widely proclaim the noble path of bodhi, honoring and cherishing my venerable teacher at all times.
With various types of unguents and exquisite fragrances, With manifold fine garments and powdered incense,
And with diverse ornaments and precious flower garlands, The Honored One among bipeds extends this offering.
All Buddhas currently dwelling throughout the ten directions, Revealing the ultimate truth to benefit sentient beings,
Universally radiate great golden light, With infinite forms and colors as an offering.
Just as the Buddha has emitted this wondrous light, To extensively make offerings to the Honored Tamer of Men,
The pure cause for the right path to enlightenment, May we proceed to the site of awakening and realize its fruit.
“Śāriputra! This is the fourth production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
Fifth, the Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought:
"The sentient beings of the world should reflect thus:

'Throughout the long night, we have been far removed from virtuous friends and have associated with evil friends; we have initiated indolence and inferior diligence; we have been shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and exhausted by weariness; we have lacked patience and love, and were devoid of all wholesome signs, such that we had no mindfulness at all.'"

How tragic it is that all sentient beings in the world are unable to reflect upon this: all living things are of one and the same flesh; whether they are preserved or destroyed, their flesh remains no different.

Those who eat and consume it are said to be without transgression and to lack the mark of transgression; they are said to be without merit and to lack the mark of merit. Even as far as the most remote regions at the edge of the ocean, all sentient beings perceive no difference: there is neither transgression nor merit.
For this reason, they are unable to discern between demerit and merit.
Because they lack such knowledge, they associate with those who hold wrong views, which increases their delusion and darkness; failing to recognize the path of virtue, they perform only sinful deeds.

Because they have extensively committed unwholesome karma, when the retribution matures, they obtain an inferior physical form; they even fall into the realm of hell to undergo the sufferings of hell—swallowing hot iron balls, being subjected to torture and flogging, and being bound with cangues and suspended—whereby their karma brings them back to life even as they approach the brink of death.
For many thousands of years they have not heard the sound of music, much less the touch of it.
This is because they do not understand the nature of sin and merit, nor do they cultivate the causes for giving; thus, the wise should keep this in mind.

"I have now resolved to give rise to this mind: I shall draw near to virtuous friends, obtain a human body, and not begrudge my own life or limb. I shall extensively practice giving and perform all manner of wholesome deeds; I shall draw near to and serve various ācāryas, diligently seeking and practicing the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka according to its requirements, summarily including even the service of providing water jars."
"This is the fifth arousal of the bodhicitta by a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Because of associating with evil friends, One deceives others with an evil mind;..."
Relying upon sinful karma and false views, I have extensively generated such evil deeds.
Beings dwelling in the most remote and desolate frontiers eat and drink to their hearts' content without any sense of satiety;
they all claim that both sin and merit lack any cause, and that there are no retributions for suffering or pain.
Seeing such karmic offenses as these, they repeatedly associate with evil friends;
being consistently harsh and malevolent, their transgressions are profound, and by this they quickly fall into hell.
Even if one should obtain a human body after a thousand transmigrations, one will soon fall back into the three miserable realms;
there, one will not see the Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened One, appearing in the world as an object of refuge,
nor will one hear the most excellent renown of all the spiritual friends in the world.
If in the future I should obtain a human body, may I extensively cultivate all virtuous and wholesome deeds;
for a human life in this world is most difficult to attain, and the lifespan of sentient beings is likewise rare.
The True Dharma of the Tathāgata is extremely difficult to hear; the appearance of Buddhas in the world is truly difficult to encounter.
Even having obtained a human body, which is itself so rare, it is even more difficult to swiftly attain the Noble Path.
If I should encounter the time when a Buddha appears in the world, I shall follow the pure teachings of the Omniscient One.
Regarding all misdeeds and transgressions arising from my three karmas of body, speech, and mind,
within this state of ultimately impermanent suffering, I vow never again to commit them.
Furthermore, because the inner mind is pure, the causes and effects of sinful karma are likewise so.
Within the midst of incomplete suffering, just as that inner mind is entirely pure,
all extremely wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are truly difficult for those lacking wisdom in this world to perform.
Except for relying upon the Ācārya, who is the supreme root of the aspiration for Bodhi—
one should know that the true path is called the Noble Path; as it is skillfully proclaimed according to one's own inclination,
one should enter the gate of non-deceptive diligence and act as the supreme root of the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Once the Bodhisattva has thus resolved their mind, they honor their teachers with the utmost reverence, offering them water jars;
having perfected both wisdom and skillful means, this constitutes the vast practice of a Bodhisattva.
“Śāriputra! This is the fifth arousal of the mind of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
Sixth, the Bodhisattva arouses this thought:
"The sentient beings of the world should reflect thus:

'Throughout the long night, I have been far removed from spiritual friends and have associated with evil associates; lacking wholesome aspirations, I was unable to be humble, respectful, and faithful toward my teachers and wise ones, nor did I praise them in a hundred ways, attend upon them, pay homage, join my palms in sincerity, or perform various virtuous deeds. Instead, I merely increased my arrogance and committed many unwholesome acts.'"

Due to the ripening of the karmic fruit and retribution of the unwholesome deeds they have committed, even if they obtain a human body, they will be emaciated and haggard, unable to sustain their lives or practice generosity.

Though born among humans, their nature is stingy and they are further impoverished; or they become slaves, driven by others and bound to them, like birds addicted to desire that fly through the air, yet remain terrified and beset by peril wherever they dwell.

Sentient beings with wrong views are likewise: they destroy the pure precepts and constantly practice the three unwholesome roots; dwelling within the four realms of existence, they are shrouded by the five hindrances; they constantly practice the six ways of failing to respect teachers and elders; they cannot follow the seven kinds of excellent and sublime Dharma; they give rise to the eight wrong paths and enter the group of those fixed in falsehood; they constantly harbor malice toward the nine grounds for resentment; and they constantly engage in the ten unwholesome courses of action.

They enter unrighteous paths with stubborn ferocity; they turn their faces toward the gates of hell and their backs to the heavenly realms; they distance themselves from spiritual friends and draw near to evil associates; they follow the inclinations of Māra, abandoning wholesome dharmas and practicing unwholesome ones; they encounter blows, terrors, and hardships wherever they go; and they perform all manner of harmful deeds.
"For this reason, I was unable to take delight in practicing generosity and other such deeds.

Now, having turned my mind toward this, I shall draw near to virtuous friends; once I have attained a human body, I will not begrudge my own life or limb as I extensively practice generosity and perform all manner of wholesome deeds. Regarding the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, I shall diligently seek it out and cultivate its practice in accordance with whatever tasks must be done, summarily including even the service of providing a water jar.
"This is the sixth resolve of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Because of associating with evil friends, arrogance increases; Through such intimacy, one wanders for many oceans of kalpas."
If among humans one receives the body of a slave, One will wander through the three realms of existence for a long night.
A human body is difficult to obtain and experienced through hardship; The marks of a supreme body are exceedingly difficult to attain, And auspicious, wondrous physical features are likewise rare;
The appearance of a Buddha in the world is most difficult to encounter.
I shall draw near to virtuous and noble friends, who reveal the correct path of practice for Bodhisattvas;
may the jewel of the bodhicitta increase extensively, and may I attain it through many koṭis of kalpas.
The body is not solid, like foam or bubbles; it is further like illusions, transformations, songs, and plays.
Just as what is seen within a dream, upon awakening one realizes that nothing is real and all is false.
The span of life draws to a close and the life-force is brief, like a flash of lightning that does not linger;
when life ends in an instant and the aggregates shift, one must abandon this unreal body to seek the true reality.
The passage of time shifts and changes with such rapidity; one must surely shatter the mountain of pride.
Within the three periods of time, which are but a hollow conjunction, beings drift through an inconceivable ocean of kalpas.
Relinquishing the body and detaching from all craving, Without begrudging even one's own life,
Eliminating arrogance and the mind of self-importance, One should always serve the venerable teacher with the utmost reverence.
The Teacher of the World is most supreme and exalted, no different from one’s own parents;
having stilled all pride and arrogance, one should serve him with reverence and diligent devotion.
Regarding the factors conducive to a bodhisattva’s unsurpassed enlightenment, and those practices shared by the supreme bodhisattvas,
may I cherish, revere, and maintain a firm resolve toward them, and may all my actions be characterized by diligent vigor.
When pride and craving arise, pride increases; one who cannot know the dharma for severing pride remains bound.
Only by the vajra of wisdom is it shattered without remainder, so that the great mountain of arrogance collapses entirely.
Causing others to cultivate the supreme conduct of bodhi, To abide most excellently at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa),
Using the True Dharma to subdue all demonic armies, And delivering the multitudes of sentient beings from the four modes of birth and their afflictions.
All those throughout the ten directions suffering from illness, unable to loathe their own impure bodies for themselves—
may I arouse a heart of compassion and vow to become the refuge for all three periods of time.
Extensively practicing the perfection of giving, Furthermore being able to train in the merit of the Buddha’s precepts,
Thoroughly contemplating the complete fulfillment of the practice of patience, I have set forth upon the supreme path of diligence.
Having perfected the pāramitā of meditative concentration, may I abide in perfect peace according to the arising of the mind;
likewise for supreme wisdom and skillful means, I vow to serve my venerable teacher and practice the paramita of generosity.
Increasing the power and majesty of these merits, With inconceivable wisdom and virtue, The aspirations of both self and others become most sublime;
Through diligent training, one becomes a perfected vessel of truth.
"Śāriputra! This is the sixth arousal of the mind of a bodhisattva.
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka*, Scroll Nineteen.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Twenty.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu...

Translated by the Imperial Preceptor for the Propagation of the Dharma, the Dharma Master of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmarakṣa, and others, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Seven, Part Three: The Perfection of Ethical Discipline. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
The Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: "Beings in the world should reflect thus:

'Throughout the long night, we have been far removed from virtuous friends and have associated with evil friends; we have initiated indolence and inferior diligence; we are shrouded in the darkness of delusion and exhausted like those who are mute; we lack vision, lack patience, and lack wholesome affection; we have no understanding of unwholesome karma and its retribution, no understanding of wholesome karma and its retribution, and no understanding of mixed karma and its mixed retribution.'"
Not knowing this for themselves, they are likewise unable to inquire of śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or various ācāryas as to what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
What is blameworthy?
What is blameless?
What is that which one should draw near to?
What should not be associated with? What should be done? And what should not be done?

What is it that, once performed, results in harm and disadvantage throughout the long night and gives rise to all manner of suffering and affliction? It is through this that pride increases, such that one cannot understand the root of wholesome karma and performs only all kinds of unwholesome deeds.
Even if one attains a human body, the faculties may be impaired; furthermore, one may be unable to sustain life among humans and unable to practice generosity.
Moreover, one may be blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired, lacking physical beauty, and be incapable of discerning between well-spoken and ill-spoken words.
"Because of such [faults], I have no desire to practice giving.

Now I must turn back this mind, draw near to virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitra), and if I obtain a human body with all faculties intact and am able to sustain my life, I shall practice giving without begrudging even my own body or life. Possessing physical strength and beauty, and being able to fully comprehend both well-spoken and ill-spoken words, I shall further inquire of my venerable teachers and wise ones: "What is wholesome?"
What is unwholesome?
What is blameworthy?
What is blameless?
What is that which should be cultivated?
What is that which should not be cultivated?
And what are those actions performed at the time [of practice] that contravene the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, while conforming to the meaning of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka?
One should draw near to and serve all ācāryas, following whatever they do.
One should grow weary of this unreal body and aspire to attain a firm, true body.
"In brief, this extends even to the service of providing water jars.
This is the seventh arousal of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
“Desiring to draw near to virtuous friends for their benefit, I have remained far away for many hundreds of kalpas,
unable to inquire about the gates of good and evil, or the retributions of faults and merit.”
Those with overweening pride fall into the hells, And among the various realms of animals and hungry ghosts;
Associating with friends who commit sinful deeds, They endure suffering for many eons without end.
Even if one obtains a human body, with impaired faculties, one will undergo saṃsāra for many thousands of kalpas;
unable to discern the gates of good and evil, nor the retributions of transgression and innocence.
If one attains a human body free from hardship and suffering, with all faculties intact and auspicious marks complete;
if one possesses these perfect human traits at a time free from calamity, it is like a one-eyed turtle encountering a floating log.
Having beheld the Lamp of the World illuminating all, and having heard the stainless Dharma within the Buddha’s teaching,
he then questioned the Honored One of the World regarding the fruits and retributions of both wholesome and unwholesome deeds.
What is the destination of the miserly?
How is it that those who are not miserly are able to practice giving?
Furthermore, what is the nature of those who are greedy, deceitful, and violators of the precepts?
Furthermore, why do they not break the pure precepts?
How is it that their minds of anger and malice remain unmoved?
And how is it that their minds are indolent and distracted?
What is the joy of diligence and meditative concentration?
What is the state of evil wisdom and the darkness of delusion?
How does one attain that true wisdom?
What is the skillful means of the bodhisattva practice?
What are the six kinds of noble conduct?
With a vast mind of loving-kindness, one excels throughout the world.
How shall beings in the evil realms be saved?
How may they delight in the Dharma with tireless hearts?
Widely and diligently seeking the treasury of bodhisattva conduct, may they dwell securely throughout the lands of the ten directions.
How does one personally approach the Honored One of the World?
How does one pay homage and cultivate all merits?
Furthermore, what is the practice-gate of Samantabhadra?
Just as I now draw near with devotion, how should I inquire of the ācārya?
I wish to hear of the venerable and honored matters of the teacher, so as to give rise to a heart of joy in the ācārya; once this mind has arisen, one is a true son of the Buddha.
With the power of merit and the power of wisdom as the predominant factors, the vast wisdom accomplished therein increases the power of wisdom;
thus, with a resolute mind, he joyfully offered the water jar.
“Śāriputra! This is the seventh production of the thought of enlightenment of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: "Sentient beings in the world should reflect thus:

'Throughout the long night, we have been far removed from virtuous friends and have associated with evil friends; we have initiated indolence and inferior diligence; we are shrouded in the darkness of ignorance and exhausted like those who are mute and dumb. Yet, all the worldly words and phrases that accord with the meaning of the teachings and accord with the words of the Dharma—because they accord with the words of the Dharma—abide in tranquility and accord with the departure from greed; they dwell together with extinction, right knowledge, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and nirvāṇa.'"

In all that I have done, I have utterly abandoned it; I am unable to comprehend the meaning of the words and the conjunction of the phrases, nor can I dwell even for a moment with Nirvāṇa. Furthermore, I am incapable of receiving, upholding, reading, or reciting [the teachings]; I lack the power, the manly strength, the manly vigor, the manly diligence, and the supreme exertion; I am without cause and without condition.

The afflictions of all sentient beings are likewise without cause and without condition; the defilement of sentient beings is without cause and without condition; the purification of sentient beings is without cause and without condition.
Relying on such causeless views, they are unable to understand the wholesome karma they have performed and instead create only unwholesome karma.

Even if one attains a human body, one's faculties may be impaired; furthermore, among humans, one may be unable to sustain life or practice giving. Enshrouded by delusion, blind, deaf, mute, and lacking physical vigor, one cannot comprehend the meaning of words or the conjunction of phrases, and so forth, failing even to dwell in harmony with *nirvāṇa*, nor being able to receive, uphold, read, or recite [the teachings].
"Because of this, I have been unable to draw near to and practice the wholesome dharmas.

I should now turn my mind back toward them and draw near to the wholesome dharmas; even at the cost of my life, I shall thoroughly understand the meaning of the words and the harmony of the phrases, and dwell together with the path of renunciation and nirvāṇa.

Regarding the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one should diligently seek, practice, receive, uphold, read, and recite it; exerting diligent effort, one should attend upon and serve the various ācāryas. By receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one becomes weary of this unreal body and aspires to attain a firm and real body, through which the supreme power of merit and wisdom shall be fully perfected.

Because they have attained full endowment through the power of merit and wisdom, they are able to accumulate the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka through their habitual practice; they draw near to and serve their various ācāryas, following them in all their activities, ranging from general duties down to the humble service of providing water jars.
"This is the eighth arousal of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Because all dharmas are in accord with their true meaning, One practices the path of cultivation within the factors of the Noble Path."
Within the principle of quiescent extinction, one enters the gate of realization, and thus attains the truth upon the path to nirvāṇa.
If one distances oneself from this Dharma, there will be no benefit whatsoever regarding all phenomena;
even if one engages with words of profit, if they do not accord with the truth, one cannot draw near to that True Dharma.
There is no power, nor is there any vigor; the capacity and function of a person are entirely absent.
There is likewise no other diligence or courage, and nothing whatsoever can be found anywhere.
One then perceives that there is neither Buddha nor Dharma, Neither father, mother, nor kinsmen;
Because of this, both good and evil karma are non-existent, And all retributions are entirely absent.
Those who hold such views regarding sinful karma repeatedly associate with them;
their roots of sin become deep, and as they remain consistently harsh and evil, they increase day by day, causing them to fall into hell for a vast duration.
Emerging from hell, one receives the retribution of an animal; in the realm of hungry ghosts, the offenses are even deeper.
Thereafter, even if one should obtain birth among humans, one will be deaf, mute, foolish, and ignorant, lacking the faculty of speech.
Due to residual karma, they further receive the retribution of being mute and speech-impaired;
their suffering increases through the defects of ignorance and delusion, and they again undergo the calamities of hell. Because they do not understand, they shall fall into ruin.
After a long period of time, one shall attain it:
a human body endowed with perfect and complete marks, with all faculties intact and superior strength increased. Abiding in purity according to the occasion, one reflects:
"If one accords with the meaning of all phenomena, one will immediately attain the path leading to liberation."
Cultivating the path to enlightenment and realizing bodhi—
this treasury of all the great Bodhisattvas, which harmonizes the meaning of the profound and correct Dharma,
is extremely difficult to encounter even after the passage of thousands of koṭis of kalpas; the arising of pure faith therein is most hard to obtain.
Whether these or other extensive and numerous teachings— the inconceivable sublime Dharma of all Buddhas—
whosoever is able to receive and uphold them through various practices establishes the supreme foundation for the enlightenment of a Buddha.
I shall personally attend upon and serve the ācāryas, honoring and placing my faith in them;
I shall do likewise for all buddhas and bodhisattvas, thereby attaining the most supreme and pure faith.
Having given rise to such a pure mind, this is the vast mind of a Bodhisattva;
with supreme wisdom and skillful means fully perfected, they constantly serve others with water jars in unflagging diligence.
“Śāriputra! This is the eighth arousal of the mind of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: "How tragic!
All sentient beings in the world, because they are attached to their own bodies and lives, are constantly pursued by all manner of meaningless and inverted actions."
What is called conduct that is without benefit?

It refers to those sentient beings who are attached to their own bodies and lives and are unable to take delight in the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). With the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) as their precursor, they are firmly grasping and shrouded by the darkness of ignorance; they pursue and destroy all matters [of spiritual practice]. This is what is called conduct that is without benefit.

Furthermore, because sentient beings cherish their own bodies and lives, they take the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as their guide; they become attached to their wives, children, and acquaintances, and with a mind of craving and clinging, they conceal themselves in the darkness of ignorance, thereby distancing themselves from all beneficial matters. This is called conduct that is without meaning or profit.

Furthermore, because sentient beings cherish their own bodies and lives, they take the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as their precursor; they look after and guard their slaves, laborers, and servants with anxious concern. This is called conduct that is devoid of benefit.

Furthermore, among all sentient beings in the world, those whose conduct is constantly pursued by meaningful benefit are as follows: if sentient beings do not begrudge their own bodies or lives and instead delight in the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), taking the bodhicitta as their guide, they skillfully cultivate the actions of body, speech, and mind; this is called conduct that possesses meaningful benefit.

Furthermore, when sentient beings do not begrudge their own bodies or lives and constantly delight in the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), taking the bodhicitta as their guide, they accumulate the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*) up to and including the accumulation of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); this is called conduct that possesses meaningful benefit.

Furthermore, when sentient beings do not begrudge their own bodies or lives and constantly delight in the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), taking the bodhicitta as their guide, they practice generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation to universally gather in all sentient beings; this is called "action with purposeful benefit."

Furthermore, when sentient beings do not begrudge their own bodies or lives and constantly delight in the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), taking the bodhicitta as their guide, they cultivate the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, and the path—the supreme factors conducive to enlightenment. This is called "action with purposeful benefit."

Furthermore, when sentient beings do not begrudge their own bodies or lives but constantly love and delight in the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma), taking the bodhicitta as their guide, they listen to and receive the instructions of their parents and ācāryas; they prostrate, praise, reverently trust, join their palms, and respectfully carry out all that is required—this is called conduct that possesses meaningful benefit.

Furthermore, when sentient beings do not begrudge their own bodies or lives but constantly delight in the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), taking the bodhicitta as their guide and always performing the affairs of the Triple Gem with a pure mind—this is called conduct that possesses meaningful benefit.
Furthermore, sentient beings may think:
"Because I cherish my body and life, meaningless and unbeneficial matters constantly pursue me.
I shall arouse diligent vigor and attend upon and serve my various ācāryas, not sparing my body or life as I follow whatever they command."
Disgusted with this unreal body, one aspires to attain a firm and real body; through the supreme power of merit and wisdom, one shall fully accomplish it.
Because of this full accomplishment, all habitual practices will be successfully realized, and upon reaching the site of enlightenment, one shall realize the sacred fruit.
"Śāriputra! This is the ninth arousal of the mind of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"If a person, out of attachment to their own body and life,
does not delight in the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) and fully accomplishes the three unwholesome karmas, such a one is merely a foolish worldling."
Those who cherish their own bodies, their wives, and all their children and kinsmen—
this mind of attachment to what is meaningless causes the deluded to revolve within the three realms.
Furthermore, regarding slaves, servants, and laborers, his unawakened mind is constantly preoccupied with them;
this attachment to what is meaningless and profitless is profound.
He amasses vast quantities of wealth and grain to support his four-footed livestock and other possessions, yet he neither uses them himself nor gives them to others.
Because this attachment to what is meaningless and unbeneficial is so deep, they guard their secret treasuries and do not reveal them.
Due to this defiled clinging to what is meaningless, those fools always cherish it with affection;
conversely, toward the benevolent mind of a bodhisattva, they abandon it and are unable to give rise to love or joy.
If one can disregard even body and life, Delighting in the supreme dharmas of enlightenment,
And brings the three types of wholesome karma to completion, This is what is called having meaningful purpose.
Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence, As well as meditative concentration and supreme wisdom—
When these are conjoined with skillful means, This is what is called "possessing meaningful benefit."
Serving one's parents as the foremost guide, and likewise honoring one's teachers and elders;
contemplating with discernment the gateway of the Triple Gem—this is what is called having meaningful benefit.
The profound treasury of all great Bodhisattvas, which universally encompasses all supreme Dharma-gates—
those who receive, uphold, recite, and widely proclaim it shall be said to possess meaningful benefit.
These sublime practices, which possess meaningful benefit, were personally proclaimed by all the Buddhas;
being in accord with the meaning as it was taught, these are called the vast conduct of the Buddha-sons.
Having generated such a great resolve, one further gives rise to pure and sincere faith;
one draws near to and serves the ācārya, providing him with a water flask and attending to all his needs.
“Śāriputra! This is the ninth arousal of the mind of a bodhisattva.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!”
The Bodhisattva gives rise to this thought: "How tragic!

All sentient beings in the world are unable to discipline their minds and intentions in accordance with reality; they oppose all the instructions of their preceptors and thus fail to obtain the wealth of the preceptor."
What is called the wealth of the ācārya?

It refers to the wealth of faith, the wealth of ethical discipline, the wealth of learning, the wealth of relinquishment, the wealth of wisdom, the wealth of shame, and the wealth of dread; these seven dharmas are called the wealth of the ācārya.
Because they do not obtain such wealth, they shall suffer the affliction of poverty that oppresses their minds.
A wise person should skillfully subdue the mind, follow all the instructions of the ācārya, and practice generosity and perform various virtuous deeds.
Why is this? Because if one can skillfully subdue the mind and practice the perfection of giving in accordance with the instructions, that person will obtain the wealth of the ācārya.
Furthermore, what is meant by the "wealth of the ācārya"?
This refers to attaining the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, which universally encompasses all the sublime practices and skillful methods of subduing for bodhisattvas.
Having understood this, one should diligently seek out and cultivate the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and extensively proclaim and expound it for others.
If one can abide securely in the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one will attain the ultimate eradication of poverty and suffering and proceed toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Having thus resolved the mind, one is immediately able to comply with the instructions of the ācārya, practicing generosity and other virtues; one grows weary of this unreal body and aspires to attain a firm, real body. One draws near to and serves the various ācāryas, following whatever they do, summarily including even the service of providing water jars.
“Śāriputra! This is the tenth arousal of the mind of a bodhisattva.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"All those sentient beings who are difficult to tame, whose inner minds are deceitful and treacherous, and who are moreover wicked—
those who oppose the instructions of their teachers and masters and are unable to endure them with patient composure."
Having recognized that these are difficult to subdue, one should follow the teacher’s instructions;
by acting according to what has been proclaimed in those teachings, one will immediately obtain the noble treasure of the Great Sage.
What are called the wealth of faith and the wealth of ethical discipline, The wealth of learning and likewise the wealth of relinquishment;
Among these, the most excellent is said to be the wealth of wisdom, With the wealth of shame and dread of blame as the seventh.
Having understood these noble riches, the seven kinds of hidden treasures will be inexhaustible;
yet if one is unable to understand them, such a person is called an unfit vessel for the Dharma.
If they are beings who are vessels for the Dharma, They shall then fully possess all Buddha-dharmas;
Free from flattery and well-disciplined, they are worthy of praise; Exerting diligent effort, they practice the conduct of giving;
With a heart that honors the sublime desire for the Dharma, They would not find it difficult to sacrifice even their own lives.
Cultivating the Buddha’s Bodhi, one becomes a vessel for the Dharma; Knowing this, one practices with constant uninterruptedness.
The Dharma-realm is equal and without distinction— Thus proclaimed by the Buddha, the Honored Tamer of Men.
This Dharma gate of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka enables one to dwell securely in awakening;
the vast Dharma as it has been taught is the true wealth of all Buddhas.
It is the gateway to the selflessness of all phenomena; it is signless and likewise devoid of the mark of emptiness.
It has no life-span and no agent, nor does it possess conceptual proliferation or any latent store.
Within the intrinsic nature of all phenomena, there is neither arising nor marks; such is their primordial state.
All phenomena are neither established nor destroyed; observe them with discernment as being fundamentally without marks.
Those who are well-disciplined act according to the instructions; following all commands, they practice skillfully.
If they attain the vision of the Buddha’s spontaneous wisdom, they enter the gate of liberation through their own objective realm.
Just as with the wealth of faith and the wealth of ethical discipline, so too are the seven factors—learning, renunciation, shame, dread of blame, and wisdom.
These unsurpassed treasures of the noble ones, when fully perfected through these seven qualities, yield inexhaustible benefit.
Hearing the treasury of the Dharma, they open wide the gates of giving; skillfully harmonizing their minds, they accord with all things.
They constantly draw near to virtuous friends and always cultivate every wholesome deed.
Holding the unsurpassed Great Bodhi in the highest reverence, they diligently practice all dharmas in this same way.
Having given rise to such a sublime mind, Like one parched with thirst seeking a drink without weariness,
I offer with a heart of vast affection and joy Pure water filling a vessel of stainless clarity.
“Śāriputra! This is the tenth arousal of the bodhicitta of a bodhisattva.

Having aroused this mind, he diligently seeks out and practices the sublime Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka; he draws near to and serves his ācāryas, following their instructions in all matters, ranging from general duties down to the humble service of providing them with water jars.”
By the power of these most excellent roots of goodness, the practitioner of the bodhisattva path attains four kinds of dharmas. What are the four?

First, they swiftly attain all wholesome dharmas as taught by the ācārya; second, they accord with the words of the ācārya; third, their practice is swiftly accomplished; and fourth, they fulfill the causal conditions for the dharma of practice.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
those who practice the bodhisattva path and are born among humans obtain four kinds of dharmas.
What are these four?
First, he instructs many people, enabling them all to abide securely in accordance with all wholesome dharmas.
Second, while dwelling in mountain caves, he causes those many people to be filled with joy.
Third, with a vast and expansive mind, many people will all come to him day and night.
Fourth, without any further exertion, upon the end of his life, he will attain rebirth in the celestial realms.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a practitioner of the bodhisattva path who is born among the gods attains four kinds of dharmas.
What are these four?
First, they obtain the foremost seat among that assembly of devas;
second, wherever they turn, that assembly of devas gazes upon their facial expressions;
third, whatever they say is received and understood.

Fourth, he goes at the proper time to the abode of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, to request a resolution of his doubts, yet does not go to the other hosts of devas; thus he obtains the enjoyment of that palace among the devas.
Śāriputra! When those who practice the bodhisattva path are born into that heaven, they attain these four kinds of dharmas.
If they are born among humans, they likewise attain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of dharma-gates.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"Having attained those lofty and supreme seats among the devas, And having gained the constant reverence and faith of the deva hosts,
Beheld and venerated by all the deva assemblies, Thus one constantly hears the well-spoken Dharma."
All that was done was by the wise; Śakra questioned the Dharma without avarice.
Having attained those exquisite palaces in that heaven, he passed away from the celestial realm and came to the human world.
Furthermore, one attains a superior birth among humans, Becoming a Wheel-Turning King who rules over the four continents;
Having passed away from the human realm, one is reborn once more, To experience supreme bliss within those celestial realms.
In the celestial realms one no longer undergoes painful sensations; honoring the venerable teacher with the crown of one’s head is the cause for this.
Through these four kinds of sublime and wondrous gates, one constantly attains such vast and great matters.
By giving rise to such a mind free from attachment, one reveres the deeds of the venerable teacher with the crown of one's head;
with a pure heart, one offers the water flask, cherishing and honoring them always without weariness.
Furthermore, they shall receive the constant veneration and offerings of all devas, humans, and nāgas;
and within the celestial realms where they are born, they shall likewise attain four kinds of dharmas.
What are the four dharmas by which one can fully know all actions performed in the past,
the accumulation of virtuous conduct and its causes, and the fact that what is done in the present life never diminishes?
Furthermore, by virtue of these wholesome dharmas, one fully understands the locus of arising and ceasing;
one knows that present arising is without movement, and thus understands the activity of all phenomena.
He was able to proclaim extensively for the sake of the devas, revealing and instructing them according to the Dharma;
having widely performed the gates of supreme practice that bring benefit and joy, he subsequently passed away from the celestial realm.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

A practitioner of the bodhisattva path attains four kinds of dharmas. Although this text mentions four dharmas, it contains only one or two, lacking the third and fourth; these were originally absent from the Sanskrit manuscript and cannot be added."
What are the four?
First, having passed away from among the devas, one is reborn among humans within a class of beings who observe the same precepts.
Second, having been born among humans, one attains five kinds of compassionate qualities in this present life.

What are the five? First, being born in this life with the arising of wholesome dharmas; second, being endowed with perfect physical appearance and deportment in this life; third, having the perfection of pure precepts in this life; fourth, having a vast retinue of followers in this life; and fifth, giving rise to contemplation of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings in this life.
"Furthermore, one shall obtain five kinds of indestructible dharmas. What are these five?

First, one's virtuous friends and spiritual mentors shall never be separated; second, one's body shall not quickly perish; third, one's wealth, joy, and enjoyments shall never be destroyed; fourth, the bodhicitta one has generated shall be firm and cannot be destroyed; and fifth, during times of famine, the dharma-joy shall be abundant and ripe."
"Furthermore, one shall obtain five kinds of rare and marvelous dharmas.
What are these five?
First, if an empty vessel is placed in a certain location, it will naturally become filled with pure water, and within that water will abound all manner of exquisite and precious jewels."
Second, when they thirst and require water, eight kinds of meritorious water will spontaneously appear before them.
Third, their bodies shall be free from all calamities, namely: poison or weapons, fire or water, the subduing power of others' majesty, or the terror of being swallowed and devoured.

Fourth, if one encounters the kalpa of weapons, the kalpa of pestilence, the kalpa of famine, the kalpa of fire disasters, the kalpa of water disasters, the kalpa of wind disasters, the kalpa of thirst and exhaustion, the kalpa of scorching heat, or the calamities of yakṣas, and is reborn within Jambudvīpa, one will immediately attain birth in the celestial realms to experience all manner of bliss; the exquisite pleasures one receives will be like those of the *vajra-līlā*.
This is a rare and marvelous Dharma.
The Buddha-spoken Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra, Fascicle Twenty.
[The Buddha-spoken Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra, Fascicle Two].

11. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao San Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Fan Translation, and the Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Fahu, et al., by Imperial Decree. Chapter Seven: The Perfection of Ethical Discipline (Śīlapāramitā), Part Four. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

Fifth, those who practice the bodhisattva path, by means of these roots of goodness, will be free from all obstacles and difficulties in this present life; they will not fall into the evil destinies in this present life; no misdeeds will be able to disturb their minds, and they will swiftly attain liberation.
These five kinds of rare and wonderful qualities are all brought to perfection by those who practice the bodhisattva path through the power of their roots of goodness.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
By the power of these roots of goodness, they further attain four dharmas that are inseparable from meditative equipoise (*samādhi*). What are the four?
First, bodhisattvas who share this vision give rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings suffering in affliction.
Second, all their male and female relatives will develop a sense of respect and affection for them.
Third, although the signs of old age approach and they gradually grow decrepit, the power and influence of their roots of virtue will instead increase.
Fourth, the wealth and profits one obtains increase a hundredfold, gradually progressing from one to three.
Furthermore, one attains three kinds of harmlessness.
What are these three?
First, being free from harm through greed; second, being free from harm through hatred; third, being free from harm through delusion.
Furthermore, they attain four kinds of dharmas of peace and happiness.
What are these four?

First, being free from all illness and affliction for a long time; second, the body not becoming withered or emaciated; third, having no lack or deficiency in enjoyments; and fourth, not being oppressed by the perils of kings, the perils of thieves, or any other such calamities.
Furthermore, one attains four kinds of honored states.
What are these four?

First, becoming a wheel-turning monarch who rules over the four great continents, governing through the True Dharma and possessing the seven treasures—the seven treasures being the wheel treasure, the elephant treasure, the horse treasure, the jewel treasure, the woman treasure, the householder treasure, and the military commander treasure—surrounded by a thousand sons, each brave and heroic, all endowed with fearlessness and the most excellent physical marks, capable of subduing enemy armies;

Furthermore, all that is practiced and enacted throughout the four great continents accords with the king’s transformation; from the high ministers and assistant officials to the minor kings, and even down to the citizens and commoners of the cities and towns, they all revere him and place their faith and trust in him.

Second, they do not become excessively attached to the pleasures of the five desires—namely, seeing forms with the eyes, hearing sounds with the ears, smelling fragrances with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, and feeling tangibles with the body—but experience these five objects without clinging;
they develop pure faith and delight in leaving the household life, swiftly attain the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and are constantly held in high esteem by humans and non-humans alike.
Third, in every place where they are born, they are preeminent in all things—supreme in wisdom, supreme in insight, and supreme in royal supernormal powers;

this is because in past lives they cultivated various virtuous deeds and possessed great renown, thereby attaining the most exalted throne of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), and were served by ministers and officials throughout the kingdom and cities, with whom they always maintained a spirit of respect.

Fourth, up until the realization of the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, which is most honored and supreme, one stands preeminent within the great assembly of all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; one is likewise preeminent among those who cultivate morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, and is further able to achieve preeminence within the dharmas of morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

These are the four kinds of reverent practices: namely, by honoring one’s ācārya and elders, attending to whatever tasks they require, and providing them with water jars; by accumulating such immeasurable merit through the reception of the Dharma and the attainment of the benefits of the Dharma, whether coming or going, one does not act in contradiction to what has been taught.
"Furthermore, by means of these roots of goodness, one attains four kinds of dharmas endowed with favorable conditions (*pratyaya*). What are the four?
First, one attains the favorable conditions of a king; 'favorable conditions of a king' refers here to the favorable conditions among the rishis."
Second, abandoning sensual pleasures and giving rise to pure faith and a joyful aspiration for renunciation—this is said to be the fulfillment of the conditions for the Dharma.

Third, for one practicing the bodhisattva path, in every birth—whether in this life, in other lives, or in all births—they attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and never abandon the great mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*)—this is said to be the fulfillment of the conditions for mindfulness.

Fourth, until they realize the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they will be surrounded by the fourfold assembly who revere, respect, and have faith in them; and even all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans will constantly surround them, respecting, honoring, and having faith in them.

Furthermore, when a practitioner of the bodhisattva path receives even a single four-line verse from an ācārya, they follow the ācārya’s instructions exactly: if told to come, they come; if told to go, they go. They recognize, "This is a root of virtue; this is not a root of virtue. They recognize, "This is blameworthy; this is blameless. They recognize, "This is to be associated with; this is not to be associated with. They recognize, "When this is done, it is without benefit and gives rise to suffering and affliction"; and they recognize, "When this is done, it brings benefit and peace. Accordingly, they do not perform what is unwholesome and practice the wholesome dharmas as instructed, remaining free of all obstacles and without contradiction.
Those who attain full ordination by means of these roots of goodness obtain four kinds of sublime qualities. What are the four? First, the excellence of pure ethical discipline;

second, the excellence of physical marks; third, the perfection of physical marks; and fourth, the attainment of the faculty of great wisdom—attaining swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, extremely rapid wisdom, profound wisdom, and wisdom of excellent discernment—and upon the dissolution of the body after death, they attain rebirth in the heavenly realms.
Furthermore, one attains four kinds of inconceivable dharmas.
What are these four?
First, one attains the secret inner treasury.

Second, by the power of their roots of goodness, none among their parents, other spiritual friends, or even devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, can perceive the crown of the head (uṣṇīṣa) of those who practice the bodhisattva path, despite their pure minds.

Third, by the power of their roots of goodness, in whatever they do, neither their parents, nor their acquaintances, nor even humans or non-humans—whether with pure or impure minds—are able to perceive the face or the two feet of those who practice the bodhisattva path.

Why is this? Those who are unable to perceive him do so because he possesses the rare marks of a bodhisattva, because he is endowed with the marks of a great man, and because he speaks the language of a great man.

Fourth, because the practitioner of the bodhisattva path possesses the power of roots of goodness, at the time of birth, the bodhisattva does not require support; he immediately stands upright and secure upon the ground, surveys the four directions, and attains supreme wisdom.

Why is this? It is because the Bodhisattva, having practiced the noble path of non-deceit and extensive learning throughout previous lives, has attained the faculty of the eye of non-deceit and the objects of the eye of non-deceit; thus, he surveys the entire trichiliocosm and perceives everything without obstruction, his divine eye being pure and surpassing that of ordinary humans.
Having attained swift great wisdom, and because they have fully perfected that great wisdom, Bodhisattvas are able to thoroughly understand the hearts of love and joy held by all sentient beings.
Why is this? Because that bodhisattva, through the wholesome deeds performed in previous lives, has been able to masterfully gather all minds.

They regard [the Dharma] with reverence, as if it were a sublime sacred medicine, as if it were various precious jewels, as if it were something extremely difficult to obtain, and as if it were the sentient beings who follow the well-taught path.
Because they have correctly heard and maintained the arising of the True Dharma, the Bodhisattva attains such wisdom of excellent discernment (*suviniścaya-jñāna*).

By virtue of possessing this wisdom of discernment, the Bodhisattva’s pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) is equal to that of all sentient beings, and so on up to their being equal in hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation;
their concordant ethical discipline is equal, and so on up to their being equal in the concordance of hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

The immovability and equality of the precepts of all sentient beings are equal, and so on, up to the immovability and equality of their hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Because the immovability of the precepts of all sentient beings is equal, the growth of the immovability of the precepts of all sentient beings is likewise equal; even so for the growth of the immovability of hearing, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, they are equal. Because the majestic deportment, the path of practice, and the diligent application of cultivation of all sentient beings are equal, all sentient beings thus seek one another.
Furthermore, it is the union of all sentient beings' morality, learning, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.

All the morality and so forth of all sentient beings are immovable; the immovability of all sentient beings' morality and so forth increases. It encompasses the majestic deportment, the path of practice, and the diligence of all sentient beings, gathering together the entire aggregate of merit. In every respect, one truthfully seeks equality, yet even this equality is such that no equality can be perceived.
Furthermore, at the most ultimate root of all things, all sentient beings mutually seek out the mark of self (*ātman*), which is equal; yet even in this equality, no equality is to be perceived.

By means of this, the practitioner of the bodhisattva path swiftly attains all karmic retributions within a single instant, achieves the arising of wisdom, and in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, fully comprehends the thousandfold mental activities of all sentient beings.

In this way, all investigations into the characteristics of a self are entirely equal; even this equality cannot be seen as an equality, for one abides in the supreme state and realizes the emptiness of the self.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva is like a lion and like a great dragon; at birth, he steps upon the ground and immediately walks seven paces, because he has brought forth the supreme karmic fruition of the site of enlightenment.
Having established himself with a single-minded purity and solemn reverence, he spoke these words:
"I am the most excellent and supreme among gods and humans.
I am able to proclaim for all sentient beings the Dharma that brings an ultimate end to birth, old age, sickness, death, and the afflictions of extreme suffering."
"Śāriputra! Thereafter, whether they be bodhisattvas or tathāgatas, they shall produce pure and wondrous sounds throughout the trichiliocosm to reveal all things."
At that time, the great earth shook universally; all were struck with awe and their hair stood on end, while celestial drums and music spontaneously resounded in succession.

Whenever that Bodhisattva stood or walked in that place, the ground trembled and light appeared; his body of wondrous color and form remained poised upon the light, motionless and steady, such that everyone was able to behold him.
Until the attainment of the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, no sentient beings whatsoever are able to see it.
This is the fourth dharma that cannot be seen.

These four kinds of invisible dharmas all arise because the Bodhisattva, in the past, attentively received the instructions of his ācārya; whether going or coming, he followed whatever was required. By the power of these roots of goodness, he has obtained the four kinds of swift dharmas of a Tathāgata.
What are the four?
First, to listen to and receive from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, as they proclaim the True Dharma without any pretense or falsehood.
Second, by the power of one's roots of goodness, the Buddha himself proclaims:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
At that very moment, his hair and beard fell away naturally, the saffron robe was donned upon his body, and he held the alms bowl; thus he attained the appearance of a bhikṣu.
Thirdly, by the power of their roots of goodness, the Tathāgata understands the mentalities of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time.
Fourth, through the arising of wisdom, they gain excellent understanding of supreme and wondrous remedies and medicines, thereby uprooting all the sickness and suffering of sentient beings.
Furthermore, by the power of their roots of goodness, they attain four kinds of faultless qualities.
What are these four?
If it is said that the Tathāgata is subject to the four kinds of perils—fire, wind, weapons, and poison—that is impossible.
Furthermore, he has attained four kinds of faultless qualities.
What are the four?

First, it is impossible that the Tathāgata could cause sentient beings who have not heard the Dharma to listen to the True Dharma, or cause sentient beings who are shrouded in ignorance to receive the verses of the Dharma.
Second, it is impossible for one who does not abide in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-citta*) to give rise to a single thought of awakening.
Third, since the Tathāgata always abides in a state of meditative equipoise, it is impossible to say that he does not practice loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Fourth, if it were said that the Tathāgata is universally able to encompass the physical forms and marks of all sentient beings, such a thing is impossible.
Furthermore, he has attained five kinds of supreme and immeasurable dharmas of the Tathāgata.
What are these five?

First, the Tathāgata’s immeasurable morality and learning; second, immeasurable concentration; third, immeasurable wisdom; fourth, immeasurable liberation; and fifth, immeasurable knowledge and vision of liberation.
“Furthermore, one attains four kinds of dharmas of the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*). What are the four?

First, the unattached and unobstructed knowledge and vision that accords with the turning [of the wheel] of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in the past; second, the unattached and unobstructed knowledge and vision that accords with the turning of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in the future; third, the unattached and unobstructed knowledge and vision that accords with the turning of all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in the present; and fourth, the accomplishment of the inconceivable gateways of the Tathāgata.”

By virtue of the inconceivable gate, one possesses the wisdom of the perfectly awakened one (samyaksambuddha) which is equal throughout the three periods of time; and this wisdom of perfect awakening is not dependent upon anything else.
By means of this inconceivable wisdom, the Tathāgata is fully able to comprehend all phenomena.
If one possesses such inconceivable wisdom, one can then understand all worldly matters, such as wind and rain.
In the world there is a wind named Anuloma (Following the Order); this wind blows upon the sentient beings of the world, rising to a height of three krośas and swirling in the air.
Furthermore, there is a wind named Like a Cloud that blows upon the world; this wind rises to a height of five krośas and swirls in the air.
Furthermore, there is a wind named Delusive Darkness that blows upon the world; this wind rises to a height of ten yojanas and swirls in the air.
Furthermore, there is a wind named Space-like Aspect that blows through the world; this wind rises thirty yojanas high and swirls in the air.
Furthermore, there is a wind named Tathāgata that blows through the world; this wind rises forty yojanas high and swirls in the air.

Śāriputra! Because it is encompassed by the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, he is able to know the characteristics and phenomena of sixty-eight thousand koṭis of wind-circles.

In the western direction there is a wind named Viśāla (Extensive), which blows throughout the world; this wind rises to a height of sixty-eight thousand yojanas and rests within the water-circle of the great earth.
Rising from the water wheel, it further extends sixty-eight thousand yojanas upward.
Śāriputra, as previously described,
beyond this calculation of trichiliocosms, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha currently dwells, teaching the Dharma and transforming sentient beings.
The lifespan of that Buddha was thirty *koṭi* years.

He had a community of thirty *koṭi-nayuta* great śrāvakas, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; they had attained mastery over their minds and reached the further shore.

There was an assembly of one hundred koṭis of great bodhisattvas, all of whom had already attained stability within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; they were those who resolved meanings and expounded the profound ocean of the Dharma through extensive learning, and who had skillfully cultivated the sublime practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
After the Buddha has remained for a thousand years, he will enter Great Parinirvāṇa; following the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for a hundred thousand years.
