Thereafter, the relics of the Tathāgata obtained will be widely disseminated, just as the dissemination of my own relics after my present Parinirvāṇa shall likewise be.

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata’s unimpeded noble wisdom is supreme and immeasurable; the maṇḍala of the wind of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is vast and perfectly complete, and all buddha-fields are likewise entirely fulfilled.
Śāriputra! In the direction above, there is a world where no Buddha has currently appeared in the world.
Therein dwell a thousand assembly of pratyekabuddhas who are presently teaching and transforming sentient beings, because they have planted roots of goodness therein that are embraced by wisdom.

Śāriputra! Because it is embraced by wisdom, the Tathāgata does not merely know those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently dwelling and teaching the Dharma in the direction above, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; rather, he is able to know all the immeasurable, incalculable, inconceivable, and incomparable Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas currently dwelling and teaching the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What roots of goodness must those who practice as bodhisattvas plant in order to fully perfect such unobstructed wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha?”

The Buddha said, “Śāriputra! If a practitioner of the bodhisattva path can skillfully subdue the mind, giving rise to the thought of respect, the thought that [the Dharma] is a holy and wondrous medicine born from the Dharma, the thought of a great treasure, the thought of something extremely difficult to obtain, the thought of supreme roots of goodness, the thought of it being as it has been taught, the thought of extreme reverence, and the thought of upholding the true Dharma, they should thus cultivate progress with diligent vigor.”

Śāriputra! The Tathāgata possesses vast and manifold supreme wisdom, the most exalted and unsurpassed wisdom of non-obstruction—immeasurable, innumerable, inconceivable, incomparable, and ineffable. Within the mere blink of an eye, he attains complete liberation regarding all that comes, goes, moves, or remains throughout as many Buddha-fields in the ten directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
Śāriputra! The liberation I have attained was swiftly gained through hearing and retaining the teachings.
That which is "thoroughly liberated" is called "well-liberated."
What is liberation?
It is the liberation from all suffering. Śāriputra!

If a person hears what has been taught and gives rise to a mind of reverence, that person will immediately be able to generate pure faith regarding what they have heard; abiding as they have heard, they will always remain inseparable from the true Dharma of all Buddhas, and whatever the characteristics of its names, phrases, and syllables may be, they will be able to receive and uphold this true Dharma.
By the power of these superior roots of goodness, one immediately attains four kinds of sublime wisdom.
What are these four?

First, the attainment of great wisdom; second, through that sublime wisdom, seeing the Buddha and being personally received by him; third, through that sublime wisdom, leaving the household life with pure faith; and fourth, through that sublime wisdom, realizing the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
These are the four dharmas of supreme wisdom.
Furthermore, one attains the four kinds of unimpeded dharmas.
What are these four?

First, being born among human beings without hindrance; second, encountering a Buddha appearing in the world and approaching him with faith and devotion without hindrance; third, leaving the household life through pure faith without hindrance; and fourth, realizing the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* without hindrance.
These are the four kinds of unhindered dharmas.
Furthermore, one attains the four factors conducive to the noble state.
What are these four?

First, one becomes a Wheel-Turning King endowed with the supreme golden wheel; second, one becomes a Great Brahmā King presiding over the Brahma world; third, one becomes Śakra, Lord of the Devas; fourth, one realizes the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attains perfect knowledge of the sphere of supernormal powers, obtaining the true eye among both devas and humans.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken these meanings, he further increased his instruction for the assembly of great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, speaking in verse:
"One should contemplate the World-Savior as the supreme cause for all sentient beings."
All boundless wisdoms are fully understood, And the immeasurable bliss of nirvāṇa is attained.
Through the excellence of coming and going, one obtains wondrous fruits;
Forever severing all causes of worldly suffering, One is thoroughly and skillfully tamed to be born among the gods, And in an instant, departs from all evil realms.
May I now swiftly behold all Buddhas, And remain far removed from all causes of suffering and hardship;
May I obtain, with complete mastery and according to my will, The boundless treasures hidden within the world.
All manner of provisions and precious jewels appear in the world according to one's thoughts;
likewise, the waters of the eight virtues are present, and all rivers, sands, ponds, and marshes are perfectly clear and still.
One is freed from the various causes of ugliness, And all afflictions of suffering will not arise;
Through the conditions of deafness, blindness, leprosy, and the like, The well-disciplined one attains the sublime fruit.
All those who are afflicted by diseases in the world— beings who are whole or maimed,
hunchbacked, lame, dwarfed, or deformed— all such defilements shall utterly diminish and vanish.
Far removed from all dissimilar characteristics, one shall obtain the most supreme and excellent retribution;
with a face fully endowed and perfectly beautiful, the well-disciplined one attains the wondrous fruit.
With physical marks so dignified and a great renown, all the devas come to offer worship;
the eight classes of beings all give rise to a heart of reverence, and all sentient beings do likewise.

"Furthermore, those who are well-disciplined obtain this benefit of the fruit: having eliminated all evil destinies, they are thereafter born within the realms of the devas and swiftly accomplish the fruit of great enlightenment."
Those who are well-tamed obtain these fruits and benefits: they skillfully understand the minds of all sentient beings and are adept at penetrating the conduct of all sentient beings.

Having taken seven steps, they emit a great sound throughout all worlds; amidst all consciousnesses, they attain great wisdom and supreme liberation, achieving the most excellent wisdom and bringing full clarity to all sentient beings.

They are well-established within wisdom; their supreme wisdom is entirely pure; they have achieved perfection in the presence of all Buddhas; their wisdom is clear and lucid regarding all essential natures; and they have attained accomplishment for both themselves and others.
If sentient beings possessed the power of wisdom, they would fully accomplish all their activities and be well able to proclaim this meaning in such a way.

However, sentient beings with few desires lack the power of aspiration; those with great greed are entirely deluded and attached; the causes and conditions of their sinful karma all increase; they accumulate immeasurable and boundless evil karma, and are unable to believe in or accept the true Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who have few desires, yet do not give rise to respect for the True Dharma, do not show reverence toward other sentient beings, and instead give rise to extreme states of hatred and defiled minds, claiming for themselves that they have already attained the fruit of Arhatship.
All those in the world who are aged, infirm, or diseased have all manner of great sufferings and afflictions gathered within their bodies.

Such a person obtains this retribution; possessing every kind of unwholesome sign, they receive in vain the food, drink, and other offerings due to an Arhat, and having committed unwholesome karma, they shall fall into hell.
If one cannot maintain those pure precepts and practices, how much less could one attain the fruit of Arhatship?
However, if one gives rise to faith and understanding by constructing various stupas and temples, and develops a mind of reverence, one will be reborn in a favorable realm.
Śāriputra, once they have thus maintained the precepts and cultivated their practice,
those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who seek to enter the treasury of the True Dharma of the Mahāyāna should draw near to their preceptors and constantly obtain immeasurable wholesome dharmas.

In this way and that way, by praising these merits, one shall obtain all manner of virtuous karmic fruits; thereafter, one’s immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, incalculable, and innumerable merits will increase even further.
Once this has been accomplished, Śāriputra,

the bodhisattva mahāsattva who dwells securely in the Bodhisattvapiṭaka attains well-disciplined and pure conduct of the precepts, fully perfected, and brings all the practices of a bodhisattva to complete fulfillment.
“What is meant by ‘the purity of ethical conduct being fully perfected’?
Śāriputra, there are ten aspects of practice for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

What are the ten? First, all sentient beings do not give rise to harm toward the bodhisattva; second, the bodhisattva does not give rise to greedy attachment toward the wealth and treasures possessed by sentient beings; third, the bodhisattva remains far removed from all... Regarding the various retinues, fourth, the bodhisattva does not deceive sentient beings;
fifth, the bodhisattva does not engage in divisive or malicious speech toward sentient beings or his own retinue;
sixth, for immeasurable eons, the bodhisattva transforms and benefits sentient beings with gentle speech; seventh, the bodhisattva...
He does not engage in frivolous speech toward sentient beings; eighth, the bodhisattva does not give rise to greedy attachment toward the requisites for life belonging to sentient beings;
ninth, the bodhisattva does not give rise to anger toward sentient beings and is able to endure all slander;
tenth, the bodhisattva remains far removed from wrong views and does not take refuge in them.
Because they lead to the realms of the gods, Śāriputra!
These ten kinds of dharmas are all the marks of a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s fulfillment of pure ethical conduct.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are ten further types of pure ethical conduct for bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
What are these ten?
First, the bodhisattva firmly upholds all precepts and practices without breaking them, remaining unassailed by ignorance.
Second, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the practice of precepts, severing all flaws and blemishes, so as not to give rise to fear amidst various perils and difficulties.
Third, the bodhisattva firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts and remains entirely distant from all matters of afflictions and defilements.
Fourth, the bodhisattva maintains pure ethical discipline and never departs from the stainless dharmas.
Fifth, the bodhisattva upholds all prohibitive precepts, constantly practicing equanimity with a mind that is ever-sovereign.
Sixth, the bodhisattva firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts, refraining from slandering wise ones and thereby attaining peace and security.
Seventh, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts and remains far removed from all faults.
Eighth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, closely guarding the sense faculties so that they do not give rise [to afflictions].
Ninth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, guarding the sense faculties so that they are fully accomplished in the beginning, middle, and end.
Tenth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, such that within right mindfulness they are universally perfected without exception.
"Śāriputra!
These ten kinds of dharmas are all fully accomplished by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Furthermore, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten further aspects of upholding the precepts.
What are these ten?
First, the Bodhisattva firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts, having few desires and being content with whatever food and drink they receive.
Second, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts because they sever greed, hatred, and delusion, giving rise to joy and contentment.
Third, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts because they do not give rise to craving or attachment toward their own body or mind.
Fourth, the Bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts and dwells in wilderness areas while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, because he remains far removed from all women.
Fifth, the Bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts and practices the dhūta austerities, because he never forgets or loses any of his meritorious virtues.
Sixth, the bodhisattva firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts because they freely accomplish all roots of goodness.
Seventh, the bodhisattva firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts because they always experience joy within noble lineages and do not fixate upon other secondary marks or signs.
Eighth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts; their words and deeds correspond with one another, and they do not give rise to deceit among humans or devas.

Ninth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts; they constantly practice self-examination within themselves, ensuring that no faults arise in their own minds, and regarding the faults of others, they do not harbor views of them but always act to protect them.
Tenth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts and, by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), transforms and benefits sentient beings without ever abandoning them.
Śāriputra, through these ten dharmas, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill and purify the practice of ethical discipline.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
there are ten further characteristics of the pure and perfect conduct of ethical discipline for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What are these ten?
First, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts and, possessing faith and understanding in the Buddha, does not give rise to retreat or discouragement.
Second, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts and is always able to protect and preserve the True Dharma.
Third, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts and always generates a sense of respect within the great assembly.

Fourth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, seeking enlightenment with a gentle and flexible resolve, never for a moment relinquishing the mind directed toward the unsurpassed fruit.
Fifth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, is always able to draw near to virtuous friends, and further accumulates all wholesome merits.
Sixth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, always remains far removed from evil associates, and is able to abandon all unwholesome dharmas.
Seventh, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, constantly giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings and conceiving compassionate concern for them.

Eighth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, constantly giving rise to a mind of compassion toward all sentient beings, and always providing rescue and protection amidst dangers and hardships.
Ninth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, delighting in the True Dharma as if wandering through a garden, giving rise to great joy and bliss.
Tenth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, maintaining a mind of constant equanimity that remains detached from both adverse and favorable conditions.
"Śāriputra!
These ten aspects of ethical conduct, the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to purify and perfect in this way.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Furthermore, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have ten kinds of pure conduct.
What are these ten?
First, the Bodhisattva firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts and is well able to subdue all sentient beings through the perfection of generosity.
Second, the bodhisattva firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts, constantly practices patience, and perpetually guards his own mind.
Third, the bodhisattva firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts and exerts diligence in all wholesome dharmas without ever retreating.
Fourth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, constantly applying himself to the collection of meditative concentrations (*samādhiskandha*) without giving rise to distraction.
Fifth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, always delighting in extensive learning within supreme wisdom (*prajñā*) without ever feeling satiated.

Sixth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, seeking the true Dharma within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, constantly cultivating the wisdom of hearing with steadfastness and without indolence.
Seventh, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, constantly investigating all impermanent phenomena, and aspiring toward bodhi without begrudging body or life.
Eighth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, constantly examining his own life-span as being like a dream or an illusion, arising and ceasing moment by moment.
Ninth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts, ensuring that all virtuous deeds regarding his own aspirations and those of all sentient beings are pure and perfect.

Tenth, the bodhisattva firmly upholds the prohibitive precepts; by the power of this observance of precepts, they vow that in the future they shall be born within the assemblies of the Buddhas, and that all sentient beings likewise attain the complete perfection of pure ethical conduct.
Śāriputra! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are all able to fulfill these ten kinds of characteristics of pure ethical discipline. Śāriputra!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus fulfills the practice of pure ethical discipline, they shall obtain various auspicious, excellent, and wondrous fruits in both the heavens and among humans.

The Bodhisattva clearly understands all the various worldly activities; the Bodhisattva is able to bestow all the various wonderful sensual pleasures of the world upon sentient beings, yet remains personally unattached to them.
When a bodhisattva practices the conduct of loving-kindness, they practice it equally toward all sentient beings, feeling mutual compassion and refraining from harm.

When a bodhisattva practices the bodhisattva path, they have deep faith in the true Dharma without falsehood; furthermore, they regard all sentient beings as their own parents, and by drawing near to and following them, they give rise to trust and affection. They maintain the perception of impermanence in every moment regarding conditioned phenomena, awaken to all conditioned activities, and are able to relinquish their own bodies and lives; thus, they attain the perfectly pure conduct of ethical discipline.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of the bodhisattvas:
"The physical marks and radiant light are wondrously beyond compare; They proclaim the gateways of the True Dharma of all Buddhas.
By firmly upholding the pure precepts, One shall attain the sublime and wondrous Dharmakāya."
Far removed from the afflictions of ignorance and blindness, Unable to be invaded by lameness, deformity, or a hundred ailments,
One who firmly upholds the pure precepts Shall attain the full perfection of all faculties.
His power is vast and beyond compare; his majestic virtue is likewise blazing and intense.
His wisdom is sharp and penetrating, transcending the world, as he subdues all demonic obstacles.
Gathering all moving beings through the power of loving-kindness, He is able to shatter the entire web of doubts;
The eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, all take refuge in him, And kings along with their subjects all offer him worship.
They are able to leave behind all fears, Abiding securely in the precepts without regression;
They do not fall into any of the evil realms, For by practicing the Great Dharma, they possess a renowned reputation.
While all sentient beings are shrouded in sleep, the Bodhisattva remains ever vigilant;
he travels throughout the four quarters, seeking the sublime Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings.
Most excellent treasures, as well as wives and concubines, they were all able to renounce because they were free from self-attachment;
seeking unsurpassed, great bodhi, they dwelt securely in the perfect and pure precepts.
For the sake of seeking the unsurpassed True Dharma, they give rise to reverence for all the Buddha-teachings;
they constantly act as teachers among the people of the world and are able to make extensive offerings at stupas and temples.
Able to eliminate all thoughts of anger, One is able to endure all ill-deeds;
Finding peace through the power of patience, One remains unmoved by any slander.
Able to ensure that words and deeds are entirely in accord, Without falsehood at any time,
One shall sit upon the Great Bodhi Mandala, Causing the three thousandfold world system to tremble in its entirety.
Yet they are able to seek all the Buddha-dharmas exhaustively, Nor do they take refuge in the realms of the gods;
Abandoning the heterodox minds of external paths, They vow to achieve unsurpassed bodhi.
Amidst all manner of weapons and poisons, which sentient beings wield to harm one another, the Bodhisattva provides protection;
for this reason, he is called the Great Wise One.
Throughout many tens of millions of kalpas, I have compassionately regarded all classes of sentient beings;
whenever I see them undergoing suffering and affliction, I cast myself away to take their place without weariness or indolence.

Most sentient beings are full of deceit; they come where the Bodhisattva dwells with the intent to plunder and create various evil karmas within Jambudvīpa. Only the Buddha’s True Dharma can eliminate and sever them.
One can bestow all manner of rare treasures and always remain close to virtuous friends;
even when sentient beings cause harm or offense, one never gives rise to thoughts of anger or malice.
In the presence of all sentient beings, one should always abandon the ways of the foolish;
having perfected the sublime conduct of the Buddhas, one never forsakes the feet of pure ethical discipline.
Always dwelling well in all Buddha-dharmas, they are also able to accord with and turn according to all dharmas;
being able to fully practice the vows and conduct of enlightenment, they attain the fruit of perfect awakening.
Having purifiedly realized the nectar-like Dharma of the three knowledges, And always dwelling well within the aggregate of ethical discipline,
One is able to perfect the cultivation of all dharmas, Receiving sublime offerings from both heavens and the human realm.
Seeking all unsurpassed dharmas, he is fully proficient in all activities;
skillfully understanding the minds of sentient beings regarding what to adopt and what to reject, he is worthy of receiving the offerings of devas and humans.
Proclaiming the supreme nectar-like Dharma, Always pure within the aggregate of ethical discipline,
Awakening to the cause of unsurpassed Bodhi, One remains entirely free from all demonic obstacles.
Having approached the Bodhi tree and sat down in steadfast composure, like the sun and moon illuminating the world,
possessing great majesty and blazing radiance, he became the most supreme in all the world.
With the supreme supramundane eye of wisdom, you have first attained fearlessness in speech;
having fully perfected the demonstration of the true path, you shall bestow fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva gives rise to no heart of attachment, Able to relinquish body, life, and wealth;
Having no craving for the world’s rare treasures, He shall realize the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.
May all beings not forsake the path to enlightenment, Fully maintaining the precepts and always being diligent,
Able to dwell securely within the True Dharma, And remain far removed from all forms of flattery and deception.
When a bodhisattva dwells securely within the aggregate of ethical discipline, even if there should be those in the world who are sycophantic or deceitful,
and they come before the bodhisattva to speak, [the bodhisattva] instructs them with words of truth.
Some may constantly carry their robes and alms bowls, yet practice much flattery and deception without sincerity;
they wish to give to the Bodhisattva but have nothing to give, while the Bodhisattva remains unmoved in right mindfulness.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has thus fulfilled and purified all practices of ethical discipline, they do not give rise to attachment or delight toward any conditioned phenomena of the world; they constantly conceive the thought of all sentient beings as their own mother; they conceive the thought of non-attachment toward the five desires; they understand that all worldly dharmas are entirely without marks (animitta); their mental conduct is equanimous and free from all treachery or malice, and they manifest and accomplish the bodhisattva path."
Why is this? When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices with a mind of equanimity, they do not depart from nirvāṇa;
yet, if they give rise to attachment through a defiled mind, it causes various dangers and evils to increase and flourish.

Because the eye is attached to forms, the Bodhisattva understands that they arise from the mind of consciousness; since afflictions are false and devoid of intrinsic nature, they are all extinguished.

Regarding the conceptual attachments that arise from various objects of perception—taking what is not a true dharma to be a wholesome dharma—the Bodhisattva knows these are delusions arising from within his own mind and thus gives rise to superior resolve. Consequently, he attains complete liberation from all afflictions, and his body is also liberated, because greed, hatred, and delusion have been entirely exhausted.
Why is this? Because this dharma of craving perishes in a single moment.
Whether there is a separate dharma of craving or a separate dharma of exhaustion, both are entirely real.
Thus, one truly understands this phenomenon of craving and brings it to true exhaustion.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, this phenomenon of craving does not truly arise within the internal mind, for it is a mere conceptual construction; therefore, if that person gives rise to discrimination regarding phenomena, it is likewise not real.
If one knows that which is real to be unreal, one is liberated from all suffering and affliction.
If that which is free from suffering and affliction is called "real," then that reality is devoid of all suffering and affliction.
The nature is fundamentally pure; this is the meaning of nirvana. It is fundamentally not a phenomenon of craving. Why is this?
Because within nirvana there are no conceptual thoughts; that place where craving is exhausted is nirvana.
If one perceives the exhaustion of craving yet it is not the exhaustion of craving, and if one perceives nirvana yet it is not nirvana, this is what is called true nirvana. Why is this so?
Greed and nirvāṇa are non-different in their intrinsic nature; they are conjoined in their fundamental nature.
The wise, regarding this, seek nirvāṇa by knowing that intrinsic nature.
If things were not real but entirely false, then within that falsity, intrinsic nature would be empty.
What is meant by "emptiness"?

It refers to the conceptual attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self," or the conceptual attachment to the nature of the self as permanent, or the conceptual attachment to the nature of the self as annihilated, or the conceptual attachment that all phenomena are entirely devoid of change.
If there were no self, no person, and no life-principle, the phenomena of greed, hatred, and delusion would ultimately not arise.

If those phenomena were to arise, this [notion of] self would necessarily exist; therefore, because the notions of "self" and "mine" arise again, all formative activities (saṃskāras) are once more initiated with respect to that which is "self" and "mine."
Śāriputra! Those who initiate all practices do so by means of four kinds of accumulated practice. What are these four?
First is the accumulation of actions of body;

second is the accumulation of actions of speech, which consists of uttering coarse and evil words based on discursive thought and investigation, because the karmic actions performed thereby cause affliction and distress to others.
Third is the practice of the accumulation of mind;

fourth is the practice of the accumulation of perception (*saṃjñā*), because of the conceptual clinging to self and others. Thus, all sentient beings are completely bound by these. In the preceding passage, four practices were indicated; of these, two within the internal [set] have their explanations, while two lack their explanatory texts.
This was not present in the original Sanskrit text and must not be added.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas see sentient beings with such physical characteristics, such conceptualizations, and such inversions, they do not yet understand how these beings are unable to practice the supreme conduct together with the Bodhisattvas."
Why is this? Because when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices together with sentient beings, he fears that they might suffer diminution, whereas he himself constantly seeks the dharma of fearlessness.
Śāriputra! Because of such conditions, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas give rise to faith and reverence toward all sentient beings, remaining free from doubt. Śāriputra!
How does a bodhisattva give rise to faith and reverence?
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva regards all sentient beings as their own parents. Śāriputra!

The bodhisattva mahāsattva regards all sentient beings without exception; throughout infinite worlds and from beginningless time, all sentient beings have at one time or another been my own parents and kinsmen.

At that time, those sentient beings, due to their craving and attachment, fall into forgetfulness; they do not remember having been parents, children, or relatives. Furthermore, when anger arises, they likewise forget all former ties as parents, children, or relatives, and consequently abandon them.
Śāriputra! For this reason, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should understand through this analogy:
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should always conceive the thought of all sentient beings as their own kinsmen.
Śāriputra!

In the past, immeasurable, innumerable, asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, and further back through unspeakably, unspeakably vast, inconceivable eons, at that time in that world there appeared a Buddha named Uttamasattva Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
He remained in the world for ninety koṭis of years, during which time there was an assembly of ninety koṭis of nāyutas of great śrāvakas, and all the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gathered together.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva within that assembly who had attained the foundations of right mindfulness and was born into a noble lineage within the royal palace.
Immediately upon his birth, the king and queen each assigned eighty-four thousand court ladies to serve as his attendants.

Thereupon, the Prince’s physical appearance was exceptionally sublime; his body was upright, pure white, and perfectly formed, endowed with all the auspicious marks, a sight that all people delighted to behold.
Consequently, when the kinsmen of the maternal clan beheld the Prince’s majestic appearance, they all gathered together to attend upon and protect him.

Śāriputra! At that time, the prince had three virtuous friends who together constructed for him an exquisite pavilion. In this way, during the three seasons—the heat, the rains, and the cold—they provided him with entertainment, so that he might travel about and dwell in comfort, each according to what was appropriate for the season.

Furthermore, there were ten million people who all arrived at that time, each playing music and sporting together; they drew near to serve and provide for him, their voices all resonating in perfect harmony.
At that time, the prince suddenly reflected upon the nature of arising and ceasing; he silenced the music and contemplated from where the sounds of the music came and from what they originated.
Where is cessation?
What is arising?
How is there cessation?
Day and night he contemplated this without ever sleeping, thinking only of impermanence and feeling weary of arising and ceasing. Śāriputra!

Having attained right mindfulness, this bodhisattva mahāsattva constantly felt weary of the sounds of music for forty thousand years; furthermore, during those forty thousand years, he took no pleasure in any of the desires of the world.

At that time, before that bodhisattva had gone forth from the household life, he had constantly and diligently practiced the four dhyānas and various samādhis, thereby accomplishing the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*).

He ascended into the air from his own residence and proceeded to the abode of the Tathāgata Most Supreme Multitude, where he approached, gazed upon, prostrated to, and made offerings to him, desiring to inquire of the World-Honored One regarding the essential points of all wholesome dharmas.
Śāriputra! At that time,
when the Tathāgata Supreme Assembly had already entered parinirvāṇa,
that bodhisattva extended his inquiry:
"O great bhikṣus and sons of good family!
Has the Tathāgata of the Supreme Assembly already entered parinirvāṇa?
"Sons of good family! [he replied.]
"The Tathāgatas of my most supreme assembly have already entered parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing these words, the Bodhisattva wept and wailed in grief, fainting and collapsing to the ground; after a long while, he finally regained consciousness.
Then that Bodhisattva, recollecting the Tathāgata, spoke these verses:
"My Buddha shines brightly throughout the world; Transcending all phenomena, he has reached the other shore.
Having utterly abandoned all heedless conduct, He has attained the accomplishment of pure and wondrous fruition."
Throughout hundreds of thousands of koṭis of kalpas, it is difficult to encounter a Tathāgata appearing in the world;
having failed to meet him for offerings due to deep defilements and obscurations, if I abandon the Tathāgata, who else will protect me?
The worldly mother is not a true friend, nor does she praise the Tathāgata;
for many lifetimes one has never heard the True Dharma, and it is difficult to encounter the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The worldly father is no true friend, for he causes me to be addicted to the five desires;
by following after those desires, my defiled mind increases, preventing me from beholding the marks of the Tathāgata.
Of my Buddha’s sixty kinds of wondrous voices, I have never heard them while in the Buddha’s presence;
thus I am unable to distinguish between good and evil, causing me to sink forever into the sea of birth and death.
Furthermore, throughout many eons, they do not fail to encounter a Buddha;
they give rise to compassionate concern for all worlds, and within that state of compassion, they are able to practice everything, fully understanding all dharmas and reaching the other shore.
Throughout many koṭis of kalpas, I have never approached or made offerings to a Buddha;
because of my negligence throughout many lifetimes, these deep obscurations prevent me from seeing the Buddha.
I have heard that the Tathāgata appeared in the world, yet having reached the Buddha’s abode, he has entered parinirvāṇa;
bound as I am by the affection for my parents, I am unable to see the Tamer of Men.
If I should encounter a Tathāgata remaining long in the world, I shall surely hear the True Dharma;
when I extensively cultivate offerings and draw near to him, may I be endowed with the hearing of the sixty sublime tones.
The sixty sublime tones are fundamentally pure, Fully possessed by all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time;
Though I am born and dwell within this world, I have not been able to hear the resonance of that Brahma-voice in person.
My birth was conditioned by karma and burdened by many obstacles; since the Buddha passed into parinirvāṇa, I have come here.
The treasury of the True Dharma of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound, and none are able to reveal it to us.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Twenty-two.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Twenty-three.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Dispersing Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, who have been conferred the Purple Robe, under Imperial Edict. Chapter Seven: The Perfection of Ethical Discipline (Śīlapāramitā), Part Six. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

At that time, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva proceeded further to the place where the Most Supreme Assembly of Buddhas had entered parinirvāṇa. Having prostrated with his head at their feet, his tears flowed profusely; he circumambulated them a hundred thousand times and then stood to one side, again reciting a gāthā:
“The Tathāgata, among all sentient beings, Has excellently taught the supreme, true Dharma;
I now give rise to a sincere mind, Vowing to seek the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.”
The Buddha possesses the true body of great wisdom; now that he has entered parinirvāṇa, I no longer behold him.
Resolving to make vows equal to those of the Tathāgata, I shall surely attain all the most excellent marks and signs.
In the past, while in a layperson's home, I failed to show reverence for the Tathāgata’s Dharma;
this has now brought me inferior and dull faculties, resulting in various demonic obstacles that come to harass and afflict me.
Now that I have not yet heard the True Dharma, I am constantly oppressed by immeasurable suffering and affliction;
may I be granted the opportunity to behold the Teacher, the Tamer of Men, and thereby awaken the roots of goodness planted in past lives.
I now utter these words of truth, Before this assembly of the eight classes of devas and nāgas;
May they bear witness to this sincere mind of mine, And may I attain the true fruit in the future.
May I, by the power of these roots of goodness, behold the Most Honored One among men;
having heard the True Dharma, may I attain supernormal powers, so that like a great dragon, I may pour down sweet rain.
May I not fall into the eight difficult states, May I remain far removed from all taints of desire,
And may I always give rise to a heart of sincere reverence for the Buddha, Such that no evil Māra or heavy obstacles can bind me.
May I always, in the presence of all Buddhas, Personally hear and uphold the treasury of the True Dharma;
May my pure and white deeds be swiftly perfected, And may I fully penetrate the boundless wisdom of the Buddhas.
May I swiftly attain true speech; through the power of truth, may I become a Buddha.
May I sit upon the great terrace of enlightenment and proclaim the Dharma of truth to benefit all sentient beings.
May I soon join the supreme assembly, Shaking the great trichiliocosm with the power of my supernormal faculties;
When surrounded by tens of millions of celestial hosts, May those who obtain benefit have their hearts rejoice.
The Buddha’s power of supernormal feats is inconceivable; Abiding in the midst of space, he is likewise difficult to behold.
By virtue of this cause of our praise of his merits, We pray that you emit pure radiance to illuminate us.
The Buddha’s supernormal powers are immeasurable; out of compassion for sentient beings, he constantly manifests them.
He causes me to hear the sublime and wondrous Dharma, which can be extolled in billions of koṭis of verses without end.
"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s mind gives rise to joy, which increases even further, as he speaks these verses: ‘If, in the past,
I received the prophecy That in this present life I shall attain the Buddha-way,
May all sentient beings follow my heart, And may all the offerings they cultivate be fully perfected.’"
The realm of true purity is inconceivable; those seeking bodhi should enter it.
If sentient beings give rise to such a mind, they shall constantly behold immeasurable Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have in the past planted deep roots of goodness in the presence of various Buddhas, having approached and made offerings to them, thereby fully accomplishing immeasurable faculties and powers."

Having passed away from here, they will be reborn in the celestial realms; for twenty koṭis of kalpas they shall not fall into the evil destinies, and for twenty koṭis of kalpas they shall not be addicted to the pleasures of the five desires.

Furthermore, in the past, he drew near to and made offerings to seven thousand Tathāgatas; at the site of each and every Tathāgata, he extensively accomplished all manner of offerings, constantly practicing the holy life at all times in order to seek unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

By the power of these roots of goodness from the past, he attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and appeared in the world, fully endowed with the ten titles: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavān, known as the Tathāgata Sāla-tree King.

In that Buddha’s assembly, various śrāvakas had all gathered together; furthermore, there were twenty koṭis of bhikṣus along with forty thousand great arhats, whose outflows were already exhausted and who were free from further afflictions. Having attained their own benefit and ended all fetters of existence, they had gained mastery over their minds and reached the other shore.

Śāriputra! The lifespan of that Tathāgata Sālarāja will be twenty koṭis of years; after his parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma will remain in the world for a full ten thousand years, and the Semblance Dharma will likewise remain for the same duration.
"The bodily relics shall be distributed throughout the world, universally honored, and extensively perform the Buddha-work.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
"For twenty koṭis of kalpas, I have never fallen into the various evil realms."
Throughout twenty koṭis of kalpas, he was never attached to the five desires.
Seven thousand Tathāgatas shall dwell in the world; during that time, he will enter parinirvāṇa.
Because he has cultivated the holy life, he attains accomplishment, and he constantly shares the desire for the Dharma with sentient beings.
Now that I have attained the path of Bodhi, I am thus named the Tathāgata Śālarāja;
throughout twenty koṭis of kalpas, I shall establish sentient beings in the fruit of Bodhi.
Awakening to the supreme cause of Bodhi, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings,
throughout twenty koṭis of years, you shall constantly preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Constantly accompanied by forty koṭis of followers, He sat together at the site of enlightenment to proclaim the True Dharma;
With all outflows extinguished without remainder, He attained the wondrous and sublime fruit of Nirvāṇa.
I have erected sixty thousand stupas for the bodily relics of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time,
and further established koṭis of jeweled banners, extending my offerings throughout ten thousand years.
The True Dharma shall abide in the world for ten thousand years; all who possess wisdom shall obtain benefit.
When this pure and wondrous sound is proclaimed, all who hear it shall find their hearts filled with joy.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfills the pure practice of ethical discipline, they give rise to antidotes toward all sentient beings; they do not produce craving or attachment toward their parents.
They initiate antidotes toward all sentient beings and do not produce indulgence or attachment toward the objects of desire."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, what are the phenomena of desire (*kāmadharma*)?
What are the counteractive phenomena (*pratipakṣadharma*)?

As for the phenomena of desire: they refer to the desire for forms when the eye perceives them, the desire for sounds when the ear hears them, the desire for odors when the nose smells them, the desire for flavors when the tongue discerns them, and the desire for tangibles when the body makes contact with them; from these, a union arises, and one develops attachment toward this union—this is called the phenomenon of desire.
Having already given rise to craving and attachment, one becomes bound; regarding these various bonds, one forms a notion of certainty.
These phenomena of bondage are ultimately false and illusory, yet because of delusion through greed, one deeply delights in such bondage.
These binding phenomena are generally of three kinds—namely, shallow, deep, and extremely deep—and all sentient beings should distance themselves from these binding phenomena.
Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) is a bond; sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch are all bonds. Why is form a bond?

It is because by accomplishing the form of body and life, one gives rise to the notion of a self (*ātman*), the notion of a person (*pudgala*), the notion of a life-span (*jīva*), the notion of permanence, the notion of indestructibility, the notion of fixed immutability, the notion of objective sensory objects, the notion of a sentient being (*sattva*), and the notion of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). All such things are the bonds of the dharma of form.

Furthermore, form (*rūpa*) is a bondage, because it constitutes the physical existence and life-force of sentient beings. That is to say, the various worldly phenomena of desire—namely, attachment to one's body, life, wife, children, and kinsmen—is called the bondage of form.

Even the desire for tactile contact is a fetter; through various defiled conditions it gradually comes to fruition, and all unwholesome karmas are accumulated therein. One becomes so attached to these desires that one cannot relinquish them even for a moment.
Śāriputra! What is desire that is without fault?
It refers to desire that is pure and stainless, being without fault; yet, it does not give rise to attachment toward the evil realms.
How is it that one does not give rise to attachment toward the evil realms?
It is by perceiving desire as being without fault. Śāriputra!
All sentient beings constantly indulge in various sensual objects, never for even a moment relinquishing them; through the retribution of this karma, they undergo the fruit of suffering everywhere.
Śāriputra! Having sequentially investigated and thoroughly examined a thousand worlds, one finds that among all evil associates, not a single person can be compared to a wife.
Why is this? Śāriputra, because all sentient beings are deluded, those who possess wisdom constantly reject them; therefore, you should know that the True Dharma is manifested.
Those who lack wisdom constantly embrace [such things]; therefore, one should know that they manifest all conditioned phenomena that are contrary to the Dharma.

Men and women, wives and concubines, become mutually attached and give rise to craving and delight. They are embraced by false paths; men and women, wives and concubines are repeatedly craved and grasped at, creating obstacles to renunciation, obstacles to upholding the precepts, obstacles to cultivating meditative concentration, obstacles to rebirth in the heavens, obstacles to nirvana, and obstacles to all pure dharmas. Furthermore, they embrace slaves, servants, and retinues; in short, they may even embrace evil friends, thereby being embraced by the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
Furthermore, the acquisition of sons, daughters, wives, and concubines is itself the acquisition of all various defilements and unwholesome roots.
Moreover, the acquisition of sons, daughters, wives, and concubines, extending even to food and drink, constitutes an obstacle that reaches its ultimate limit:
it is an obstacle to the desire to see the Tathāgata, an obstacle to the desire to hear the True Dharma, and an obstacle to the desire to associate with the Noble Assembly.
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision—the Dharma that is pure and immaculate—cannot be seen by any of the noble assembly due to their obstructions.

Within the course of time, they seek accomplishment but encounter obstacles; they seek the seven treasures of the noble ones but encounter obstacles. Instead of faith in the true Dharma, they develop attachment to what is contrary to it; even those who break the precepts, are stingy, possess evil wisdom, and lack shame or remorse are all embraced [by such conditions], and instead of the seven treasures of the noble ones, they embrace what is contrary to them.
Furthermore, they embrace sons, daughters, wives, and concubines, which is to say, they embrace the sufferings of disease, sores, ulcers, pain, fierce fires, and venomous snakes.

Moreover, they embrace the houses where their sons, daughters, wives, and concubines dwell as if they were burial mounds; within those mounds, they raise cries of lamentation, and when no kinsmen or friends are present to hear them, their delusion and confusion increase.
This illusory dharma acts as an obstacle to all wholesome dharmas.
To speak briefly, Śāriputra:
for a person who has broken the precepts, all manner of unwholesome dharmas are like the frost and hail of the world that destroys all things; the destruction of wholesome dharmas is likewise so.
Furthermore, they are addicted to men, women, wives, and concubines, like a person craving flavor who licks a sharp sword or eats hot iron balls and various impure things.

Moreover, though their bodies are filthy, out of greedy attachment they adorn themselves with incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments as offerings, like decorating oneself with the most grievous instruments of suffering in hell.

Furthermore, to take in and employ various slaves and servants; to take in and accept various wretched, dark, and emaciated persons who are subject to all manner of contempt; and to take in and accept various domestic animals such as camels, donkeys, pigs, and dogs—this is precisely to embrace all forms of suffering and affliction.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding the taking up of sons, daughters, wives, and concubines:
it is better to enter a great city of blazing hot iron with flames extending for a thousand yojanas than to take up parents, sons, daughters, wives, or concubines.
If one constantly gives rise to such a mind of defiled attachment, one will immediately fall; how much more so when experiencing various objects of sensory contact?

Why is this? All causes of suffering take the dharma of greedy attachment as their root; it damages the root of wholesome dharmas, is the root of sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction, the root that binds one to wholesome dharmas, the root of filth and evil, and the root of being born blind—it is not the root of the pure eye of wisdom.
It is as if one were constantly treading upon ground of glowing iron; it causes this person to fall entirely into the wrong path.
For what reason is she called a "wife"?

Because of the actions of a wife: she is able to endure as if carrying a heavy burden, and she willingly accepts and bears that heavy burden for a long time without abandoning it, undergoing various sufferings that oppress her body and mind and cause her harm.
It is for such reasons that one is called a wife.

Likewise, because sentient beings give rise to craving, they become slaves; because of their attachment, they lack self-mastery; they are subjected to beatings and bonds, yet they submit with full trust, developing even greater veneration and following all commands;
it is for such reasons that one is called a wife.
To speak of it fully and extensively, Śāriputra, it is immeasurable: furthermore,

that which is called the heavy burden consists of the five aggregates— form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness— and these five aggregates are known as the great burden, which one is unable to cast off.
Men and women, wives and concubines, become kin through the power of past causes and conditions. Śāriputra!

These are the conditions for breaking the precepts, the conditions for destroying right practice, the conditions for wrong views, and the conditions for delighting in food and drink; they are the conditions for the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals. They create obstacles to supreme wisdom and close the gate to Nirvāṇa. Because of these causes and conditions, all suffering is accumulated; this is what is called "kin from past causes."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
A mother’s lineage also possesses many faults.
It is said that this lineage involves immeasurable and boundless matters such as illusory transformations; if someone follows along with these, they will give rise to faults."

All demonic activities are as if held in the palm of one's hand; the various delusive illusions and manifold faults of Pāpīyān’s retinue and the māras’ daughters—manifested through frivolous minds, mocking minds, deranged minds, and monkey-like minds—are well able to display such deceptions.
For these reasons, it is called the maternal lineage.
Śāriputra, furthermore, this illusion is also called a village; there, royal cities and four-way crossroads are established, and the world of sentient beings is vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable.
For these reasons, it is called the "village of delusive illusions.
Śāriputra, such delusive desires and their faults lead one to fall into the evil destinies.

Śāriputra! It is like a magician who performs deceptive illusions; amidst a great assembly, he prepares various magical implements and is able to extensively manifest all manner of illusory phenomena. The deceptive illusions of women are just like this.

Śāriputra! Sentient beings in the world are bound by seeing that woman; sometimes they are bound by hearing her voice, sometimes by the touch of her hand, sometimes by giving rise to thoughts of attachment through her singing and dancing, sometimes by being deluded by her charms when in union, or sometimes by her weeping. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they are bound in every situation, serving as her messengers and even becoming her slaves.
Śāriputra! It is just as when the ripening crops of the world are destroyed by heavy rain and hail. Śāriputra!
The mother’s lineage is likewise; she can destroy the husband’s lineage and can also destroy all pure dharmas. Śāriputra!
The faults of all sensual desires—which lead to rebirth in the evil destinies—cannot be understood by any fool, yet they instead embrace wives, concubines, and kinsmen. Śāriputra!
These bodhisattvas, through the power of skillful means, are able to distance themselves from the faults of sensual desires and matters that are without benefit.
Why is it that all foolish ordinary beings reject and turn their backs on the true Dharma, instead giving rise to ignorance and the notion that they are not true men?

One should conceive of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Mahāsattvas as Great Beings (*mahāpuruṣa*), and should abandon the notion that they are not Great Beings. One should not give rise to thoughts of anger; rather, one should cultivate correct practices toward those in the happy realms as Great Beings, and not engage in wrong practices by regarding those in the miserable realms as not being Great Beings. One should not direct oneself toward the destinies of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals, nor should one direct oneself toward the breaking of precepts. One should take no pleasure in dwelling even for a moment among those who break the precepts, but should instead take pleasure in directing oneself toward the most supreme and excellent, unobstructed, and unhindered Buddha-wisdom of all unsurpassed True Dharma. Furthermore, one should take pleasure in directing oneself toward the cultivation of remedies for all unwholesome dharmas.
"May I, in the future, let out the lion's roar; may I not delight in following unwholesome dharmas and letting out the roar of other beasts."
May I, in the future, manifest a body of golden hue like that of the Buddha, never again taking birth as an ordinary, mundane being.
May I always be the foremost leader in guiding the world toward virtue.

Furthermore, among human beings, they are free from all perils and hardships; they sleep and eat in peace, lacking nothing, and always obtain pure and exquisite food and drink in full abundance, yet they do not feel weary of or abandon coarse and simple worldly fare.

I constantly aspire to cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) in a place of tranquility, swiftly attaining the most supreme and excellent *samādhi*. May I focus one-pointedly on a single object, remaining far removed from the defilements and obstacles of agitation and distraction; may I always sport within the various gates of the Buddhas' concentrations, while likewise distancing myself from the various states of concentration belonging to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and taking no pleasure in relying upon the various states of concentration of all foolish ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, they do not dwell with attachment to the five aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; they do not dwell with attachment by relying on earth, water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness; they do not dwell with attachment by relying on the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; nor do they dwell with attachment to this world or other worlds.

Furthermore, although they may see, hear, perceive, or cognize the realm of sublime touch, as well as the tranquil contemplation they have realized, they likewise do not delight in relying upon or dwelling therein.
May those who always rely upon meditative concentration according to reality, though delighting in the cultivation of samādhi, never cause harm to their own or others' bodies.
May they always bring the wisdom of the Buddha to perfection, and have no longing for any conditioned affairs of the desire realm.
“Śāriputra! The wise Bodhisattva-mahāsattva has four kinds of dharmas for transcendence. What are these four?

First, renunciation of the desire realm; second, renunciation of the realm of all sentient beings; third, renunciation of those who acknowledge kindness but do not repay it and whom one does not associate with; fourth, renunciation of all ascetic practices.
One should give rise to these four kinds of renunciation.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the miserable realms, even upon seeing the most excellent maternal lineages, he does not give rise to a mind of lustful attachment; rather, he should give rise to four kinds of perceptions.
What are the four? First, the perception of diminution;
second, the perception of peril and difficulty; third, the perception of the impurity of excrement and urine; and fourth, the perception of the filth of pus and blood.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells within the evil destinies, they should further give rise to three kinds of perceptions.
What are these three?
First, the perception of her as a mother; second, the perception of her as a sister; third, the perception of her as one's own daughter;
these three perceptions should be brought forth.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should always skillfully explain, cultivate, and contemplate [the teachings], and they should faithfully accept all the sūtras.
As I observe the world, there is not a single person who, throughout immeasurable kalpas, has not been born by a mother or nurtured by a father.

As for all sentient beings who circulate through and sustain one another, every single sentient being has at some time been my father or mother; or having been called "mother" in the past, they have now returned to being called "wife" in this present life.
Those practitioners should train themselves thus: "I shall abide in conduct that is not in conflict with that of foolish ordinary beings.
Such modes of conduct are in accordance with this.
With craving as his mental focus, he concentrates his inner mind and reflects thus:
"Regarding this mind of craving, how does one perceive that which has arisen and that which has not yet arisen?"
If one should feel craving for the various forms within the eye,
that practitioner must remain firm in their inner mind and investigate the arising of attachment within their own eyes.
How can seeing arise within the eye?
How can self-nature see self-nature?
How can the eye itself see the eye itself?

In this way, one's own eye is composed of the four great elements; because it relies upon various conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since it is not of intrinsic nature, yet one gives rise to attachment toward it, that mind of attachment likewise lacks intrinsic nature.
Why is this? That nature does not exist, and this mind is likewise non-existent; it is due to conceptual differentiation that attachment arises.
While all foolish worldlings dwell in non-discrimination because they lack understanding, I now delight in dwelling within discrimination and thus give rise to the aspiration for progress.
"Why is this? Such physical forms are not dharmas of merit; they are objects of desire for contemplation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Mutually harmonizing to form a single meaning, herein there is no differentiation of meaning;
nor does it arise from a solid internal mind, but is called an accumulation by virtue of craving.”
How can one truly be true amidst reality, yet give rise to attachment for the four great elements?
These phenomena are like tiles and wood; one should not give rise to a mind of craving or delight toward them.
From the grasping at a self, pervasive conceptualization arises; from what is unreal, it accumulates.
Within the unreal, craving is born; in reality, craving is unfindable.
Even if one were to search throughout the ten directions, the true nature of craving cannot be found;
yet, having formed attachments to what is unreal, the mind of craving arises and accumulates once more.
If one thus gives rise to such investigation, examining this cycle thoroughly from all sides,
then at the time of investigating according to its progressive intensification, true craving cannot be found.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Twenty-Three.
7. The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Twenty-Four.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperially Appointed Court Disperser and Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of Sanskrit Transmission, and Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, under Imperial Edict. The Seventh Chapter, the Remainder of the Perfection of Ethical Discipline (Śīlapāramitā), concludes as follows: At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"What I have now proclaimed is progressively more excellent than all other sūtras; you should believe and understand it in accordance with the faculties and powers [of sentient beings]."

Śāriputra! Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like foam and bubbles that cannot be grasped or touched; within foam and bubbles there is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-span, no individual (pudgala), no mind-born, no youth, no agent, and no experiencer.
Understanding all phenomena in this way as unarisen and devoid of all marks, how could there be anyone therein who feels craving?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like a mirage, arising from the accumulation of all afflictions and craving; they are without self, without person, without sentient being, without life-span, without individual (pudgala), without mind-born, without youth, and without agent or experiencer, both in the past and the future.
Understanding that such conditioned phenomena do not proceed and are free from all marks, how could there be anyone therein who possesses craving?
Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like the plantain tree, for their substance is not real.
Within the plantain tree there is no self, no person, and so on, up to being free from all marks; how, then, could there be anyone therein who feels craving?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like magical illusions, produced through the accumulation of inversions; within these illusions there is no self, no person, and so on, up to being free from all marks. Within this, how could there be anyone who feels craving?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like those seen in a dream; because the various forms and appearances therein are not real, within this dream there is no self and no person, up to and including the absence of all marks. Within this, what could there be that is subject to craving?
Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like echoes, for they arise through conditions.
Within an echo there is no self, no person, and so on, up to being free from all marks; how, then, could there be anyone here who feels craving?
Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like reflections, manifested according to various karmas and delusions.
Within these reflections there is no self, no person, and they are even devoid of all characteristics; how, then, could there be anyone therein who feels craving?
Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like floating clouds; their gathering and dispersal lack a fixed substance, and they are not ultimate.
Within these floating clouds, there is no self and no person, even to the point of being free from all marks. How, then, could there be anyone therein who feels craving and attachment?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like flashes of lightning, perishing in an instant; within this lightning-flash there is no self and no person, even to the point of being devoid of all marks. Within this, what could there be that is subject to craving?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like space, devoid of self and what belongs to a self; within these empty phenomena, there is no self and no person, even to the point of being free from all marks. In this state, who could there be to harbor craving and attachment?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like those who are ignorant and deaf, possessing no conscious awareness; they are also like insentient things such as grass, trees, walls, fences, tiles, and pebbles, which possess no conscious awareness. Within these ignorant, deaf, and insentient phenomena, there is no self and no person, even to the point of being free from all marks (*nimitta*); how, then, could there be anyone therein who feels craving?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), which are in constant flux; they are also like a wind-kite, a mere assemblage of conditions. Within these conditioned phenomena, there is no self and no person, even to the point of being devoid of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*). In this context, who could there be to harbor craving?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are all false and provisional, mere accumulations of all that is impure. These provisional phenomena are without self and without person, even to the point of being free from all marks; how could there be anyone within them who feels craving?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like reflections in a mirror; they manifest according to objects, appearing and vanishing in an instant, and are thus phenomena subject to disintegration. Within these mirror-reflections, there is no self and no person, even to the point of being free from all marks. In this state, how could there be anyone who feels craving?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth are like a well of suffering, where the four snakes and two rats of the sufferings of old age, sickness, death, and birth mutually assail and press upon one another. Within this well of suffering, there is no self and no person, even to the point of being free from all marks; how, then, could there be anyone here who feels craving and attachment?

Furthermore, these eyes and so forth have no real limit; it is only when the ephemeral faculties are invaded by the law of death that a limit is perceived. Within this limit, there is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-span, no pudgala, no mind-born, no youth, no agent, and no experiencer. Understanding them thus as being free from all marks, what room is there here for one who feels craving?

Śāriputra! The dharmas of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are likewise. If a bodhisattva mahāsattva’s inner mind is firm and truly corresponds with reality, they will never fall into the dharmas of craving;
it is impossible for them to fall into craving.
Śāriputra, to truly feel weary of and detached from the phenomena of craving—this is called the pure conduct of ethical discipline of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva has thus perfected this pure conduct of ethical discipline, they do not cause harm to any sentient beings; they are able to benefit even the most minute of sentient beings, and they do not begrudge their own body or life, relinquishing everything to all without exception.
Or, having received the kindness of others, they are able to repay it, ensuring that the enjoyments of both self and others are fully perfected.
Furthermore, in all circumstances, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva would rather lose their own life than engage in various forms of perverse desire;
they would rather lose their own life than deceive sentient beings through false speech or divisive talk, and they always maintain contentment with their own kin and retinue.

It would be better to lose one’s life than to engage in frivolous speech; rather, one should always utter words of loving-kindness, gentleness, and compliance, as well as words that are certain and upright. One should always protect oneself and not give rise to craving for the sensory objects of others.
It would be better to lose one’s life than to give rise to anger; even when reviled by others, one should never be shaken, but be able to endure all harsh words.
It would be better to lose one’s life than to give rise to wrong views.

Why is this? Because they take refuge in the Buddhas with a mind that never regresses; they constantly uphold the prohibitive precepts without transgression; furthermore, they do not delight in worldly wisdom or eloquence, but study only the Buddha-wisdom, firmly maintaining the prohibitive precepts, remaining forever free from fault, and distancing themselves from all perilous, evil, and defiled phenomena.

Firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts, they remain far removed from all evil afflictions and habitual tendencies, constantly achieving pure and superior conduct, and increasing their former practice of universally bestowing food and drink.
Firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts, one acts with sovereign ease according to one's will, dwelling in peace, happiness, and auspiciousness.
Maintaining all the prohibitive precepts, one does not give rise to slander toward the wise, remaining undeluded in right mindfulness throughout the beginning, middle, and end.

Within the observance of ethical discipline, one remains free from all censure and reproach; no faults whatsoever arise, the sense faculties are constantly and closely guarded, and within the observance of ethical discipline, one possesses great renown.
They constantly embrace all wholesome dharmas; having few desires and being content, they always know their proper measure regarding those worthy of offerings.
Joyfully upholding the precepts, they sever all攀缘 (pān-yuan, mental attachments); they always practice with rectitude.
Maintaining all the prohibitive precepts, they constantly examine their threefold actions and delight in dwelling in the wilderness.
Firmly upholding the prohibitive precepts, they always give rise to a sense of weary detachment toward women, while constantly loving and delighting in the noble lineages of the sages.
He steadfastly maintains the prohibitive precepts, vowing never to gaze upon the beautiful sights of the world, remaining without flaw in his dhūta practices.
Upholding all the prohibitive precepts, he causes his own roots of goodness to arise from within himself rather than through others, ensuring that his words and deeds are in accord.

Upholding all the precepts, they do not give rise to falsehood toward gods or humans; they constantly generate a compassionate mind that ever increases in excellence, and without any intent to harm sentient beings, they give rise to great compassion.

They constantly maintain the prohibitive precepts and endure all matters of suffering and affliction; they joyfully uphold the precepts and delight in all dharmas, yet remain without attachment, constantly practicing the conduct of equanimity.

Maintaining all the prohibitive precepts, they always practice equanimity toward favorable and adverse conditions; they are constantly able to examine their own faults and transgressions; they always protect others by conforming to their minds, and are skillfully able to subdue all sentient beings.
While upholding all the precepts, they are able to fulfill the dāna-pāramitā;
while upholding all the precepts, they are able to fulfill the śīla-pāramitā, their resolute mind being such that no one can surpass it.
While upholding all the precepts, they are able to fulfill the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), reaching the ultimate consummation in all wholesome dharmas.
While upholding all the precepts, they are able to fulfill the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*), never giving rise to weariness within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
While upholding all the prohibitive precepts, they are able to fulfill the dhyāna-pāramitā, cultivating the wisdom derived from hearing without ever interrupting it.
While upholding all the prohibitive precepts, they are able to fulfill the prajñā-pāramitā, being resolute and joyful in their intimacy with spiritual friends.
Firmly upholding all the precepts, they accumulate the factors conducive to enlightenment and distance themselves from evil associates.
By upholding the precepts, they always remain far removed from perilous hardships and, regarding their own bodies, they constantly give rise to a sense of weary detachment.
Maintaining the various precepts while being able to investigate the perception of impermanence, they are further able to renounce their own life-span.
Maintaining the various precepts, they never take pleasure in dwelling long in the world, but always remain far removed from all contrary conduct.
Maintaining all the prohibitive precepts, one’s own mind remains perpetually pure and free from all feverish afflictions.
Maintaining all the prohibitive precepts, one stays far removed from craving and attachment, remaining humble rather than arrogant.
Observing all the precepts, being pure and straightforward without guile, speaking with gentle and soft words in accordance with reality;
observing all the precepts, one attains great renown that pervades everywhere while remaining self-disciplined.
They maintain all the prohibitive precepts and are constantly free from anger; they delight in tranquility and benefit sentient beings through virtuous speech.
They maintain all the prohibitive precepts, speaking according to reality without any contradiction, and gather in sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
Maintaining all prohibitive precepts and constantly protecting the True Dharma, they shall never lack for the wealth of their own Dharma.
All wise ones who are fully endowed with this aggregate of ethical discipline are able to practice the various deeds of a bodhisattva.

Śāriputra! By means of this perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*), the bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to give rise to a courageous mind; all demonic activities (*mārakarman*) and their retinues are completely obscured, and all afflictions and disturbances likewise do not appear.
Chapter Eight: The Perfection of Forbearance (Kṣānti-pāramitā), Part One.
“Śāriputra, what is the perfection of forbearance of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?”
This bodhisattva mahāsattva, in order to protect the precepts, rouses heroic vigor and practices the perfection of patience in its fullness.

While practicing this conduct, they are able to endure all worldly afflictions and harmful matters; whether it be cold, heat, hunger, or thirst; fierce winds or scorching sun; or when mosquitoes, gadflies, leeches, and venomous insects collectively come to disturb them, they are able to accept it all with composure.

If sentient beings come to revile one another with harsh speech, or seek to harm the bodhisattva’s body and life, at that time the bodhisattva’s mind is free from fear; he gives rise to neither anger nor affliction, nor does he harbor resentment, being able to endure all such acts—whether already committed, currently occurring, or yet to be committed.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s fulfillment of the cultivation of the perfection of patience.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Throughout the long night of the past, I have constantly cultivated this dharma of the contemplation of patience.

Even if all sentient beings were to come and revile me, inflict anger upon me, strike me with blows, or slander me with various harsh and evil words, at such times I would not give rise to resentment, nor envy, nor malice; nor would I, in response to their harmful actions, inflict harm upon them in turn.

Śāriputra! Having personally accomplished the contemplation of patience, I constantly give rise to a heart of compassion, taking pity on sentient beings who increase their anger, hatred, and jealousy, and fall into the midst of afflictions; furthermore, by means of various skillful expedients, I awaken them so that they may attain liberation and obtain sublime rewards.

If sentient beings reject and turn their backs on Bodhisattvas, refusing to follow their virtuous guidance and instead increasing their evil conduct, they will constantly receive ugly and undesirable retributions in all places.

Why is this? Because the karma of malice is a cause of ugliness; it is unwholesome karma, defiled karma, inferior karma, the karma of a non-noble person, and the karma of one who is not a virtuous friend; therefore, it should not be committed.

One should know that the unwholesome karma of hatred can lead one toward rebirth in the three evil destinies, can lead one toward the realm of Yama, and can lead one toward the path of the hells or birth among animals, becoming a retainer in the realm of Yama.
