In this way, various unwholesome karmas of anger and hatred can lead one toward the destiny of the destitute and inferior yakṣas, and can lead one toward the destiny of the destitute and inferior pretas.
Such unwholesome karmic actions as malice can lead one toward poverty, low birth, and ugliness among human beings. Śāriputra!
I myself have never cultivated such modes of conduct in the past, and a bodhisattva mahāsattva likewise should not cultivate such modes of conduct.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
In this context, what are these distinct phenomena?
And what are these various distinct practices?"

The wholesome dharmas we cultivate are associated with them, whereas those they cultivate are associated with unwholesome dharmas; these are distinct dharmas and distinct modes of practice. Śāriputra!
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should train themselves by following me in this way. Why is this?

When Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are training, even if there are sentient beings who come to harass and disturb them, they do not give rise to thoughts of anger or malice, nor do they direct their attention toward the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). They constantly reflect upon themselves and practice the contemplation of patience (*kṣānti*), thereby bringing to maturity the roots of goodness in all sentient beings.

Śāriputra! Suppose there were someone who, with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, and mani-jewels, filled the four great continents and used them as a gift; it would not equal practicing this perfection of patience.
Why is this? Because by means of patience, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to cause sentient beings not to fall into saṃsāra, but to proceed toward the path of outflows-free realization.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not give rise to a mind of anger, but should constantly bring to mind mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Sangha. Why is this?

By the power of this merit from taking refuge, one shall attain the accomplishment of immeasurable roots of goodness, and shall also cause all sentient beings to mindfully recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
While maintaining this reflection, one should constantly attain awakening, considering: "What is wholesome and what is unwholesome for me and for sentient beings?
If I do not keep the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha in mind, I will be perpetually bound by the afflictions of anger, hatred, and evil conduct."
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"If one gives rise to anger, it is not the correct principle; if one is able to practice patience, that is the correct principle.
A Bodhisattva should distance themselves from all karmic actions of anger."
When practicing the perfection of patience, one should first bring to mind the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
By the power of these Three Jewels, all sentient beings may be led to practice this same conduct.

"Śāriputra! I have already accomplished such a mode of practice and attained unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment. I turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings; may all Tathāgatas grant me their acceptance."
"Good son!

When you give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, you shall turn the sublime wheel of Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, and you shall attain the supreme, unimpeded analytical knowledge and immeasurable wisdom and vision of all Buddhas."

When a bodhisattva cultivates this perfection of patience through such modes of practice, they counteract the misconduct of anger and malice; furthermore, they should also bring to mind that in the eastern direction there are worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, wherein dwell Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who currently abide, teach the Dharma, and benefit sentient beings.
At that time, those bodhisattvas were granted a prophecy by that Tathāgata:
"Sons of good family!
I too have already resolved upon this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and I teach the Dharma to sentient beings to transform and instruct them."

"In this way, there are likewise worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below; in those places, there dwell Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, currently residing and teaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings."
At that time, those bodhisattvas were granted a prophecy by that Tathāgata:
"Sons of good family!

I too have already resolved upon this *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind; I teach the Dharma to all sentient beings for their transformation and guidance, always delighting in praising the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), making the lion’s roar, and forever remaining far removed from all evil practices such as anger and malice."

"If there are sentient beings who delight in performing various kinds of beneficial deeds, and the Bodhisattva at that time sees those sentient beings performing such deeds, he likewise follows suit in performing all manner of meaningful benefits; how, then, could there be any distinction therein between various difficult and easy tasks?"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of patience in this manner toward all sentient beings."
If one does not train in accordance with this, they are not my virtuous friend;
if one can act in accordance with it to bring about beneficial purposes, they are called a virtuous friend.
Therefore, understanding that non-harming is the beneficial purpose, I shall take great delight in it and never abandon sentient beings while performing all manner of beneficial deeds.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Throughout billions of kalpas, I have borne the burdens of sentient beings' lack of virtue;
When I see sentient beings undergoing suffering, I have never for a moment abandoned them to remain at ease."
Sentient beings possess the fundamental nature of seeking benefit; they act as virtuous friends by instructing one another.
Even when encountering various evils and afflictions, they always endure them for the sake of that benefit.
Pervading all of Jambudvīpa, and likewise throughout the Buddha-fields,
they fill them entirely with every kind of precious treasure, bestowing them all for the sake of spiritual friends.
If someone were to take up a sharp sword and come to sever my limbs and members,
through the power of patience I would give rise to a mind of loving-kindness, remaining forever free from fear of any suffering or affliction.
Should there be those who are wrathful and full of hatred, persistently coming to harass with bitter malice, he extols them through the power of patience;
dwelling securely in the endurance of suffering, he is never troubled.
Should there be those who, bearing swords, staves, or poisons, seek to inflict harm out of malice,
one should endure all such evil deeds for the sake of the roots of goodness that benefit sentient beings.
I shall not now follow the ways of the foolish, nor shall I practice those inferior deeds;
I will extensively cultivate the causes for supreme benefit and proceed toward the unsurpassed fruit of Nirvana.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) in this way:

Suppose that for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *kalpas*, someone were to strike him with various weapons such as clubs, tiles, stones, and other implements; for a short time he might fall to the ground in a swoon, his life nearly coming to an end, only reviving after a long while."
At that time, the bodhisattva reflects thus:
"How marvelous! I have now regained my life once more; thereafter, I shall practice and train in this most supreme and excellent perfection of patience."
Suppose someone were to come to me and request my head, eyes, marrow, bones, flesh, hands, and feet, continuing in this manner for as many great eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River.
At that time, I shall never harbor any stinginess, nor shall I give rise to any unwholesome states such as anger, malice, or hatred. Why is this?
If I were to give rise to anger, malice, or any such unwholesome states, the roots of goodness I have accumulated over hundreds of thousands of kalpas would surely be scattered and destroyed.

I shall now further consolidate and accumulate the roots of goodness planted throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas so that they may not be lost or destroyed, thereby practicing for the sake of the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which is difficult to attain.
Why is this? O Śāriputra, we, the assembly of bodhisattvas, take the power of patience as our armor. Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva should not allow their mind regarding the Great Vehicle to regress, nor give Māra an opportunity, lest they fail to achieve the rare and unsurpassed *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One should not allow the bodhicitta to regress or become distracted, thereby permitting demonic activities (*mārakarman*) to create various obstacles.
What are these demonic activities? They are as follows:

attachment to one’s own food and drink is a demonic activity; attachment to the three robes is a demonic activity; discriminating in one's teaching and conversion is a demonic activity; causing others to praise oneself for the sake of gain and offerings is a demonic activity; delighting in practices for one’s own benefit is a demonic activity; severing various pure dharmas is a demonic activity; and even interrupting others' quiet seclusion, obstructing the cultivation of merit and wisdom, hindering others from approaching their preceptors (*ācārya*), and cutting off others' practice of the bodhisattva path—these are all demonic activities.
Śāriputra! If a bodhisattva mahāsattva should turn back from the path to enlightenment or give rise to a distracted mind, all evil Māras will immediately find an opportunity.
Why is this? Because various demonic obstacles, throughout the long night, watch for an opportunity to enter the bodhisattva’s mind, thereby causing anger and malice to increase.

Śāriputra! In the past, when I was firmly maintaining the prohibitive precepts and practicing the perfection of patience, I attained mastery of the wholesome dharmas; my name at that time was the Rishi.

At that time, there was a great Māra who manifested as a multitude of five hundred men; all were valiant and filled with great wrath. For five hundred years, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they pursued one another day and night, manifesting great fury. Whether on roads, in towns, villages, or the homes of laypeople, or in the midst of wildernesses, they constantly used anger, falsehood, and unreality to delude sentient beings.
Śāriputra! For five hundred years, those hosts of Māras constantly harbored great malice toward me and gave rise to various transgressions.
At that time, I contemplated and reflected deeply; out of compassion, I gave rise to a mind of great loving-kindness and extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the sake of those hosts of Māras.
At that time, having heard the Dharma, all the evil karmic actions of those māra hosts were completely extinguished. Śāriputra!
When I had thus taught this Dharma to those māra hosts, I caused all sentient beings to mature their roots of goodness so that they would attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Furthermore, for the sake of those sentient beings who are deceitful, corrupt in precepts, delight in unwholesome dharmas, and are difficult to tame, as well as those with excessive greed, hatred, and delusion, he acts as a virtuous condition so that they may attain maturity in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"I vow that when I attain perfect enlightenment in the future, I shall be the very first to deliver all sentient beings and lead them to nirvāṇa. Śāriputra!

At that time, I shall eliminate all deluded thoughts and constantly give rise to right mindfulness; I shall be fully endowed with virtuous conduct that benefits sentient beings, never abandoning it for even a moment throughout the three periods of time."
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva advances in the quest for anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should fulfill the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

If a bodhisattva experiences within his own body various kinds of malignant diseases and extremely heavy afflictions, even unto the suffering of death—whether already arisen or yet to arise—the bodhisattva at that time, being fully endowed with the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*), is able to endure them all.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva should firmly abide in the bodhisattva perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
That is to say, one should understand that the absence of anger is called the bodhisattva’s patience, and the absence of harmful intent is called the bodhisattva’s patience.
This is called the patience of a bodhisattva; speech free from contention is called the patience of a bodhisattva; non-violence is called the patience of a bodhisattva;
protecting one’s own life is called the patience of a bodhisattva; protecting the lives of others is called the patience of a bodhisattva;
and constantly guarding the actions of body, speech, and mind is called the patience of a bodhisattva.
When one inwardly examines with discernment while undergoing humiliation and practices the conduct of patience, this is called the bodhisattva’s patience;
when one remains far removed from craving and attachment, this is called the bodhisattva’s patience; when one accords with the retribution of karma, this is called the bodhisattva’s patience;
when one purifies the actions of body, speech, and mind, this is called the bodhisattva’s patience; and by the power of patience, one further attains—
To obtain the supreme and wondrous bliss of humans and devas is called the patience of a bodhisattva;
to further obtain the perfect and excellent marks and signs of a bodhisattva is called the patience of a bodhisattva;
and to further obtain the Tathāgata’s profound, wondrous, and pure Brahma-voice, as well as the firm accumulation of wholesome conduct by a bodhisattva, is called the patience of a bodhisattva.
To endure humiliation and remain far removed from all worldly afflictions is called the bodhisattva’s patience.
When others seek out every fault, the bodhisattva does not give rise to malice toward them; this is called the bodhisattva’s patience.

In brief, they shall even attain the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the eighteen unique qualities, and all supreme dharmas—great kindness, great compassion, great joy, and great equanimity—in their entirety and perfection.
It should be understood that this bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of patience, if someone should come to him in anger to harass or harm him, the bodhisattva at that time understands it to be illusory; as if facing an echo, he does not retaliate. Even if they strike or kill him, the bodhisattva scrutinizes them and understands them all to be like illusions or magical transformations, and likewise does not retaliate.
Even if someone should come and praise them in various ways, they do not take delight in it. Why is this?

Because the Bodhisattva takes as their retinue the genuine merits that are naturally perfected within themselves; they do not become attached to worldly dharmas, they are able to repent and apologize for their own faults, and they do not give rise to disparagement toward the faults of others, performing great Buddha-work to bring the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) to perfection.

Furthermore, they reflect that all the karmic deeds of sin they have committed are entirely false and illusory, and they are able to renounce all conflicting practices and meaningless matters. Śāriputra!
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
*The Buddha-Spoken Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattva-Piṭaka*, Fascicle Twenty-Four.
*The Buddha-Spoken Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattva-Piṭaka*, Fascicle Two.
Fifteen:

Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Preceptor of the Silver Light and Merit Court, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, Purple-Robed Śramaṇa, Subject Fahu, and others, by Imperial Decree. The Remainder of Chapter Eight: The Perfection of Forbearance. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

The perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is as follows: it is the ultimate patience regarding one's own person; that which involves the notion of a self and so forth is not ultimate patience.
Why is this? When others come with anger to harass and disturb him, he is able to endure it, for neither the mind nor its objects can be apprehended.
The bodhisattva then reflects as follows:
"What is hatred? What is patience?
Within the enumeration of dharmas, how could there be hatred toward the sense bases such as the eye?"

Furthermore, he investigates and observes that patience regarding the twelve sense bases is likewise unattainable; through successive penetration and understanding, he finds that the characteristics of sentient beings and so forth are entirely non-apprehendable.

Furthermore, this patience is not ultimately real; even the name "patience" is like an echo in an empty valley. This is called suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self; one should form such an understanding regarding patience and the like.

Furthermore, this patience is also not ultimate, for it involves the conceptualization of superiority and inferiority regarding the practice of patience, such as thinking, "In regard to these dharmas, I am without error, whereas that person is in error."
Furthermore, this forbearance is not truly ultimate; that is to say, to think "I am liberated regarding these phenomena, while others are not" is inconsistent with the practice of forbearance.

Furthermore, this patience is also not ultimate; that is to say, regarding these dharmas, one conceives two kinds of marks within the practice of patience, thinking, "I abide in the right path, while they do not abide in the right path."
Furthermore, this forbearance is not truly ultimate; that is to say, one is able to endure regarding these dharmas and regarding emptiness, yet one cannot endure regarding views;
one is able to endure within the signless, yet one cannot endure within the signful;
and while one is able to endure all things within the wishless and the desireless, one cannot endure within the wished-for and the desirous.
Regarding patience: if one is able to endure when the object of focus is non-accumulated, yet cannot endure when the object of focus is accumulated;
if one is able to endure at the point where afflictions are exhausted, yet cannot endure within the realm of afflictions;
and furthermore, if one is able to endure in what is wholesome, yet cannot endure in what is unwholesome...
One is able to endure; that is, one can endure regarding what is faultless but cannot endure regarding what is faulty,
one can endure regarding untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena but cannot endure regarding tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena,
and one can endure regarding supramundane (*lokottara*) phenomena but cannot [endure] regarding mundane (*laukika*) phenomena.
If one is able to endure while being able to endure pure phenomena but unable to endure defiled phenomena,
or if one is able to endure the phenomena of nirvāṇa but unable to endure the phenomena of saṃsāra,
such forms of patience possess counteractive factors and are therefore not ultimately real.
What is called ultimate patience?
It is when one can accord with emptiness, such that regarding seeing and non-seeing, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
When one can accord with emptiness, regarding having aspirations and seeking, or being without aspirations and without seeking, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
If one can accord with emptiness, then amidst the accumulation of objects of perception, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
If one can accord with emptiness, then regarding both pure phenomena and defiled phenomena, there is neither existence nor non-existence.
If one can accord with emptiness, then regarding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, they are neither existent nor non-existent.
If one can accord with emptiness, then regarding faults and the absence of faults, they are neither existent nor non-existent.
If one can accord with emptiness, then regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) as well as the dharma of nirvāṇa, they are neither existent nor non-existent.
This is called ultimate patience (*kṣānti*). Why is this?
It is because all phenomena of the past, future, and present are fundamentally non-arising; thus, the conditions are inexhaustible and patience is inexhaustible.

If, regarding these phenomena, they are neither conditioned nor unconditioned, nor are they a combination; if they neither increase nor decrease, and are without arising or perishing; if they are neither a creator nor a nourisher—because they do not arise, this is called "inexhaustible," and this is taught as true patience.
Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva is able to practice in this manner, it is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā) of the great bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

When that bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to practice these practices corresponding to a bodhisattva, all Māras and their retinues, along with their demonic activities and disputes, will completely cease to appear; this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s accomplishment of the supreme perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).
Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Vigor (Vīryapāramitā), Part One "Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is called the perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct associated with the perfection of diligence, he first causes the works of Māra to vanish and cease to appear.”

Next, one should arouse non-retrogressive, fully endowed, and courageous diligence; disregarding body and life, with firm and heroic resolve, one should seek to cultivate this sublime Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and furthermore, be able to transcribe, uphold, hear, read, and recite it, as well as explain its meaning and intent for others.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva also teaches others to hear, transcribe, receive, uphold, recite, and explain the meaning and intent of various sūtras for the sake of others.

Śāriputra! It is, for example, as if there were a person who practices the path of truth, wielding various adamantine weapons to battle a hundred men without fear, valiantly confronting the enemy host and not begrudging his own life or body.

The bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing the perfection of vigor is also like this: they should firmly initiate the most supreme vigor, seeking the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka without ever abandoning it, and resolve upon the practice of superior understanding with non-retrogressive vigor.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices with firm and resolute diligence, they do not begrudge their body or life. Within this trichiliocosm—beings born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or by transformation; those with form or without form; those with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—even down to those included within the category of sentient beings—if, throughout the course of an entire kalpa, passing through moments, *lava*s, and *muhūrta*s, such that they have never previously taken birth since ancient times but only now take birth to obtain a human body, they shall likewise apply themselves with diligence to reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding [the teachings], even expounding them for others so that they may receive and uphold them."
Śāriputra! I shall now delight in speaking a parable to clarify this meaning.
It is as if there were a person who practices the path of true correctness; wielding a sharp sword, he is able to resist evil companions and sever their lives, thereby achieving complete victory.

Śāriputra! It is the same for that bodhisattva mahāsattva: with a single-minded resolve to arouse courageous diligence and a heart free from fear, they are fully able to receive and uphold the true Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka.
Śāriputra!

A bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to fulfill the practice of diligence of the stage of non-retrogression, and furthermore, can swiftly fulfill immeasurable powers of diligence, namely: the valor of pure mind, the valor of ethical discipline, the valor of patience, the valor of diligence, the valor of samādhi, the valor of supreme wisdom, and the valor of supreme conduct.

Śāriputra! Although a bodhisattva mahāsattva can thus give rise to such heroic vigor, he never for even a single thought-moment gives rise to an intention to kill; this is not like an evil friend who gives rise to a heart of heroic vigor and is able to commit murder.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra! I say that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is like Brahmā, like Śakra, the Lord of Devas, and like Mount Sumeru, remaining unshakable. Possessing great loving-kindness and great compassion, as well as excellent resolve, he further attains the sphere of the superknowledges (abhijñā) of the stage of non-retrogression. He skillfully knows the various mental activities of sentient beings; his mind is as equal as the great earth toward all, and his mind is equally impartial like water, fire, wind, and space. Furthermore, he is able to eliminate all faults such as greed, hatred, and delusion."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Suppose a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva were to take seven treasures filling worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and offer them as a gift; this would not equal the merit of hearing this sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka, reflecting upon it with diligence, and being able to practice it so as to attain the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and others should practice with such tranquil contemplation. Śāriputra,
if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva can thus extensively and accordingly practice and train, they will attain the fulfillment of immeasurable and vast roots of goodness.
By hearing this perfection of diligence (*vīryapāramitā*), one is able to accomplish the most supreme and wondrous fruit.
Why is this? Śāriputra!
Because they are resolutely devoted to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva, for the sake of hearing, reciting, copying, upholding, and explaining to others the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, should arouse courageous and diligent effort.
In this way, as one proceeds through various perils and difficulties, one shall likewise go forth with firm resolve and without weariness or hardship.
How does one who finds it difficult to depart succeed in departing?
It is by means of the wondrous path to Nirvana, which prevents Māra Pāpīyān from finding an opportunity.
Regarding these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the path of yoga, they exert courageous diligence in seeking the way to nirvāṇa through the three vehicles.

Within the three evil realms, they cause all sentient beings to be able to sever the dharmas of affliction, and through the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, and so forth, as well as extensive learning and cultivation, they seek liberation.
If there are sentient beings who perform unwholesome deeds and are indolent, one should give rise to compassion for them and cause them all to develop courageous diligence. Śāriputra!
When the wisdom of Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas increases, they may distance themselves from sentient beings who are indolent, or they may dwell together with those who are diligent.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
it is because they seek only the most supreme, foremost, and pure liberation that is nirvāṇa.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of diligence, they cause all sentient beings to practice it as well; moreover, they are able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, skillfully explaining right conduct so that all may awaken, in order to lead them into the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
“Brave and diligent, entirely without hindrance, Always attaining a noble height beyond compare,
Within the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, He is called the Great Wise One who upholds it.”
Contemplating the meaning of the unsurpassed True Dharma, one attains the gateway of inconceivable wisdom;
further seeking liberation within the True Dharma, one shall receive the Tathāgata’s personal prophecy.
Bravely cultivating supreme wisdom, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree in right contemplation,
he causes all māras to tremble and submit entirely, by virtue of his power of wisdom and diligence.
Universally manifesting all pure precepts, Able to practice every worldly activity,
Furthermore able to benefit and bring joy to all sentient beings, Possessing perfect diligence without diminution.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

“After my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years, if there are sentient beings who practice this practice and who delight in and uphold these sūtras, they shall attain immeasurable, supreme wisdom, a mass of merit, wealth, nobility, and majesty; and they shall also attain the Tathāgata’s ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four right efforts, loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, as well as the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha and all other Buddha-dharmas—in short, they shall gather them all together and understand each one clearly.”

With a mind attained to purity, one dispels the activities of Māra, causes all sentient beings to exhaust the suffering of birth and death and turn toward the path to Nirvāṇa, and furthermore, at that time, completely relinquishes all favorable and adverse conditions.

Śāriputra! At that time, there will be sentient beings endowed with wisdom and skillful means who seek to advance toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; who maintain pure precepts, constantly delight in extensive learning, practice various meditative concentrations, cultivate the work of wisdom and supreme liberation, as well as the knowledge and vision of liberation; who strive for the Buddha-dharma, delight in the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings, eliminate wrong views, joyfully seek right view, and emerge from saṃsāra by practicing the noble path and expounding the true Dharma.

Furthermore, at that time, he shattered all demonic obstacles, causing greed, hatred, and delusion to be entirely extinguished; he severed the darkness of ignorance and gave rise to luminous wisdom. Śāriputra!
If one is able to hear and receive such a Dharma as this, one will be able to grow all roots of goodness and accumulate the most supreme diligence.
If one can thus hear the True Dharma, Māra shall find no opportunity, and one will give rise to no doubt regarding any of the Buddha-dharmas.
Śāriputra! At that time, those sentient beings, endowed with the power of merit and practicing correctly within their own minds, shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Furthermore, these sentient beings will be able to hear and recite the various sūtras, delighting in receiving and upholding them with extreme joy; likewise, they will experience great joy in receiving, reciting, practicing, and accomplishing the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. I declare that such persons shall achieve accomplishment within the teachings of all Tathāgatas.

Furthermore, if there should be someone who does not specialize in reading and reciting, but because of certain causes and conditions comes for a time to listen and receive [the teaching], and with focused attention feels love and joy, giving rise to great delight, they too shall obtain the most supreme and foremost firm diligence.
In this way, Śāriputra, one is able to explain even a small portion of the true and subtle characteristics of the sublime Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka to others. Śāriputra!

It is like this: suppose there were fruits in the waters of the great ocean, fully matured and endowed with both color and fragrance, floating upon the surface. A man, seeing such fruits, gave rise to great courage and heroic diligence, entering the great ocean; seeing the waters surging violently, he disregarded the danger of drowning and, grasping the fruits with both hands—whether one, two, or three—he emerged from the great ocean.
Thereafter, he went to that secluded place to observe the fruit and tasted its flavor.
He then thought to himself:
"In the past, I did not recognize this fruit; I was likewise ignorant of its color, fragrance, and delicious taste."
Again he thought to himself:
"I shall summon great courage and go once more to the great ocean to retrieve those fruits.
However, the fruits did not appear; he saw only the waves of the sea surging violently, and giving rise to distress, he withdrew at that time.
However, I thought of how this fruit was of such exquisite color, fragrance, and flavor, so wonderful and lovely that I regretted not having taken more of it earlier.
Śāriputra, after my parinirvāṇa,

during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish, if there are sentient beings who possess even a slight degree of faith and understanding in generosity, ethical discipline, supreme wisdom, and diligence, they shall be just like this as well.

For these reasons, regarding the various sūtras—having heard their praise, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting them, and even expounding them for others, even as much as a single four-line verse—they are harassed by Māra Pāpīyān; thus they are unable to establish themselves in receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting, nor can they perform various offerings and praises to bring them forth, and for this reason, they abandon them all.

Furthermore, even those who have successively heard, recited, praised, and upheld [the teachings] in small measure, yet contemplate and practice them in secluded places, will find themselves vulnerable to Māra, who will cause them to constantly falter and retreat in all circumstances.
Then that practitioner spoke these words: "Alas, alas!

I am one who has declined within the unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgata; you do not allow us to hear or uphold the True Dharma, such that even for the duration of a muhūrta, I am unable to bring to mind the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Again, when the community of bhikṣus is possessed by Māra, they are unable to hear, read, or recite the various sūtras.
At that time, Māra Pāpīyān appears before the great assembly and disparages them in various ways:"
"These various sūtras were not spoken by the Buddha; they are merely worldly, false, and artificial embellishments. Śāriputra!
When the bhikṣus in that great assembly heard these words, because they were all under the influence of Māra's power, they would not listen to or accept them in any respect.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person, having heard this True Dharma, Causes all hosts of Māras to depart entirely,
And within all the Buddha-dharmas, Attains resolute faith and eliminates doubt."
If there are sentient beings of meager merit who cannot hear this True Dharma,
it is because those sentient beings lack merit that, even upon hearing it, they are unable to give rise to faith and understanding.
There may be those endowed with the power of merit who, upon hearing and upholding [this teaching], give rise to faith and understanding;
by hearing even a little of this True Dharma, they are able to dispel all demonic activities.
Thus, those sentient beings of meager merit do not give rise to faith in this True Dharma;
because of their lack of faith, they fall into evil destinies, like those born blind who see nothing.
If there are those who possess the power of merit and have deep faith and understanding in this True Dharma,
by virtue of that deep faith they will be born in the happy realms, as swiftly as butter dissolves when cast into water.
A certain class of sentient beings with little merit, upon hearing the Dharma, give rise to afflictions from one to another;
those people suffer distress throughout the long night, and because of their ignorance, they do not attain liberation.
Having utterly abandoned the Buddha’s Bodhi, they swiftly fall into the evil destinies.
“Śāriputra! The Tathāgata possesses a dharma of pure and immaculate wisdom. Śāriputra!”

Among the fourfold assembly, if there are certain bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa and at a time when the Dharma is about to perish, hear, recite, delight in, and uphold these various sūtras.
If there are certain sentient beings who, in all circumstances, are unable to find joy in receiving, upholding, reading, or reciting [the teachings],
the Tathāgata knows each and every one of them.

Furthermore, if sentient beings, having heard this sūtra, can initiate right practice and cultivate it according to the principle, they shall obtain four kinds of dharmas that are fully endowed with purity, stainlessness, and non-obstruction.
What are the four?

First, obtaining the unobstructed dharma of the fully perfected, pure, and stainless perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Second, obtaining the unobstructed dharma of always encountering the Tathāgata and beholding his various sublime marks, which are fully perfected, pure, and stainless. Third, obtaining the unobstructed dharma of being able to see the Tathāgata Maitreya, which is fully perfected, pure, and stainless. Fourth, obtaining the unobstructed dharma of the power of all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) that are in accord with reality, which is fully perfected, pure, and stainless.
Śāriputra! One who has attained these four kinds of dharmas that are complete, pure, stainless,
and unobstructed— Śāriputra!

If, after my parinirvāṇa, at a time when the Dharma is about to perish, there are those who practice the Mahāyāna according to such modes of conduct and cultivate the corresponding practices, and who initiate the practice of sublime diligence—furthermore, receiving, upholding, reciting, and explaining the sūtras for others, and causing them to be heard in succession—then those sentient beings will encounter ten kinds of demonic activities (*mārakarman*). The wise should fully understand them all; they must not comply with these demonic activities, but should instead further arouse courageous diligence to accomplish the work of the Buddha.
What are called the ten kinds of demonic deeds?

Śāriputra, if there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to the desire to receive, uphold, read, and recite the various sūtras, at that time Māra Pāpīyān comes to harass and disturb him; this is the first demonic deed. A wise person should understand this and must not comply with it.
"Śāriputra!

If there is a bhikṣu who conceives a desire to receive, uphold, read, and recite the various sūtras, and at that time Māra Pāpīyān comes to harass him, causing diseases to arise in his eyes—this is the second work of Māra. A wise person should recognize this for what it is and must not become discouraged."
"Śāriputra!

If there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to the desire to receive, uphold, read, and recite the various sūtras, and at that time Māra Pāpīyān comes to harass him, causing various painful illnesses to arise in his body—this is the third work of Māra. A wise person should understand this and must not become discouraged."

Śāriputra! If there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the various sūtras, gives rise to the desire to receive, uphold, read, and recite them, yet causes his mind to become distracted and finds no delight in abiding in its original state—this is the fourth work of Māra. A wise person should understand this and must not comply with it.

Śāriputra! If there are bhikṣus who, having developed a desire to receive, uphold, read, and recite the various sūtras, instead give rise to extreme anger and engage in mutual contention, causing those sūtras to be unable to be established, this is the fifth work of Māra. A wise person should understand this and should not comply with it.

Śāriputra! If there are bhikṣus who, regarding the various sūtras, give rise to the desire to receive, uphold, read, and recite them, yet cause one another to grasp at them and engage in strife, thereby falling together into royal peril; if they give rise to malicious speech as sharp as poisonous arrows and mutually inflict harm upon each other—such conduct prevents the various sūtras from circulating and causes them to swiftly regress due to the karma of contention. This is the sixth work of Māra; the wise should understand this and must not comply with it.

Śāriputra! If there is a bhikṣu who gives rise to the desire to receive, uphold, read, and recite the various sūtras, at that time Māra Pāpīyān comes to entice him and cause him to dwell in the houses of laypeople; furthermore, he incites various disputes and quarrels. Through such conduct, he is unable to receive and uphold the sūtras and causes them to be slandered. Because of the karma of dispute, his practice is swiftly destroyed. This is the seventh work of Māra; the wise should understand this and must not comply with it.

Śāriputra! At that time, when the Dharma is about to perish, there may be a group of young bhikṣus who have not long since gone forth into this Dharma; they shall delight in receiving and upholding the various sūtras, possess firm faith and understanding, and resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, having heard this sutra, that bhikṣu was filled with great joy.
His preceptor then said to the young bhikṣus: "This is not the Buddha’s bodhi;
it is not the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya; it should not be accepted or upheld."
When the bhikṣus heard these words, for a short time they did not believe or accept the Buddha’s bodhi.
Furthermore, those bhikṣus said to one another:
"In the past we cultivated the Dharma of the Buddha’s bodhi, but now it causes us to take no pleasure in its cultivation."

All the power of their past roots of goodness will be severed and extinguished; instead, they will be caused to fall into defiled states, and even at the end of their lives, they will be reborn in the evil realms to undergo great suffering and affliction.
Śāriputra! You should know that these are the words spoken by Māra, which thus accumulate the karma of the various hells.
That sentient beings slander the Triple Gem and do not comply with the Buddha’s words—the Tathāgata fully knows this throughout the three periods of time.
Furthermore, when sentient beings initiate diligence and cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna, the Tathāgata is likewise able to know this.
Śāriputra! I now cause all bodhisattvas to give rise to four kinds of conceptions.
What are the four?

First, to be well-disciplined regarding one's own actions; second, to skillfully observe what is well-cultivated and practiced; third, not to take pleasure in observing the deeds of others, but to give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings; and fourth, to practice walking, standing, sitting, and lying down in empty and secluded places, while guarding the minds of both oneself and others in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus are called the four kinds of conceptions.
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha*, Fascicle Twenty-five. 2.
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha*, Fascicle [Twenty-five].

The Twenty-sixth [Chapter], translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others—Śramaṇas of the Imperial Court, recipients of the purple robe and conferred the title of Great Master of Indian Translations, Silver Light Grand Master, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, under the Imperial Edict. Chapter Nine, Part Two: The Perfection of Vigor. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

At that time, those sentient beings will frequently give rise to wrong views and harbor perverse attachments; the bhikṣus who preach the Dharma will also become few, and they will be held in contempt by others, failing to engender respect, nor will they be honored, approached, or supported with offerings.
There were certain bhikṣus who taught what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma, and took no pleasure in approaching the True Dharma.

Even when they saw someone who felt reverence, respect, and made offerings toward the various sūtras, or who possessed great power and offered manifold praise, they would together treat them with contempt and arrogance.

Śāriputra! At that time, those bhikṣus who have attained freedom from desire will joyfully accept and uphold [the teachings], whereas those who have not yet attained freedom from desire will take no pleasure in accepting and upholding the sūtras; they will instead follow the faction of Māra before the great assembly. This is the eighth work of Māra. The wise should understand this and must not follow it.

Śāriputra! If there is a bhikṣu who, though having conceived a fondness for various sūtras and engaging in their upholding, recitation, explanation, and transcription, commits acts of theft out of a desire for gain by conforming to the ways of worldly sentient beings, he repeatedly directs his attention toward three matters.
What are the three?
They are attachment to clothing, food and drink, and various bedding and furniture.
To pursue these three matters excessively is the ninth work of Māra; the wise should understand this and must not comply with it.

Śāriputra! If there are bhikṣus who practice the conduct corresponding to these Mahāyāna sūtras, and are able to arouse the most supreme diligence, copying them, receiving and upholding them, delighting in reading and reciting them, and explaining them extensively for others;

At that time, that bhikṣu was possessed by Māra; obscured by the hindrances of karma and afflictions, he accorded with and took delight in defiled phenomena, constantly engaged in frivolous discourse, and was addicted to sleep.

Even while asleep, they take pleasure in and remain attached to various defiled phenomena; furthermore, they are addicted to the affairs of seductive women and deeply delight in conforming to such modes of conduct. They take no pleasure in copying, receiving, upholding, reciting, or extensively explaining the sūtras to others.
Śāriputra! At that time, those bhikṣus who conceive love and joy for the teaching of the Tathāgata do not wish for the extinction of the Tathāgata’s holy doctrine.
Those who do not conceive such love and joy—evil-doing bhikṣus possessed by Māra—desire to cause the Buddha-dharma to be swiftly extinguished.
This is the tenth work of Māra. Śāriputra,
these ten dharmas should be understood one by one by all who possess wisdom, and they should not be followed.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"At all those places where they dwell, obstacles of Māra arise due to their karma;
they utterly abandon all pure dharmas and take no delight in discerning what is beneficial."
Excellence of wisdom diminishes while poor wisdom increases; they do not abide within the True Dharma.
Delighting in hearing what is contrary to the Dharma, they are able to practice it all, and thus fall into the miserable realms as their destiny.
Thus, as they passed away in succession, those who concealed their faults for the sake of protection,
yet held their preceptors and teachers in high esteem, all fell simultaneously into the evil realms.
Throughout ten million billion kalpas, for the sake of benefiting the world, I have practiced asceticism;
always contemplating skillful means for sentient beings, I have caused them all to remain far removed from the fires of the three poisons.
At that time, I realized great enlightenment and was able to turn the pure, wondrous wheel of Dharma;
among gods and humans there was no one equal to me, and I was acclaimed as the foremost in both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
I must not now abandon them; sentient beings in this world are exceedingly difficult to encounter.
I shall cause all those hosts of Māra to retreat and disperse, so that they may all be freed from suffering and attain peace and happiness.
Furthermore, within the paths of delusion and darkness, they uphold the true and virtuous practices such as the six perfections;
being in complete accord with all the Buddha's teachings, they are able to attain the path to enlightenment.
Having heard and received such teachings as these, they are further able to expound the true emptiness and establish others in right faith;
for this reason, they are able to remain free from all hosts of Māras.
Within this supreme reality, if one rejects the true Dharma,
taking what is unreal for the real, one will be unable to remain far removed from the hosts of Māras.
If there are sentient beings who, in the presence of the Buddha, Give rise to firm and joyful reverence,
When hearing such a sublime Dharma, They shall obtain auspicious and supreme benefit.

When sentient beings of right faith rejoice, and when all those who are subject to Māra experience suffering and distress as they perform wholesome deeds everywhere, the hosts of Māra come vying with one another to terrify them.
At that time, Māra assumed the guise of a bhikṣu, skillfully uttering words of deception to swiftly stir up turmoil among the assembly,
claiming that the path to bodhi was not true.
Saying, "My dharma is the true cause," you should have sought firm abiding;
yet, having first given rise to such conceptual proliferation, you then treat it with contempt and further slander it.

At that time, those bhikṣus were possessed by Māra; because they believed Māra’s words, they became heedless, saying, "This dharma is not the Buddha-vehicle," and thereby abandoned the path to nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, turning their backs on perfect awakening and uniting with all sensory objects, they do not have faith or acceptance in the Buddha’s Dharma;
because they are already burdened by the coarse heaviness of clinging to the view of self, they swiftly fall into the miserable realms.
Even if there should be a few bhikṣus who, moreover, delight in what is not the truth,
they will each, within the emptiness of the Mahāyāna Dharma, seek out one another's faults.
Even if one encounters the most supreme and true Dharma, because of distraction and confusion, one does not listen or practice it;
furthermore, giving rise to fear toward its principles and abandoning the true Dharma, one has no place of refuge.
At that time, there will be no one to preach the Dharma; the people will be numerous yet lacking in faith and understanding.
Even if such teachers of the Dharma should exist, everyone will utterly abandon them and refuse to listen or accept their words.
If, during the final age of the World-Honored One, you are further able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, many demonic obstacles will invade at that time;
do not give way to despondency or retreat on this account.
If in the future there should be a community of bhikṣus who develop firm faith and understanding in the Dharma,
they would rather lose their own lives than fail to uphold it steadfastly, thereby swiftly attaining the realization of the perfect and eternal fruit.

At that time, Śāriputra and the great bhikṣus, having heard within the great assembly that those who practice the Mahāyāna are able to practice the True Dharma amidst all perils and difficulties, each gave rise to vast, immeasurable, firm, and courageous power of diligence.
With such a mode of practice, one listens to, recites, copies, upholds, successively teaches, and extensively explains to others this true Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Furthermore, he spoke these skillful similes:
"Suppose there is a person who is well able to guard his ancestral treasury, yet seeing that his wealth and treasures are gradually diminishing, he gives rise to anxiety and distress."

As I now see that the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—so difficult to attain—which Śākyamuni Tathāgata cultivated over immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, is gradually declining and vanishing.

We bhikṣus are likewise filled with shared grief and affliction; we ought each to give rise to vast, immeasurable, and courageous diligence, firmly upholding and guarding the precious treasury of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva’s true Dharma.
Again, the bhikṣu said:

"Suppose there is a man who has an only son, handsome and exceptionally fine; when his parents see him, their hearts are filled with joy, and they gaze upon the features of their son without ever turning their eyes away for a moment."
His son suddenly fell into that perilous place; a large bird seized him and carried him away, and he fell once more onto a high and precipitous spot on the edge of the hell realms.
At that time, his parents exerted great courage and strength to seize him and bring him back.

Just as I do now, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if there should be a true person who conceives great faith and reverence for the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure and desires to seek liberation, they will at that time receive, uphold, read, recite, and practice according to the teachings.

I entrust this unsurpassed Dharma-treasure of the Tathāgata to you for mutual preservation; you must likewise guard it with diligence, ensuring that it is not defiled or destroyed by those wicked people.
Furthermore, the bhikṣu said:
"Suppose, for example, in this world, military forces have gathered and are drawn up in battle formations, intending to fight one another.

At that time, there may be a few sentient beings among the crowd who, seeing those armies, feel no fear or weakness of heart as they stand before them, protecting the troops so that they do not engage in combat."

Furthermore, among the multitude there were many who were courageous; seeing these troops, their hearts were free from fear or weakness as they stood before them, and in this manner, through successive efforts, they established their martial merit.

Just as now, after my parinirvāṇa when the Dharma is about to perish, if there are sentient beings whose inner resolve is firm who protect and uphold the True Dharma, who draw near to virtuous friends, who delight in seeking liberation, and who don the armor of steadfastness to rouse the power of vast diligence and shatter the hosts of Māra.

In the same manner, if one applies even a small portion of refined and subtle discernment toward the Jewel of the Dharma, it is likewise so; even if one explains a single four-line verse to others, causing them to rejoice, and leads them to accept the Buddha’s words with faith, free from doubt or slander, and further instructs many sentient beings to rejoice in and praise the unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, thereby establishing them therein.
At that time, the bhikṣus spoke at length, providing immeasurable parables.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"In terms of the actual characteristics of such practice, I say that the mass of merit obtained by this person is like space—limitless and impossible to exhaust through description."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, such persons will be difficult to find. I declare them to be superior men, supreme men, courageous men, and great men; they have attained a share of the Buddha-dharma, do not delight in the quiet seclusion of the self-benefiting Hīnayāna, but practice only the firm and correct conduct of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, they take no pleasure in praising the reputations of themselves or others, but take pleasure only in praising the merits of the Mahāyāna.
Śāriputra, even at the time of their death, they shall likewise uphold, recite, and study this True Dharma, and attain decisive, superior understanding of true emptiness.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In the future final age, there will also be a great proliferation of bhikṣus who violate the precepts and slander the True Dharma, taking great pleasure in practicing the non-Buddhist scriptures of the various worldly outsiders."

Śāriputra! In this evil age of the five corruptions—the corruption of the kalpa, the corruption of afflictions, the corruption of sentient beings, the corruption of views, and the corruption of lifespan—if there should be a bhikṣu who, with courageous vigor, can overcome all strife and abide in peace, constantly aspiring never to be separated from the Bodhi of the Buddhas, he should practice visualization during the three periods of the day and night and remain well-established therein.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Those who draw near to the Tathāgata’s treasury of the True Dharma Are able to shatter all suffering of old age and death.
They do not apply themselves to practices for their own benefit alone, But always delight in bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings."
Within the True Dharma taught by me, those who can establish it with reverence and delight are worthy of being my tamer; they are truly the disciples of the Tathāgata.
If one does not delight in hearing the true Dharma, And furthermore cannot dwell well within it,
That person will fall into the evil realms, Like a wheel swiftly sinking into the sea.
Throughout the course of a thousand koṭis of kalpas, it is extremely difficult to encounter a Buddha appearing in the world;
yet such a person is possessed by Māra, and even if they do encounter a Buddha, they give rise to weariness and indolence.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Ninety-one kalpas ago, at that time, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
Within that Buddha-dharma, there were six groups of bhikṣus: first, Sudarśana; second, Sunetra;

third, Priyakārin; fourth, Bhadraśrī; fifth, Yaśas; and sixth, Tīkṣṇadaṃṣṭra. They gave rise to and clung to views of self, person, sentient being, life-span, as well as the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Constantly acting with arrogance and contempt, they would call one another together and go into the wilderness, where they constantly discussed various evil deeds, each claiming for themselves that they practiced a hundred kinds of wholesome actions.
Furthermore, he gathers ten, twenty, or even fifty others to form a group, teaching them his own practiced methods in succession, and makes this vow:
"If you violate my instructions, you shall surely suffer harm."

Having spoken these words on their practice, they departed in separate directions; some entered villages, some reached towns and cities, and others went to the houses of themselves or others, even as far as royal capitals.
At that time, one of them reached a certain village, gathered his own kindred, and again taught them to increase or diminish the Buddha’s words.
Śāriputra! How does mental engagement increase or diminish the Buddha’s word?
At that time, those of such a kind firmly cling to the existence of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span, thinking: "If there is no self, who is it that comes and goes?"
Who is it that sits or lies down?
Who is it that speaks or remains silent? Who is it that gives?
Who is the experiencer?
Who is it that eats and drinks?
Who suffers and who rejoices?
"Who is it that experiences even a single itch or a single pain?
At that time, someone in the assembly spoke these words:
"If one says there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span, such a person is not my good friend."

"Śāriputra! At that time, the men, women, boys, and girls of that village, having heard these words, all took pleasure in those who held the view of a self as their virtuous friends, and said to one another:
'In the past, there were wise ones who understood reality as it truly is.'"
A true spiritual friend is one who speaks of the absence of self, person, sentient being, or life-span.
Regarding such a person, whom I previously held in high esteem, I should no longer draw near to them, nor should I honor or make offerings to them.
"Śāriputra! Later, during the second half of the month, those six groups of bhikṣus gathered together again. Among them, one bhikṣu said:
'I have successively converted five hundred clans to become my followers.'"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin had a śrāvaka bhikṣu whose outflows were exhausted and who was free from further afflictions, having attained the fruit of arhatship."
Having understood this, he entered those five hundred villages and spoke these words to the men and women, boys and girls:
"The Dharma they teach consists of coarse and evil speech, untruthful speech, and speech devoid of benefit."
Then, among that assembly, the Arhat spoke these verses:
"If one does not understand the True Dharma, That person is obscured from the path of the true sages.
Since you cling tenaciously to false teachings, You will certainly fall into the various evil realms."
Having spoken these verses, the group of six bhikṣus became greatly incensed and were unwilling to accept them with faith.
At that time, the Arhat, moved by great compassion, praised the Buddha and further spoke this gāthā:
“The true Dharma taught by our Buddha Is that all conditioned things are utterly impermanent.”
Within all phenomena there is no self; they are neither solid nor permanent.
Furthermore, all conditioned formations are produced through volitional effort; because their essence is unreal, they are empty and yet more empty.
Fools, deluded and confused, cling tenaciously to them, giving rise to agitation within these illusory dharmas.
Having spoken these verses, he further addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
"Within the Dharma taught by all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, there is absolutely no self, person, sentient being, or life-span."
At that time, the Arhat, knowing that the assembly of bhikṣus did not delight in or accept his teaching with faith,
spoke again in verse: "If one gives rise to views and attachments regarding giving and receiving, And further recognizes the existence of conceptualization through sensation and contact,
Failing to have faith and follow the Dharma of non-self— They shall all fall into the various evil realms."

"Śāriputra! At that time, those sentient beings will place their trust in and accept all the words spoken by men, women, boys, and girls regarding false dharmas. Consequently, sixty-eight thousand people, due to their wrong views, will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, all fall into the Avīci Great Hell, where they will experience extreme suffering."
Furthermore, within the hells, they are born with many tongues, each tongue as vast as a thousand-petaled lotus flower; upon these tongues, iron plows are used to furrow and tear them apart.
Moreover, hell-wardens take up hundred-edged mallets to strike and pierce the offenders.
Additionally, hot iron balls rain down from the sky; these balls, fiercely blazing, strike the bodies of the offenders.
Furthermore, those iron balls transform into masses of fire with extremely fierce flames; each sinner perceives these raging fires burning their own bodies.
Once this retribution is exhausted, they emerge from hell and shall fall again among the thousand-headed fish.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:

"When sentient beings fall into hell, amidst immeasurable hundreds of thousands of masses of fire, lightning flashes in the sky and fire rains down; the bodies of these sinners undergo extreme suffering."
A single body further undergoes all sufferings; fierce flames and weapons descend from the sky, filling a hundred yojanas, as each person sees their own body filling the midst of hell.
Each person further beholds upon their own tongue sharp-pointed arrows fiercely coming to strike, and keen knives slicing the tongue into segment after segment;
only then do they realize this is the most extreme suffering within all suffering.
Because they followed false friends and, through repeated intimacy, came to cherish and revere them, they abandoned the assembly that maintains pure precepts;
for this reason, they have fallen into this state of extreme suffering.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Because those six groups of bhikṣus are false and unreal, they too shall likewise fall into the Avīci Great Hell."
That hell is one hundred yojanas in extent, and each individual perceives their own body filling the entirety of the prison.
Within each of those bodies there are a thousand mouths, and within each mouth two tongues arise, each tongue being four yojanas in length and breadth.

Upon each of their tongues, five hundred iron plows plow and tear them asunder; furthermore, hot iron is used to seize and cauterize the tongues, such that the suffering of these offenders prevents them from speaking.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of koṭis of various instruments of torture come from above to beat their heads.

Thus they undergo these punishments for a full hundred thousand koṭi-nayutas of years; having finished this retribution, they again enter various other hells to undergo the sufferings of punishment, all in the same manner.
Why is this? Because that person has constantly slandered the teachings of all Buddhas and thus incurs such a transgression.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
During the time of that Buddha, there was also a householder living in a lay residence named Ananda.
His family was wealthy and prosperous, possessing abundant treasures and wealth that he enjoyed according to his heart's desire.

Furthermore, he possessed in full all the gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, pearls, and coral accumulated by his ancestors; all his treasuries were likewise overflowing, and his slaves, servants, and the populace of the city were compliant with his commands, never lacking for anything that pleased him.
At that time, the elder delighted in serving the Nirgrantha heretics; he practiced false teachings and gave rise to wrong views.
The elder’s wife was named Viśvabhūti; her appearance was exceptionally wonderful, upright, and pure, and she possessed such perfect physical features that all who saw her found her pleasing.
A son was born, exceptionally handsome and distinguished, with a perfect countenance and a body so pure white that all people loved him.
In the past, this son had planted various roots of goodness before immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of Buddhas.
When the son was first born, he opened his mouth three times and laughed, saying these words:
"For what reason have I now been born into this family of those with wrong views?
When the mother heard her son speak these words, she was struck with terror and alarm; her hair stood on end, and she abandoned her child, fleeing in frantic agitation.
At that time, there were many women who, having witnessed this event, all gathered together and questioned one another.

Upon hearing it said that her son had spoken such words, the women were struck with further alarm and fear and fled in all directions; yet they returned again to observe and deliberate, saying to one another:
"Is this newborn child a deva?"
Is it a nāga?
Or is it a yakṣa, rākṣasa, asura, garuḍa, kiṃnara, mahoraga, kumbhāṇḍa, piśāca, or some other human or non-human being?
Having conceived this doubt, the newborn son said to the women:
"You who are endowed with auspicious marks of a human being, for what reason have you abandoned me and fled in such panic and agitation?"
At that time, the youth addressed the assembly of women with these verses:
“You women of supreme auspiciousness, why do you not feel fear for the evil realms?”
I now cause you to realize the truth, so that you may entirely distance yourselves from all perils and hardships.
My own parents and kinsmen are not at all true friends to me;
I shall now eliminate their false views for them, so that they do not give rise [to rebirth] in the perilous and evil realms.
"Śāriputra! At that time, the parents of the youth and the entire assembly, having heard these verses spoken by the youth, went together to where he was."
At that time, before his parents, the youth spoke again in verse:
"All the treasures and wealth within my storehouses, The five grains, my home, and all my furnishings— Quickly renounce these for me to give as alms;
I shall go forth under the Buddha to become a śramaṇa."
Seeing Vipaśyin Buddha dwelling in the world, peerless among those within the three realms;
that Buddha’s sun of wisdom illuminates the world—I vow to leave the household life to become his disciple.
Having received the instruction in the Buddha’s true Dharma, To bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings,
As that Buddha’s sun of wisdom shines upon the world, I vow to renounce the householder’s life and become his disciple.
Our Buddha is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, adorned in their entirety;
that Buddha’s sun of wisdom shines upon the world, and I vow to leave the household life to become his disciple.
Even if throughout thousands of koṭis of kalpas, one has never heard the name of this Buddha—
rare as the udumbara flower to encounter— I vow to leave the household life and become his disciple.
"Śāriputra! At that time, his parents said to the youth:

'Since you are able to thus give rise to a pure mind and leave the household life to go forth under the Buddha, we now bestow upon you all the ancestral treasuries and twenty *koṭis* of gold, silver, and precious jewels that we possess, so that you may in turn practice giving yourself.'"
Then his parents spoke these verses:
"All the wealth and treasures we now possess, We entrust them all to you to bestow as gifts;
By virtue of the pure mind you have aroused, May you bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings wherever you go."
All gold, silver, and various precious gems, Grain, dwellings, and all necessary provisions—
Because you have given rise to a pure mind, Swiftly practice relinquishment for the benefit of sentient beings.
Mats, bedding, and various articles of enjoyment, Scented ointments, flower garlands, powdered incense, and the like—
Through the arousal of a pure mind, you shall swiftly practice giving wherever you go.
The Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel—these are the most supreme and excellent fields of merit.
By extending a mind of extensive generosity toward them, one brings true benefit and happiness to all.
Then the youth spoke again to his parents in verse:
"I wish to go to the place where the Buddha dwells, Before the World-Honored One, Mahāvīpaśyin,
To perform vast and immeasurable offerings, For the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings."
Whether gods or humans, all such multitudes who delight in seeking every form of happiness—
now that I have gone before the World-Honored One, may you all likewise go there together.
When the youth had spoken this verse, he reflected thus, surveyed the four quarters, and said to his parents:
"I shall now go to the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin."
When the assembly heard these words, they were each filled with wonder and doubt, and said to one another:
"How is it that this boy, born but a single day ago, can engage in such a discourse with his parents?"
"And yet, how is it that he can walk with the lifting of his two feet?
At that time, an assembly of eighty-four thousand koṭis gathered together, each reflecting and saying to one another:
"Is this youth perhaps a deva?"
Is this a nāga?
Or is it a yakṣa, rākṣasa, gandharva, asura, kiṃnara, mahoraga, or one of the human or non-human beings?
Then that youth, together with the multitude, went at once to the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin.
At that time, as the youth led the assembly along, ten thousand parasols appeared in the sky to cover them from above, and a voice resounded loudly in the air, saying:
"Let no harm come to them from cold, heat, wind, or rain."
Furthermore, a golden net appeared in the sky, completely covering it from above.
Moreover, exquisite celestial flowers, various powdered incenses, and diverse wonderful perfumes rained down from the sky, while a cool, gentle breeze wafted these fragrances abroad.
Furthermore, along the path, fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground and celestial jewel-robes rained down; the celestial flowers that fell accumulated to a height exceeding the knees.

Along the path, immeasurable ponds of water possessing the eight virtues appeared spontaneously, and within each pond were countless *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers as offerings. Moreover, exquisite pavilions made of the seven precious gems appeared spontaneously.
Furthermore, as they traveled, various horns and conch shells resounded spontaneously without being struck, emitting subtle and wondrous sounds that sang praises in song.
To their left and right, immeasurable precious jewels were naturally arrayed in adornment.
At that time, as soon as the youth took each step, a flower appeared for him to tread upon; once he had stepped on it, it vanished and was no longer seen.
Then, while on the road, the youth looked back and observed for a moment, speaking these verses:
"In this world there is right principle and wrong principle; That which I now practice is the supreme path."
Not proceeding upon any path that is not the right one, I have therefore gone to the Honored One of Right Principle.
Throughout nayutas of kalpas, I have at times obtained a human body;
furthermore, I have encountered the Tathāgata appearing in the world, and am endowed with the power of faith, understanding, and wisdom.
“Śāriputra! When that youth had spoken these verses, eighty-four thousand devas and humans in the sky all praised him together, reciting this gāthā:
‘Excellent, excellent, O Great Wise One! You are able to proclaim the supreme ultimate truth.’”
"Having completely abandoned all that is irrational, one is therefore able to practice the true and correct path. "Śāriputra!
At that time, the youth further spoke these verses to the assembly of devas:"
“Those who are able to practice the true path extensively explain the attainment of harmony;
but for those who stubbornly cling to what is not the true path, how could they attain the principle of correspondence?”
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Twenty-six.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Twenty-seven.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperial Preceptor of the Western Heaven, Silver Light Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject [Dharmapāla], by Imperial Decree. Chapter Nine, Part Three: The Perfection of Vigor. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."
Then the assembly of devas, facing the youth, spoke again in verse:
"Those who possess craving for sensual pleasures, Who find no escape from all objective realms,
And who, due to ignorance, follow what is not the right principle, Shall fall into the hells and the evil destinies."
If one seeks to go forth from home upon the true path, one should abandon the enjoyment of all sensory objects;
he who can reveal these various correct principles is called one who accords with the world.
"Śāriputra! At that time, the youth addressed the assembly of devas and spoke again in verse:
'I now speak for you, O assembly of devas; You have not yet understood the True Path.'
"I shall now explain this true principle of such correspondence so that you may fully understand it.
Having spoken these verses, the youth, together with the great assembly, proceeded at once to the presence of the Tathāgata Vipaśyin.

Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and withdrew to stand to one side. He gazed up at the Tathāgata Vipaśyin without averting his eyes for even a moment.
At that time, the youth was filled with great joy and spoke these verses:
“Endowed with the three types of knowledge, you bestow the nectar of immortality; You are able to bring about the welfare and benefit of the world.”
I bow my head to the Dragon, Elephant, and Lion King; for this reason, I now constantly praise and pay homage to him.

The light of the Buddha’s wisdom is most rare and marvelous, like the sun and moon illuminating the world, and like the appearance of the udumbara flower—firmly established and abiding in wondrous marks and signs.
Sentient beings in the world are burdened by many obstacles; they cannot understand the noble path of the Buddha.
Like those born blind and ignorant, they fail to realize that they are falling into perilous and evil ways.
May I, in the future, attain perfect enlightenment, just like the World-Honored One Vipaśyin;
may I cause all sentient beings to leave behind all sufferings and extinguish the fires of the three poisons to attain refreshing coolness.
Furthermore, may immeasurable sentient beings, following me, extensively make such vows;
hearing the Buddha expound the Supreme Vehicle, may they all attain the revelation of the path to Bodhi.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the youth further said:
"Homage to Vipaśyin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who skillfully expounds the essential points of the Dharma."
At that time, a multitude of eighty-four thousand koṭis of people also spoke these words:
"Homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin, who skillfully expounds the essential Dharma."
Thus he sighed three times, ending and beginning again:
"May I, in the future, all attain the realization of Right and Equal Enlightenment, just as the Tathāgata Vipaśyin skillfully expounded the essential teachings."

At that time, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin, knowing that the boy and the assembly of eighty-four thousand koṭis of people were capable of receiving the prophecy, manifested a supernormal transformation; from his face he emitted a great radiance named "Decisive Victory," and that light further possessed immeasurable varieties of colors and forms, namely blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, crystal, gold, and so forth.

Such physical forms pervaded immeasurable worlds, shining with brilliant clarity; they extended upward through the Brahma-world to the very limits of the realm of form, completely eclipsing the radiance of the sun and moon.
That light returned once more to the crown of the Buddha’s head, circling it to the right in a graceful swirl for hundreds of thousands of turns,

and then suddenly vanished. Śāriputra, at that time, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin had a personal attendant bhikṣu who, having witnessed this miraculous manifestation of light from the Buddha, immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, gazed up at the Honored One’s countenance, and asked in verse:
