“Vipaśyin Buddha is most rare and marvelous; among all the noble ones, he is the most venerable of sages.
I now inquire of the Sugata, the Honored One: by what causes and conditions does this radiance appear?”
At that time, the bhikṣu again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For what cause and condition do you manifest such great supernormal transformations and emit this radiance?”
We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of great compassion and pity, will dispel our doubts for us and expound upon this matter.

Furthermore, there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of people currently standing before the Buddha who wish and desire to hear it; we shall listen with sincere and earnest hearts. For the sake of all sentient beings, please compassionately reveal and teach it.
The Tathāgata, with great compassion, is the eye of the world; he rescues and protects all beings as houses provide shelter for everyone.
We only pray that the Tathāgata, out of his great kindness and pity, will sever the net of our doubts.

Furthermore, regarding all the mental activities, conceptualizations, karmic actions, and various doubts of sentient beings in the past, future, and present, there is nothing that the Tathāgata does not fully know.
Furthermore, regarding all sentient beings in all Buddha-fields, the Tathāgata thoroughly understands every distinction of wisdom and speech throughout the three periods of time.
The Tathāgata is the sovereign king of all dharmas, fully endowed with the eight kinds of vocal resonance and possessing mastery over all his preaching of the Dharma.
For what cause and condition does he manifest such great supernatural powers and emit this radiance?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will sever all our nets of doubt and utterly extinguish all our sorrows, lamentations, sufferings, and afflictions.
We now make this triple request with single-minded concentration, joining our palms in reverent homage, desiring to hear [the teaching].
"Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin said to his personal attendant bhikṣu:
'Do you see this youth standing before me with palms joined in reverence?'"
"Yes, indeed, Sugata!
I have now seen it.
The Buddha said:

“Bhikṣus! In the past, this youth already drew near to, praised, honored, and prostrated before eighty-four thousand koṭi-nayutas of Buddhas; he made offerings of robes, bedding, and various medicinal decoctions, planting roots of goodness and constantly practicing the holy life in order to achieve perfect enlightenment.”
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣu! Do you also see these eighty-four thousand koṭis of people standing before me with palms joined?"
"Yes, indeed, Sugata!
I have now seen it.
The Buddha said:

"In past lives, all these people were once the parents of this youth; in birth after birth, there was none who did not receive his instruction and resolve their minds toward enlightenment in successive future lives, vowing never again to receive a female body and being able to practice in accordance with his teachings, until they all together resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
"I have now bestowed upon him the prophecy of his future Buddhahood; for this reason, I manifest great supernormal powers and emit this radiance.
At that time, the Tathāgata Vipaśyin spoke these verses for the sake of his personal attendant bhikṣu and the assembled multitude:
"You see before you this great assembly, Who has all gathered here following the youth."
Eighty-four thousand koṭis in number, listen with single-minded concentration as I speak;
the Buddha has attained mastery over the teaching of the Dharma, and I now address you, O bhikṣus, with my own words.
I know that throughout many eons, the youth has drawn near to and made offerings to various Buddhas;
furthermore, in the presence of immeasurable Buddhas, he has with firm resolve sought to leave the household life,
practicing the most supreme and pure conduct, and is further able to bring benefit and happiness to the multitudes of devas and humans.
Furthermore, these great assemblies present here, numbering eighty-four thousand koṭis, have been my parents in birth after birth;
I have constantly and without interruption taught and gladdened them.
Furthermore, in the past, throughout incalculable eons, you extensively made boundless great vows;
in every lifetime, you were all my parents, together seeking unexcelled, supreme Bodhi.
Abiding thus in liberation from birth and death, you should follow me and practice together, aspiring for supreme and wondrous bodhi.
I now bestow upon them my personal prediction: they shall certainly attain perfect enlightenment; therefore, I manifest this great supernormal power.
I am able to cause all within your minds to be free of doubt while walking, standing, sitting,
or lying down. You gods, nāgas, and the assembly of humans— numbering in the many nayutas before me—
shall together hear this and receive my personal prediction that before long you shall become Honored Ones Among Two-Legged Beings.
"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, the boy was filled with joy and leaped for gladness. He quickly went before his parents and, uttering words of truth, spoke this verse:
'These eighty-four thousand beings Were all my parents in the past.'
"Since we have simultaneously and together resolved upon bodhicitta, what now becomes of us, your parents? Śāriputra,
at that time, the parents spoke this verse to the youth:
“As you have said, all these people have each and every one of them already resolved upon bodhicitta;
I now take refuge in the Omniscient One, and my vow is no different from yours.”
Thus you shall advance toward the ultimate path;
you are now born from my own body, and having together resolved upon the mind of truth, may we both achieve the fruition of Bodhi.
"Śāriputra! At that time, the boy spoke these verses to his own parents:
'If I should first attain Buddhahood, I vow to reveal [the path] to all without exception. "
"May my parents and all these people together attain unsurpassed, great Bodhi.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
at that time the Tathāgata Vipaśyin spoke these words to that youth and the assembly of people:
"I now bestow upon you the prediction of your future Buddhahood.
Do not give rise to doubt or confusion; comfort yourself well and do not harbor further divergent views. Why is this?
In the past, you were the Great Lord Devaputra; at that time, I already bestowed upon you the prediction of your future buddhahood.

After that, for ten million nayutas of kalpas, you shall not fall into the evil realms. Furthermore, after another ten million nayutas of kalpas, you will be born into the lineage of a universal monarch (cakravartin) and attain buddhahood, known by the name Mahākāruṇika Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, endowed with great renown.
His father’s name was Śuddhodana, free from all dullness and ignorance;
his mother’s name was Māyā, free from all sorrow and affliction.
At that time, his son was also like my own son, named Rāhula.
Having appeared in the world, he sought to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Once he had accomplished the path to enlightenment, that Buddha’s lifespan was a full hundred thousand years.
The light of that Buddha is able to universally illuminate lands of one hundred thousand yojanas.
All sentient beings within that world—whether they have a karmic connection with him or not—all receive the touch of the Buddha’s illuminating light.
At that time, within the Buddha’s light, there gathered a great assembly of hundreds of koṭis, nayutas of koṭis, and hundreds of thousands of nayutas of koṭis of great śrāvakas.

Furthermore, there was another assembly of one koṭi, all of whom were great arhats; they were fully endowed with pure dharmas, their outflows were exhausted, they were free from further afflictions, their minds attained mastery, they possessed the eight liberations, and had acquired the six supernormal powers.

"Śāriputra! Such great arhats as these all gather together; furthermore, an immeasurable multitude of great bodhisattvas all gather together; and furthermore, all the parents of those buddhas from their past lives also gather together."

At that time, the Tathāgata Mahākāruṇika taught the Dharma to convert and transform immeasurable asaṃkhyeya sentient beings, causing them all to abide in the stage of non-retrogression. Having brought about the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, he then entered parinirvāṇa at that very moment; his True Dharma remained in the world for one koṭi of years.
The relics of that Buddha will be widely disseminated throughout all worlds, no different from the dissemination of my own relics after my parinirvāṇa. Śāriputra!

When these words were spoken, all the true sons of noble family gave rise to courageous and vast diligence; they engaged in investigation and reflection, observing the world with a mind intent on the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, never turning back.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who give rise to right mindfulness, which becomes increasingly superior and uninterrupted in mind, as they resolutely seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus, for immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he made the vow to transform and benefit sentient beings within the flow of saṃsāra while seeking the bodhi of a Buddha. Śāriputra!

At that time, I also made this vow: until the end of cyclic existence, I shall don the armor of diligence to transform and benefit sentient beings; throughout an entire kalpa, I shall fulfill my vows of diligent practice, with courageous and vigorous effort, never turning back from my mind, and may I attain Bodhi.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is the irreversible courageous diligence of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of irreversible courageous diligence, even if they were to see this trichiliocosm filled with masses of fire, for the sake of seeking the unexcelled perfect enlightenment of a Tathāgata, they should arouse courageous diligence, enter into that fire, and be able to endure it without giving rise to weariness."
When those bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, they immediately attain the fulfillment of the vows of diligent practice for one entire kalpa.
Furthermore, when those bodhisattvas hear this Dharma, their courageous diligence in non-retrogression increases immeasurable roots of goodness.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices irreversible, courageous, and diligent effort, seeking to realize nirvāṇa for the benefit of all sentient beings, he remains pure, unmixed, constant, and firm; he gives rise to great compassion toward both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and performs corresponding actions toward all sentient beings."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice courageous diligence, remaining entirely free from indolence; at all times, whether lifting or lowering the feet, they never depart from the mind of enlightenment (bodhicitta). They should perceive the Three Jewels as always present before them, neither abandoning any sentient beings nor conforming to any afflictions."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice courageous diligence, remaining entirely free from indolence; they shall dedicate all the power of their already arisen and yet-to-be-arisen roots of goodness toward the right path of enlightenment, and further cause those roots of goodness to increase without end."
Śāriputra! Just as the waters of a hundred rivers flow into the great ocean and are never exhausted, so too is this dedication of roots of goodness toward bodhi;
it is likewise inexhaustible. For this reason, it is called "non-retrogressive, courageous, and energetic perseverance."

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices non-retrogressive, courageous diligence, they are entirely free from indolence; they accumulate roots of goodness for all-knowledge through all correct practices and are further able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings. For this reason, it is called 'non-retrogressive, courageous diligence.'"
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

To speak briefly now, the mass of merit obtained by bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, up to and including all sentient beings, and even the mass of merit obtained by śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, whether they be those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa), does not equal the mass of merit obtained by a single hair-tip of the Tathāgata; how much less so the mass of merit contained within all the pores of the Tathāgata’s entire body?"
Because the Tathāgata has accumulated a vast mass of merit through his practice over immeasurable eons,

even if one were to possess a truly accumulated mass of merit equal to a hundredth or a thousandth part of the Tathāgata’s actual realization of such a mass, it would not equal even one of the Tathāgata’s marks of a great man (mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa), let alone all of his primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana).

Furthermore, all aggregates of merit do not equal even a single mark of the white tuft of hair between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows, resembling a white conch or the moon; how much less so the merits contained within its hundreds of thousands of coils?

Moreover, all aggregates of merit do not equal even one of the Tathāgata’s marks of the invisible crown of the head, let alone the merits produced by all the marks and signs of a Great Man, including the *uṣṇīṣa* and the various faculties, numbering hundreds of thousands of *koṭis*.

Furthermore, all aggregates of merit do not equal even a single aspect of the Dharma taught by the sound of the Tathāgata’s great Dharma-conch; how much less so his vast Dharma-sound, which can universally pervade immeasurable worlds, causing the faculties of all sentient beings to become harmonious and giving rise to joy, so that they may attain excellent discipline according to their respective inclinations, and thus develop understanding and realization regarding this rare *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

In this way, the bodhisattva, following the example of the Tathāgata throughout immeasurable worlds, utters a great sound so that all sentient beings may hear it; donning the armor of diligence and generating a firm resolve, they delight in practicing the non-retrogressive, courageous, and vigorous conduct of a bodhisattva.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices with vigor and never retreats, even if one were to cause all sentient beings throughout the entire trichiliocosm to fully achieve the power of resolute understanding (*adhimukti-jñāna-bala*), and if those sentient beings were to subsequently achieve and possess the power of wisdom (*jñāna-bala*) by following this Bodhisattvapiṭaka of the True Dharma, compared to the former merit, it would not equal even a hundredth part, a thousandth part, a hundred-thousand-millionth part, or even an *upaniṣad* part."

To speak briefly, may all sentient beings throughout this trichiliocosm be caused to attain the wisdom-power of the *srotāpanna*, the wisdom-power of the *sakṛdāgāmin*, the wisdom-power of the *anāgāmin*, and the wisdom-power of the *arhat*; furthermore, may they attain the wisdom-power of the ten faiths, the ten abidings, the ten practices, the ten transferences, and the stage of non-retrogression, as well as the rank of a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Thus it should be extensively explained, until all sentient beings in immeasurable worlds are universally caused to attain the wisdom-power of a Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood.

If any sentient beings, having heard in this way of the Tathāgata’s powers of non-conceptual and conceptual wisdom and so forth, are neither startled nor terrified, they shall at that time gradually come to delight in the profound power of wisdom.

Compared to the aforementioned merit, this does not equal even one part in a hundred, one part in a thousand, one part in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions, one part in an asaṃkhyeya, or even one part in an upaniṣad.

Moreover, the bodhisattva, desiring to arouse courageous and vigorous diligence, would rather relinquish his body, life, head, eyes, marrow, brain, and all other limbs than take pleasure in even a momentary interruption in the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s power of wisdom.
Abandoning such [worldly concerns] with courageous diligence—this, I say, is called the bodhisattva’s practice of non-retrogressive diligence.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in this way for the stage of non-retrogression, even to the point of generating a single mind that universally enters into the infinite and boundless varieties of mental activities of all sentient beings of the past, future, and present; and even if those sentient beings are fully possessed of all afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, they should nevertheless turn back and enter into the mind of the bodhisattva."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, through the power of wisdom, employs various analogies and expressions to investigate thoroughly; thus he arouses courageous and diligent effort, seeing that all sentient beings are being scorched and boiled by desire, hatred, ignorance, and the like.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, through various skillful means, causes all suffering and affliction to be universally stilled, so that they are extinguished without remainder like ashes; he further causes them to cultivate the path leading to Nirvana. I call this the Bodhisattva’s practice of non-retrogressive diligence.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the diligence of non-retrogression, it consists of wholesome actions of body, wholesome actions of speech, and wholesome actions of mind. Indeed, all aspects of the perfection of diligence are never apart from the cultivation of these actions of body, speech, and mind; yet among these three types of action, the mental volition that gives rise to diligence is the most supreme."
What is the most excellent diligence of mental action?
It is both non-conceptual and conceptual.
What is non-conceptual?
It refers to the bodhicitta.
How does it possess conceptual differentiation?
It means giving rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings.
What is non-conceptualization?
It refers to the realization of the principle of selflessness through patience and wisdom.
What is conceptualization?
It means being able to embrace all sentient beings.
How is it non-conceptual?
It means that although one is able to embrace all sentient beings, there is no grasping at signs.
What is conceptualization?
It refers to the wearying detachment from saṃsāra.
What is non-conceptualization? It refers to the total non-apprehension of anything within the three realms.
That which is with conceptual differentiation refers to the relinquishing of wealth and treasures according to one's inclination.
That which is without conceptual differentiation refers to being without grasping at signs regarding giving.
That which is with conceptual differentiation refers to having an accumulation regarding the observance of precepts.
Non-conceptualization refers to not grasping at signs regarding the observance of precepts.
Conceptualization refers to the patient endurance of suffering.
Non-conceptualization refers to the mind having no dwelling place within each moment.
That which is with conceptual differentiation refers to the dharmas capable of initiating all roots of goodness.
That which is without conceptual differentiation refers to constant meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
That which is with conceptual differentiation refers to that which has been accumulated within meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
Non-conceptualization refers to the mind being constantly determined, dwelling in immovability.
Conceptualization refers to cultivating the wisdom of hearing without satiety.
Non-conceptualization refers to skillful concentration upon the internal mind.
That which has conceptual differentiation refers to the extensive exposition of all phenomena within the wisdom derived from hearing.
That which is without conceptual differentiation refers to having no recollection or mental engagement whatsoever regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
That which has conceptual differentiation refers to that which is actively cultivated within wisdom.
Non-conceptualization refers to being free from all conceptual proliferation regarding all phenomena.
Conceptualization refers to the accumulation and cultivation of all holy practices (*brahmacarya*).
Non-conceptualization refers to the complete relinquishing of the very nature of all wisdom.
That which possesses discrimination refers to being able to bring the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) to perfection.
That which is without discrimination refers to the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
That which possesses discrimination refers to constantly contemplating and reflecting upon meditative visualization (*saṃjñā*).
Non-conceptualization refers to maintaining constant right mindfulness within the internal mind.
Conceptualization refers to being skillful and adept in all four right endeavors (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Non-conceptualization refers to being able to transcend all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Those with conceptual discrimination are those who, clinging to the signs of words and letters, seek liberation.
Those without conceptual discrimination are those who, regarding vast merit and reward, universally abide in signlessness.
That which involves conceptual differentiation refers to being well-versed in the faculties and dispositions of all sentient beings.
That which is free from conceptual differentiation refers to being skillfully able to observe all dharmas of the roots of virtue without apprehending anything.
That which possesses conceptual differentiation refers to the cultivation of the various powers (*bala*).
That which is without conceptual differentiation refers to that state wherein there is no impairment.
That which possesses conceptual differentiation refers to the ability to give rise to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Non-conceptualization refers to the wisdom that is free from conceptualization regarding all phenomena.
Conceptualization refers to being able to seek progress toward the right path.
Non-conceptualization refers to viewing all miraculous transformations as being like empty space.
That which possesses conceptualization refers to the ability to accumulate [merit] within the gateways of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
That which is without conceptualization refers to abiding in calm abiding (*śamatha*) with a single object.
That which possesses conceptualization refers to the accumulation [of insight] within special insight (*vipaśyanā*).
Non-conceptualization refers to skillfully entering into the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Conceptualization refers to being skillfully able to enter into and understand all phenomena of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Non-conceptualization refers to being skillfully able to fully comprehend that which is not a phenomenon of causes and conditions.
"Having conceptualization" means being attached to the sound of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Being without conceptualization" means practicing the practice of the true Dharma (*saddharma-caryā*).
"Having conceptualization" means adorning the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Non-conceptualization refers to the dharmakāya being free from all adornments.
Conceptualization refers to the adornment of speech.
Non-conceptualization refers to the ability of the noble ones to remain in constant silence.
That which is with conceptual differentiation refers to the arising of aspiration based on the three gates of liberation.
That which is without conceptual differentiation refers to the absence of a dominant self.
That which is with conceptual differentiation refers to being able to remain far removed from the four types of demonic activities (*māra-karman*).
Non-conceptualization refers to the ability to abandon the seeds of the habitual tendencies of afflictions.
Conceptualization refers to the ability to skillfully understand and apply expedient means (*upāya*).
Non-conceptualization refers to knowing and seeing reality as it is through wisdom.
Conceptualization refers to having objects of perception that arise apart from objective referents.
Non-conceptualization refers to being free from transcendent views.
That which is with conceptualization refers to views accompanied by mental ideation;
that which is without conceptualization refers to views consisting of mental action (*manas-karman*).
This is called the vigor of mental action, the most preeminent among all forms of vigor. I declare this to be the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of non-retrogressive vigor.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the non-retrogressive application of energy in this manner, they practice these five kinds of supreme and most excellent dharmas, and swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
What are the five kinds of most supreme and sublime dharmas?

First, to constantly contemplate the appearance of a Buddha in the world; second, to be able to draw near to all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); third, to always encounter auspicious times; fourth, to constantly accumulate all roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) and always cause them to be firm and stable; fifth, to follow and study the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ complete categories of precepts until they are perfected.
"These are called the five kinds of most supreme and wondrous dharmas; by means of these, a bodhisattva swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"If bodhisattvas were to be separated from these five kinds of most supreme and wondrous dharmas, would they be able to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"

If bodhisattvas do not constantly keep in mind the appearance of Buddhas in the world, cannot draw near to spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), or do not encounter favorable times, they will be unable to accumulate the dharmas of the various roots of goodness (kuśalamūla) and fail to make them firm; they will be unable to train in accordance with the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas' perfection of the categories of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) and thus remain incomplete.
Thus, by being far removed from these five most supreme and exquisite dharmas, one cannot swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
that one should attain it while contravening them is impossible.
Śāriputra! How does a lay bodhisattva remain far removed from five kinds of dharmas? It is as follows:
suppose a royal minister dwells among a great assembly, relying on his power and majesty to intimidate many people, and further says to the assembly:
"I can perform various tasks for you," he says;
yet, through mere deception, he does not actually do them, even to the point of remaining established in such matters as false and deceptive speech.
Śāriputra! Because of such falsehoods, one cannot be reborn in the heavenly realms or other auspicious destinies; likewise, through such modes of conduct, one cannot encounter favorable times.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, regarding this mode of practice, a lay bodhisattva who merely provides for their own sustenance and necessities is unable to benefit others, nor can they encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world; indeed, they cannot swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Moreover, when a lay bodhisattva dwells within a city or town, there are various obstacles and difficulties that constantly cause affliction.
What are these obstacles and difficulties found in cities and towns?

Śāriputra! There are Tathāgatas who appear in the world and attain perfect enlightenment, preaching the Dharma for the sake of devas, humans, asuras, and others to instruct and transform them. Their teaching is excellent in the beginning, middle, and end; its meaning is profound and far-reaching, its phrasing is skillful and elegant, and it is fully endowed with the characteristics of the pure and holy life (brahmacarya), surrounded by and revered by the fourfold assembly.

Although one may draw near to, make offerings to, and pay homage to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās, yet because the villages, cities, streets, and houses therein are inhabited by common people, kings, ministers, elders, and householders, one is unable to fulfill the aggregate of pure ethical discipline due to these causes and conditions; I call this an obstacle within the city.

If a lay bodhisattva is thus attached to and delights in the five desires, they will be unable to keep the Buddha’s appearance in the world in mind, and will not even be able to swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a lay bodhisattva proclaims the practice of secular laws, there are many obstacles and difficulties.
That is to say, parents, sons and daughters, wives and concubines, slaves and servants, sisters and brothers, friends, and kinsmen act as obstacles throughout the long night."

Śāriputra! Such dharmas create various obstacles and difficulties for lay bodhisattvas; furthermore, they take no delight in the appearance of a Buddha in the world, and thus they are unable to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Twenty-Seven.
The Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Twenty-Eight.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperial Preceptor for the Transmission of Sanskrit, Grand Master of Compassionate Enlightenment, conferred the purple robe and the title of Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, under the auspices of the Western Heaven, by imperial decree. Chapter Nine, Part Four: The Perfection of Vigor. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Householder bodhisattvas who, regarding the true nature of the sūtras spoken by the Tathāgatas, do not delight in extensive learning even after having heard them; who do not delight in practicing fewness of desires; who likewise do not have faith in or accept similar sūtras; and who further give rise to slander toward the Mahāyāna teachings of those Tathāgatas—all such persons fall into the various evil destinies.
What are called the various evil destinies?

They are the realm of Yama, the hungry ghosts, and the animals; furthermore, the borderlands, those with improper ethical discipline, and even if one attains a human body, it is incomplete, defiled by heavy obscurations, and possessed of all manner of false views.

Śāriputra! Regarding such places of reproach and aversion, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas remain far removed from them and take no pleasure in being born there; indeed, they cannot swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* [unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment] therein.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when a lay bodhisattva relies upon those of great power and influence—namely kings, ministers, and commoners, as well as wealthy and eminent persons—it increases their anger; the words they utter become largely deceitful and false; they accumulate evil deeds to delude others, and furthermore, they give rise to arrogance and contempt."
Because of such unwholesome speech, this person falls into the evil realms, with a body that is emaciated and possessed of all manner of inauspicious marks. Śāriputra,
these are called the five dharmas of a lay bodhisattva.

Due to these causes and conditions, they will be unable to encounter the appearance of Buddhas in the world, nor will they be able to draw near to spiritual friends. They will fail to encounter auspicious times, and all the roots of goodness they have accumulated will be utterly destroyed. They will be unable to follow and learn from bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who uphold the precepts, and so forth, until they are unable to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"If a person practices these five kinds of dharmas, Their supreme wisdom will not increase;
Furthermore, being far removed from the Honored Tamer, They shall not swiftly attain perfect enlightenment."
Because they deceive all sentient beings, like the ministers and servants of a royal house,
they sever all the power of their roots of goodness and will be unable to encounter the appearance of a Buddha in the world.
Furthermore, some cause sentient beings to tremble with fear, commanding them to be seized, bound, and beaten;
having thus committed such evil deeds, they remain forever estranged from the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Furthermore, by violating the pure precepts of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, one gives rise to the suffering of illness;
for a moment, one fails to encounter auspicious times and remains perpetually distant from all Buddhas.
Parents, wives, children, and all kinsmen constantly engage in unrighteous conduct without interruption;
having no desire to hear the True Dharma, they fall into delusion from which it is difficult to escape.
Even if one encounters a Buddha’s era and seeks to draw near him, one may not succeed in a single instant;
or again, when one desires to delight in the life of renunciation, they will come vying with one another to create obstacles.
Sometimes, having heard this true Dharma, they preach the reality of emptiness wherever they go;
yet others, giving rise to a mind of resentment, declare that this is not the true Dharma.
Such various obstacles and difficulties as these do not even amount to one-sixteenth [of the consequences];
because of this cause of slandering the True Dharma, one will be born blind in life after life, seeing nothing at all.
They cannot see the Honored One, the Perfectly Awakened; even if they should see him, they do not give rise to pure faith.
They shall obtain an incomplete human body and later fall among all the animals.
If a person turns toward the Buddha’s bodhi and gives rise to love and joy for the bodhisattvas,
all obstacles and difficulties will be completely eliminated, and they will be well able to cultivate true and correct practice.
All parents and their retinues, as well as all other classes of sentient beings,
he repeatedly guides to leave the household life, swiftly enabling them to be gathered and led back to the Right Path.
Having first been guided by my mother alone, she was further able to praise [the path] and inspire me to go forth;
I then proceeded to the presence of the Blessed One, the Sugata, and resolved my mind upon awakening to great bodhi.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are five other such qualities of a renunciant bodhisattva by which they likewise distance themselves from spiritual friends; they cannot encounter the appearance of a Buddha even for the duration of a finger-snap; the power of all the roots of goodness they have accumulated is thereby destroyed; they are unable to train in accordance with bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who uphold the precepts; and they are unable to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

What are the five dharmas? First, violating the pure precepts due to improper reflection; second, slandering the True Dharma due to lack of faith; third, being addicted to gain and profit as well as delighting in fame and reputation; fourth, clinging to the view of self and entering into various perils and difficulties; and fifth, giving rise to envy toward the virtuous conduct of others.

Śāriputra! A renunciant bodhisattva who is fully possessed of these five qualities will likewise remain far removed from spiritual friends and will be unable to encounter the appearance of Buddhas in the world. To speak briefly, such a person will not even be able to swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Śāriputra! For this reason, it is like a hungry dog, emaciated and haggard, with skin and bone standing together, who suddenly sees a dry bone and conceives the thought of eating it. It then goes to a secluded place and licks and gnaws at it with all its might, injuring its own mouth so that blood smears upon the bone; yet, unaware of its own folly, it gives rise to craving, ultimately gaining nothing despite its fullness.
At that time, there were kṣatriyas, brahmins, elders, and householders who came from afar; seeing this starving dog gnawing on those dry bones, they were moved to profound pity and lamentation.
At that time, the starving dog thought to itself again:
"That one who has come will take away my delicious food.
Thereupon, the dog let out a harsh sound, with malevolent eyes, snarling and barking furiously.
"Śāriputra, what do you think?
If those people were to see these dry bones entirely devoid of flesh and blood, would they attempt to seize them?"
Śāriputra said:
“No, World-Honored One.”
"No, Sugata. The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“How did that dog manifest such a sign?
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“World-Honored One!”

Because the dog was hungry, it gnawed on that dry bone as if it were the taste of nectar; due to its deluded arising of craving, it manifested such evil sounds and eyes, barking and howling with distress, fearing that the crowd of people would seize it away.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“After my parinirvāṇa, there will be bhikṣus who, regarding their own clans and even down to the impurities of excrement and urine, will give rise to deep attachment and be bound by it.”
With such modes of conduct, they cannot achieve even a single moment of buddha-work.
Those bhikṣus whom I am now describing are like those hungry dogs within the Buddha-dharma.
Not only does the Tathāgata thus censure and revile them, but if any sentient beings see those bhikṣus acting in such a manner, they likewise slander them like that starving dog.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, for the sake of extensively bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, seek the wisdom of a Buddha; they would even renounce their own bodies and lives, let alone give rise to hatred or envy toward the virtuous deeds of others.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are other foolish people in the world who, out of attachment to their own livelihood and a craving for worldly wealth, food, and drink, become slaves; they are bound by them and subjected to punishment, servitude, and being driven about."
Within other clans, they associate with those who are deceitful and false; out of greedy seeking, they further give rise to envy toward others. Śāriputra!
Just as that bhikṣu, for the sake of craving gain and offerings, sees a newcomer arrive among those clans and then gives rise to a heart of malice and jealousy, saying this to the newcomer:
"I have resided here since long ago. From where have you all come?
Now, the elders among this clan first made a vow, saying:"
"If all clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine are to be given exclusively to me," if one speaks thus, how can those who arrive later obtain them?
"Because of this, three kinds of faults arise.
What are the three?
First, attachment to one's dwelling place; second, a lack of joy in one's original abode; and third, being able to understand worldly dharmas while being unable to understand supramundane dharmas."
Furthermore, that bhikṣu does not find pleasure in dwelling among this clan of householders, and that bhikṣu speaks these words:
"There are three kinds of dwellings:
first, dwelling in a place of affection and delight; second, dwelling in a place of harmony; and third, dwelling in a place of reality."
"You elders have committed many transgressions; you should therefore give rise to deep reverence for me and praise and extol my Dharma.
Thus spoke Śāriputra.
Because of this, the fault of giving rise to hatred and jealousy within that lineage causes all pure dharmas to diminish and vanish.

"Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are other lineages characterized by much envy and falsehood. Whether they observe the precepts or do not observe them, they all distance themselves from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattvas and do not follow their training."
These analogies should be understood in this way.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the past, immeasurable, boundless, vast, and inconceivable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, at that time and in that period, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Jinaśikhin Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. That Buddha remained in the world for ninety koṭis of years.

In that Buddha’s assembly, there were furthermore ninety nayutas of great śrāvakas, all of whom were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions; they had attained their own benefit, achieved mastery over their minds, and reached the further shore.

At that time, there was also a householder named Sūcitta, whose family was immensely wealthy and possessed a vast retinue. He was endowed with abundant riches and treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, mother-of-pearl, agate, coral, amber, and pearls—all of which he enjoyed in great abundance. Furthermore, his male and female slaves, servants, elephants, horses, chariots, and various storehouses were all overflowing.
At that time, the elder father begot two sons:
the first named Viśuddhavāsa and the second named Viśuddhadhara;
they were handsome in countenance, possessed of perfect physical marks, and a joy for all who beheld them.
Suddenly, at one time, he ascended a great multi-storied pavilion and wandered about in playful ease.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:

“That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jitāmita, in the early morning, having dressed and taken his bowl, was surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus as they preceded and followed him, entering that great city to beg for alms in due order.”

That Buddha’s marks and signs were like a mountain of gold, and like a vast, exquisite, and supreme golden banner; he dwelt in *śamatha* with his sense faculties well-restrained, like a dragon-elephant that is most wondrously pure; like a great lake free from all dust and defilement; like the great ocean filled with precious jewels; like Śakra, Lord of Devas, surrounded by the gods; and like Mahābrahmā, serene and adorned; he was fully perfected, pure and bright, with a mind harmoniously composed and faculties tranquil.
At that very moment, those two youths beheld the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Victorious and Exalted One, Śrīghana.

These two youths then praised the Tathāgata for having arrived from afar, saying that the Buddha’s body, with its marks and signs of excellence, was infinite, boundless, and perfectly complete; gazing up at the World-Honored One, their hearts could never be satiated.
"Śāriputra!
At that time, the youth Viśuddhavāsa had already previously beheld the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jyotirasa, and he spoke to the youth Viśuddhadhara, saying:
'Have you ever, in the past, beheld the Tathāgata Jyotirasa?'"
"The virtues of this Buddha are boundless; among all sentient beings, he is the Great Compassionate Father.

Then the youth Viśuddhadhara said, "In the past, I have never before seen this Buddha, the World-Honored One, so fully endowed with the marks and signs of excellence and so exceptionally sublime in his majestic power."
Then the youth Viśuddhavāsa said:
"In the past, I have already seen this Tathāgata Jyeṣṭhottara; I pray that in the future I may be exactly like this Buddha, without any difference."
"Śāriputra! At that time, the youth Viśuddhavāsas spoke these verses:
'May I in the future be like the World-Honored One, Surrounded by a multitude of bhikṣus. "
If I may attain a form resembling that of the Tathāgata, I shall again be called the Most Supreme Honored One.
Now, with these offerings of food and drink, for the sake of seeking unsurpassed bodhi, I renounce all my houses and dwellings;
may I, in the future, achieve perfect enlightenment.
Just as the moon is supreme among the many stars, who would not feel refreshed upon seeing it?
Among all sentient beings, the Buddha is most honored; who would not renounce the home life to seek liberation?
"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard these words, the youth Viśuddhadhara spoke again in verse:
"Do not speak such words now, Nor shout them out to the four quarters."
"Listen now to my words of truth: how may one swiftly attain the path to Bodhi?
"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard these words, the youth Viśuddhavihārin spoke again in verse:"
"Do not take delight in this path, nor give rise to a mind of hatred or envy;
for the well-spoken words I have now uttered shall lead you to attain the path of Bodhi."
Regarding all the worldly riches and treasures, you must not give rise to a heart of stinginess;
since I am even able to relinquish my own body and life, I therefore speak these words so that you may fully understand.
I give you all these houses and dwellings, as well as all my wealth and treasures;
I shall now go to the presence of the Buddha to leave the household life and seek the prediction of enlightenment.
Who, having seen the thirty-two marks of excellence, would not find them delightful?
Who would not practice for unsurpassed bodhi?
Do not give rise to thoughts of inferiority or weakness regarding this.
My house and its wealth and treasures, my parents, kinsmen, and all my friends—
I am able to renounce all of these in order to seek out and go to the presence of the Buddha.
Even if one were to spend thousands of millions of kalpas, it would be extremely difficult to hear that a Buddha has appeared in the world;
for the Buddha is the great light of the world, and to encounter the Buddha’s light is likewise difficult.
The Buddha came to the royal city to perform his transformative work, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus;
like the pure moon in a cloudless sky, he shone universally throughout the world.
Just as when the thousand-rayed sun appears, The four-way crossroads and all streets are brilliantly illuminated,
So too does the Buddha, as he travels through the city to transform beings, Universally radiate light in this same manner.
Just as Mount Sumeru is the king of mountains, And like the appearance of exquisite jewels,
So too is the Buddha among the assembly of bhikṣus, Pure and majestic in this same way.
Blazing with radiant light and great majesty, Universally able to illuminate all sentient beings,
The Tathāgata, supreme among two-legged beings, Is fully endowed with such sublime physical marks.
The Buddha entered the royal city to wander and transform beings, manifesting immeasurable and great supernatural transformations;
all devas, nāgas, spirits, and sentient beings who saw him were filled with joy and paid him reverent homage.
Having seen the thirty-two kinds of sublime marks, who would not seek the True Dharma?
If one delights in practicing the Lesser Vehicle, this is called the inferior and weak view of a fool.
I behold the Unsurpassed Honored One among Men, Whose marks and signs are dignified and rare in the world;
I now approach the Well-Gone One, the Honored One, To seek the path of unsurpassed bodhi.
"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard these words, the youth Viśuddhadhara spoke again in verse:
'I have no fondness for the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), Yet I am also able to go to the presence of the Buddha.'"
Now, within this great celestial palace, I vow to cast away my very life and body.
Furthermore, I perceive that my body is entirely illusory; thus, I am able to relinquish both body and life.
To seek the unsurpassed, great wisdom, I shall likewise proceed to the presence of the Buddha.
The affection between parents is most profound and weighty;
House, wealth, possessions, and all objects of desire— I am now able to renounce them all entirely, And vow to proceed to the presence of the Buddha.
If I may obtain what I wish, like the World-Honored One, And be praised and accepted by the Buddha,
Having renounced all that I possess, I shall go forth under the Buddha as his disciple.
"Śāriputra! At that time, the youth Viśuddhavihārin descended calmly from the great tower and immediately proceeded to where the Tathāgata Jyotiruttama—the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—was staying."

At that time, the youth Viśuddhadhara again gave rise to a courageous mind within the great multi-storied pavilion; disregarding his own body and life, he descended swiftly and, by virtue of his diligence, arrived first at the place of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jyeṣṭhottama.

Śāriputra! When the youth Viśuddhavāsa had arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, he took a most excellent Dharma robe worth one *koṭi* of Jambūnada gold and offered it to the Tathāgata, speaking these verses:
“The excellent robes I now offer, I do not seek for the sake of beautiful physical marks;”
May I in the future be like the World-Honored One, Supreme, most venerable, and praised as foremost.
Possessing pure and great wisdom, Well-established in the power of diligence,
Adorned with the thirty-two marks of excellence, May I attain the fruit of one who is honored among two-legged beings.
Furthermore, having accomplished the ten powers of knowledge and being well-established in the four fearlessnesses,
may I in the future be like the World-Honored One, supreme, most venerable, and acclaimed as the foremost.
May I, within the Buddha’s True Dharma, abide like the Buddha in the mass of light;
may I expound all dharmas as a gift to sentient beings, causing all without exception to attain awakening.
The exquisite robes I now offer do not seek after marks of physical beauty;
may they bring about the attainment of pure Great Bodhi, so as to extensively deliver the boundless multitudes of humans and devas.
Furthermore, these most excellent robes I offer, seeking the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata,
so that I may abide in the gate of the non-dual True Dharma and subdue all those of external paths.
Furthermore, may I bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, causing them to be entirely free from greed, hatred, and delusion;
may ignorance, craving, and existence be all eliminated, so that they may attain the unconditioned nectar of the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s pure Dharma universally brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings,
causing them to leave behind birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as extinguishing the various afflictions of sorrow and lamentation.
Furthermore, may I preach the Dharma to benefit all—gods, nāgas, humans, and non-humans;
may all sentient beings, whether with perception or without perception, awaken themselves and awaken others, and pay homage to one another.
May I abide in all Buddha-fields, universally emitting light that illuminates the ten directions;
amidst great darkness and the torment of heat, may I provide for them the cool flavor of ambrosia.
In the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, they cause all to be free from attachment;
completely distancing themselves from objects of aversion and affection, they constantly proclaim the pure Dharma of the Tathāgata.
“Śāriputra! When the youth Viśuddhadhara had arrived before the Buddha, he further took a pair of exquisite leather sandals and offered them to the Buddha.
Having made this earnest offering, he spoke these verses:”
“May I become like the Buddha, the Most Honored One among the assembly;
may I be like a great dwelling as a refuge and protection, causing all sentient beings to leave the evil realms and further enabling them to expound the true and correct path.”
All the various desires found in the world—these are called the coarse objects of the foolish;
may I remain far removed from all conditioned things and always encounter the Buddha appearing in the world.
Beholding the Buddha’s radiance illuminating the world, I shall make offerings to the Honored One Among Two-Legged Beings;
For the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, I vow to seek the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi.
Furthermore, with the most excellent incense, flowers, and the like, With various banners, streamers, and precious parasols,
For the benefit of all sentient beings, I take these to offer to the Great Awakened One.
With exquisite garments and food and drink, With beds, mats, bedding, and various medicines,
For the benefit of all sentient beings, I offer these to the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, holding drums and various musical instruments, With songs of praise and wondrous melodies,
To benefit all sentient beings, I make offerings to the World-Transcending Honored One of Radiant Light.

Furthermore, holding various precious and exquisite foods and drinks—the most supreme flavors found in the world—I offer them to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, for the benefit of all sentient beings. May they be used as an offering.
Having performed such vast offerings, he sought to go forth as a renunciant under the Buddha Tathāgata;
for the benefit of all sentient beings, he vowed to practice every pure conduct.
Furthermore, I vow that all sentient beings alike shall not be born amidst the delusions of false paths;
may they cause billions of sentient beings to dwell securely and peacefully in the Eightfold Noble Path.
May I not be born in this realm of desire, In the most inferior borderlands or places of reproach;
Having distanced myself from all heedlessness, May I always remain close to heedfulness.
Furthermore, may I not be born in the various evil realms; may I always wish to be born among families of faith.
Having been born, may I give rise to the supreme mind, and may I behold the Tathāgata and remain ever in his close proximity.
Having seen [the Buddha], one should give rise to this pure mind, and with flower garlands, scented unguents, and so forth,
along with various drums, music, and offerings, one should seek supreme understanding for the benefit of all beings.
May I, throughout many millions of eons, constantly perform vast acts of offering;
having renounced the world and distanced myself from all realms of desire, may I practice every form of pure conduct.

"Śāriputra! Those two youths, having offered various musical instruments and hymns of praise to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jinaśikharin, immediately conceived a pure mind for that spot of earth and constructed a vihāra out of red sandalwood, four yojanas in length and breadth, and half a yojana in height."
Having thus fashioned them, they offered them to the World-Honored One and further spoke these words:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately accept them.
Those two youths, before the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śrīghoṣa, entreated the World-Honored One and spoke in verse:
“May the Buddha dwell peacefully in my vihāra, which has been praised by all the Buddhas of the past.
Now I give rise to this mind of pure offering; may the Buddha, out of compassion, graciously accept it.”
If the Buddha were to dwell permanently in my vihāra, Thoroughly knowing the minds of beings numbering in the millions Throughout the three periods of past,
present, and future, May I likewise be so in the future.

The Buddha, relying on this vihāra, reached the further shore; He attained the right efforts and the bases of psychic power, And fully understood each of the four sublime practices; I offer this vihāra in the same manner.
I pray that the Tathāgata Jinaśekhara, together with the entire assembly of bhikṣus,
will accept this vihāra for half a month, receiving offerings, honoring, and constantly showing them respect.
Having now approached, revered, and made offerings to this Tathāgata,
I have given rise to this faith and sought to leave the household life, shaving off my topknot hair and donning the Dharma robes.
Having thus renounced the home life and gone forth, one should universally seek all that is beneficial and pleasant;
one should always practice in accordance with what is wholesome and take delight in such true Dharma.
When the two youths had spoken these verses, the youth Viśuddhavāsa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
May I swiftly attain perfect enlightenment in a future age, emitting a great radiance no different from that of the World-Honored Buddha."
Then the youth Viśuddhadhara again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
May I always serve as a guide for those on perilous and evil paths.”
"Śāriputra! At that time, the youth Viśuddhadhara stood to one side before the Tathāgata Jyotiruttama, joined his palms in reverence, and made this vow:

'May I, within the Buddha-dharma, never again sit or lie down, but remain perpetually free from sleep; and for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, may I seek the Unsurpassed Way while always remaining far removed from all indolence.'"

One should rather renounce everything, even one's own life, until even the sinews, skin, blood, and flesh are completely withered; furthermore, remaining far removed from all indolence, one should give rise to vast and courageous diligence to seek the path to Bodhi.
"Śāriputra! At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśuddhavihārin spoke these verses to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśuddhadhara:
'I shall together with you give rise to a mind of equanimity, And practice the conduct for unsurpassed bodhi.'"
I now likewise exert the power of diligence, for the benefit of all sentient beings.
I shall distance myself from all desires, even at the cost of body and life; I shall not shrink from my flesh and blood withering away.
May I practice and cultivate this throughout a thousand kalpas, with a mind of diligence and resolve set upon the path to Bodhi.
Always contemplate dwelling in the wilderness, And delighting in the quietude of mountain retreats;
Seeking the unsurpassed, great wisdom, One attains mastery over the purity of all phenomena.
"Śāriputra! During those thousand years, that Bodhisattva Viśuddhadhara never once slept or succumbed to indolence for even the duration of a finger-snap, much less experienced dreams."

Furthermore, for a thousand years he did not seek to sit at ease; except for the necessities of nature, he did not even kneel on his right knee for as long as a finger-snap, let alone sit or lie down.

During those thousand years, that bodhisattva would go on almsround with his bowl at mealtime; yet he did not look upon those who gave to him to see if they were men or women, boys or girls. With a mind dedicated to transforming and benefiting sentient beings and practicing equanimity in his conduct, he would return to his dwelling, contemplate the three worlds, and only then eat.

Having eaten thus, he did not give rise to even a single thought of hunger or thirst at a time when it was not mealtime, nor did he give rise to thoughts of sweet, sour, salty, bland, bitter, or pungent flavors.
Furthermore, during those thousand years, he did not go begging for food outside of the proper time for alms.
During that same period of a thousand years, the Bodhisattva dwelt beneath trees, seeking the path to enlightenment with single-minded diligence, without even looking to see what kind of tree it was.
Furthermore, for a thousand years, he never once changed the Dharma robes he wore even for a moment.
During those same thousand years, that bodhisattva did not give rise to any discursive thoughts regarding sensual desires, nor did he do so regarding any forms of harm.

Furthermore, for a thousand years, he did not give rise to a single thought of investigation or reflection regarding his own parents, brothers, sisters, or various kinsmen, nor regarding the sun, moon, or other such phenomena.
Furthermore, for a thousand years, he never had even a single thought of affection or attachment toward his house or dwelling.
Moreover, during those thousand years, he never once gave rise to the intention to look upon the sun, the moon, or the stars.
Furthermore, during those thousand years, he never once took shelter against a wall or among trees to dwell therein.
Moreover, throughout those thousand years, he never applied any clarified butter or oils to his body.
Furthermore, throughout those thousand years, he never once felt even a single moment of indolence regarding his own person;
nor, throughout those thousand years, did he ever experience a single moment of weariness.
Furthermore, during those thousand years, he did not even accept ghee or oil; he delighted solely in single-minded diligence because he sought to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
During those thousand years, that bodhisattva remained untiring in both body and mind.

Furthermore, while practicing the conduct of diligence for a thousand years, he did not give rise to a single thought of shaving his beard and hair; at that time, the Four Great Heavenly Kings came before him and, touching his head with their hands, his topknot hair fell away of its own accord.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings took these hairs and erected a stūpa upon a pure ground.
Furthermore, throughout a thousand years, the Four Great Heavenly Kings knew that the Bodhisattva had fully accomplished all his virtuous deeds.
At that time, for another thousand years, even when it was hot, that bodhisattva did not take pleasure in staying in the shade of trees.
Furthermore, for another thousand years, even when it was cold, he likewise did not take pleasure in covering his body with clothing.
Furthermore, for a thousand years, he likewise did not engage in speech or frivolous discourse with the sentient beings of the world.
"Moreover, Śāriputra, at that time,
a Māra king suddenly appeared, named Mūḍhasmṛti (Deluded Thought)."
Then the Māra Mūrdhaja commanded the various Pāpīyasas to construct a forest of swords and a bridge of swords for those two bodhisattvas, Viśuddhavāsa and Viśuddhadhara.
At that time, Māra the King and Pāpīyān wandered about in a state of frantic agitation, shouting aloud:
"I have now created this Forest of Famous Swords!

When Māra the King uttered these words, throughout the trichiliocosm—from the upper reaches of his own palace down to the very limits of the earth—all hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Māras, Pāpīyāns, devas, and their retinues heard and learned of it; they all assembled together, filled with terror, desiring to plot his harm.
Śāriputra, at that time, that bodhisattva dwelt with single-minded diligence, remaining unshakable.
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha*, Fascicle Twenty-Eight. Part 5:
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha*, Fascicle Two.

19. Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, the Imperially Enfeoffed Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Fahu (Dharmapāla), together with others, holding the rank of Silver Light Luogudafu and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Vigor, Part Five. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Viśuddhadhara neither walked nor followed his mind along the bridge-path in that Forest of Swords.
Those celestial Māras produced great evil sounds, seeking to terrify and harass the Bodhisattva.
At that time, the two Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, Viśuddhadhara and Viśuddhavāsa, both listened attentively.
Furthermore, the sons of the gods in the void praised them with these words:
"Those two Bodhisattvas are fully capable of practicing such right conduct; they possess such great compassion and such valor."
Those two bodhisattvas focused their thoughts exclusively on the Buddha for a thousand years.

At that time, the Tathāgata Jyotirasa had completed his work of transformation and entered parinirvāṇa. After the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, the devas in the sky saw this and addressed them, saying:
"O sons of good family!
"Vijayottama Tathāgata has already entered parinirvāṇa.
Upon hearing these words, the two bodhisattvas immediately proceeded to the place where Vijayottama Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, to the couch upon which he was laid.

Having arrived, they stood to one side with palms joined in reverence; out of compassionate longing, they called the Tathāgata to mind, not casting their eyes away for even a moment during those seven days, as they paid him honor and offered praise.
At that time, the two bodhisattvas practiced the bodhisattva path with courageous diligence, seeking the benefit and happiness of sentient beings as if carrying a heavy burden.
At that very moment, they stood before the Buddha as if entering parinirvāṇa, and were reborn in the Brahma world.

Having been born in the Brahma Heaven, he again came to the stūpa of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Jyeṣṭhottara; for forty thousand years, he circumambulated it, prostrated, and made various offerings. Furthermore, for seventy thousand years, he held up banners and canopies as an act of worship and reverence, and again offered exquisite incense, flowers, food, and drink to the temple.

Those two bodhisattvas, having exhausted their lifespans among the Brahmā devas, were again reborn in Jambudvīpa, born into the noble lineage of a universal monarch (cakravartin), and attained the knowledge of past lives.
Once he was born, they said to one another:
"We should practice the conduct of heedfulness.
At that time, the Bodhisattva spoke these verses:
“‘We have been born into this supreme royal lineage, Attained great supernormal powers, and escaped all calamities;
We vow that we shall always practice with heedfulness, And draw near to the path of unsurpassed bodhi.’”
Noble status, wealth, abundance, and all sensual pleasures—these phenomena are swiftly subject to decay and cannot be relied upon;
the wise should fully understand this and aspire to the supreme, great Bodhi.
If a person seeks this path to enlightenment, they should renounce all the pleasures of wealth and desire;
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they should seek to go forth from the household life and cultivate the most supreme and pure conduct.
In the past, throughout immeasurable eons, I and all sentient beings were full of many cravings;
our desire for the pleasures of the five senses blazed fiercely, such that we said there was never enough in their enjoyment.
I have now awakened to the nature of all sensual pleasures;
having resolved to renounce all nobility, wealth, abundance, and kin, I shall go forth into homelessness and strive with diligence for the sake of the path to Bodhi.
In the past, at the same time we were sixteen years old, we left our homes to renounce the world in search of liberation;
shaving off our hair and donning the dharma robes, we practiced the holy life for a thousand years.
Furthermore, at that time they entered nirvana together, and were subsequently reborn in the Brahma world;
having there again relinquished their lifespan, they were born here among the noble clans of Jambudvīpa.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

At that time, there was another Buddha who appeared in the world, named Most Supreme Valiant Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

Those two bodhisattvas went to where that Buddha was, attending upon and making offerings to him, honoring and praising him; they conceived pure faith, left home for the homeless life, shaved off their hair and beards, donned the dharma robes, and practiced the holy life for ten million eons (*koṭi-kalpa*).

Śāriputra! Those two bodhisattvas, throughout immeasurable ages, have already encountered hundreds of thousands of buddhas, drawing near to and making offerings to them; at the abode of each and every buddha, they fully cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya), honoring, praising, revering, and making offerings to them.

Śāriputra! After that time had passed, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhadhara first attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, being named the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Vīryaparākrama. That Buddha remained in the world for ninety *koṭi* years, and there was an assembly of ninety *koṭi-nayuta* great *śrāvaka*s who all gathered together.

Śāriputra! At that time, during the era of the Tathāgata Vīryavīra, the Bodhisattva Viśuddhavihārin was a universal monarch (cakravartin). He honored and praised that Buddha, and further provided him with various offerings of exquisite clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicinal requisites, serving both that Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus for a period of three months.

Śāriputra! At that time, after the Cakravartin King had made his offerings, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vīryavikrama, wishing to inspire great awakening in the Cakravartin King, spoke these verses:
“If one practices the supreme practice of vigor, And yearns for all the joys of the Buddha-dharma,..."
If sentient beings are addicted to the pleasures of desire, all meaningful benefits will be extremely difficult to attain.
If one does not distance oneself from the pleasures of desire, one harms both one’s own welfare and that of others;
therefore, one should completely renounce them and seek the supreme qualities of all Buddhas.
I now cause you to do likewise: having cast aside all former kinsmen and made boundless great vows, quickly seek to achieve the fruit of Bodhi.
Having seen me already having attained the Buddha-way and turning the wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park,
if you give rise to attachment toward various desires, you will not be able to swiftly achieve great Bodhi.
All Buddhas teach the departure from all desires; No further birth occurs within the phenomena of heedlessness.
The wise who follow this with virtuous faith Are able to distance themselves from all karmic obstructions.
You carry a heavy burden with impaired wisdom; how can you abide in teachings that lack benefit?
If you do not awaken to the nature of all desires, the Buddha has taught that they are all causes of suffering.

When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the Wheel-Turning Sage King attained great awakening; he completely renounced all worldly things—kingdoms, cities, wives, children, parents, kinsmen, ministers, attendants, and the officials and commoners of all small towns and villages—as well as his wealth, treasures, and storehouses.
Standing before the Buddha, he spoke these verses:
"Even if my body’s flesh should all wither away, And I perish in the midst of the wilderness,
I vow to renounce my kingdom, cities, and all palaces, In my longing for the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha."
Furthermore, he roused great diligence to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings;
in a vast and remote wilderness, he left his home to renounce the world and joyfully engage in spiritual practice.
May I forever vow to renounce all sensual pleasures, To distance myself from sinful karma and delusion;
If one clings to any form of defilement, One should turn away from the path to Bodhi.
All desires and royal sovereignty— I vow to renounce them all;
Within the teaching of the Blessed One, I aspire to go forth and practice the holy life.
The wise person stays far removed from all objects of desire, Vowing to practice the path to enlightenment;
They should give rise to a mind of diligent and courageous effort, For if one indulges in defilements, they turn their back on the Buddha-way.
I have now cast aside those realms of desire, as well as kingship and sensual pleasures;
diligently seeking liberation through the Buddha’s Dharma, I vow with vigor to swiftly attain Bodhi.

When the Wheel-Turning Sage King had spoken this verse, he immediately drew near to that Buddha to make offerings, gave rise to great faith and reverence, left his home to renounce the world, shaved off his hair and beard, and donned the dharma robes.
After the King had gone forth, at that time there were again sixty hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of people who likewise gave rise to great faith and reverence, abandoning their homes to go forth.
When that Tathāgata Viryavīrya had completed his transformative activities, he entered parinirvāṇa at that time.

Upon seeing the Buddha’s extinction, the Cakravartin King was overcome with grief and distress; after collecting the relics and making offerings to them, he too reached the end of his life and was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.

After that deva has passed away, he will again descend to be born in Jambudvīpa; at that time, he shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, named Sukṛtacara.

That Buddha remained in the world for one *koṭi* of years, and there was an assembly of *koṭi-nayuta* great *śrāvakas* who all gathered together; they were all great *arhats*, whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions, having attained their own benefit, gained mastery over their minds, and reached the further shore.

Furthermore, there was an assembly of one hundred thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who had attained non-retrogression and dwelt on the stage of non-retrogression, vowing to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
That Buddha continued to teach the Dharma and transform immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* sentient beings, performing deeds of great benefit before entering *parinirvāṇa*.

After that Buddha’s passing, his True Dharma remained in the world for a full *kalpa*; thereafter, his bodily relics were distributed and venerated with offerings and respect, exactly as my own relics will be distributed after my passing, without any difference.
Śāriputra! That Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Viśuddhavihārin constantly follows and studies the practice of the Bodhisattva’s perfection of diligence, yet never grows weary or indolent.
This is because in the past, due to relying upon certain beings who fashioned jeweled necklaces,

he gave rise to envy. Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, while seeking the path to awakening, gives rise to envy toward other families, you should know that at that time there are three kinds of fear.
What are the three?
First, begging for alms in improper places; second, engaging in conversation with those with whom one should not speak; and third, conceiving envy toward other bhikṣus upon seeing them.
In such places, one increases the fault of envy exclusively; for this reason, one regards the realm of hell as one's own home.
Thus, those who practice diligence there are like blind people in dangerous, remote regions, being born under the influence of false views and captured by them.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, seeing other bhikṣus give rise to anger, they do not even look at them, yet they conceive a mind of jealousy, inciting others to wrathful contention, assuming extremely evil expressions, and uttering coarse and savage words.
By these causes and conditions, they fall into the path of the hells as if it were their own home.

Having established the seeds for rebirth there, even if they obtain a human body, they are born in various perilous and difficult places, in borderlands, or among those with wrong views; they are possessed by them, their minds lack compassion, they delight in much harm, and they are devious toward others while delighting in much compliance.
Śāriputra! When that bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to envy toward other clans, he should reflect upon these three kinds of fear.
Having spoken thus, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:
“It is marvelous, World-Honored One!

That a bodhisattva mahāsattva, upon hearing such characteristics of practice from the Tathāgata, does not give rise to envy toward those families, but attains great and wholesome benefit and achieves liberation.”
Again, Śāriputra said:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!

We, the assembly of śrāvakas, also wish to hear this essential teaching: how is it that one does not give rise to envy toward those families, yet attains deliverance from the path of hell, and achieves liberation from all the perilous and evil paths such as congenital blindness?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“Since there is no causal basis for it, let this matter rest.
Śāriputra said:
"How may we avoid all slander, refrain from giving rise to wrong views, and always be born in the Central Land, where we may see the Buddha, hear the Dharma, and practice the path of the śrāvaka?
When they had spoken thus, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"Excellent, excellent!"
It is well that you are able to inquire about such meanings of the Dharma from the Tathāgata. Śāriputra,
if there are sentient beings who delight in practicing the secular texts of non-Buddhist outsiders, you should not speak of this to them.
If there are those who, with reverence, faith, and understanding, aspire to train in the Buddha-dharma,
you should speak to them.
Why is this so, Śāriputra?
If one does not distance oneself from worldly and non-Buddhist scriptures, I declare that to be the root of strife; this is a hardship within the Buddha-dharma. Śāriputra!

If a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses firm faith and understanding, does not give rise to negligence, and throughout the long night investigates and contemplates with discernment, giving rise to a mind that seeks to protect all sentient beings, they will then be able to approach the Tathāgata to inquire about the meaning of the Dharma.
Having heard this Dharma, they rejoice with delight and practice according to the teaching.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
if there are sentient beings who seek nirvāṇa through inferior and weak diligence, not only is it difficult for them to attain it, but they will further increase three kinds of faults."

That is to say, they are attached to gain, honor, and reputation; furthermore, they take pleasure in friends, kinsmen, and various retinues, and for the sake of their own sustenance, they constantly and greedily seek out unrighteous profit.
Because they pursue through these three matters, they cannot be liberated from the three evil realms.
Due to this inferior and weak diligence, they fall into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and the realm of Yama, thereby obstructing their birth in the heavenly paths.
Furthermore, within the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), they constantly give rise to strife and contention. Śāriputra!

Those sentient beings are unwilling to believe in or accept any wholesome dharmas; they constantly associate with evil friends, take no pleasure in dwelling in places of tranquility, and instead delight in staying in the houses of laypeople.
I heard several elders making this statement:
"If he remains thus established, we vow to provide him with food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine, and to attend upon him with offerings."
At that time, the bhikṣu and the elder spoke to one another, saying:
"If one dwells in the wilderness, who else could be so close?
It is for this reason that I now feel affection and reverence toward him."
Because of this, the bhikṣu developed a deep attachment and remained in the householder’s home.
Having stayed for a long time, he and the various clans and their relatives developed mutual craving and affection.
Suddenly, a bhikṣu arrived from a distant land and came to that clan. At that time, the resident bhikṣus, out of greed and attachment, gave rise to jealousy and said to him:
