"I am originally pure and also widely learned; I claim for myself the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat."
Thus they produced such false, deceitful, and crooked evil speech.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
at that time other bhikṣus also spoke these words:
"I shall not seek to dwell long in this householder's home.
Śāriputra, those resident bhikṣus were mutually hateful and jealous, acting in ways that were unrighteous and harmful.

Furthermore, there is another class who, regarding the Mahāyāna Dharma, utter malicious speech and engage in mutual contention, and concerning the various sūtras, they practice false conduct and mutually slander one another.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, those sentient beings who,

having heard for even a moment this true Dharma consisting of the sounds, names, phrases, and syllables of the sūtras spoken by the Buddha Tathāgata, develop a resolute conviction [in it] yet subsequently give rise to slander toward it— such individuals, by their very nature, are certain to fall into the evil destinies."

Śāriputra! Furthermore, if one gives rise to hatred and envy toward those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who possess irreversible diligence, such a mode of conduct will likewise lead to rebirth in the evil destinies.
At that time, having heard these words, Śāriputra and all sentient beings ceased to harbor envy regarding virtuous deeds. "Śāriputra!
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the non-retrogressive conduct of diligence within the perfection of diligence, they conceive the thought of rescuing and delivering all sentient beings."
All sentient beings are constantly scorched and boiled by three kinds of maladies.
What are these three?
They are greed, hatred, and delusion.

I shall, for those sentient beings, gather and harmonize the Buddha’s true Dharma as a great panacea to cure the diseases of the feverish afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion in all sentient beings; I declare this to be the practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of diligence of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
all sentient beings are constantly born into feverish affliction. Why is this?

It means that the diseases of the three poisons increase at all times; whether born among the gods or among humans, or even in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or the Yama-loka, all are scorched and boiled by the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion.

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees those sentient beings suffering from the affliction of feverish distress, they conceive the thought of rescuing and delivering them; furthermore, they reflect that the medicinal herbs and remedies of the world are incapable of treating these three kinds of diseases—how, then, can these three kinds of diseases be eliminated?
Only the Buddha-Tathāgata has attained the Great Dharma-body, acting as a Great Physician King to cure the grave illnesses of the three poisons and the feverish afflictions of all sentient beings.

All Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are likewise so: their bodies are the medicine of the Dharma and they act as Great Physician Kings, fully able to rescue and heal all sentient beings, causing the three poisons and feverish afflictions to be entirely extinguished.
Śāriputra! The various medicines and treatments of this world can never cure the diseases of the three poisons.

Only the Tathāgata and the great Bodhisattvas, acting as great kings of physicians, bestow the medicine of the Great Dharma, which is able to extinguish and eliminate the feverish afflictions of the three poisons for all sentient beings.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I correctly understand the realm of all sentient beings as taught by the Tathāgata...”
"What do you think?
Is it not the case that, unlike the realms of earth, water, fire, wind, and space, the realm of sentient beings alone is immeasurable and boundless?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"It is so, it is so! It is just as you have said, Śāriputra."

The realm of the common lot (nikāya-sabhāga) of those sentient beings is likewise not something that can be seen by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; only the Buddha’s divine eye (divyacakṣus) can illuminate it entirely. Śāriputra!

All the devas, humans, and asuras within the trichiliocosm, including the immeasurable and boundless beings born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or by transformation; those with form and those without form; those with perception, without perception, and neither with nor without perception—within all such realms of sentient beings established therein, and throughout the entire range visible to a Buddha’s divine eye, whether in a single kṣaṇa, a lava, or a muhūrta, they have not obtained a human body until now. Only at this moment have they finally attained it.

Śāriputra! Even if all such persons were like the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, who skillfully treats all manner of diseases, they would still ultimately be unable to cure the feverish afflictions of the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion in even a single person.

Furthermore, even if one were to compound various kinds of the greatest and most excellent medicines in quantities as high as Mount Sumeru, one would still be unable to cure the single disease of greed, hatred, and delusion.

Even if they were all like the King of Physicians who Sustains Life, each remaining in the world for a kalpa of lifespan, and they were to pound, sift, and compound great medicinal elixirs in quantities exceeding Mount Sumeru until they were utterly exhausted, they would still be unable to effect even a slight cure for the diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion within a single person.
Śāriputra! Only the Tathāgata possesses the medicinal elixir of the pure Dharma, complete with skillful means, which accords with the diseases of the three poisons as they manifest.

If sentient beings suffer from the feverish affliction of greed, the Tathāgata teaches them the method of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as a compounded medicine; this can heal all such feverish afflictions of greed belonging to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of asaṃkhyeyas, even to those that are unspeakable and incalculable, bringing them all to complete recovery.

Furthermore, for all sentient beings afflicted by the feverish disease of hatred, the Tathāgata preaches the medicine of the harmonious Dharma of great loving-kindness (*maitrī*); this is able to cure the feverish disease of hatred in such immeasurable, even unspeakable and incalculable, sentient beings, so that they are all completely healed.

Furthermore, for all sentient beings afflicted by the feverish disease of delusion, the Tathāgata has taught that the harmony of dependently arisen phenomena serves as the medicine; this cures and completely heals the feverish disease of delusion for immeasurable—even to the point of being unspeakable and incalculable—sentient beings.

By means of this analogy, one should understand that the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is able to use such medicinal teachings of the Tathāgata to heal the immeasurable, boundless, and even unspeakably incalculable sentient beings, completely extinguishing the burning afflictions of the three poisons; this is precisely the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

Śāriputra! Thus abiding in the dharmakāya, the bodhisattva mahāsattva further, through the power of the dharmakāya’s empowerment, causes the heat and affliction of the three poisons of immeasurable, boundless, even unspeakable and incalculable sentient beings to be entirely extinguished so that they do not arise again; they are entirely extinguished so that they do not arise again.
The Buddha said,
“Śāriputra! In the past,
throughout immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I have fully understood all such dharmas.”
Furthermore, at that time, a Buddha appeared in the world named Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
That Buddha-Tathāgata bestowed upon me this prediction:
"After the passing of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Twenty-Nine.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Thirty.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others—Śramaṇas of the Imperial Court, recipients of the purple robe and the title of Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, who were granted the rank of Silver Light Luoguo Dafu and Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices—by Imperial Decree. Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Vigor, Part Six. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

Having attained the fulfillment of the Dharma-body in the presence of the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara, I was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven as the Devaputra named Jyotiṣprabha. I served as the lord of the Śakras, possessing great majesty and virtue, endowed with great supernormal powers, my fame renowned everywhere, sovereign and unimpeded.

Furthermore, at that time, there were eighty-four thousand great cities in Jambudvīpa, as well as numerous towns and villages; those villages were filled with hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of sentient beings.

Furthermore, at that time, when the kalpa of pestilence arises, sentient beings with evil karma reach the point where the conditions for disease ripen; they develop scabies, sores, carbuncles, and skin eruptions, as wind, bile, and phlegm accumulate within their bodies.
At that time, there were also hundreds of thousands of kings of physicians who prepared excellent medicines to treat the diseases of sentient beings,
curing them completely. "Furthermore, Śāriputra,
those sentient beings who had no refuge, no protector, and whose ailments remained uncured, cried out in a loud voice:"
"Is it a deva, nāga, yakṣa, gandharva, rākṣasa, human, or non-human?
Can they cause my illness and all its sufferings to be liberated?"
"I am able to relinquish all my wealth and possessions; I vow to serve as your slave, providing whatever you require and attending to your every command at will. Śāriputra!

It is because I possess the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, that I am able to see those who are "without sight"—those whose bodies are afflicted by various diseases such as scabies, leprosy, carbuncles, and skin rashes, or by the accumulation of wind, bile, phlegm, chills, and fevers, which have fully matured and pervaded their entire forms.

There were none who heard them; those sentient beings cried out in a loud voice, saying, "It is because we possess the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, that we are able to hear."
Toward those sentient beings, I give rise to great compassion and feel profound pity, forming this thought:

"For those without refuge, I shall become their refuge; for those without protection, I shall become their protector; for those who have not been healed, I shall bring about their healing, so that they may attain peace and happiness."
"Śāriputra! At that time, concealing my Śaṅkara form, I went not far from the great city of Kuru and suddenly manifested through transformation as a sentient being named Sumu."
Again, dwelling in mid-air, he spoke these verses for the sake of all those suffering from disease in Jambudvīpa:
"Not far from that city of Kurujāṅgala, There is a manifested being named Sumu;
If one comes there to eat his limbs, All diseases shall be completely healed."
"You sentient beings, do not be afraid; those who eat thus will give rise to joy.
They will be free from resentment and hatred already removed; this is the great medicine of Jambudvīpa."
"Śāriputra! When all sentient beings within these eighty-four thousand great cities, districts, towns, and villages heard this sound, they immediately rushed toward the great city of Kuru."
He went to Sumu and took a small portion of his limbs to eat, yet Sumu’s limbs were not diminished at all.
At that time, Sumu spoke these verses:
"Because the path to enlightenment is truly not in vain, I have attained an inexhaustible mass of wisdom."
"His words are true and not deceptive; may my own limbs likewise never be exhausted.
Śāriputra, at that time, all those who were ill in Jambudvīpa gathered at the place of Sumu and took portions of his limbs to eat.
Through inexhaustible wisdom, although they have been severed in this manner, they arise again after being severed.
Yet, once they have arisen once more upon the limbs, there is no diminution.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When all those who were ill ate the limbs of the body consumed by Sumu, their various ailments were healed, and they attained peace, security, and happiness, receiving the reward of freedom from disease.
In this way, all those who were ill throughout the entire continent of Jambudvīpa were completely cured, attaining peace, security, and happiness, and receiving the reward of freedom from disease.
"At that time, all the sentient beings on the continent of Jambudvīpa—whether men, women, boys, or girls—all spoke these words:
'As we reflect upon it, by eating this sumu, our illnesses have been cured and we are now at ease and happy.'"
"We should personally attend upon and make offerings to him.
At once they gathered together and went to Sumu, surrounding him on all sides as they spoke this verse:
"You who can act as our refuge and savior, You are the King of Physicians and the Excellent Medicine."
"What shall we do now?
We pray that you will grant us offerings without any stinginess. "Śāriputra!..."
At that time, knowing that these sentient beings had attained peace and security, I manifested the form of a great Śūkarā (Boar) and stood before the multitude, saying:

"I now have no further use for royal cities, kingdoms, districts, towns, villages, houses, wealth, or goods; nor for gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, or other exquisite jewels; nor for elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, palanquins, carriages, or vehicles; nor for men, women, boys, girls, male and female slaves, attendants, food, drink, clothing, bedding, seats, medicines, or provisions; nor for gardens, groves, ponds, or lakes. Such objects of pleasure as these are all no longer of use to me."

I instruct you only thus: you must sever the taking of life and never do it again; you must sever stealing and never do it again; you must sever sexual misconduct and never do it again; you must sever false speech and never do it again; you must sever divisive speech and never do it again; you must sever frivolous speech and never do it again.
"In short, you must sever harsh speech, greed, hatred, and wrong views, never to commit them again.
Then, that Mahāśakara spoke these verses for the sake of all those people:
"Even if one possessed many koṭis of wealth and treasures, In quantity as vast as Mount Sumeru,"
Food, drink, clothing, and exquisite celestial maidens— Such offerings as these are of no use to me.
If you were to provide such various offerings, It would not equal practicing the ten paths of wholesome action,
Each of you together giving rise to a heart of loving-kindness and compassion, And constantly guarding them at all times.
The Bodhisattva does not delight in wealth and profit, but is able only to uphold the ten wholesome karmas;
if you all can practice them together, I shall call this true worship.
Food, drink, clothing, and bedding; elephants, horses, chariots, and various precious jewels—even up to exquisite celestial maidens—I now accept none of these at all.
Listen now to my words of truth: you should cultivate the ten paths of pure wholesome action;
arouse hearts of loving-kindness and compassion toward one another, and always maintain them in all circumstances.
If you can embrace such teachings as these, the path of the ten wholesome karmas will remain ever pure.
Having spoken this verse, he addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"At that time, amidst the great assembly, I proclaimed the essential points of the Dharma, teaching with purity and without admixture, thereby instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them."
Having spoken this Dharma, he vanished from sight.

At that time, among the men, women, boys, and girls on the continent of Jambudvīpa who had consumed *soma*, not a single person fell into the evil realms until the end of their lives; instead, they were all simultaneously reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three, where they enjoyed every pleasure amidst a wondrous assembly.

"Śāriputra! Those persons and sentient beings, having heard this Dharma in that celestial realm, were instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened; they attained definitive understanding regarding the three vehicles, namely: the vehicle of the śrāvaka, the vehicle of the pratyekabuddha, and the unsurpassed vehicle of omniscience."
"In those heavens, some shall enter parinirvāṇa, some have not yet entered parinirvāṇa, and some are currently entering parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha said, "Śāriputra!"

Observe how the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells securely in the Dharma-body; why is it that he is said to have attained great supernormal powers, to possess great majestic virtue, and for his fame to be heard everywhere?
At that time, I alone was able to sacrifice my own body and life to bring all sentient beings to maturity in the Nirvāṇa of the three vehicles.
When he had spoken thus, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva being fully endowed with the dharma-body?”
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“The dharma-body of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is firm and solid, like a vajra, possessing no characteristic of destruction; it is exquisite, true, and neither born nor extinguished.”

Furthermore, because the Dharmakāya does not spare its own life or body in order to deliver sentient beings, for this reason fire cannot burn it and no object can destroy it; moreover, it is as firm and solid as a vajra, possessing no characteristic of disintegration.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the irreversible perfection of diligence, they thus abide in the fulfillment of the dharmakāya; they bring sentient beings to maturity without begrudging their own bodies or lives, and they are free from verbal expression, conceptualization, and discursive imagination.

Furthermore, one knows that this body is like empty space; because the body is free from various characteristics, one is able to enter into and understand all phenomena as being likewise free from various characteristics.
Because they are free from characteristics, one does not discriminate between this body and these dharmas.
If the body is already free from characteristics within the realm of characteristics, it is likewise so for all dharmas.
If one can personally become detached from even a single characteristic, one is thereby able to enter into the understanding that the bodies of all sentient beings are devoid of characteristics.
Because the bodies of all sentient beings are devoid of characteristics, one is thereby able to enter into the understanding that the dharma-realm is devoid of characteristics.
Because the dharma-realm is free from characteristics, one is free from characteristics regarding all phenomena.
One should train in this way until even the most subtle of phenomena cannot be apprehended.
By means of the suchness of one's own person, one is able to accordingly understand the suchness of the persons of all sentient beings.
By means of the suchness of the bodies of all sentient beings, one is able to accordingly understand the suchness of one's own body.
By means of the suchness of one's own body, one is able to accordingly understand the suchness of all phenomena.
By means of the suchness of all phenomena, one is able to accordingly understand the suchness of one's own self;
by means of the suchness of one's own self, one is also able to comprehensively understand the suchness of all Buddhas.
By means of the *tathatā* (suchness) of all Buddhas, one is able to thoroughly understand the *tathatā* of one's own self;
by means of the *tathatā* of one's own self, one is likewise able to accordingly understand the *tathatā* of the past, future, and present.
By means of the suchness (tathatā) of the past, future, and present, one is able to accordingly understand the suchness of one's own self.

Furthermore, the suchness of the past is not in contradiction with the suchness of the future; the suchness of the past is also not in contradiction with the suchness of the present; the suchness of the present is not in contradiction with the suchness of the past; and the suchness of the future is also not in contradiction with the suchness of the past.

Furthermore, the suchness of the past is not in conflict with the suchness of the future; the suchness of the future is also not in conflict with the suchness of the present; the suchness of the present is not in conflict with the suchness of the future; and the suchness of the future is also not in conflict with the suchness of the present.

Because present suchness is not in contradiction with past suchness, and past suchness is likewise not in contradiction with present suchness; furthermore, it is the same for past suchness in relation to future and present suchness.

Furthermore, the suchness of those aggregates, bases, and elements is the suchness of these aggregates, bases, and elements; the suchness of that defilement and purification is the suchness of this defilement and purification; the suchness of that nirvana and samsara is the suchness of this nirvana and samsara; the suchness of those formations is the suchness of these formations, and the suchness of all formations is likewise so.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

Because it is as described, because it is without distinction, because it is not something to be abandoned, and because it is not a reflection, even *tathatā* (suchness) does not possess even the slightest characteristic."
Why is this? Suchness is without marks; that which is spoken of as such is the mark of the Tathāgata.
Likewise, the suchness that encompasses cause and effect—what is spoken of as that is also the mark of the Tathāgata.
When that bodhisattva perceives these various marks as being without fabrication, he perceives the mark of the Tathāgata as non-contentious.
Since all phenomenal marks do not move therein, that is the mark of the Tathāgata.
If it is not the wisdom of true suchness (*tathatā-jñāna*), how can one observe the body of the Tathāgata?
To observe the body of the Tathāgata with equanimity is to realize the equality of one's own body.
By observing the equality of one's own body, one realizes the equality of all bodies as being no-body.
By observing all bodies through the equality of non-body, one is able to observe this very body.
Therefore, knowing that all bodily characteristics are dependently originated, one realizes that this own *dharmakāya* is definitively indestructible; it is likewise so for all *dharmakāyas*.

Having attained such a Dharma-body, he is able to discern that which is not the aggregates, bases, or elements; through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing all sentient beings, he is able to transform and deliver them, performing all manner of beneficial deeds.

Śāriputra! It is, for example, like the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, who compiles and combines various great and excellent medicines to bestow upon those suffering from many ailments; he creates the form of a young girl, as wondrously beautiful as a most supreme and pure pond, fully adorned and dwelling in perfect composure, whether moving, walking, sitting, or lying down at the proper or improper times, and is further able to perform those most excellent and sublime tasks.
Furthermore, at that time, the most eminent, most excellent, great clansmen, householders, and lay devotees all came to see that maiden who prepared the medicine.
Then, after the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, had universally applied such a touch, all those who were ill attained happiness, lightness, and tranquility, becoming free from the affliction of disease.
Śāriputra, you should know that only the unique King of Physicians who sustains life can cause the diseases of sentient beings to be cured, for no other physicians possess such power.

Śāriputra! It is the same for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who has realized the Dharmakāya: even when reaching the bodies of sentient beings—whether men, women, boys, or girls—who are being scorched and boiled by greed, hatred, and delusion, and having made contact with them all over, all those diseases are completely cured, and they attain freedom from all feverish afflictions.
Thus it is because the bodhisattva has attained purity through the power of their former vows.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not act for the sake of material goods, food, drink, or other such things for the sustenance of the body; rather, they possess thorough penetration regarding all taking and discarding within the dharmakāya. Yet, out of compassion for sentient beings, they may accept food and drink, nor do they abandon their physical life or body; furthermore, regarding the power of the dharmakāya, they neither take up nor discard, nor do they diminish it.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

although the dharmakāya of a bodhisattva mahāsattva is without arising or cessation, because they are able to manifest arising and cessation, they are further able to bring sentient beings to maturity."

One thoroughly understands the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and further knows that these phenomena have no collective assembly; one fully comprehends both the place of their arising and the place of their cessation.
Regarding that Dharma-body, the food of Dharma, the power of Dharma, and the constant reliance upon the Dharma, the mind has nothing to manifest.
"This is called the perfection of diligence that never regresses in maturing sentient beings through the ripening power of former vows.
At that time, the World-Honored One, in order to clarify this meaning further, spoke these verses:
"Now I have attained a vajra-body, Indestructible and non-dispersing, for the Buddha knows it thus."
Swords cannot wound them, nor can fire burn them; when delivering sentient beings, how could they ever fail?

Delivering sentient beings from the harm of fierce fires, as if they had obtained the supreme medicine of coolness—once sentient beings have gained such knowledge and vision, it is like obtaining all manner of food and drink.
Even unto the non-conceptualization of the dharma-realm, there is only the single dharmakāya and no other body;
there is no person, no self, and no māṇava, for one has thoroughly realized that all phenomena arise through conditions.
Contemplating how one can practice asceticism, one extinguishes conditions and thus severs the causes of suffering;
the aggregate of form is as insubstantial as a bubble on water, the aggregate of sensation is like a mass of foam,
perception is like a mirage appearing in the heat of thirst, and formations are observed to be as hollow as the core of a plantain tree.
Furthermore, like various illusory arts and performances, all diverse things are instantly devoid of inherent characteristics.
The wise, understanding that all conditioned activities are not solid or real,
perceive that the requisites produced are like flashes of lightning and like waterfalls cascading down high mountains.
The desire for wealth is likewise like a reflected image; it is more swift than the flight of an arrow.
Knowing that all things change like floating clouds, no wise person finds delight therein.

Having experienced the various exquisite pleasures of food and drink among the gods and humans of the three realms, one later falls into the midst of extreme suffering in hell; having seen this, one finds no delight in the celestial realms.
That which has no support is like the beasts; this person relies on that which is free from birth and death.
The Bodhisattva shall attain the Great Dharma-body, which remains without arising or ceasing even through the cycles of formation and destruction.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the practice of the irreversible perfection of diligence, they should train in this way."
It is heard that the world is entirely filled with all manner of unwholesome dharmas, yet people likewise fail to understand their corresponding remedies.

For example, sentient beings in the world possess three great maladies—namely, the great malady of greed, the great malady of hatred, and the great malady of delusion—and they fail to recognize these three great maladies of sentient beings, nor do they know the three great medicines for them.
What are these three?
For the great malady of greed, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) serves as the great panacea.
For the great malady of hatred, the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*) serves as the great panacea.
For those with the great malady of delusion, the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) serves as the supreme medicine;
yet they do not understand this at all.
Even if a King of Physicians were to treat other ailments, though they might be temporarily cured, it would not be ultimate, for such treatment cannot cure every disease.

Those who possess wisdom should not follow and train in such ways; rather, they should train in the dharmas that serve as antidotes taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Acting as great physicians who have mastered all unsurpassed wholesome dharmas, they cause all diseases to be completely purified and healed—this is the ultimate goal.
One should not follow or learn even a small portion from the medical kings practiced in other worlds.

Rather, one should accumulate, pound, sift, and compound the supreme medicinal elixir of the Dharma; once its sound is heard, the great disease of greed, the great disease of hatred, and the great disease of delusion will all be completely cured.
Śāriputra!

This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of diligence when practicing the non-regressive path; it is the accumulation, refinement, and compounding of this sublime medicinal elixir of the Great Dharma, which none of those śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas can possess. Only the Tathāgata—the Unsurpassed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Awakened One—acts as the Great King of Physicians, gathering all roots of virtue, refining and compounding them into the Great Dharma Medicine. Blowing the Great Dharma Conch, he produces a profound and wondrous sound that reaches throughout the trichiliocosm so that all may hear and know it. This enables immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of *kaṅkara*—in short, even unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings—to have these three great diseases of greed, hatred, and delusion entirely cured.

Śāriputra! For example, within the forests of the Snowy Mountains there is a great medicinal king-tree named Free from All Poisons; any sentient beings dwelling within a hundred yojanas who smell its fragrance will have all their poisons completely eliminated.

Śāriputra! If one anoints conch shells and drums with the great medicinal king-tree that is free from all poisons and blows or beats them, then whatever sentient beings there may be who possess insect venom, medicinal poison, gaseous poison, or any other kind of poison, once they hear this sound, all their poisons will be completely eliminated.
"Śāriputra!
This king of great medicinal trees, which is free from all poisons, cannot be known by any physicians whatsoever; only the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, alone is able to know and understand it."

Śāriputra! As for the great medicinal drug of the sublime Dharma of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, they are able to collect, grind, and compound it; even śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot do so, whereas only a Tathāgata can. For this reason, having mastered all wholesome dharmas and acting as a Great King of Physicians, he is able to cure all the ailments of all sentient beings.

One is able to collect, grind, and blend these medicinal dharmas, blowing the great Dharma conch to produce a profound and wondrous sound that reaches throughout the trichiliocosm so that all may hear and know it. This enables immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of *kaṅkara*—to speak briefly, even unto unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings—to have their greed, hatred, and delusion entirely extinguished upon hearing this sound.
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva accumulate the wealth of the Dharma?
In what places is it applied as a gift?
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva applies the wealth of the Dharma, they accumulate it solely within the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

Śāriputra! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the irreversible perfection of diligence, they should train themselves in this way: regarding the true Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, they should receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain its meaning; whether writing it themselves or causing others to write it, they should even go so far as to explain it extensively to others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In the distant past, after such successive eons—vast, inconceivable, and incalculable (asaṃkhyeya)—at that time there was a Buddha named Padmottara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. That Buddha had a great assembly of eighty koṭis of śrāvakas gathered together; all were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were free from further afflictions, having attained mastery of mind and reached the further shore."
The lifespan of that Buddha will be eighty thousand years; his True Dharma shall remain in the world for five hundred years, and the Semblance Dharma shall likewise endure for the same length.
After that Tathāgata Padmottara has entered parinirvāṇa, all his relics shall be no different from those of my own after my extinction.

Śāriputra! After the Tathāgata Padmottara has entered parinirvāṇa, one hundred years later, there will be a bodhisattva who, passing away from another direction, will come to be born into a royal family.
At that time, he spoke these words to his mother:
"For what reason have I now been born into this family of unrighteousness?
From this day forth, I shall also practice in accordance with that True Dharma."
For these reasons, it is called the Practice of the True Dharma (*saddharmacaryā*).
This concludes the thirtieth fascicle of the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-bodhisattvapiṭaka-saddharma-paryāya*, spoken by the Buddha. Fascicle Thirty-one.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperial Preceptor for the Propagation of the Sanskrit Canon, Silver Light Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and the Great Master of Compassionate Enlightenment who was conferred the Purple Robe, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Nine: The Perfection of Vigor, Part Seven. "At that time!"

Śāriputra! For the sake of maturing his roots of goodness, that youth Dharmacārī, at the age of twenty, gave rise to pure faith; he left home to go forth, assumed the appearance of a bhikṣu, received full ordination, and dwelt in meditative seclusion within a great forest grove in an araṇya.
In the midst of the void, various worthies and sages came secretly to instruct him on such matters of benefit, saying to the bhikṣu:
"Regarding the bodhisattva-piṭaka of the True Dharma, you have attained non-retrogressive diligent practice; possessing great renown, you shall become a Buddha."

At that time, having heard these words from the noble ones, that bhikṣu was filled with great joy and attained what he had never experienced before; he then sought the true Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka everywhere—in cities, villages, kingdoms, royal palaces, and among all the people wherever they might be.
Furthermore, he went to the saṃghārāma and respectfully paid homage to and questioned the assembly of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs:
"What is called the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka?"
Regarding the ācāryas and the Buddha-dharma, how should a bodhisattva further serve, attend upon, and train in them?
I now wish to seek the true Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka from these venerable ones, and I shall come to hear and receive it, whether in its names or its syllables.
Those bhikṣus replied, “This is not within our knowledge.
They then thought to themselves in secret:
"The words of those noble ones must not be false.
I have never heard or received the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; how then could I practice non-retrogressive diligence?"
He asked again: "Venerable Elder!
In what direction does that Tathāgata Padmottara reside?"
"I pray that you grant me your instruction. He replied, "O Bhikṣu!"
"The Tathāgata Padmottara resides in this location.

He immediately proceeded to the indicated place; having arrived, he circumambulated it three times to the right, prostrated with his head at the feet [of the Buddha], and standing before the Buddha, spoke these words:
"I shall now sit cross-legged here, and until I am able to hear this True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka from the Tathāgata Padmottara, I vow not to rise from this spot."

"Śāriputra! During these seven days and nights, this bhikṣu did not slacken in his vigor in that place; with such steadfastness exceeding seven days and nights, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, he beheld the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnagarbha in the world-system of the East, and heard him expound eight Dharma-gates."
These eight kinds of Dharma-gates enable one to practice and study in accordance with the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

At that time, having fully heard these inconceivable eight Dharma-gates which are unsurpassed, that bhikṣu rose from his seat in that place and was likewise able to expound upon the non-retrogressive conduct of diligence within the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Furthermore, for sixty full years, he taught and transformed immeasurable koṭis of devas and humans in cities, villages, kingdoms, and royal palaces, causing them to abide in the Three Vehicles.
At the time of his death, that bhikṣu made this aspiration:
"May I be born among the human class within the buddha-fields.
Having passed away from there, he was reborn in the family of a householder on the continent of Jambudvīpa.
Having been thus born, he then gave rise to this thought and resolved to practice the conduct of the True Dharma (*saddharmacaryā*).
By reason of these causes and conditions, he was given the same name as his predecessor, "Practice of the True Dharma" (*Saddharmacaryā*).
Having conceived pure faith, he left the household life to enter homelessness, assumed the appearance of a bhikṣu, and received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Not long after he had gone forth, he again came to dwell in the presence of the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.

For sixty thousand years, throughout cities, villages, kingdoms, and royal palaces, he was able to expound and propagate the practice of the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; he taught and transformed immeasurable koṭis of devas and humans, bringing them to maturity in the three vehicles—namely, the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, and the unsurpassed Mahāyāna.
At the time of his death, he again made a solemn vow; by the power of that aspiration, he obtained a human body in Jambudvīpa, born into a royal lineage.
Immediately upon his birth, sages in the sky proclaimed:
"O sentient being, you have transcended all phenomena."
For this reason, he was given the name *Sarvadharmātikrānta-sattvaparipācaka* (One Who Transcends All Dharmas and Ripens Sentient Beings).
For twenty years, he gave rise to right faith, left the household life for homelessness, assumed the appearance of a bhikṣu, and received full ordination.
Through the power of right mindfulness that transcends all phenomena, he dwells in the presence of the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka. Śāriputra,

this bhikṣu who transcends all phenomena severed all doubts regarding the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and was able to expound it throughout cities, villages, kingdoms, and royal palaces for a full sixty thousand years.
After this number had passed, he caused immeasurable koṭis of devas, humans, asuras, and others to resolve upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At the time of his death, he further made a vow, saying:
"May I obtain a human body."
He was born into the great Śāla clan of elders on the continent of Jambudvīpa.
Immediately upon his birth, a voice arose in the sky, and the noble ones proclaimed:
"You have attained right mindfulness within the realm of sentient beings."
For this reason, he was given the name "One Who Has Attained Right Mindfulness for Maturing Sentient Beings.
Over the course of twenty years, he gave rise to right faith, left the home life to become a renunciant, assumed the appearance of a bhikṣu, and received full ordination.
Because he previously contemplated with perfect accuracy the most supreme and excellent accomplishment of extensive learning, he taught the Dharma for sixty years to transform and instruct others.
Throughout cities, villages, kingdoms, and royal palaces, he is now able to further expound the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka for all sentient beings, severing all their doubts and delusions.

Furthermore, exceeding that number, he taught and transformed four koṭis of devas, humans, asuras, and others, bringing them to maturity in the three vehicles—namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the unsurpassed Buddha vehicle of wisdom.
Śāriputra! Having made this vow, the bhikṣu Samyagdharmanirdeśa immediately passed away and was reborn in the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, in that same region as before.
Śāriputra! That bodhisattva mahāsattva brings sixty koṭis of devas, humans, asuras, and others to maturity, causing them all to fully accomplish the three vehicles.

Śāriputra! Among those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, there was no interval; within the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratnagarbha, they attained inconceivable, supreme, and most excellent perfection of learning.
Upon passing away from that life, he immediately attained rebirth within the royal lineage of the world-system of the Tathāgata Padmottara.
Those whom he had previously taught—sixty koṭis of devas, humans, asuras, and others—all were born together with him there as his retinue.
Furthermore, at that time, a Buddha appeared in the world, named Uttaramatīśvara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
That Buddha’s lifespan was eighty koṭis of years, and the lifespan of the people in that land was likewise equal.
That Buddha had a great assembly of eighty koṭis of śrāvakas gathered together, all of whom were arhats.
Each individual śrāvaka likewise had a great assembly of eighty koṭis of śrāvakas, all of whom were pure mahā-arhats.
Furthermore, at that time, there was a prince named King Vīryadatta, who was accomplished in extensive learning and possessed clear,

penetrating wisdom. Śāriputra, at that time, the prince, together with his own retinue of eight hundred million, went simultaneously to the place where the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Uttaramati resided.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the World-Honored One, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata Uttara-caryā, knowing the boy’s past causes and conditions and the thoughts in his mind, preached the Dharma for him.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra, saying:

“When the youth King Vīrabhadra heard of such practices cultivated in accordance with his former lives, he was filled with great joy. Together with eighty koṭis of his own retinue, he conceived pure faith, abandoned the household life for the homeless one, assumed the appearance of a bhikṣu, received full ordination, and throughout the rest of his life constantly practiced the holy life to seek the path to enlightenment.”
At that time, the Tathāgata Most Supreme Conduct addressed the great assembly:
"This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva King Receiving Valor, after my parinirvāṇa, shall next become a Buddha appearing in the world, named Tathāgata Great Diligence, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."

After that Tathāgata of Supreme Conduct has entered parinirvāṇa, having made offerings to all his relics and upheld the True Dharma, one shall subsequently attain the fruit of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Śāriputra! The lifespan of that Tathāgata Mahāvīrya is half an eon.
There is an immeasurable assembly of great śrāvakas, numbering twenty nayutas each, all of whom are pure great arhats, who have gathered together.
Śāriputra!

When this non-retrogressive bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of vigor, having heard the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, he sequentially upholds, recites, and reads it, and explains it to others, until he is born within that world-system of the Tathāgata Mahāvīrya.

Śāriputra! If a son of good family or a daughter of good family abides in the Mahāyāna, they will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. While practicing with non-retrogressive diligence, they shall definitively hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and even explain it extensively for others.
Why is this? Śāriputra,
these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to seek the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka in this way, practicing the conduct of non-retrogressive diligence.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of diligence.
Chapter Ten: The Perfection of Meditative Concentration, Part One. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice and advance in the bodhisattva’s dhyāna-pāramitā?

Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should first distance himself from the faults of defiled desire and all unwholesome dharmas; by means of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), he gives rise to joy and bliss—this is called entering and understanding the practice of the first dhyāna.

Śāriputra! Next, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should distance himself from applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and internally induce a state of mental one-pointedness that is pure and immaculate; by means of that meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he gives rise to joy and bliss. This is called entering and understanding the practice of the second dhyāna.

Śāriputra! Next, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should abandon craving and practice mindfulness with clear comprehension (*smṛti-samprajanya*). Although he experiences only sublime pleasant sensations, even as his body is clearly comprehending, he observes the state of equanimity, mindfulness, and the departure from joy—just as those noble ones do—thereby practicing the sublime pleasure. This is called entering and understanding the practice of the third dhyāna concentration.

Śāriputra! Next, the bodhisattva mahāsattva should first sever pleasure, pain, and the afflictions of equanimity; being without pain or pleasure, with equanimity and mindfulness purified, this is called entering and understanding the practice of the fourth dhyāna.

He attains, as it truly is, a perfectly pure, singular, and unmixed state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita-citta*), free from all other factors and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Without departing from this concentration, he is able to perform the activities of that dhyāna, and furthermore, he brings to perfection the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and their associated cognitive activities.
What are called the five kinds of supernormal powers?

First, the divine eye; second, the divine ear; third, knowledge of others' minds; fourth, recollection of past lives; and fifth, the power of miraculous transformations. These are what are called the five kinds of supernormal powers.
Furthermore, how does a bodhisattva fulfill the supreme practice of the supernormal knowledge of the divine eye, up to the supernormal knowledge of the power of psychic travel? Śāriputra!

This Bodhisattva dwells in accordance with reality within a state of meditative equipoise that is perfectly pure, singular and unmixed, free from secondary afflictions, and characterized by a mind devoid of desire for sentient beings; yet, they are able to initiate supernormal powers such as the power of the psychic bases. This is called the "activity of knowledge regarding supernormal powers."

Furthermore, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he is able to observe the various signs of sentient beings—such as their initial birth, decline, and death, as well as their beauty or ugliness—and their rebirths in happy or miserable realms, whether superior or inferior. He even knows the distinctions in the karmic actions of sentient beings: those who are fully possessed of evil conduct of body, speech, and mind; who give rise to wrong views and slander the noble ones; and who further accumulate the causes of karma based on wrong views, such that when their bodies perish and their lives end, they fall into the miserable realms of the hells (*naraka*).

Furthermore, he knows that those sentient beings possess virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind; they give rise to right view and praise the noble ones, and by accumulating the karmic causes of right view, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they are reborn in a happy destination or the celestial realms.
Śāriputra! With the pure divine eye, which surpasses that of humans, he is able to fully know all sentient beings who have accumulated evil karma. Śāriputra!

This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s purified divine eye is the most excellent among all sentient beings; its perception of forms and characteristics is clear and entirely without obstruction. It surpasses that of all devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, śaikṣas, aśaikṣas, great arhats, and the assembly of pratyekabuddhas; it is supreme, most excellent, most extremely clear, and unsurpassed.
Furthermore, this divine eye is the most supreme among all paths of renunciation.

Possessing such a divine eye, Bodhisattvas perceive all sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions—whether coarse or subtle, superior or inferior, distant or near—and through this divine eye, they understand all material forms without any obstruction.

Furthermore, with this divine eye, one sees as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven; excluding the formless realm, one can fully comprehend all the infinite sentient beings in the worlds of the ten directions—whether they are born or pass away—as well as their karmic causes and all causal faculties, whether they increase or decrease, or whether they are superior or inferior.
Furthermore, one sees all the meritorious adornments of the Buddha-fields throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
One also fully understands the pure aggregate of ethical discipline, its stable abiding, and its attainment of sublime and wondrous fruits of retribution.

Furthermore, that purified divine eye surpasses that of humans; all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, and the assembly of Bodhisattvas see it all—including the correct mindfulness and correct awareness of those noble beings, their mastery of spheres of experience, their dignified deportment and path of practice, as well as their realization of the Dharma of liberation, their attainment of the gates of *dhāraṇī*, and their abiding in wisdom and skillful means, whereby they are able to enter into and understand all perfections.

That eye is unimpeded, for it does not see any forms; that eye is unattached, for it is unstained by any forms. That eye is liberated, meaning it is free from all views; that eye is pure, its very essence being luminous and clean. The eye has no dependence, being detached from all objective spheres; the eye has nothing to grasp, being free from all afflictions. The eye has no obscuration, being free from all doubt and delusion; the eye does not give rise to discursive thought, being free from obstructive phenomena. The eye attains radiance, illuminating all dharmas; the eye follows wisdom, remaining beyond the sphere of consciousness. That eye is unattached, being free from those things difficult to subdue, as well as from all afflictions such as ignorance and darkness.
The eye can discern the illusory transformations of all sense faculties; furthermore, its visual characteristics are invincible, and it gazes upon all sentient beings with equanimity.
That eye is pure, free from discursive thought, and its stainless nature is luminously radiant.

Furthermore, that divine eye manifests before him according to his mental intention and matures into the Buddha-eye; this eye is free from greed and hatred, transcending all opposition and conformity.
Moreover, that divine eye accords with reality in its practice of the methods for the sphere of meaning, and it abides in great compassion toward sentient beings.

Furthermore, that divine eye gives to all who come seeking alms without exception; it feels no anger even upon seeing those who have broken the precepts; it constantly protects those who have fallen away; it constantly exerts and encourages those who are indolent; for those who are distracted, it manifests the factors of meditative concentration; for those with impaired wisdom, it reveals the eye of right wisdom; for those on false paths, it awakens them to the true path; and for those of inferior resolve, it guides them toward the supreme knowledge and vision of the Buddha.

Furthermore, that divine eye, regarding the supreme supernormal power of the knowledge of all modes of knowledge, becomes decisively manifest through one-pointed concentration on the path to enlightenment. Śāriputra!
This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s ability to fulfill the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-abhijñā*) and the activities of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

what is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s attainment of the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*) and the fulfillment of the activities of wisdom regarding the supreme practice of supernormal powers?

Śāriputra! This bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the purified divine ear that transcends that of humans; he is able to hear the sounds of humans and non-humans throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions—namely, the sounds of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and other humans and non-humans; the sounds of noble beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas. This is called the purified divine ear of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Furthermore, he hears the sounds of all sinful karmas: the sounds of the hells, the sounds of the animal realm, and the sounds of the realm of Yama; even down to the subtlest sounds of butterflies, bees, scorpions, mosquitoes, gnats, and the like; as well as all vocal karma produced by sentient beings and the wholesome or unwholesome mental activities directed toward objects—all these he fully knows.
He fully understands the roots of wholesome and unwholesome vocal karma that are produced, as well as their causes and effects.

He understands that when vocal karma is characterized by the defilement of craving, it is expressed through greed; when vocal karma is characterized by malice, it is expressed through harsh abuse; and furthermore, he understands that vocal karma characterized by delusion is likewise expressed through both greed and malice, as well as through harsh abuse.

If verbal karma is manifested solely by abusive speech, then anger follows that manifestation of abusive speech; and if that verbal karma is also manifested by the darkness of delusion, one can fully comprehend it as being accompanied by delusion.

Furthermore, through the wisdom of the supernormal power of the divine ear, one understands with reality the skillful means for generating [insight], thereby subduing the karma of speech and conforming to purity.
By being able to counteract and purify the karma of speech, one is likewise able to counteract all greed, hatred, and delusion, causing them all to become pure.
Furthermore, with that divine ear, they hear the voices of both the noble ones and those who are not noble.
Having heard them thus, they do not give rise to attachment or dwelling upon the voices of the noble ones, nor do they harbor hostility toward or seek to refute the voices of those who are not noble.
Furthermore, one attains great loving-kindness toward the voices of noble beings and arouses great compassion toward the voices of those who are not noble.
Regarding all sounds, which have no beginning or end, one understands them as they truly are through definitive wisdom.
Furthermore, with that divine ear, they hear the sublime Dharma taught by all those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the entirety of the worlds in the ten directions without exception.
Having heard it, they keep in mind the faculties of those to be converted; they give rise to no delusion or darkness, but rather embrace all beings, never losing mindfulness.
Just as those sentient beings enter into understanding according to their respective faculties, they realize that all phenomena are of a single equal flavor.
Furthermore, having heard the Dharma taught by one Buddha or two Buddhas, they do not create mutually obstructive distinctions of phenomena.
The Sutra on the True Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Thirty-one.
The Sutra on the True Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Thirty-two.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperial Preceptor for the Propagation of the Sanskrit Canon, Silver Light Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, Śramaṇa Subject Fahu, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Ten, Part Two: The Perfection of Dhyāna. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have explained those practices of upholding [the Dharma] in the past; by virtue of hearing their voices through these present roots of goodness, one obtains what was taught during both appropriate and inappropriate times—whether during a formal assembly, at the time of preaching the Dharma, or when teaching outside of such times—and having heard it, one is able to explain it through individual analytical practice.

Furthermore, when preaching the Dharma, whether during a formal assembly or for a single bhikṣu, he preaches the Dharma and provides authentic prophetic declarations for them; yet he does not speak that which would cause harm to others, nor does he provide prophetic declarations that are not in accordance with reality. Instead, he selects the relevant principles and meanings, employing skillful means to sustain and guide others, and preaches to them with a mind that is pure and stainless.
If one hears with certainty sounds such as those resembling forms and gives rise to joy, then for the sake of causing that hearing of sounds resembling forms and so forth, there is certain joy.
Furthermore, when preaching the Dharma in the midst of a multitude, one empowers that sound with the divine ear-consciousness so that all sentient beings may understand it;
thus, those sentient beings who hear this Dharma may indeed comprehend it.

Furthermore, if sentient beings hear this Dharma or have not yet fully understood it, they attain the purity of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) in that regard; consequently, their ear-realm (śrotradhātu) and wisdom-realm (jñānadhātu) also attain purity.
Since my auditory faculty has attained purity, these sentient beings likewise attain purity, and they achieve skillful liberation within that auditory faculty.

According to the meanings of the words and phrases as they are spoken, and through the eloquent expressions of all sentient beings, I cause the beings of the five destinies who hear the sound of the Dharma to fully awaken and enter into it.
Furthermore, within this divine ear-element, they achieve the divine ear of a Tathāgata, and therein their mind remains free from confusion.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s perfection of the wisdom-action of the supernormal power of the divine ear.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva fulfill the supernormal knowledge of others' minds and the cognitive activity of its correct practice?
Śāriputra, [it is as follows:]..."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva can fully comprehend the minds of all sentient beings throughout all worlds in the ten directions without exception, reaching back to their past limits, as well as comprehending their present minds.
Furthermore, he is able to fully comprehend the various mental states of sentient beings in the past, whether their minds were coarse or subtle, and the causes thereof:
whether this sentient being’s cause for the highest state of mind, or this sentient being’s cause for a middling state of mind, or this sentient being’s cause for the lowest state of mind;

and whether this sentient being’s faculty is associated with generosity, this sentient being’s faculty is associated with ethical discipline, this sentient being’s faculty is associated with patience, this sentient being’s faculty is associated with diligence, this sentient being’s faculty is associated with meditative concentration, or this sentient being’s faculty is associated with supreme wisdom.

Furthermore, the faculties of these sentient beings have great loving-kindness as their cause; the faculties of these sentient beings have great compassion as their cause; the faculties of these sentient beings have great sympathetic joy as their cause; the faculties of these sentient beings have great equanimity as their cause.

Furthermore, the faculties of these sentient beings have the Great Vehicle as their cause; the faculties of these sentient beings have the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle as their cause; the faculties of these sentient beings have the Śrāvaka Vehicle as their cause.
Moreover, these sentient beings are fully endowed with the power of all causes of virtue, and they are fully endowed with the power of all conditions of virtue.

Furthermore, if a sentient being possesses the power of unwholesome causes and conditions, that very being will, through the correspondence with the power of those causes and conditions, be born into an inferior lineage.

Furthermore, if a sentient being is fully endowed with the power of virtuous causes and conditions, that very being, through the correspondence of those causes and conditions, will be born into a noble lineage.

Furthermore, there may be sentient beings whose mental states are pure but whose craftsmanship is not; or there may be sentient beings whose craftsmanship is pure but whose mental states are not; or there may be sentient beings whose craftsmanship is pure and whose mental states are also pure; or there may be sentient beings whose mental states are not pure and whose craftsmanship is also not pure.
"Śāriputra!
These sentient beings possess the wisdom of their past faculties, causes, mental activities, and conduct, which corresponds exactly to my wisdom for teaching the Dharma accordingly.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s power of knowing the minds of others."
Furthermore, through the power of knowing the minds of others, he understands that this sentient being practices the cause of giving and will obtain the fruit of giving in a future life;
likewise, this sentient being practices the cause of pure ethical discipline and will obtain the fruit of pure ethical discipline in a future life.
Furthermore, this sentient being, by practicing the cause of patience, will obtain the fruit of patience in future lives.
Moreover, this sentient being, by practicing the cause of diligence, will obtain the fruit of diligence in future lives.
Furthermore, these sentient beings, by practicing the cause of meditative concentration, will attain the fruit of meditative concentration in future lives.
Moreover, these sentient beings, by practicing the cause of superior wisdom, will attain the fruit of superior wisdom in future lives.
Furthermore, these sentient beings practice the causes for the Great Vehicle and will attain the fruits of the Great Vehicle in future lives.
Moreover, these sentient beings practice the causes for the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle and will attain the fruits of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle in future lives.
Furthermore, this sentient being practices the causes for a śrāvaka and will attain the fruit of a śrāvaka in a future life.
Moreover, this sentient being practices the causes for the mundane world and will attain the mundane fruit in a future life.

Śāriputra! Whether by these causes and conditions or those causes and conditions, one should truly understand that in future ages these sentient beings will possess such faculties; thus, one should be able to bring those sentient beings to maturity without becoming weary, even understanding the root of their minds through wisdom, and preaching this True Dharma to those who are proper vessels for it.
Furthermore, what is gained from preaching the Dharma?
It is to ensure that no other dharmas or other karmic actions are performed.
If sentient beings, within the present life, engage in extensive investigation and reflection regarding the practice of all dharmas, they shall know them all as they truly are.
Furthermore, when his mind is attached to greed, he knows that mind of attachment to greed as it truly is;
when his mind is free from greed, he also knows that mind free from greed as it truly is.
When he is possessed of a mind of hatred, he knows as it truly is that he is possessed of a mind of hatred.
When he is free from a mind of hatred, he also knows as it truly is that he is free from a mind of hatred.
When he is possessed of a mind of delusion, he knows as it truly is that he is possessed of a mind of delusion.
When he is free from a deluded mind, he knows that he is free from a deluded mind as it truly is.

Whether it concerns the defilements or the obstructed minds of these or those sentient beings, he is able to understand them all as they truly are; having understood them as they truly are, he teaches the Dharma for the sake of their deliverance from afflictions.

Furthermore, when he goes among the assembly and observes in this way—having thoroughly examined all those present in the gathering, whether here or there—he then preaches the Dharma to all sentient beings.

Śāriputra! This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva thoroughly understands the wisdom regarding the faculties and natures of these sentient beings throughout their past and future limits; yet his own mind abides in nothing, nor does it abide in the minds of others.

Why is this? Because this bodhisattva mahāsattva, through the understanding of wisdom, has a mind that abides nowhere; through the understanding of mindfulness, has a mind that abides nowhere; through the understanding of insight, has a mind that abides nowhere; through the understanding of inclination, has a mind that abides nowhere; through the understanding of superior wisdom, has a mind that abides nowhere; through the understanding of awakening, has a mind that abides nowhere. Having severed habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), all latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and the harsh afflictions, being stainless, radiant, and free from all faults, he clearly understands all phenomena and is profoundly able to penetrate the differences in the mental activities of all sentient beings, yet his mind abides nowhere.

Śāriputra, to thus understand the mental states of sentient beings through such modes of activity—this is called the perfection of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s knowledge and activity of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

what is meant by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*) and the perfection of the cognitive activity of its correct practice?
Śāriputra, [it is as follows:]..."

In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva possesses the supernormal power of recollecting past lives in all its infinite varieties regarding all sentient beings in all worlds throughout the ten directions without exception.

Whether for one day, two days, three, four, or five days; or ten, twenty, up to fifty days; or for a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, or immeasurable hundreds of thousands of births; even for a hundred eons of formation and destruction, a thousand eons of formation and destruction, a hundred thousand eons of formation and destruction, or immeasurable hundreds of thousands of eons of formation and destruction—he fully knows all sentient beings of those past times: their names, their clans, their lineages, their physical appearances, their forms, their dwellings, their food and drink, their duration of life, their experiences of suffering and pleasure, their various births and deaths, and the span of their lifetimes, as well as their passing from that life and being reborn here.
Furthermore, one knows that for oneself and for all sentient beings, this recollection of past lives is not of only one kind.
Regarding the prior limit of oneself and the prior limit of other persons (*pudgala*), this recollection of past lives is not of only one kind.

Furthermore, through the power of mindfulness of one’s own past roots of goodness and the power of mindfulness of the past roots of goodness of others; and through the maturation of one’s own roots of goodness for the sake of awakening, causing other sentient beings to mind those roots of goodness and resolve upon the mind of awakening; and furthermore, because all causes of past suffering and pleasure are in accordance with impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so forth—since they accord with impermanence, suffering, non-self, and so forth—one does not delight in physical forms, does not delight in enjoyments, does not delight in retinues, does not delight in wealth and abundance, does not delight in being a Wheel-Turning Sage King, does not delight in being Śakra, Lord of Devas, does not delight in being Mahābrahmā, and does not delight in being a World-Protecting Heavenly King. One finds no love or delight in sovereign power over any place of birth, nor in any sensual pleasures.
He reflects correctly:
"In this state, one does not undergo saṃsāra for the sake of maturing sentient beings.

Realizing that it is merely the accumulation of past afflictive actions—conforming to impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and so forth—he feels intense remorse and gives rise to great renunciation.
Regarding all unwholesome karmas of the present, even unto the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), he develops a sense of revulsion and refrains from committing them again.

He causes his past roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) to become vast and fully matured in the root of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Furthermore, he is able to accumulate present roots of goodness, eliminate all perilous and difficult circumstances, and bring to maturity the seeds of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. Through the power of right mindfulness as a condition, he ensures that these continue without interruption, maturing the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Furthermore, because this right mindfulness is stabilized by self-mastery and the empowerment of the dharmadhātu, it remains unshakable and thus free from disturbance; likewise, the karma of matured meditative concentration is also free from affliction.
Regarding śamatha, through self-mastery the mind is free from confusion, and one thereby embraces vipaśyanā.
Because of the lack of timidity in direct perceptual wisdom (*pratyakṣajñāna*) and because of the lack of forgetfulness due to correct mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*), one experiences great bliss.
The accumulation of all conditioned formations is not realized through another; because of this accumulation of formations, one proceeds toward the further shore and is able to reach it entirely.

Because of this accumulation of formations, through the power of the object of right mindfulness, there is no loss or forgetfulness regarding the past or the present. This is called the perfection of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s supernormal knowledge of the recollection of former abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-karma*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva achieve perfection in the supernormal power of the base of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi*) and the wisdom-action of its correct practice?
Śāriputra, [it is as follows:]..."

This bodhisattva mahāsattva, having severed all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), is able to fully cultivate the meditative concentration of the basis of psychic power of desire; having severed all conditioned formations, he fully cultivates the meditative concentration of the basis of psychic power of diligence; having severed all conditioned formations, he fully cultivates the meditative concentration of the basis of psychic power of mind; and having severed all conditioned formations, he fully cultivates the meditative concentration of the basis of psychic power of investigation.
Because by means of desire, effort, mind, and investigation, one gathers and masters all phenomena, thereby being able to cultivate them so as to achieve liberation.

Furthermore, through the repeated cultivation of these four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), one attains the supernormal power of the miraculous movement (*ṛddhividhi*) right before one's eyes and gains the enjoyment of those manifold kinds of supernatural transformations.
Furthermore, this miraculous power constantly observes all sentient beings, and each individual miracle is capable of taming every sentient being.
Moreover, this miraculous power can universally manifest itself—whether as a body, as power, or through empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Furthermore, each and every one of those bodily forms is able to go forth and subdue all classes of sentient beings.

Moreover, each and every one of those bodily forms can further manifest as the body of a Buddha, or the body of a Pratyekabuddha, or the body of a Śrāvaka, or the body of Śakra-devendra, or the body of Mahābrahmā, or the body of a Lokapāla, or the body of a Cakravartin King.
Furthermore, each and every manifested physical form further manifests such forms as are able to go forth and subdue all sentient beings, as well as all stubborn classes of animals.
Furthermore, those manifested physical forms preach the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings.

Moreover, they can manifest such power as to universally subdue the most intense hatred and pride of all sentient beings—namely, the strength of a great athlete, up to the strength of four parts of Nārāyaṇa, up to half a Nārāyaṇa, up to a full Nārāyaṇa, and even such powers as these:

lifting Mount Sumeru, sixty hundred thousand *yojanas* high, with only two fingers, and hurling that mountain eighty-four thousand *yojanas* away; just as one might pick up a single *āmra* fruit and cast it from here to another world-system, yet the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s power of supernormal knowledge (*ṛddhividhi*) involves no movement at all.

Furthermore, one can take this vast trichiliocosm, from the bottom of the water realm up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, place all sentient beings within it upon the palm of one's hand, and remain there for the duration of kalpas, while universally manifesting all paths of practice.

Furthermore, for the sake of those sentient beings who are characterized by pride, overweening pride, and extremely heavy anger, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes the power and capability to subdue such pride, overweening pride, anger, and so forth, and then teaches the Dharma to them.
Furthermore, by relying on those bases of supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*), one attains the wisdom of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
Within that wisdom of empowerment, one immediately attains such methods of empowerment as these:
one may empower the great ocean so that it becomes the size of a cow’s footprint, and likewise empower a cow’s footprint so that it becomes the size of the great ocean;
Furthermore, at times he may empower a mass of fire to become a mass of water, and again empower a mass of water to become a mass of fire.
In short, he empowers all phenomena—whether superior, middling, or inferior—to mutually transform into one another.

They shall likewise attain such accomplishments that no one among the gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas who comes before them in this world will be able to shake, transform, or cause their appearance and disappearance.
Furthermore, in this world, there is no one who shares this empowerment method except for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who alone possesses it.

Moreover, through the power of the conditions of skillful empowerment, he extensively expounds the sublime Dharma to those sentient beings characterized by pride, arrogance, and extreme wrath, causing them to attain the utmost joy.

Furthermore, those who cultivate the bases of supernormal power (ṛddhipāda) do not fall into or perish within the realm of Māra, nor among the retinues of celestial Māras or the various afflictions (kleśa); they transcend them with mastery and are able to enter into and understand the realm of the Buddha.
Toward all sentient beings, he does not inflict even the slightest harm, but remains in accord with and conforms to all roots of virtue.
This is called the perfection of the wisdom-action of the supernormal power of the divine realm for a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
“Śāriputra! Furthermore, what is called the supernormal powers (abhijñā) of a bodhisattva mahāsattva?
And what is called wisdom (jñāna)?”
To correctly observe the characteristics of forms with that divine eye is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
That knowledge of illusory phenomena which does not engage in correct practice is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one truly hears [the Dharma] regarding all sentient beings, this is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
However, if neither [the self nor] past faults can be apprehended therein, this is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If one thoroughly understands all mental activities, this is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
To maintain correct practice without ceasing the wisdom that knows the cessation of the mind, this is called knowledge (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
To recollect the past limit without obstruction is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
If one’s knowledge regarding the three periods of time is entirely without obstruction, this is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, to travel at will to all buddha-fields is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
To possess unimpeded wisdom regarding the fields of empty space is called knowledge (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
To establish the stages of phenomena is called supernormal power (abhijñā).
To investigate phenomena is called wisdom (jñāna).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Skillfully guiding and transforming all worldly beings is called supernormal power (abhijñā).
Being entirely free from attachment to all worldly things is called wisdom (jñāna).
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
To transcend all Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
