To transcend all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
What has been thus described is called the perfection of the activity of supernormal knowledge.
Moreover, Śāriputra!"

One should know that all the distractions of the afflictions, as well as the mental states and sustaining wisdom of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ practice of meditative concentration, up to and including the defiled minds and distractions of all sentient beings, as well as the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas’ practice of meditative concentration and so forth, are to be understood as being accumulated.
Śāriputra! This Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells having universally accumulated [these qualities]; this is called *samāhita*.
Furthermore, all these sentient beings are also called *samāhita*.
The mind is always equanimous; this is called samāhita.
The mental faculty is always equanimous; this is called samāhita.
Skillful equanimity is called samāhita.
When the mind is profoundly deep and equanimous, this is called samāhita.
Equanimity in giving is called samāhita.
Equanimity in maintaining the precepts is called samāhita.
Equanimity in patience is called samāhita;
equanimity in diligence is called samāhita;
equanimity in meditative concentration is called samāhita.
The equality of supreme wisdom is called *samāhita*.
The equality of all phenomena is called *samāhita*.

If one attains equality regarding all phenomena, that is the equality of all sentient beings and the equality of all enlightenment; to enter into and understand this universally is what is termed *samāpatti*.
Furthermore, if one universally enters into and understands all phenomena as being like space and so forth, this is called *samāpatti*.

Furthermore, if one universally and equanimously enters into and understands the signless (*animitta*), the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and the practice of non-accumulation (*anabhisaṃskāra*), this is called *samāpatti*.
Furthermore, if one universally enters into and understands the sounds of all phenomena, this is called *samāpatti*.

Moreover, regarding all circumstances—whether beneficial or non-beneficial—if the mind is as even as the earth, as even as water, as even as fire, as even as wind, and as even as space; if it dwells well, being high above agitation and free from dullness below; and if it remains unshakable throughout all paths of practice, this is called *samāhita*.
To be without conceptual differentiation regarding the very nature of one's conduct on the path is called *samāpatti*.

Although one’s speech may be abundant, it is free from verbal faults; it is neither high nor low and is without agitation. When one accords with, follows, and accomplishes the meanings and principles of all worldly phenomena at their proper times, yet remains able to transcend the eight worldly concerns, has no attachment whatsoever to any afflictions, and stays far removed from the realms of clamor, discursive thought, and investigation—such practice of the Dharma is called *samādhi*.
Furthermore, he is able to manifest all the crafts and activities of the world, yet he does not abandon their specific characteristics.

However, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters into and understands the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) with equanimity, while further giving rise to wisdom and skillful means (*upāya*). He is not bound by the conditions of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), but observes sentient beings with equanimity and enters into understanding through skillful means such as tranquility and supreme tranquility; this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Causing the Buddha’s wisdom not to manifest before one is called skillful means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, if one enters into the understanding of all phenomena with equanimity and is not bound by them, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, that all phenomena are entirely without grasping or abandoning is called skillful means (*upāya*).
That there is no conceptualization or discursive thought regarding that dharmadhātu is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
If one enters into the realization of the equality of the Buddha-body without giving rise to a manifest realization, this is called skillful means.
To maintain mindfulness of that Dharma-body without dwelling anywhere is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
To enter into and understand the equality of the characteristics of the Buddha’s voice, and to fully comprehend the wondrous Brahma-sound, is skillful means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, to contemplate that dharmas are ineffable is wisdom.
Moreover, to enter into and understand equality at the moment of the vajra-mind, and to be able to abide therein most excellently, is skillful means.
To maintain right mindfulness therein without distraction is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, to enter into and understand that former vows with equanimity, thereby being able to bring sentient beings to maturity and abiding in the most supreme state, is skillful means (*upāya*).
To contemplate that all sentient beings lack a real self is wisdom.
To contemplate those roots of goodness as being realized yet without anything realized is skillful means.
Furthermore, to contemplate that they are rootless and free from dwelling or attachment is wisdom.
Furthermore, to enter into and understand the equality of buddha-fields so that they manifest as pure is skillful means;
to contemplate those lands as being equal to space is wisdom.
Furthermore, to mindfully contemplate entering into and realizing the equality of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), thereby manifesting its adornments, is skillful means.
Furthermore, to mindfully contemplate that cessation or all defiled phenomena is wisdom.
If one enters into and understands the turning of the wheel of Dharma with equanimity, yet is able to respond universally to the capacities and conditions of beings, this is skillful means.
Furthermore, to be mindful that in that turning there is nothing turned is wisdom.
To enter into and understand the equality of all practices leading to enlightenment, and to be able to manifest their relinquishment, is skillful means.

Furthermore, to be mindful that those [practices] are neither associated with nor accompanied by any secondary afflictions among all phenomena; to possess the sublime bliss of the Tathāgata’s wisdom and meditative concentration, free from all feverish distress; and to fully comprehend and subdue all objective referents, whether characterized by signs or signless—this is skillful means.

All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in a state that is neither fixed nor non-fixed; because they have skillfully attained renunciation and are thus correspondingly associated with it, this is their wisdom.

Furthermore, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the inexhaustible perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*), such that no demonic activities can find an opportunity against them, and they achieve stable abiding as a vessel for the teachings of all Buddhas.
Śāriputra! Through the wisdom and skillful means thus described, those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are able to transcend the perfection of meditative concentration.
The Buddha-spoken Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra, Volume Thirty-two.
The Buddha-spoken Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Sūtra, Volume Thirty-three.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others—Śramaṇas of the Imperial Court, recipients of the purple robe, Grand Masters of the Transmission of Sanskrit, and Silver Light Luoguo Dafu, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments—by Imperial Decree. Chapter Ten, Part Three: The Perfection of Dhyāna. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain non-retrogressive supernormal powers; whether through mental intention or through physical action, all are the playful exercises of their supernormal powers.
Furthermore, he dwells extensively in various places, manifesting all manner of activities.
Whatever he does, his power of supernatural knowledges and wisdom is supreme in the world.

Although his deeds possess all the requisite marks, he is skillfully able to discern them and further realizes through direct experience the foremost dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The supernormal powers of a bodhisattva manifest the characteristic of inexhaustibility, like space pervading all places.

The supernormal powers of a bodhisattva manifest all appearances, whether material or immaterial, and are further able to accord with and enter all sounds, yet they remain equal regarding sounds from the past limit.

The bodhisattva’s supernormal powers observe the mental activities of all sentient beings; their essential nature manifests in accordance with conditions, and throughout all kalpas, it follows their thoughts without interruption from the past limit to the future limit.
Everything consists solely of the manifestation of miraculous transformations; they appear decisively before one without any distinct characteristics.

The bodhisattva’s supernormal powers reach the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*); having observed the temporal divisions, there is no transgression of them. These powers surpass the mundane world and provide definitive discernment of all phenomena, such that they are difficult for any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha to fathom.

The meaning of the bodhisattva’s supernormal powers is profoundly deep; they terrify and destroy the various māras, subjugate non-Buddhists, and are able to maintain all Buddha-dharmas within the site of enlightenment, aspiring to seek perfect awakening.

Turning the wheel of the true Dharma according to their respective dispositions, they skillfully discipline all sentient beings until they reach the stage of empowerment (abhiṣeka), attaining mastery over the Dharma.
"Śāriputra!..."

This irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, in all his activities, is entirely free from conceit; his mind is pure, perfectly and rightly disciplined, radiant, and autonomous. Having abandoned all defiled desires and secondary afflictions, he is subtle and tranquil, and he brings all wholesome karma to full accomplishment.

One gives rise to right reflection regarding meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and samāpattis; thus, within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), there is no bondage whatsoever. Why is this so?

This means that they are completely liberated from the bonds of the afflictions of birth and karma, as well as from all inverted attachments; therefore, they are entirely without fetters within saṃsāra, yet they do not destroy the Mahāyāna and fully realize all Buddha-dharmas.
Yet that Buddha-dharma, though sought thoroughly throughout the ten directions, is ultimately unattainable.
Furthermore, all dharmas accord with the Buddha-dharma; therefore, the Buddha-dharma is itself all dharmas.

If all phenomena are sought according to reality, they cannot be found; whether within the path of calculation or that which is beyond calculation, one transcends them equally, without even the slightest remainder.

This teaching states that there is neither non-existence nor the absence of non-existence; if one can thoroughly understand both existence and non-existence, one will consequently have no attachment whatsoever to them.
Furthermore, the meaning of all phenomena is not something to be clung to; if one clings to such meanings, it does not constitute the great benefit of the Dharma.
Furthermore, if one abides in neither the meaningful nor the meaningless, even when perceiving the meaningful, one’s wisdom remains unimpeded.

If wisdom is unimpeded, there is no conceptual construction (*parikalpa*). If there is no conceptual construction, there is no opposition (*pratigha*). If there is no opposition, there is no abiding. If there is no abiding, there is no interruption. If there is no interruption, there is no vain activity. If there is no vain activity, there is no delusion. If there is no delusion, there is no "I" or "mine. If there is no "I" or "mine," there is no contention. To be without contention is the Dharma of a śramaṇa.
If being free from contentious debate is the dharma of a śramaṇa, then it is like space and like a level palm.
If it is likened to space and like a level palm, then one does not fall into the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
If one does not fall into any state whatsoever, then there is no shape-color (*saṃsthāna-rūpa*), no manifest-color (*varṇa-rūpa*), and no distinct states (*avasthā*).
If there is no shape-color, no manifest-color, and no distinct states, then one thus accords with awakening.
If one can thus awaken in accordance with reality, then one awakens in that very manner.
How, then, are this awakening in accordance with reality and that which is awakened to explained?
That is to say, if one realizes that those infinitesimal dharmas are all unapprehendable, this is called "conformity with awakening and that which is awakened to.
One should enter into and understand this with equanimity; thus, one will be able to accomplish the marvelous qualities of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
What is the marvelous quality of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva?
It is said: in loving-kindness there is no self; in compassion there is no sentient being; in sympathetic joy there is no life-principle;
in equanimity there is no person (*pudgala*). In giving, there is no mind of regret; in maintaining ethical discipline, there arises a mind of tranquility.
Through patience, one gives rise to that inexhaustible mind; through diligence, one gives rise to that supreme mind; through meditative concentration, one leaves behind that distracted mind;
through transcendent wisdom, one is free from that mind of conceptual proliferation; through the foundations of mindfulness, one is free from the mental attention of mindfulness-objects;
through the right efforts, one follows that mind of arising and ceasing; through the bases of psychic power, one leaves behind that mind of frivolous play; and regarding faith and diligence—
In mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom, one gives rise to the mind that enters into understanding through unimpeded spontaneity and equanimity;
in the five faculties and five powers, one gives rise to the mind that cannot be damaged or subdued; in the seven factors of enlightenment, one gives rise to the mind that discerns bodhi;
in the eightfold noble path, one gives rise to the mind of correct understanding through investigation; and in śamatha, one gives rise to...
With that mind of equanimity, he gives rise to the mind of wondrous, all-pervading knowledge that observes the Noble Truths through *vipaśyanā*;
he matures sentient beings by giving rise to that originally pure mind; he embraces the True Dharma within that *dharmadhātu* with a mind free from confusion;
he gives rise to the mind of non-apprehension regarding the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and regarding non-retrogression...
Generating a mind free from transition while turning the earth; generating a signless mind regarding the signs obtained;
generating a mind that accords with the three realms while adorning the site of enlightenment; generating a mind that embraces sentient beings while subduing the hosts of Māras;
generating a mind that accords with awakening regarding the self-nature of all phenomena; and regarding the turning of the wheel of Dharma...

One gives rise to that mind which does not turn toward anything; regarding great nirvāṇa, one gives rise to that mind which accords with the equality of the intrinsic nature of saṃsāra as it manifests. Śāriputra!
What has been thus described constitutes the marvelous quality that a bodhisattva mahāsattva achieves regarding both the awakening that accords with reality and that which is awakened to.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what is meditative concentration?

It means that bodhisattvas have no attachment to those meditative concentrations; they are able to bring the samādhi of the Tathāgata to perfection, and moreover, they do not delight in the flavor of the joy of meditation."

Although these bodhisattvas experience physical well-being, they remain free from attachment; furthermore, while constantly delighting in meditative concentration, they always cherish great compassion. For these reasons, they allow themselves to remain amidst the defilements of the afflictions.
Furthermore, by not regressing from meditative concentration and equipoise, one becomes weary of and detached from the desire realm due to these conditions.
Moreover, by cultivating the activities of supernormal powers within meditative concentration, one comes to thoroughly know the mental activities of all sentient beings due to these conditions.
Furthermore, by penetrating the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) within meditative concentration, one attains mastery over the mind through these conditions.
Moreover, by attaining the knowledge of meditative equipoise (*samāpatti-jñāna*) within meditative concentration, one pervades all realms of form and formlessness through these conditions.
Furthermore, they attain the ultimate tranquility of meditative concentration; for this reason, they seek to increase their mastery in the *samāpattis* of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
Moreover, they remain undisturbed within meditative concentration; for this reason, they abide in the most ultimate state.
Furthermore, they constantly practice the remedies within meditative concentration; for this reason, they do not abide in the habitual tendencies of that continuity.
Moreover, they attain supreme wisdom within meditative concentration; for this reason, they become foremost among all worldly beings.
Furthermore, through meditative concentration, they first thoroughly understand the mentalities of sentient beings; for this reason, they become the most supreme among all sentient beings.
Moreover, through meditative concentration, they always exercise mastery in accordance with their joy regarding the Triple Gem; for this reason, they obtain the inexhaustible merits of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, having attained the highest excellence in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he remains constantly in a state of equipoise (*samāhita*) due to this cause.
Moreover, having attained mastery over meditative concentration, he is able to bring all activities to fulfillment by virtue of this cause.
Furthermore, within meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they have no apprehension whatsoever; by virtue of these conditions, they attain great wisdom (*mahā-prajñā*).
Śāriputra! This is the meditative concentration of a bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, what serves as the precursor to the perfection of meditative concentration (dhyānapāramitā)?

It is as follows: it is preceded by a resolute mind; preceded by a one-pointed mind; preceded by an undistracted mind; preceded by a settled mind; preceded by a mind of śamatha; preceded by a mind of samādhi; preceded by the samādhi of the faculties; preceded by the samādhi of the powers; preceded by the samādhi of the right [limbs of enlightenment]; preceded by the liberations of concentration; preceded by the nine successive attainments; preceded by non-contradiction; preceded by wholesome dharmas; preceded by the subduing of the enemies that are the afflictions (kleśa); preceded by the fulfillment of the aggregate of samādhi; preceded by the samādhis of bodhisattvas; and preceded by the samādhis of the Buddhas."
Śāriputra! Such a dharma of tranquility is called the practice undertaken by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, which takes the perfection of meditative concentration as its precursor.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Through dhyāna, liberation, and the pāramitās, One constantly practices such conduct for many kalpas;
The mind remains unattached to worldly dharmas— This is called the Samādhi of Quiescent Illumination.”
If one thoroughly penetrates the perfections, Adorned like lightning, supreme and most exalted,
And through courageous effort leaves all defilements behind— This is called the Moonlight Samādhi.
Accomplishing the light of virtue of the precepts free from sorrow, One attains sovereign mastery over all phenomena;
This dharma is as lofty and courageous as Mount Sumeru, And is called the Samādhi of the Light of Dharma.

Upon that ground adorned with the jewel of the Dharma, The sublime purity of the dhāraṇī of the True Dharma, This mind is able to discern the minds of others; It is called the sovereign turning of the wisdom of the True Dharma.
Samādhi can surely crush and sever all afflictions, Like a banner or a jeweled net, it is without obstruction;
Within the ten powers, it excels in liberation, And is named the Samādhi that Shatters the Power of Māra.
Victorious, invincible, and like a lamp on Mount Sumeru, he is named Wisdom-Light Pure Eye;
because he was able to join his palms and utter words of praise, he attained the samādhi of the Ground of Wondrous Sustenance.
Because they are able to enter into and understand emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as the stage of tranquility;
through the wisdom of mindfulness of dharmas and mastery of merit, they attain the boundless samādhis of all Buddhas.
The Nāga King Sutanu, whether coming or going, is ever tranquil;
with pure vision, his eyes do not blink, for his concentration is named "the state far removed from all diverse perceptions."
The Vajra-samādhi is like the vajra-ground, Lofty, manifest, and immovable as Mount Sumeru;
Its pure sound revolves universally, The samādhi that is far removed from afflictions.
The vast characteristics of all merits are like space, without limit;
Fully increasing wisdom and mindfulness, their eloquence in preaching is inexhaustible.
Observing sentient beings so as to cause them to act virtuously—boundless, inexhaustible, and indestructible;

through loving-kindness one can harmonize and soften, through compassion one cultivates roots of goodness, through joy one enters supreme delight, and through equanimity one abandons the two obstacles.
Liberation is firm, giving rise to joy; like a supreme lotus or a vajra-banner, the ocean of wisdom and the light of wisdom are both unmoving—this is called the samādhi of the meaning of the Dharma.
The ocean of light of infinite liberation, adorned by the Tathāgata’s concentration, wisdom, and vows;
the supreme, perfectly awakened, wondrous tranquility—this concentration is named the Dharma of Immovable Subjugation.
May the light adorn the buddha-fields, causing the minds of all sentient beings to be entirely joyful;
may they always accord with the path of perfect enlightenment—this is the perfection of the Adornment of the Jewel Topknot.
Swift as the wind and without limit, Like the ocean treasury that holds all manner of jewels,
He bestows the true nectar of the gate of liberation, Opening the *samādhi* of the seven flowers of awakening.
The meaning of great supernormal powers is wondrously embraced; Thoroughly penetrating the boundless, all are perfected.
Universally manifesting such a Buddha-realm— This is called the Samādhi of the King of Accumulated Stone Mountains.
If one cultivates the perfection of meditative concentration, abiding securely in the sphere of equipoise,
the immeasurable gateways of a bodhisattva’s merit— this is called the samādhi of tranquility.
In meditative equipoise, whatever he attends to, all his spoken words are exemplary;
even in the midst of walking, sitting, and other postures, he is thus always without negligence.
Furthermore, these phenomena are most profoundly tranquil; they are without self, without person, and without a life-principle.
They are neither conceptualization nor non-conceptualization; only by this, and with nothing remaining, does one reach the further shore.
If one cultivates the perfection of meditative concentration, the ocean of boundless merit thereby attained—
those wise Bodhisattvas should, out of compassion, regard all sentient beings.
11. Chapter on the Perfection of Superior Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā). Chapter Eleven, Part One. At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"What is the perfection of superior wisdom of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas?"

Śāriputra! When bodhisattvas practice the non-retrogressive bodhisattva conduct, they ultimately uphold, recite, hear, and extensively expound this sublime and beneficial Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka for the sake of others, thereby attaining the marks of supreme wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding that supreme wisdom, what are its characteristics and how is it entered and understood?
It means that one enters and understands the characteristics heard through supreme wisdom according to one's own inclination.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of that which is heard?

They are: the characteristic of aspiration, the characteristic of intention, the characteristic of wholesome harmony, the characteristic of spiritual friends, the characteristic of transformation, the characteristic of dedication, the characteristic of nobility, the characteristic of reverence, and the characteristic of circumambulation to the right.

The characteristic of supreme mastery; the characteristic of intimacy; the characteristic of not listening to external objects; the characteristic of service; the characteristic of mental attention (*manasikāra*);

the characteristic of non-distraction; the characteristic of being like one seeking a treasure; the characteristic of being like one seeking a physician; the characteristic of extinguishing all suffering and illness;
the characteristic of mindfulness as a vessel; the characteristic of penetrating awakening (*bodhi*); and the characteristic of awakening through antidotes.
The characteristic of entering the wisdom of the Buddha; the characteristic of listening without weariness; the characteristic of gathering the gift of Dharma;

the characteristic of having no regret after giving; the characteristic of delighting in associating with those who have heard much; the characteristic of skillfully manifesting joy and acceptance; the characteristic of great joy pervading the body;
the characteristic of the mind being greatly at ease and pleased; the characteristic of listening without fatigue; and the characteristic of delighting in hearing the true Dharma.
Delighting in hearing the characteristics of right practice; delighting in hearing the characteristics of not contacting ignorance;

delighting in hearing the characteristics of the *pāramitās*; delighting in hearing the characteristics of the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; delighting in hearing the characteristics of the means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*);

delighting in hearing the characteristics of skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*); delighting in hearing the characteristics of the holy life (*brahmacarya*); delighting in hearing the characteristics of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); [delighting in hearing] the four...

The characteristic of the foundations of mindfulness; the characteristic of delighting in hearing about the four right efforts; the characteristic of delighting in hearing about the four bases of psychic power;
the characteristic of delighting in hearing about the twelvefold dependent origination; the characteristic of delighting in hearing about impermanence, suffering, non-self, and tranquility;

the characteristic of delighting in hearing about the liberations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the characteristic of delighting in hearing about the practice of not accumulating unwholesome roots; delighting in...
The aspect of accumulating roots of goodness through hearing; the aspect of delighting in hearing the solitary [teachings]; the aspect of delighting in hearing the turning of the wheel of Dharma;
the aspect of having no distracted thoughts amidst defilements; the aspect of the thought to subdue all afflictions; the aspect of turning toward the wise;
the aspect of drawing near to the noble and holy ones; the aspect of distancing oneself from non-discipline; and the aspect of delighting in...
They delight in hearing about the marks of a sage; they delight in hearing about the marks of the five faculties; they delight in hearing about the marks of mindfulness and investigation;
they delight in hearing about the marks of the seven factors of enlightenment; they delight in hearing about the marks of the eightfold noble path;
and they delight in hearing about the marks of the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four immeasurables, and eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha.
“Śāriputra! Within this very [state], one hears the cultivation of wisdom. Why is that?
This refers to generating a desire for the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka; having heard it, one is able to comprehend it; having comprehended it, one is able to practice it.

If one has the aspiration to hear the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one forms a wholesome union and draws near to spiritual friends—whether through transformation, through being gathered, by turning to the right, or through supreme mastery. One draws near to those of great learning without listening to external objects, abiding in great learning with diligent mental attention. One regards it as seeking a treasure, as seeking a physician, as the means to extinguish greed, hatred, and delusion, and as the act of upholding the teachings. Thus, one penetrates the essential meaning of all phenomena and causes wisdom to increase within one’s disposition, listening and receiving them without weariness.

Having heard of generosity, they are able to give with courage; having heard the teaching on ethical discipline, they are able to guard pure precepts; having heard the teaching on patience, they are able to practice forbearance; having heard the teaching on diligence, they are free from indolence; having heard the teaching on meditative concentration, they do not become distracted; and having heard the teaching on supreme wisdom, their minds aspire to the joy of exhausting the outflows and to the excellence of extensive learning. Furthermore, having heard the Dharma, their bodies and minds experience serenity and delight.
Having heard the Mahāyāna, one gives rise to superior aspiration; having heard the matters of gathering [the roots of virtue], one practices gathering them in mind;
having heard of the four foundations of mindfulness, one establishes mindfulness of body, feeling, mind, and phenomena;

and having heard of the four right efforts, one causes unwholesome states that have already arisen to be eliminated, is able to abandon those not yet arisen, and causes wholesome roots that have already arisen to increase.
He is able to initiate wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen; upon hearing the teaching on the cessation of strife, both body and mind attain pliancy;
upon hearing the teaching on meditative concentration, his mental activity becomes resolute;
and having heard the four immeasurables, he gives rise to great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings, great compassion toward those attached to pleasure, and...
One gives rise to great joy toward all true dharmas and great equanimity toward unwholesome states;

having heard of the five faculties, one is able to practice with the mind through faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; having heard of the seven factors of enlightenment, the mind attains awakening regarding all phenomena;
and having heard of the eightfold noble path, one is able to give rise to the mind directed toward Nirvāṇa.

If one wishes to train in the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four immeasurables, eighteen unique qualities, and even the infinite Buddha-dharmas, one should thus resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Having heard this, they are able to understand it; having understood it, they are able to cultivate it.

Śāriputra, that such various characteristics of what has been heard are entered into and comprehended at will—this is the practice of the perfection of supreme wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) of the bodhisattva mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of superior wisdom, they are able to receive, uphold, read, recite, hear, and extensively explain the supreme meaning and benefit of this sublime Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka for others, thereby attaining the correct practice of all dharmas."
What is the correct practice regarding all phenomena?
It refers to establishing correct practice within these phenomena exactly as they have been taught. Śāriputra!
Regarding "right practice of the Dharma," it refers to following and embracing all dharmas. Why is this?
Because non-attachment to dharmas is itself right practice; it is impossible for one who dwells in attachment to possess such practice.
It is impossible to seek liberation within the phenomena of a person (pudgala).
To have no attachment to the phenomena of a person is called right practice.
To attain freedom from doubt is indeed possible.
Therefore, for all practitioners, to accord with and embrace this True Dharma without obstruction constitutes right practice.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If one is without grasping, without seizing, without arising, and without ceasing regarding all phenomena and the revered Dharma; and if one likewise does not seize even upon those phenomena that accord with correct principle—such as this is what is called right practice."
As I have now said, there is not even the slightest thing, nor is there anything to be seen; such non-seeing and non-grasping is the characteristic of all dharmas.
What is this characteristic?
It is called "having characteristics" and "being without characteristics."
Why is this so? This characteristic is itself without characteristics; therefore, it is called "signless.
Furthermore, regarding these characteristics, there is no cognitive apprehension whatsoever within all phenomena.
This signlessness is without seeing and without grasping.
What has been thus described constitutes right practice.
Therefore, one should cultivate this right practice, so as to realize all phenomena directly and attain non-obstruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"If one does not give rise to fixed views regarding the Bodhisattva-piṭaka,
such wise ones shall attain abiding in right practice."
Furthermore, if one engages in grasping at these phenomena,
or gives rise to extremist views, this is not correct practice.
Although phenomena are unattainable, do not form a conceptual understanding of them as being empty.
How much more so this true and sublime Dharma, which is not like empty space.
If the Dharma were like empty space, there would be no one in the world who could comprehend it;
because there would be no comprehension, this would not constitute the correct practice.
Furthermore, this sublime and true Dharma is neither grasped nor not grasped;
therefore, regarding what is dharma or non-dharma, one should not give rise to attachment.
Because there is no grasping, this itself constitutes the characteristic of the Dharma.
Within such modes of practice, it is called "right practice.
Furthermore, regarding this sublime and correct Dharma, there has never been any attachment;
by understanding it through conformity, none can cause harm.
Because there is nothing to be harmed, wisdom has no objects of understanding;
within such modes of practice, this is called "right practice.
Furthermore, those who possess wisdom abide in the merit of few desires.
Within this True Dharma, one should practice with proper application.
If one dwells well in virtue and conducts oneself according to the right rules of conduct,
then in whatever direction one goes, one will accordingly attain purity.
Because their orientation is pure, they know this True Dharma;
thus, in every place, they can thoroughly understand the mentalities of sentient beings.
Furthermore, once those wise ones have understood those mentalities, [they act accordingly].
Within such modes of practice, one is able to proclaim the True Dharma.
Furthermore, this profound Dharma penetrates the ultimate truth;
regarding such meanings, one always attains certainty.
Furthermore, those who possess wisdom, whose learning is as vast as the great ocean,
because it is so deep and broad, practice immeasurable merit.
Without relying on mere words or their literal meanings, they are able to penetrate the correct principle.
Regarding immeasurable words and meanings, they attain firmness and immovability. "Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of the perfection of superior wisdom, having heard these supreme benefits of the meaning of this True Dharma of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, and even going so far as to explain them extensively for others, they are able to obtain the light of superior wisdom."

Among all phenomena, they are able to completely eliminate the darkness of ignorance and the cataracts of blindness; they swiftly achieve accomplishment in the light of supreme wisdom; they understand wholesome and unwholesome phenomena as they truly are; and until the end of their lives, they will ultimately sever all unwholesome phenomena.
"Having heard all wholesome dharmas as they have been realized, one is able to proclaim them within sublime tranquility.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Just as when entering a place of darkness, The various forms and appearances before one [remain unseen],"
That eye cannot be seen, yet fire can dispel the darkness.
Likewise, throughout the present eon, there are those who undergo birth and death;
regarding wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, they do not listen and thus remain ignorant.
By hearing this Dharma, one should refrain from committing transgressions and abandon what is unwholesome;
thus, one can swiftly proceed toward Nirvāṇa.
One should delight in associating with teachers and friends, thereby increasing the wisdom born of hearing.
Because that wisdom is pure, one attains the meaning of sublime bliss.
That wise person who understands the meaning of what they have heard perceives the departure from non-Dharma;
being courageous in the pure Dharma, they attain supreme and wondrous bliss.
If, having heard the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, one abides in the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
illuminating the world with light, one truly practices the conduct of enlightenment (bodhicaryā).
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka, Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Thirty-Three.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha,
Volume Thirty-Four.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Minister of Silver Light and Rank of Lu.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Dharma-pāla, a Subject and Grand Master of the Propagation of the Dharma (Chuanfan Dashi), who was conferred the purple robe and the title of Chief of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Shiguanglu Qing). Chapter Eleven: The Perfection of Superior Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), Part Two. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of the perfection of supreme wisdom, they should cultivate a pure aspiration for the sublime meaning and benefit of the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka;

they should regard those who uphold, read, and recite the true Dharma as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), and with courageous diligence and a perfectly integrated mind, they should give rise to right vows and the four right endeavors, thereby attaining non-obstruction regarding all phenomena.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"By honoring spiritual friends, one becomes a teacher of the Dharma;
Acting as the assembly that listens to the Dharma, one dwells constantly in right practice."
Not begrudging their own bodies or lives, they are most supreme in their diligent effort;
abiding within the wisdom of reality, they attain the purity of transcendent insight.
Having personally realized the True Dharma, their pure faith reaches all things without exception.
Through awakening to renunciation, as the Buddha has extensively revealed,
and like those wise ones who have thoroughly mastered the meaning of words and phrases,
by constantly practicing pure conduct, one attains entry into the stages of training.
Regarding all aspects of defilement and purity, one is entirely without attachment;
because there is no attachment, there is no diminution in regard to the Dharma.
Through diligence and aspiration, the body swiftly attains pliancy.
Having heard this Dharma, their wisdom increases and they are free from loss of mindfulness;
dwelling constantly in mindful wisdom, they comprehend both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
By training in the Supreme Vehicle, they master the power of mindfulness and insight.
Knowing the intentions of those sentient beings, as I have known them throughout the long night,
and because of training in this Dharma, they attain supreme wisdom and purity;
having understood the intentions of sentient beings, they reveal the True Dharma for their sake.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

a bodhisattva mahāsattva gives rise to right view regarding the subtle, pure, and luminous dharma-gate of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and toward all noble ones (ārya), and practices in accordance with what the Buddha has taught."
One should train in this way for two reasons.
What are these two?
First, obtaining the speech and sounds of others; second, exercising one's own mental attention.

If bodhisattvas are unable to hear the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva Piṭaka regarding the practices of yoga, or if, having heard it, they find mere partial joy and contentment in the samādhi-gates of the profound Dharma and Vinaya, you should know that they harbor overweening pride and have fallen into the net of Māra; they remain within birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, as well as the secondary afflictions.
Attached to the pleasures of the five desires, they continue in the cycle of saṃsāra.
For this reason, the Tathāgata says that those sentient beings follow after outflows (āsrava) and are incapable of liberation. Śāriputra!

If there are those who associate with Dharma masters and, having heard this True Dharma, understand it thoroughly, they will not commit offenses and will distance themselves from what is non-beneficial; their wisdom derived from hearing will increase, they will behold wondrous Nirvana, and through pure vigor, they will attain supreme and sublime bliss.

In this way, it should be known that for a bodhisattva mahāsattva, this constitutes the attainment of corresponding practice by upholding, reciting, and even hearing this marvelous Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, its legal principles, and its supreme benefits, and by extensively revealing and explaining them to others.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
If a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not hear this true Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, they will be unable to attain the corresponding mental state, for it is utterly contrary to the Noble Path."
The Tathāgata speaks thus because those sentient beings are constantly attentive to liberation from old age and death.
What is this "corresponding intention"?

It means that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is free from both correspondence and non-correspondence; this is the corresponding intention, and regarding this corresponding intention, one attains the absence of further designations.

Furthermore, regarding the mind associated with a bodhisattva: it is said that no sound can be produced by it, nor can any sound be produced by arhats; yet the sounds they emit are ultimately unfindable. When one investigates them throughout the past and the future, how could they possibly arise?
Wherein do they cease?

If one penetrates the sounds uttered in the past, then the past has already ceased; if one penetrates the sounds uttered in the future, then the future has not yet arrived; if one penetrates the sounds uttered in the present, then the present does not abide.
Thus, that which has been said and that which remains to be said have been sought everywhere and are found to be entirely unobtainable.
One should train in this manner regarding the associated mind:
"O Śāriputra!..."
If a bodhisattva who is engaged with the mind trains in this manner, how does he investigate?

It is said that this bodhisattva observes that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is fundamentally extinguished; he observes that the self-essence of all phenomena is fundamentally quiescent; he observes that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is equal; he observes that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen; he observes that all phenomena are ultimately non-emergent; he observes that all phenomena are ultimately non-accumulative; and he observes that all phenomena are ultimately without cessation.

At this time, it is said that even the contemplation of reality as it is is not an object of contemplation; thus, it is neither an object of contemplation nor not an object of contemplation. To speak of this is called the "intention of investigation," and one should train in this manner.

If there are bodhisattvas who, regarding this true Dharma, are clouded by doubt and ignorance such that they are unable to enter into understanding—claiming that this Dharma is not a gate to liberation, severing all diligent effort and failing to give rise to penetration—it will in no way correspond with their minds.
Furthermore, the right view regarding these phenomena is precisely the vision of suchness (*tathatā*).
How is it that the vision of suchness regarding all phenomena is [itself] "no-view"?
It is what is called "non-seeing."
Such non-viewing is the non-arising of designations; where there is no arising of designations, there is no accumulation.
How is there no accumulation?
It means that regarding designations, there is no opposition.

By means of these teachings, the Tathāgata observes that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without arising and without activity; through this, within right view, he attains the practice of authentic deliverance (*samyagnairyāṇika*).
Furthermore, what is the cause of this practice of authentic deliverance?
It means that all phenomena are themselves the Buddha-dharma.

Therefore, those who seek the practice of authentic transcendence should uphold, recite, read, hear, and explain to others this sublime and beneficial meaning of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, until they attain a mind that is in accord with this True Dharma.
This is called the practice of authentic renunciation.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva practices the perfection of transcendent wisdom, they correctly and skillfully awaken to this subtle, pure, and luminous dharma-gate, and by observing the sense base of the mind, they attain understanding of the arising of the mind."
What is the sphere of mind (manāyatana)?
How does one enter into understanding?
It is this: that bodhisattva, within the locus of the empowerment of samādhi and the locus of the investigation and analysis of vipaśyanā, [enters].
The supreme object of aspiration; the object of the mind’s longing; the state of uninterrupted continuity;
the state of impermanence; the state of causes and conditions; the state of dependent origination; the state devoid of self, person, or life-principle;
the state that neither abides nor does not abide, neither departs nor does not depart; the state where cause and effect are neither accumulated nor destroyed; emptiness.
It is the sphere of habitual practice regarding signlessness and wishlessness, yet it is not a sphere grasped by emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness;
it is the sphere grasped by *samādhi* and *samāpatti*, yet it is not a place where *samādhi* and *samāpatti* arise through dependence;
it is the sphere grasped by the knowledge of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), yet it is not the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); it is the sphere of observing non-arising, yet it is not...
The sphere of practice for renunciation; the sphere of observing that all sentient beings are without self;
the sphere of not abandoning great compassion; the sphere of seeing terror in all forms of birth; the sphere of having a mind that clings; the sphere of renouncing greed;

the sphere of not abandoning the active manifestation of dharmas associated with greed; the sphere of relinquishing the pleasures of the five desires; the sphere of not abandoning the joy of the Dharma; [the sphere of] detachment...
Śāriputra, one gives rise to and enters into understanding all such dharmas: the locus of all conceptual proliferation and the locus of not abandoning skillful means. Śāriputra!
This is called the entry into understanding the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*).
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
regarding that sphere of mind, how is it described as the path of right principle?"
That which is called the path by means of intention, the path by means of the gateway, the path by means of the face-gateway,
the path by means of cause, the path by means of synthesis, the path by means of non-contradiction,
the path by means of the absence of dispute, the path by means of equanimity, the path of neither entering nor not entering, and the path of the absence of conceptual proliferation.
The Path is that which is without disparagement; this is the Path. It is without increase; this is the Path. It is without decrease; this is the Path. It is without arising;
this is the Path. It is without transformation; this is the Path. It is without antidote; this is the Path. Suchness is the Path.
The limit of reality is the Path. The Tathāgata is the Path. Non-differentiation is the Path. Thusness is the Path.
This path is the equality of the three periods of time; this path is the non-abiding in the discrimination of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

this path is the non-abiding in the eye-element, the form-element, and the eye-consciousness-element; this path is the non-abiding in the ear-element, the sound-element, and the ear-consciousness-element;
this path is the non-abiding in the nose-element, the odor-element, and the nose-consciousness-element; it is the non-abiding in...
The tongue element, taste element, and tongue-consciousness element are the path; not abiding in the body element, touch element, and body-consciousness element is the path;

not abiding in the mind element, mental-object element, and mind-consciousness element is the path; that which accords with ultimate truth is the path; that which accords with right knowledge is the path;
that which accords with sūtras of definitive meaning is the path; that which accords with the correct...
The Dharma is the path. Śāriputra,
this is what is called the path of right principle.

Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters into and understands the path of correct principle with a discerning mind, through this observation there is nothing to be observed; thus, it is neither non-observation nor not non-observation.
This is called the "investigating intention. "Śāriputra,

if a bodhisattva-mahāsattva possesses an associated intention regarding this true Dharma yet remains in delusion and blindness, saying that 'this Dharma is not a gate of liberation,' thereby severing all diligent effort, failing to give rise to superior progress, and lacking any penetration— such an intention is entirely inconsistent with that [true Dharma]."
Furthermore, for all sentient beings, such right view is precisely the vision of *tathatā* (suchness).
Moreover, what is meant by the vision of *tathatā*?
It is that which is called "non-viewing."
When there is no view, no further designation arises, up to and including the absence of any corresponding name, as has been explained in detail previously.
Regarding this practice of the perfection of superior wisdom within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, one should train in this manner.
"Furthermore, as there is no self in the mind, so too is there no self in all phenomena.
If all phenomena are without self, then likewise there is no self in any sentient beings."
To observe in this manner is the observation of the mind.

Furthermore, the realm of saṃsāra and the realm of nirvāṇa are in equal correspondence; likewise, the essential nature of afflictions corresponds with the essential nature of all phenomena. Regarding that correspondence and non-correspondence, there is no attachment whatsoever, and one attains resolute conviction through the observation of the mind.
Furthermore, all the bodhisattva’s corresponding activities are without exception: he sustains all sentient beings without abandoning them, and he upholds the true Dharma without contradiction.
Śāriputra! This is called the mark of what is heard by a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has attained the corresponding mind.
When one enters into understanding through the mind and observes in this way, that supreme wisdom sees suchness and remains unshakable.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the practice of the perfection of supreme wisdom, they attain the dwelling of supreme wisdom, because it is not shared with any conditioned phenomena."
That which is called ignorance up to old age and death do not coexist with it.
Furthermore, from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) up to the sixty-two views concerning the beginning and the end, none of them coexist with it.
Whether it be the eight worldly dharmas—whether disparagement or praise—it dwells together with none of them.
From the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements, up to all objects of mental engagement, it dwells together with none of them.
Furthermore, he does not coexist with pride, overweening pride, false pride, nor even the twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Moreover, he does not coexist with any afflictions whatsoever—whether superior, middling, or inferior; coarse or subtle.
Furthermore, they do not dwell together with ignorance, darkness, blindness, obscurations, or fetters, nor with any inferior qualities whatsoever.
Moreover, they do not dwell together with the māra of afflictions, the māra of the aggregates, the celestial māra, or the māra of death, nor with any karmic activities of the māras whatsoever.

Furthermore, they do not dwell together with any view of a self, a person, a sentient being, a life-span, a nourisher, a spirit, a soul, a human being, or a youth, nor indeed with any view of a self whatsoever.

Furthermore, they do not coexist with karmic obstructions, afflictive obstructions, dharma obstructions, view obstructions, retribution obstructions, or cognitive obstructions, nor even with any continuous habitual tendencies.
Furthermore, they do not dwell together with conceptualizations and discriminations regarding the obstruction of signs, nor with any entanglements of what is seen, heard, sensed, or known.

Moreover, they do not dwell together with stinginess or generosity, violation of precepts or upholding them, anger or patience, laziness or diligence, distraction or meditative concentration, or faulty wisdom or supreme wisdom; indeed, they do not dwell together with any of the perfections that lack their respective antidotes, nor with what is wisdom and what is not wisdom.

Furthermore, regarding all perverse retributions—whether permanent or impermanent, wholesome or unwholesome, with fault or without fault, saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, and even all methods of erroneous counteraction—he never dwells together with them.
Furthermore, they do not coexist with various Buddha-dharmas, various buddha-fields, or various sentient beings.
Moreover, they do not coexist with the conventional and the ultimate, the wise and the ignorant, nor even with the mental attentions and characteristics of all sentient beings.

Furthermore, he does not dwell together with superior wisdom or superior conduct, nor with the conditioned nature of phenomena, nor even with anything produced by the abiding of mind, mentation, and consciousness.
Śāriputra, this is the practice of the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s perfection of superior wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), which does not dwell at all with such immeasurable conditioned phenomena.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,

when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the conduct of the perfection of superior wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they are able to dwell securely in the Bodhisattva Piṭaka and, through superior wisdom, discern all phenomena, thereby attaining ten kinds of skillfulness."

What are the ten? First, skill in the aggregates; second, skill in the elements; third, skill in the sense bases; fourth, skill in the truths; fifth, skill in correct knowledge; sixth, skill in accordance; seventh, skill in wisdom and consciousness; eighth, skill in the factors of enlightenment; ninth, skill in the noble path; and tenth, skill in dependent origination.
What is called skillfulness regarding the aggregates?

It refers to these five aggregates as being like a mass of foam, like a bubble on water, like a mirage, like a plantain tree, like a magical illusion, like a dream, like an echo in a valley, like a shadow, like a floating cloud, and like a reflection in a mirror.
That which is called the aggregate of form is like a mass of foam; within that mass of foam there is no self, no person, no sentient being, no life-force, no individual, no mind-born, and no youth.
If the nature of the world is thus, then the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is likewise.
This is called skillfulness regarding the aggregate of form.
As for the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), it is like a bubble upon the water; within that bubble there is no self, person, being, life-force, soul, mind-born, or youth.
If the nature of the world is thus, then the nature of the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is likewise so.
To speak of this is called skillfulness regarding the aggregate of feeling.

As for the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha), it is like a mirage; within that mirage there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span. To speak of this is called skillfulness regarding the aggregate of perception.

That which is called the aggregate of formations is like a plantain tree; within that plantain tree there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span. To speak thus is called skillfulness regarding the aggregate of formations.

That which is called the aggregate of consciousness is like an illusion; within that illusion there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span. To speak thus is called skillfulness regarding the aggregate of consciousness.
Furthermore, it is said that these five aggregates are the characteristics of this world’s momentary transformation and disintegration.
If the nature of this world is thus, then the nature of that world is likewise so.
What is their essential nature?
It is the nature of suffering and impermanence.
The essential nature of those aggregates is likewise thus.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of superior wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by which they attain skillfulness regarding the aggregates (skandha-kauśalya).
Furthermore, what is meant by skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu-kauśalya*)?
It is as follows: the earth element is the dharma-element, and the dharma-element has no characteristic of coarseness or roughness.
The water element is the dharma-element, and the dharma-element has no characteristic of softness or pliancy.
The fire element is the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm has no characteristic of heat.
The wind element is the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm has no characteristic of movement.
The eye-consciousness element is the dharma-realm; the dharma-realm has no characteristic of looking.
The auditory consciousness element is itself the dharma-element; in the dharma-element, there is no characteristic of sound that can be manifested as an object.
The olfactory consciousness element is itself the dharma-element; in the dharma-element, there is no characteristic of fragrance that can be smelled.
The tongue-consciousness element is itself the dharma-element; within the dharma-element, there is no characteristic of tasting flavors that can be cognized.
The body-consciousness element is itself the dharma-element; within the dharma-element, there is no characteristic of feeling tangibles that can be perceived.
The consciousness element is the dharma-element; the dharma-element has no characteristic that can be observed.
Thus, the self-nature element and the dharma-element are non-dual and undifferentiated.
Furthermore, the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm are non-dual and undifferentiated.

The realm of saṃsāra and the realm of nirvāṇa are non-dual and undifferentiated; this realm of emptiness and the realm of all phenomena are non-dual and undifferentiated. Because they are empty by nature and free from conceptual construction, they are non-dual and undifferentiated.

By entering into and understanding the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), one enters into and understands the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*); thus, one enters into and understands through such definitive discernment even up to the immeasurable realms. Śāriputra!
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of superior wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), by which one attains skillfulness regarding the elements (dhātu-kauśalya).
Furthermore, what is meant by skillfulness regarding the sense bases (āyatana-kauśalya)?
That is to say, this eye-base is fundamentally empty, as are the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-bases; therein there is neither a self nor anything belonging to a self.

When that bodhisattva thus understands, as they truly are, the essential nature of the eye up to the essential nature of the mind, then there is no analytical determination, no manifold determination, and no virtuous determination; regarding wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, they do not proceed with a dualistic appearance.
This is called skillfulness regarding the bases (*āyatana-kauśalya*).
Furthermore, this skillfulness regarding the bases refers to the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*).
When one perceives forms with the eye and thereby gives rise to revulsion (*nirveda*), such revulsion is not the correct practice (*samyak-pratipatti*).

Furthermore, regarding the sphere of the ear and the sphere of sound, the sphere of the nose and the sphere of odor, the sphere of the tongue and the sphere of taste, the sphere of the body and the sphere of tangibles, and the sphere of the mind and the sphere of mental objects—from these, up to the arising of revulsion toward the mental consciousness—such revulsion is not the correct practice.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva should accumulate and realize great compassion in both the states of the noble path and those that are not the noble path; they should cause sentient beings in all perilous and difficult non-noble paths to abide in the right path, and they do not abandon them even within the states of the noble path itself.
Śāriputra! This is called the practice of the perfection of superior wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, by which one attains skillfulness regarding all bases.
Furthermore, what is meant by "skillfulness in understanding the truths"?
This skillfulness regarding the truths is fourfold: namely, the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path.
What is the knowledge of suffering?
It is the non-arising of the aggregates; this is the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of origination?
That is to say, because one is detached from the accumulation of craving, this is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
What is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*)? Because, once ceased, it does not arise again, this is the knowledge of cessation.
What is the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*)?
It is because within the equal Dharma no equality can be apprehended; this is called the knowledge of the path.

If a bodhisattva possesses such wisdom regarding these four truths yet does not realize them [as a final cessation] while maturing sentient beings, this is called skill in the truths (*satyakauśalya*).

"Furthermore, there are three kinds of skill in the truths (*satyakauśalya*): namely, conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*).
What is conventional truth?
It refers to all conceptualizations, sounds, speech, and written characters, as well as all worldly activities; this is conventional truth."
What is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*)?
It means that the mind has no object of perception; how much less so for words and letters—this is the ultimate truth.
What is the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*)?
It means that all characteristics are a single characteristic, and this single characteristic is the absence of characteristics;

this is the truth of characteristics (*lakṣaṇasatya*). That bodhisattva is untiring in teaching the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), does not lose correct practice regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and accords with the signless (*animitta*) within the truth of characteristics; this is the true characteristic.
This is called the bodhisattva’s skill in the truths.
Furthermore, there is but one truth, which is not of two kinds; namely, the truth of tranquility—this is the single, actual truth.
Regarding all that is equal and unequal, one is able to engage in the truly wondrous activity of conforming [to them], and thus attains skillfulness regarding the truths.
