Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Silver Light Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject Dharmapāla, and others, by Imperial Decree. Chapter Eleven: The Perfection of Superior Wisdom (III). "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains such skillfulness regarding the truths, they thereby understand that the five aggregates are suffering; if the characteristic of suffering of the five aggregates is brought to cessation so that it is like space, this is the Noble Truth of Suffering.

Furthermore, these five aggregates follow along with afflictions, craving, and views; if one causes the grasping of these causes—craving, views, and so forth—to not arise and not aggregate, this constitutes the Noble Truth of Origination.

Moreover, these five aggregates are ultimately subject to extinction; if one causes them to not be produced in the past, not to arise in the future, and not to abide in the present, this constitutes the Noble Truth of Cessation.

If one is able to realize and penetrate the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, and the knowledge of cessation through the continuity of wisdom, and is thus able to skillfully subdue the mind and lead it toward right practice, this constitutes the Noble Truth of the Path.

Furthermore, regarding this clear realization of the truths, being able to investigate, reflect upon, and exhaustively examine them constitutes the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the truths.
Furthermore, the analytical knowledge that understands all feelings as suffering, up to and including those feelings that are drawn forth and grasped, is the Noble Truth of Suffering.
To understand, as it truly is, how the causal conditions of feeling give rise to the accumulation [of formations], is the Noble Truth of the Origin.

Furthermore, if one attains pliancy regarding feeling, then one does not regard that feeling as feeling; rather, by further observing that which is not-feeling as cessation, one realizes and attains cessation—this is the Noble Truth of Cessation.

Furthermore, regarding the path that has been undertaken: just as in the world one accumulates and strives for progress, that which is neither mere undertaking nor the path itself, yet causes suffering to cease and leads toward right practice—this is the Noble Truth of the Path.
If one perceives these four truths as equal and ultimately without perception, this is purity; this is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the truths.
Furthermore, to give rise to direct realization regarding cessation, and to be further able to not give rise to observation regarding suffering—this is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
If there is a condition that gives rise to existence and yet remains detached from existence—this is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
To know that all arising is fundamentally non-arising and that cessation is nothing that ceases is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
To seek and examine such a path according to its various types, thereby causing entry into that knowledge, is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
If one can abide securely in such knowledge of the truths, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skill in the truths regarding the practice of the perfection of superior wisdom.
“Śāriputra! Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain four kinds of skill in correct knowledge (*saṃprajanya*).
What are these four?
First is correct knowledge of meaning, second is correct knowledge of phenomena, third is correct knowledge of worldly treatises, and fourth is correct knowledge of eloquence.
What is correct knowledge of meaning?
That is to say: regarding the various ultimate phrases of phenomena, it is the wisdom of continuity, the wisdom of causes, the wisdom of conditions,
the wisdom of accumulation, the wisdom of penetrating the boundless, the wisdom of entering into and understanding dependent origination, the wisdom of discerning the dharma-realm,

the wisdom of entering into and understanding true suchness in accordance with it, the wisdom of not abiding in the limit of reality, and the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena as they truly are— [it is] the investigation [of these].
The wisdom of signlessness; the wisdom regarding the wishless within wishing, and the wisdom regarding the non-practiced within practicing;

the entry into the single wisdom of correct principle; the wisdom that enters into the understanding of selflessness; the understanding that there are no sentient beings; the realization that there is no life-span;
the ultimate wisdom that there is no person (pudgala); the unobstructed wisdom regarding the past; and regarding the future...
The wisdom of immeasurable knowledge regarding future lives; the wisdom that pervades all places in the present life;

the wisdom that the aggregates are like magical illusions; the wisdom that the sense bases are definitively empty; the wisdom that the elements are beyond measure; the wisdom of inner bodily tranquility;
the wisdom that there is no pervasive movement externally; the wisdom of renouncing sensory objects; and the wisdom of mindfulness abiding nowhere.
The wisdom that penetrates non-entry; the wisdom of superior insight and observation; the wisdom that thoroughly penetrates the Four Noble Truths:
the wisdom that all sufferings are existence, the wisdom that all origins are formations, the wisdom that all cessations are signless, and the wisdom that all paths are renunciation;
the wisdom that discriminates all dharma-terms; the wisdom that skillfully understands all faculties; and the power of the [spiritual] strengths that is invincible.
The wisdom of subduing and overcoming; the wisdom empowered by *śamatha*; the wisdom of the radiance of *vipaśyanā*;
the wisdom that perceives the arising and ceasing of all magical illusions; the wisdom that is undeluded regarding all mirages; the wisdom that sees no reality in all dream-objects;
the wisdom that understands all echoes as dependently originated; the wisdom that [perceives] all reflections as...
The wisdom that synthesizes all; the wisdom that perceives a single characteristic within manifold characteristics; the wisdom that perceives no union within perfect union;
the wisdom that finds nothing to be attained within all pliancies; the wisdom that penetrates sounds and speech in the Śrāvaka vehicle;
the wisdom that understands dependent origination in the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; and the wisdom that accumulates all roots of goodness in the Supreme Vehicle.
What has been stated in this manner constitutes a bodhisattva’s correct knowledge of meaning (*artha*).

Furthermore, regarding correct knowledge of meaning: if one accords with the meaning, then all phenomena (*dharma*) accord; that meaning which is thus accorded is the very nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Why is this? Because the meaning of all phenomena is ultimately like space.
If their meaning is like space, then the meaning of all phenomena is ultimately without marks.
If the meaning of phenomena is signless, then the meaning of all phenomena is ultimately wishless.
If the meaning of phenomena is wishless, then that meaning of those phenomena has nothing toward which to proceed or realize.
If the meaning of phenomena has nothing to be realized, then the meaning of all phenomena is ultimately devoid of a life-principle and devoid of a person.
If there is no person (pudgala) in this meaning, then one penetrates the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa) within that meaning.

If it is said that there is neither abiding nor exhaustion regarding this meaning, and one attains realization and knowledge of the meaning thus spoken, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, will rejoice and grant their seal of approval; such is the true and correct knowledge of that supreme wisdom as it truly is.
If one possesses correct knowledge of superior wisdom as it truly is, then there will be no fault in any circumstance; this is called a bodhisattva’s correct knowledge of meaning.
What is called correct knowledge of phenomena?

This refers to the wisdom that penetrates and understands the true Dharma: whether wholesome or unwholesome, faulty or faultless, with outflows or without outflows, mundane or supramundane, conditioned or unconditioned, defiled or purified, saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) or the realm of gnosis—these are fundamentally equal from the outset, with nothing to be awakened to.
This is called a bodhisattva’s correct knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).

Furthermore, regarding the correct knowledge of phenomena: one is able to correctly know the mind that acts with craving (*rāgacarita*), namely: false craving, firm craving, subtle craving, vast craving, and the boundless observation of past craving, as well as the entry into understanding present craving according to its conditions.

Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who have internal craving but not external craving; or those who have external craving but not internal craving; or those who have both internal and external craving; or those who have neither internal nor external craving.

Furthermore, there may be greed for forms but not for sounds; greed for sounds but not for forms; greed for both forms and sounds; or neither greed for forms nor for sounds. There may be greed for forms but not for odors;

greed for sounds but not for odors; greed for odors but not for tastes; greed for tastes but not for tangibles—and so on, with various permutations regarding greed for the objects of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch. Through such non-beneficial gateways, one enters into the understanding of twenty-one thousand types of greedy conduct, twenty-one thousand types of hateful conduct, and twenty-one thousand types of deluded conduct.

Thus, regarding the twenty-one thousand types of conduct consisting of greed, hatred, delusion, and those with equal proportions [of the three poisons], there is the wisdom that understands the eighty-four thousand modes of mental activity as they have been described;

the wisdom of the corresponding modes of practice as they have been described; the wisdom that is neither more nor less [than what is required]; the wisdom that transcends the hundred realms of desire; the wisdom of the distinguished vessel of the Dharma; and the wisdom of true speech. To speak thus is called a bodhisattva’s correct knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*).
"What is correct knowledge of worldly treatises?
It refers to the thorough understanding of all sounds and wisdom.
One is able to thoroughly understand the voices of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans."
Regarding the sentient beings of the five destinies—whether coarse or subtle, high or low—he understands their speech, which flows in a continuous, unbroken succession of sounds and syllables.

Whether they speak of one, two, or many; whether in male voices, female voices, or voices that are neither male nor female; whether in extensive or concise discourse, in vulgar or elegant speech; whether speaking of the past, future, or present; and whether consisting of a single syllable or corresponding to many syllables—he understands them all completely.
This is called correct knowledge of worldly treatises.
Furthermore, regarding correct knowledge of worldly treatises: it consists in being matured in the phrasing, clear in the meaning, free from all fear, and without fault.

Regarding the conventional and the ultimate, through the knowledge and vision of one’s own mind, one employs profound and skillful various adornments to cause all sentient beings to give rise to joy; this is called a bodhisattva’s correct knowledge of worldly treatises.
"What is the bodhisattva’s eloquence of correct awareness?
It is eloquence that is non-abiding and uninterrupted in speech; eloquence of swift and true prophecy;
eloquence that definitively attains the fruit; eloquence according with whatever is asked; and eloquence that is without loss or interruption."
The eloquence of cessation; the eloquence of non-contention; the eloquence of delighting in the sublime Dharma; the eloquence of abiding in patience;
the eloquence of profundity; the eloquence of skillful means; the eloquence of the conventional and the ultimate;
the eloquence of establishing all generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and supreme wisdom; and the eloquence of establishing mindfulness.
The eloquence of the foundations of mindfulness, right exertions, bases of power, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the noble path;
the eloquence of entering into and understanding the knowledge of all truths, concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis;
the eloquence of awakening to all vehicles; the eloquence of understanding the mental activities of all sentient beings; and being free from stammering.
eloquence of speech; eloquence of speech free from harshness; eloquence of speech free from confusion;
eloquence of speech that is smooth and supple; eloquence of speech that is pure; eloquence of speech that is liberated;
eloquence of speech that is unobstructed; eloquence of speech that is honored; and eloquence of speech that is compassionate.
The eloquence of speech that is appropriate, the eloquence of speech that is without flaw, the eloquence of speech that is sweet,
the eloquence of speech that is refined and smooth, the eloquence of speech that is without disparagement,
and the eloquence of speech that praises the noble ones; [with these] one can penetrate the sentient beings of infinite lands and, by means of them...

With a single expression of wondrous Brahma-sounds, such eloquence enables one to skillfully expound the Dharma for other sentient beings and individuals; it is for this that the Buddha grants his seal of approval.
If he were to teach a Dharma that does not lead to transcendence, how could he be able to reach the end of all suffering and accomplish right practice?
Śāriputra, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful eloquence within the practice of the perfection of superior wisdom.
"What is the skillfulness of conformity for a bodhisattva?
There are four kinds. What are these four?"

First, to follow the meaning and not the letter; second, to follow wisdom and not consciousness; third, to follow sūtras of definitive meaning and not sūtras of interpretable meaning; fourth, to follow the Dharma and not the person.
What is the meaning? What are the words?
That which consists in entering into and understanding the practice of supramundane dharmas is called the meaning.
Thoroughly understanding worldly phenomena is called the letter (*vyañjana*).
Bestowing sublime bliss upon that which is disciplined and composed is called the meaning (*artha*).
Subduing and restraining through the absence of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is called the letter.
If one is able to fully describe saṃsāra, this is called the meaning (*artha*).
To extensively reveal that which is non-apprehensible is called the phrasing (*vyañjana*).
If one is able to universally praise the virtues of nirvāṇa, this is called the meaning.
The absence of conceptual differentiation regarding the essential nature of the dharma of nirvāṇa is called the letter (vyañjana).
If it is explained according to the respective stages of the three vehicles, this is called the meaning (artha).
Wisdom that penetrates only a single teaching is called the "text.
To expound upon generosity for the sake of all sentient beings is called the "meaning.
The purity of the three spheres is called the "text."
If one can proclaim and expound the majestic deportment of the three karmas and accumulate all the merits of the dhūta practices, this is called the "meaning.
That the superior practices of purity in body, speech, and mind are all ungraspable—this is called the "letter."
If one can proclaim the firm endurance of anger, resentment, vexation, envy, arrogance, and conceit, this is called the meaning (*artha*).
To attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is called the letter (*vyañjana*).
To be able to expound upon all roots of goodness with leaping joy and diligent effort is called the meaning (*artha*).
To practice that diligence without entering or dwelling [in it] is called the letter (*vyañjana*).
If one can expound upon the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*), this is called the "meaning.
Knowledge of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is called the "letter.
Regarding the faculty of wisdom, extensive learning and the dhāraṇīs are called the "meaning."
The meaning is ineffable; this exposition is called the "letter.
If one can reveal and demonstrate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma), this is called the "meaning.
If there is the realization of the fruit through the practice of these factors of enlightenment, this is called the "letter."
If one can reveal and teach the truths of suffering, its origin, and the path, this is called the meaning (*artha*).
The direct realization of the truth of cessation is called the letter (*vyañjana*).
If one correctly reveals and teaches [the dependent origination] beginning with ignorance and ending with old age and death, this is called the meaning.
If it is said that from the cessation of ignorance up to the cessation of old age and death, this is called the letter.
If it is said that one accumulates serenity and insight, this is called the meaning.
The knowledge of clear liberation—this is called the letter.
If one can discern the categorized practices such as greed, hatred, and delusion, this is called the meaning (*artha*).
If the mind remains unmoved within liberation, this is called the letter (*vyañjana*).
If one can reveal and explain all obstructive phenomena, this is called the meaning (*artha*).
If one realizes the unobstructed wisdom of liberation, this is called the letter (*vyañjana*).
If one correctly reveals and skillfully praises the immeasurable Triple Gem, this is called the meaning.
If one speaks of the nature of phenomena as free from craving and the qualities of the unconditioned, this is called the "letter.

If one speaks of the bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind of awakening, the cultivation of meritorious qualities, and so forth, up to the terrace of enlightenment, this is called the "meaning."

To speak of the characteristics of the single mind and the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment of the knowledge of all modes, down to their concise summary in accordance with the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dharma—this is called the "letter."
Furthermore, if all sounds, speech, letters, and even the unspeakable meaning are collectively referred to as "meaning," then what is a sutra of provisional meaning?
That is to say, regarding the words spoken, if one understands them extensively and in detail exactly as they were spoken, this is called a sutra of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
What is a sutra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?
Regarding the meaning spoken, if one penetrates it extensively and thoroughly exactly as it was spoken, this is called a sutra of definitive meaning.
Furthermore, it is said that for certain individuals there is no possibility of transcendence; such teachings are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
The teaching that one can indeed transcend through the very Dharma as it has been taught is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains skillfulness in accordance with the practice of the perfection of transcendent wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
What is the bodhisattva’s skillfulness in words and phrases?
This means that bodhisattvas are well able to practice the perfection of superior wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) regarding these two dharmas.
What are the two dharmas?
First, skillful consciousness; second, skillful knowledge.
What is consciousness?
It abides by means of four bases. What are these four?

First, consciousness abides in dependence on form; second, consciousness abides in dependence on feeling; third, consciousness abides in dependence on perception; fourth, consciousness abides in dependence on formations—this is what is called consciousness.
What is wisdom? It is said that if one thoroughly understands the five appropriated aggregates, this is called wisdom.
Furthermore, if one thoroughly understands the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element, this is called consciousness.
Furthermore, if one abides in the four kinds of dharmadhātu and is well able to discern that dharmadhātu, this is called wisdom (*jñāna*).

Śāriputra, it is further said regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*): the eye observing forms is its manifestation; the ear hearing sounds is its manifestation; the nose smelling odors is its manifestation; the tongue cognizing tastes is its manifestation; the body feeling tangibles is its manifestation; and the mind knowing phenomena is its manifestation—this is called consciousness.
Furthermore, if the internal body is tranquil and there is no external pervasive activity, and the wisdom follows along with phenomena without grasping at anything, this is called *jñāna* (gnosis).
Moreover, if one gives rise to pervasive conceptualization and grasping, this is called *vijñāna* (consciousness).
Absence of grasping, absence of appropriation, and the manifestation of non-aversion—this is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, the thorough understanding of consciousness as it abides in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) subject to arising and ceasing—this is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is devoid of pervasive consciousness, and because wisdom that is unconditioned does not abide in arising and ceasing—this is called wisdom.
What are the definitive (*nītārtha*) and non-definitive (*neyārtha*) sūtras?
That is to say, if what is taught leads toward the path, it is of provisional meaning (neyārtha);
if it leads toward the fruit, it is of definitive meaning (nītārtha).
To speak of conventional practice is of provisional meaning.
The teaching of the ultimate truth is definitive;
that which leads toward karmic activity is provisional.
The exhaustion of karma and afflictions is definitive.
Furthermore, the afflicted portion (*saṃkleśabhāga*) is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
If one speaks of the purified portion (*vyavadānabhāga*), that is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
To cultivate revulsion toward that saṃsāra is of provisional meaning.
Realizing the non-dual nature of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa is definitive meaning;
skillful literary expression is provisional meaning.
That which is profound and difficult to understand is definitive meaning.
To take delight in and desire various words and phrases is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
To give rise to certainty regarding even a few words and phrases is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Furthermore, various expressions such as "self," "person," "individual," "life-principle," "mind-born," "young brahmin," "agent," and "experiencer"—whether they imply a sovereign or lack a sovereign—are of provisional meaning.

To not give rise to the notions of a self, a person, a human being, or even a *pudgala* regarding the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
What, then, are the *pudgala* and phenomena (*dharma*)?

That is to say, if one abides in the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*) regarding all phenomena, yet by giving rise to that very view further abides in the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the realm of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*), this is called both the person and the phenomenon.

Furthermore, regarding *pudgalas*: there are ordinary *pudgalas*, virtuous ordinary *pudgalas*, *pudgalas* who follow by faith, *pudgalas* who follow the Dharma, the eight types of *pudgalas*, *pudgalas* who have entered the stream, *pudgalas* who return once more, *pudgalas* who do not return, *pudgalas* who are worthy of offerings (*arhats*), *pudgalas* who are pratyekabuddhas, and *pudgalas* who are bodhisattvas.

If a single person appears in the world, they are still able to bring forth manifold sublime joys; out of profound compassion for the assemblies of gods and humans in that world, they perform all manner of beneficial deeds.

How much more so for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who dwells in the conventional world and, for the sake of all persons, causes all sentient beings to enter into and understand the meaning and benefit through the sounds spoken by the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said: "This teaching is called 'the Dharma' because it causes each and every sentient being to accord with it, and they joyfully desire to be led toward and established in its meaning.
What is meant by 'Dharma'?"
That which is called non-action and non-non-action, non-abiding and non-non-abiding, is fundamentally equal in all places and universally identical in its basis.

Furthermore, the characteristics of all phenomena are by nature empty; there is neither equality nor inequality. Free from all conceptual discrimination and without any object of attachment, they are all transcendent.

This explains that by practicing in accordance with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), one attains non-retrogression; therefore, through this gateway of correct principle, one gains entry into and understanding of the nature of all phenomena.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s attainment of four kinds of skillful means in accordance with the perfection of superior wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means regarding merit and wisdom?
The gateways of practice for bodhisattvas are of two kinds. What are these two?
First is the practice of merit; second is the practice of wisdom.
What is meritorious action?
It refers to the meritorious action of generosity, the meritorious action of ethical discipline, and the meritorious action of meditative cultivation.
Abiding in a mind of equanimity and great compassion, one causes all sentient beings to repent their transgressions and universally inspires them to give rise to all roots of goodness.
The Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Thirty-Fifth.
4. The Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvapiṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Thirty-Six.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperial Preceptor of the Three Baskets, Silver Light Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject, under Imperial Decree. Chapter Eleven: The Perfection of Supreme Wisdom (IV). "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

All those in training (śaikṣa), non-returners (anāgāmin), and pratyekabuddhas should first give rise to such a superior resolve regarding this meritorious activity; they shall attain the stage of non-retrogression and become Buddhas in their next life.

Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas should likewise give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy regarding this; they should also rejoice in all roots of goodness within these meritorious practices of all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present, and they should entreat all Buddhas to turn the sublime wheel of Dharma.
Within these meritorious actions, all roots of goodness for enlightenment are collectively dedicated.
To those who have not yet resolved upon bodhicitta, they are exhorted to do so; to those bodhisattvas who have already resolved upon bodhicitta, they teach the dedication of merit.

One should gather the poor through material offerings; provide medicine to those who are ill; draw near to and show compassion for those who are timid and weak; protect those who have violated the precepts with the Dharma; and lead them out of the retribution of their offenses so that they may abide in nirvana.
One should honor and make offerings to one’s preceptors and ācāryas as if they were the Buddha, the World-Honored One; one should be diligent and courageous in places where the Dharma is taught.
One should seek out Dharma masters and go to them even if it requires traveling a hundred yojanas; one should delight in hearing the true Dharma without ever becoming weary or satisfied.

One should have no expectations regarding those who preach the Dharma, but should always draw near to them, honor, and make offerings to them, never becoming weary or indolent, as if toward one’s own parents.
Furthermore, among meritorious deeds, one should not give rise to agitation or confusion in body, speech, or mind, and remain free from all faults.
Dwelling in the stupas and temples of the Buddhas, they gather the roots of all goodness and the merit of Brahma, perfecting the primary and secondary marks to adorn their transformation bodies.

They distance themselves from verbal faults to adorn their vocal karma, adorn their single-mindedness with resolute understanding, adorn the Buddha-fields with the playful exercise of supernormal powers, and adorn the characteristics of the Dharma with pure wisdom.

Hearing that True Dharma, one becomes free from all obstacles and attains non-obstruction; one rejoices in and praises the teacher of the Dharma, does not give rise to attachment toward the Dharma taught, and likewise does not cause the destruction of such an adorned gateway to liberation.

By offering various gardens and groves to the Buddha and the Sangha, thus adorning the Bodhi tree of the Buddha; by planting all roots of goodness and having compassion for all beings, purifying karma and afflictions to attain the state beyond birth and extinction—one thus adorns the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
By making inexhaustible vows to bestow all manner of delightful objects, one obtains the hand of inexhaustible jewels that is perfectly complete.

By remaining free from frowning and being as even as the palm of one's hand, and by delighting in giving to all, one first attains a countenance that is dignified and majestic, and subsequently becomes a sight that all sentient beings joyfully behold.
By bestowing radiant and pure adornments upon all sentient beings, one attains a light that universally illuminates everything;
through the power of eloquent praise, not merely from habitual practice, the treasury of ethical discipline and merit becomes entirely purified.
Born among humans and devas, their karma of the ten paths of wholesome action is likewise pure; their supernormal powers and transformations are never in vain.

Following the teachings of all Buddhas, they give rise to no discrimination; with a profoundly pure mind, they impartially transform others, becoming objects of love and respect for all sentient beings.
One should teach the supreme Dharma and the practice of resolute belief according to one's capacity, thereby being able to encompass all meritorious conduct.
Furthermore, one should give rise to the mind of omniscience, possess the seven noble riches with faith as the precursor, and be loved and respected by all the world.
Therefore, it is determined that by first providing guidance, one is able to bring to perfection all Buddha-dharmas and all wholesome dharmas.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillfulness in meritorious action.
"What is the skillfulness in the wisdom-practice of the bodhisattvas?
It refers to the arising of cognitive understanding regarding causes and conditions.
What are causes and conditions?"

That is to say, with a profound mind, they take delight in following and understanding the assemblies of the Dharma; they diligently seek out virtuous friends and abide in the wisdom of the Buddhas, rather than relying on the wisdom of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and they engender supreme faith and joy toward the masters of discourse.

The one who preaches the Dharma, having recognized that the listener’s inner faculties are fully matured, possesses no stinginess regarding wisdom and continuously expounds the profound and sublime Dharma for them.
Those who hear the Dharma should practice in such a way as to be in accord with the seeking of the Dharma; thus they will be able to be in accord with this practice of wisdom.
What is meant by being in accord with the seeking of the Dharma?

This means that having obtained some slight meaning from a Dharma teacher, one reflects upon and weighs it during the first and last watches of the night, investigating: "In what way is this logical and in what way is it illogical?

Through such successive inquiry, until the mind reaches the state of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*), one becomes free from all obstacles and untainted by defilements; thus, one attains the knowledge of liberation and initiates authentic practice.

Regarding this profound Dharma, the vast Dharma, the boundless Dharma, and the Dharma that surpasses all non-Buddhist paths, his wisdom and understanding penetrate it thoroughly and constantly radiate light. Most supremely exalted, he rises above the mountain peaks; with courageous diligence, he does not cast off his heavy burden. He practices sublime conduct with a mind focused on a single object; rich in the cultivation of mental attention, he does not abandon the dhūtas. Always delighting in the joy of the Dharma, he does not engage in worldly ways; seeking the supramundane Dharma, he remembers it without forgetfulness and proclaims it accordingly for others.

The disciples of the Noble Lineage were all filled with joy; they cultivated superior conditions for guidance, upheld the prohibitive precepts, and adorned themselves with a sense of shame and remorse. They turned toward the Buddha-way, whereby all ignorant ones who were shrouded by the darkness of ignorance naturally distanced themselves from it and attained the pure eye of wisdom—vast awakening, profound and wondrous awakening, and supremely wondrous awakening.

By means of the wisdom of observation, one is further able to discern the merits of both oneself and others, thereby bringing the karmic retribution of pure and matured deeds to full completion and purification.
This is the skillful mastery of the wise conduct of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
"Furthermore, a Bodhisattva seeking wisdom practices four kinds of giving toward a Dharma teacher. What are these four? They are:
birch-bark paper, pens, ink, and so forth;
an exquisite Dharma seat; all manner of requisites for support; and verses of praise for the assembly of the Dharma."
These are the four kinds [of qualities] that are accomplished within the practice of wisdom.
Furthermore, within the practice of wisdom, one should achieve four kinds of protection toward the Dharma teacher.
What are the four? First, guarding the body;
second, guarding wholesome qualities; third, guarding one's dwelling place; and fourth, guarding the assembly of those to be converted. These are called the four.
Furthermore, within the practice of wisdom, one accomplishes four kinds of heavy burdens. What are these four?
They are the Dharma, wisdom, material wealth, and bodhi; these constitute the four.
Furthermore, within the practice of wisdom, one accomplishes the five powers:
first, the power of faith, which is resolute conviction in the Dharma;
second, the power of diligence, which is the earnest pursuit of extensive learning.
Third is the power of mindfulness, which never forgets the bodhicitta.
Fourth is the power of meditative concentration, which is certain and equanimous regarding all phenomena.
Fifth is the power of superior wisdom, which further delights in extensive learning.
These are the five kinds [of practices] by which one attains perfection within the conduct of wisdom.
Furthermore, within the conduct of wisdom, one accomplishes four types of ethical discipline (*śīla*). What are these four?
These are called the four: the precept of the true Dharma, the precept of diligent pursuit of the Dharma, the precept of certainty in the Dharma, and the precept directed toward Bodhi.
Furthermore, those who diligently pursue the Dharma achieve four kinds of patience within the practice of wisdom.
What are the four?
First, when wicked people come to destroy, revile, or insult one, one should not retaliate, but should instead respond with kind words and offer an apology;
second, one is able to endure wind, sun, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, and so forth.
Third, to attend upon and serve one's preceptors and teachers;
fourth, to abide in the great dharma-patience regarding the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
These are the four kinds.
Furthermore, one accomplishes four kinds of diligence. What are these four? They are:
the diligence of extensive learning, the diligence of dhāraṇī-retention, the diligence of eloquent exposition, and the diligence of right practice; these are the four kinds.
Furthermore, within the practice of wisdom, one further accomplishes four kinds of supreme concentrations.
What are these four? They are:
the tranquility of signlessness, one-pointedness of mind, entry into the concentration of supernormal powers, and the realization of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; these are called the four.
Furthermore, within the practice of wisdom, one accomplishes four dharmas. What are these four? They are:

non-abiding in all existences, the absence of intrinsic nature, the lack of a sovereign master in the arising and ceasing produced by the four conditions, and exclusive resolute faith; these are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, one accomplishes four kinds of skillful means. What are these four?

First, conforming to and turning with the world; second, conforming to and turning with the sūtras; third, conforming to and turning with the Dharma; and fourth, conforming to and turning with wisdom.
These are the four kinds [of qualities] by which one attains fulfillment within the practice of wisdom.
Furthermore, one accomplishes the four paths of unimpeded knowledge. What are these four?
The so-called pāramitās, the seven factors of enlightenment, the branches of the noble eightfold path, and the knowledge of all modes—these constitute the four kinds of unobstructed paths.
Furthermore, one accomplishes four kinds of tirelessness. What are these four? They are:
tirelessness in extensive learning, tirelessness in eloquent exposition, tirelessness in investigation and reflection, and tirelessness in wisdom; these are called the four kinds.

Furthermore, within the practice of wisdom, one thus knows and sees, while simultaneously conforming to all sentient beings and all buddha-fields through generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and sublime wisdom, as well as loving-kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity.
Why is this so? Śāriputra!

To whatever extent bodhisattvas are resolute regarding all forms of knowledge, they take such knowledge and vision as their precursor. If they abide in this wisdom and attain penetration into the conduct of omniscience, they will be protected and remembered by the majestic spiritual power of all Buddhas; no Māras or similar beings shall find an opportunity against them, as they universally assemble for the sake of the knowledge of all-knowledge.
“Śāriputra!
This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains skill in the practice of knowledge within the perfection of superior wisdom.
What is the skill of the bodhisattvas in the applications of mindfulness?
The Bodhisattva’s foundations of mindfulness are of four kinds.
What are these four?

First, the foundation of mindfulness that contemplates the body by means of the body; second, the foundation of mindfulness that contemplates feelings by means of feelings; third, the foundation of mindfulness that contemplates the mind by means of the mind; and fourth, the foundation of mindfulness that contemplates phenomena by means of phenomena.
What is the application of mindfulness by observing the body with the body?

Śāriputra, when these bodhisattvas cultivate the observation of the body, they observe the prior limit of the body, the posterior limit of the body, and the present body. Yet this body arises from inversion, perishes according to causes and conditions, is without movement, without action, without intrinsic nature, and without grasping.
For example, just as the various external mountain forests, medicinal herbs, seeds, and so forth arise from causes and conditions, they likewise lack intrinsic nature and are devoid of grasping.

Furthermore, this body is like a wall, a tile, a pebble, grass, or wood—an image; that is to say, the aggregates, bases, and elements are without grasping, empty, without self or what belongs to a self, impermanent, subject to rapid decay, unsubstantial, phenomena of inversion, objects of wearying detachment, and lacking solidity.
All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should contemplate in this way: they should joyfully and diligently seek the solid body.
Why is this? Because it is the body of the Tathāgata.
The body of the Tathāgata is the Dharma-realm body, the vajra body, the indestructible body, the firm and solid body, and the most supreme and wondrous body among all things within the triple world.
When practicing this contemplation, one should know that ordinary beings are coarse, heavy, defiled, and possessed of all manner of faults;
yet they are further able to leave behind all such faults and attain the most wondrous physical marks of a Tathāgata.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the bodies of all sentient beings: by what are they produced such that their continuity remains unbroken?
It is through the immeasurable powers of the four great elements and the *ālaya-vijñāna*—their capacity for creative activity, grasping, and perfuming (*vāsanā*).

For example, just as the external great elements—the earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element—possess various doors, various locations, various names, various characteristics, and various substances, by means of which all sentient beings sustain their life-faculties (*jīvitendriya*).

The arising of the four great elements of the body is likewise thus: there are various gates, various locations, various names, various characteristics, and various substances; it is because of these that all sentient beings likewise maintain their life-faculty.
One contemplates the body as impermanent through its specific characteristics, yet does not feel weary of or seek to escape saṃsāra;
one contemplates the body as suffering through its specific characteristics, yet does not delight in abiding in nirvāṇa.
One contemplates the body as selfless through its specific characteristics, yet does not abandon the transformation and deliverance of sentient beings.
One contemplates the body as empty and quiescent through its specific characteristics, yet does not fall into ultimate extinction.
By contemplating the body through its specific characteristics, one remains detached from it yet does not abandon wholesome dharmas.
One who is thus able to contemplate the body with the body should understand that it is neither solid nor desirable.

By observing the internal body, one knows that afflictions cannot be accommodated; by observing the external body, one realizes that various afflictions do not gather together, thereby achieving pure bodily action and attaining a pure and adorned physical form, which is praised and revered by all devas and humans.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains the application of mindfulness by observing the body with the body.
How do the bodhisattvas observe feelings with the application of mindfulness of feelings?

That is to say, regarding all those sensations of suffering, pleasure, and so forth, Bodhisattvas should skillfully comprehend them through wisdom and expedient means. They should harbor no sense of attachment or stinginess toward pleasant sensations; when they perceive the touch of suffering experienced in the evil realms, they give rise to great compassion without any thought of ceasing it; and regarding the touch of both painful and pleasant sensations, they remain free from ignorance, clearly understanding them through mindfulness.
In this way, one gains the vision of liberation regarding suffering, pleasure, and that which is neither suffering nor pleasure.
Yet, through wisdom and skillful means, bodhisattvas act toward sentient beings either to bring them to fulfillment or to cause them to distance themselves [from such states].

However, these sentient beings lack understanding regarding the attainment of renunciation; they indulge in pleasant sensations as they arise, seek to eliminate painful sensations as they occur, and fail to attain pliancy by conforming to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) regarding sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant. [The Bodhisattva] gathers them in through great skillful means and teaches them the sublime Dharma, so that these sentient beings may likewise attain pliancy.
By what causes and conditions are such feelings said to exist?
It is said that when there is accomplishment in the wholesome, there is pleasant feeling; when there is accomplishment in the unwholesome, there is painful feeling.

Furthermore, in this regard, the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span give rise to various kinds of feeling, namely: grasping-feeling, appropriation-feeling, perverted-feeling, conceptualization-feeling, wrong-view-feeling, feeling arising from the perception of the eye up to the perception of the mind, feeling arising from the perception of forms up to the perception of phenomena, and even all feelings produced with eye-contact as a condition.

To state it briefly: even down to the various feelings produced with mental contact as a condition regarding internal and external phenomena—whether they be painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—are called "feeling."
"Furthermore, within the aggregate as a whole, there may be one type of feeling, namely that which is indicated by a single moment of mind;
two types of feeling, namely those indicated by the internal and the external;
or three types of feeling, namely those indicated by the past, the future, and the present."
The four feelings refer to what is manifested by the four great elements.
The five feelings refer to the mental attention toward the five aggregates.
The six feelings refer to the pervasive conceptualization of the six sense bases.
The seven feelings refer to the seven stations of consciousness.
The eight feelings refer to that which is associated with the eight wrong paths.
The nine feelings refer to the nine abodes of sentient beings.
The ten feelings refer to the ten paths of wholesome action.

This extends to the total summary of all various types of feelings and mental attentions; therefore, one should know that the feelings of sentient beings are immeasurable, and their mental attentions are likewise immeasurable.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas contemplate pleasant feelings, they see sentient beings dwelling at the limit of saṃsāra; they cause wisdom to arise in them and reveal to them wholesome and unwholesome feelings.
Śāriputra! This is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the application of mindfulness by observing feelings with regard to feelings.
What is the bodhisattvas' application of mindfulness by observing the mind with regard to the mind?

This means that all bodhisattvas, maintaining secret protection through unwavering right mindfulness, observe this mind as arising and ceasing with extreme rapidity—devoid of form or characteristics and lacking any place of abiding; it is neither within, nor without, nor in between.
One knows that the very subtlest atom of the initial resolve is utterly devoid of mental characteristics, such that its spatial dimensions cannot be apprehended at all.
All the roots of goodness accumulated by that mind are likewise utterly devoid of even the subtlest atom, and are without spatial dimensions.
Furthermore, one dedicates this mind toward bodhi;
regarding its own essential nature, there is nothing for the mind to cognize, nothing for the mind to observe, and nothing for the mind to enter.
The Buddha said:
"Therefore, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Why is this?

It is because the bodhicitta and that wholesome mind do not function together; furthermore, the mind of roots of goodness and the bodhicitta do not function together; furthermore, the mind of roots of goodness and the mind of dedication do not function together; and furthermore, the mind of dedication and both the bodhicitta and the mind of roots of goodness do not function together at all."
One should observe in this manner and not give rise to fear; subsequently, one will attain the profound dependent origination of unimpaired cause and effect.

Now, the mind of dharmatā is the very nature of sentient beings; thus, it likewise belongs to the causes and conditions of all phenomena, being unmoving, unconditioned, and without a sovereign master. It is like a covering obscuration, characterized by its non-commonality with [the phenomenal].
Therefore, one should know that this mind of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-citta*) also does not function in common [with other minds].
What is the nature of phenomena and what is the obscured mind?
As for the mind of the nature of phenomena, it refers to that state wherein nothing at all is bestowed.
Furthermore, if one dedicates all that exists to universally cover and adorn the Buddha-fields, this mind is an obscuration.
Just as those illusory transformations are utterly quiescent and pure in a single kṣaṇa, it is called the mind of dharmatā.
Furthermore, if one gathers various precepts and dedicates them toward all swift supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), this mind is an obscuration.
Just as a dream is ultimately exhausted and utterly vanishes without remainder, it is called the mind of *dharmatā*.
Furthermore, if one delights in the power of patience up to the dedication that universally covers and adorns, this is an obscuration of the mind.
Just as a mirage is ultimately devoid of the characteristics of body and mind, it is called the "mind of dharmatā."
If one further arouses all diligence and dedicates it toward the fulfillment of all Buddha-dharmas, this is an obscuration of the mind.
Like the moon in water, which is neither grasped nor seen, it is called the mind of dharmatā.
Furthermore, if one dedicates all dhyānas, liberations, samādhis, and samāpattis toward the samādhis of the Buddhas, this constitutes an obscuration.
That which is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, and non-indicative is called the mind of dharmatā.
If one further uses wisdom to analytically explain all pure phrases and meanings, dedicating them toward the fulfillment of the wisdom of all Buddhas, this constitutes an obscuration.
These various designations are called the "mind of dharmatā."
Furthermore, if there is any interruption in the various roots of goodness, this constitutes an obscuration.
A mind that arises without causes is called the *dharmatā*-mind.
If, however, it arises due to the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), this constitutes an obscuration.
Liberation from the six sense objects is called the mind of dharmatā.
If, moreover, there is anything to be severed or extinguished within the realm of the Buddha, this constitutes an obscuration. Śāriputra!

When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices in this way, observing the movements of the mind, they abide in supernormal powers; having attained those powers within a single moment of mind, they are able to discern the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, and having known them, they preach the Dharma to them in accordance with their respective natures.

Furthermore, abiding in great compassion, having attained that great compassion, one is able to transform and deliver all sentient beings without weariness; through the empowerment of this contemplative practice, this mind is inexhaustible and undying.

Furthermore, even if one enters the limits of saṃsāra and severs all fetters, if one does not give rise to conceptual thoughts or intellectualizing regarding this mind, but transcends all conditioned phenomena, such that it cannot be reached by any śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha, one will abide securely in this mind until all Buddha-dharmas are perfected.
This mind, in a single kṣaṇa, is able to enter into equal correspondence with supreme wisdom and will certainly achieve the fruit of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s application of mindfulness by observing the mind with the mind.
*The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka*, Fascicle Thirty-Six.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha,
Scroll Thirty-Seventh.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of the Western Heaven, Silver Light Grandee.

Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Dharma-pāla, a Subject and Grand Master of the Propagation of the Dharma (Chuanfan Dashi) who received the purple robe, together with others, including Shi Guanglu Qing Cijue: The Chapter on the Perfection of Supreme Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), Part Eleven, Section Five. The Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"How do the Bodhisattvas practice the application of mindfulness of phenomena by observing phenomena?"

This means that bodhisattvas, by means of the eye of noble wisdom, perceive all phenomena and attain realization therein; even when they contemplate the nature of phenomena at the seat of enlightenment, they do not see anything at all, not even so much as a mote of dust.

If the liberation of emptiness is itself the liberation of signlessness, the liberation of wishlessness, the liberation of non-arising, the liberation of non-birth, the liberation of non-action, the liberation of non-nature, and the liberation of dependent origination, then bodhisattvas should contemplate all phenomena in this manner.
What is called "Dharma"?
It refers to the meaning of no-self, the meaning of no person, the meaning of no sentient being, and the meaning of no life-span; this is called Dharma.
What is non-Dharma?

That is to say: the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, the view of a life-span, the view of permanence and the view of annihilation, the view of existence and the view of non-existence—these are called non-Dharma.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
This dharma and non-dharma encompass all dharmas and non-dharmas. Why is this so?
That is to say, the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—are that which can universally and fully comprehend all phenomena; these are the dharmas.
Deep-seated attachment to the view of a self and so forth is that which is contrary to the dharma; these are the non-dharmas.

Therefore, when a bodhisattva practices the contemplation of phenomena (dharmānupaśyanā), they see nothing whatsoever, even down to the most subtle degree; they attain liberation from all phenomena and the path to enlightenment, becoming entirely free from obstacles, and they do not give rise to thoughts of great compassion based on attachment or biased views toward sentient beings.
He is free from afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Why is this?

Because, having understood the definitive meaning and entered into the realization that both persons and phenomena are empty (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), there is no accumulation of afflictions; rather, he is able to awaken to the fact that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those afflictions is itself the nature of awakening (*bodhi*), and that the nature of awakening is itself the nature of affliction.
Thus, the foundations of mindfulness are equal in all phenomena, just like space.

Furthermore, when bodhisattvas practice the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*), they are able to counteract [obstacles] regarding the Buddha-dharmas; they contemplate all sentient beings until they exhaust the wisdom of their births, realize that unconditioned state (*asaṃskṛta*) through the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), and do not abandon the limit of non-arising (*anutpādakoṭi*).

Thus, by penetrating the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), one immediately attains stable abiding in the mindfulness of all phenomena. One does not give rise to attachment or delight toward the teachings of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; rather, one resolutely abides in the applications of mindfulness of the Buddhas, never forgetting them and remaining free from delusion. Even unto the final limit of the application of mindfulness to phenomena, one is able to expound immeasurable uncommon realms, entering into and understanding all Buddha-dharmas with equanimity, causing the minds of all sentient beings to rejoice, and naturally knowing and comprehending all demonic māras.
This is called the application of mindfulness that contemplates phenomena by means of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā-smṛtyupasthāna*). Śāriputra,
it is through these four kinds of skillfulness in the applications of mindfulness that bodhisattva mahāsattvas attain proficiency in the perfection of superior wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
“What is the skillfulness of bodhisattvas regarding the factors conducive to enlightenment?
There are seven kinds of factors conducive to enlightenment. What are these seven?”

First is the awakening factor of mindfulness; second is the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena; third is the awakening factor of energy; fourth is the awakening factor of joy; fifth is the awakening factor of tranquility; sixth is the awakening factor of concentration; and seventh is the awakening factor of equanimity. These are called the seven.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It refers to being mindful of the dharmas realized, observing, discerning, analyzing, selecting, and comprehending them.
Furthermore, one should be mindful of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) of those dharmas in accordance with awakening, just as one realizes through mindfulness that all dharmas are empty.
This is called the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the investigation-of-dharmas factor of enlightenment (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the discernment by means of wisdom within the aggregate of eighty-four thousand teachings; having investigated them according to the Dharma, that which is of definitive meaning is understood as being of definitive meaning, that which is not of definitive meaning is understood as not being of definitive meaning; that which is conventional is understood as being conventional, that which is ultimate is understood as being ultimate; that which is intentional is understood as being intentional, and that which is definitive is understood as being definitive—just as one has thus discerned them.
This is called the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the factor of enlightenment of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to the discernment of phenomena through reflection and the resulting knowledge and understanding; it is the delight in cultivating meditative concentration, tranquility, and pliancy. One should, by the power of diligent effort, subdue those attachments, and with a longing for the path to enlightenment, remain without retreat or abandonment of one’s burden.
This is called the factor of enlightenment of diligence (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*).
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-sambodhyaṅga*)?

It refers to delighting in hearing the sound of the Dharma; with a pure mind, one does not give rise to weariness or fatigue. Free from all objective attachments and the bonds of afflictions, one’s sincere aspiration and longing reach such a point that even the hairs on one's body stand on end as one attains the great Dharma-joy.
This is called the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It refers to being free from all obstacles such as lethargy and agitation within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), thereby causing both body and mind to attain pliancy.
This is called the enlightenment factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is the enlightenment factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It refers to the profound abiding of the wisdom that understands all phenomena through a mind in meditative equipoise (*samāhita-citta*), observing that the nature of all phenomena is entirely equal.
This is called the enlightenment factor of samādhi.
What is the enlightenment factor of equanimity?

It refers to the mind being unmoved by phenomena associated with sorrow or joy; neither increasing nor decreasing in regard to worldly phenomena; conforming to the noble path; and being without dwelling, without movement, and without affliction regarding oneself, others, or both together.
This is called the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Śāriputra,
bodhisattva mahāsattvas attain such skillfulness in these seven types of enlightenment factors within the perfection of superior wisdom.
"What is the bodhisattvas' skillfulness regarding the noble path?
It consists of eight kinds. What are these eight?"

First is right view, second is right discrimination, third is right speech, fourth is right action, fifth is right livelihood, sixth is right effort, seventh is right mindfulness, and eighth is right concentration; these are called the eight.
What is right view?

It refers to a vision that transcends all worldly realms, which does not arise from the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, or the view of a life-span; nor does it arise from the view of permanence or annihilation, the view of existence or non-existence, the view of good or evil, up to and including the view of nirvana.
This is called right view.
What is right discernment?
It refers to discerning greed, hatred, delusion, and all other afflictions so that they do not arise.
To discernfully analyze ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, causing them to be firmly established—
this is called right discernment.
What is right speech?

This means that regarding the words of one's own friends and those of others, there is no distinction between "self" and "other"; being fully endowed with such correspondence, one enters the path of equanimity.
This is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*).
What is right action (*samyak-karmānta*)?
This means that regarding the retribution of dark karma, one ensures it is not produced and causes it to be completely exhausted;
regarding the retribution of white karma, one brings together its own kind so that goodness reaches full maturity.
This is called right action.
What is right livelihood?

It means that a disciple of the noble lineage, bearing the heavy burden for the sake of the noble path, maintains and nourishes his physical life so as to increase and fulfill it; he does not seek through confusion, deception, evil means, or excessive seeking; he does not give rise to regret or vexation regarding the gains obtained by others; and he does not give rise to delight or attachment toward whatever gain and sustenance he himself receives.
This is called right livelihood.
What is right effort?
It refers to not exerting diligence toward wrong conduct, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the secondary afflictions.
Entering the path of the Noble Truths and proceeding toward the fruit of Nirvana while being able to give rise to great diligence in accordance with that goal—
this is called Right Effort.
What is Right Mindfulness?

This means that one abides in the right path through this mindfulness, remaining free from the deviousness and the faults of saṃsāra; furthermore, even regarding the vision of the path to nirvāṇa, one should remain detached within such mindfulness, so as to be without confusion concerning the noble path.
This is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration?
It refers to the correct realization of equality, which is the equality of all phenomena; abiding in samādhi, one is able to transcend that very correct realization.
Furthermore, when a bodhisattva abides in samādhi, they are able to liberate all sentient beings and can also transcend even prior correct realization.
This is called right concentration.
Furthermore, the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones of the past, present, and future, have equally revealed the inexhaustible Noble Path to all bodhisattvas within the Eightfold Noble Path. "Śāriputra!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who is skilled in the Noble Path should cultivate the factors that assist the path.
What are these factors that assist the path?
They are śamatha and vipaśyanā; these are called the factors that assist the path.

What is śamatha? It refers to causing the mind to be detached and tranquil, becoming utterly still and reaching the state of supreme tranquility; it involves guarding the sense faculties so they are unmoving and unshakable, without fluctuation; the mouth is strictly guarded and free from flattery or deceit; the mind is one-pointed; it remains far removed from clamor and all perils, delighting in dwelling in solitude.

He maintains his body and life in purity and well-being, remaining constantly careful and discreet in his deportment and conduct, even to the point of being fully endowed with the knowledge of the proper time, the appropriate portion, and the correct measure for sustenance.
Even if one hears slander, one should practice patience and, with an even deeper mind, always delight in solitary meditation (*pratisaṃlayana*).

Therefore, one should apply the mental attention (*manasikāra*) of the factors of concentration to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; through skillful means and unimpededly, one dwells in the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), from the first dhyāna up to the eighth dhyāna.
Regarding śamatha, one should first practice it.
I say that there are furthermore immeasurable modes of śamatha; one should also accord with these modes, and this is called śamatha.

What is vipaśyanā? It refers to observing the emptiness of all phenomena within the domain of wisdom; observing that there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span; observing those five aggregates as being like illusions and transformations; observing the eighteen elements as being the nature of the dharma-realm; observing the twelve sense bases as being like an empty village; observing that the faculties such as the eye function differently according to their respective objects; observing that all dependent origination is without contradiction; and observing that the views of sentient beings are ultimately and utterly removed.
Furthermore, one contemplates that causes inevitably bring about their results; one contemplates results as if they were directly realized before one;

and through contemplating all things with correct penetration, one transcends even further. Moreover, vipaśyanā refers to seeing all phenomena as being like space—without marks, without aspiration, and without distinction.
One contemplates that there is no cause and no place of arising or ceasing; seeing nothing to be attained, one attains the state of having nothing to observe.

Within this state of having nothing to observe, one further scrutinizes and contemplates the absence of anything to observe; knowing that the observer is likewise thus, such contemplation is contemplation according to reality. Through contemplation according to reality, one is able to attain the true skillfulness of *vipaśyanā*.
These bodhisattvas do not fall away from this practice, nor do they dwell with attachment to any roots of goodness. Śāriputra,
this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains such factors conducive to enlightenment within the perfection of supreme wisdom.
"Furthermore, there are four aspects of skillfulness regarding the right path for bodhisattvas.
What are these four?

First, the desire to prevent unarisen sinful and unwholesome dharmas from arising; second, the desire to eliminate and sever sinful and unwholesome dharmas that have already arisen; third, the desire to give rise to wholesome dharmas that have not yet arisen; and fourth, the desire to cause wholesome dharmas that have already arisen to endure long-term without being impaired."
Cultivating various contemplative practices so as not to forget them, and generating a mind of diligence to embrace right aspirations—
these are all designations for the profound mental attention that seeks to prevent the previously mentioned unwholesome dharmas from arising;
likewise, generating a mind of diligence to embrace right aspirations and profoundly observing with the deep mind are also designations for the same.
Why is this? It is because the Dharma is without accumulation and is liberation through the profound mind; this is called wholesome dharma.
What is called unwholesome dharma?
This refers to that which is counteracted by morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
What is the counteraction regarding morality?
It refers to the violation and falling away from the names and the practices of morality.
What is the counteragent regarding meditative concentration?
It refers to the arising of a distracted mind within the aggregate of samādhi, which destroys noble practice.
What is the counteragent regarding wisdom?

This refers to repeatedly giving rise to views regarding all phenomena and forming obstructive understandings; it is the tendency toward the aggregate of superior wisdom that destroys the absence of views—this is called that which is counteracted by morality, concentration, and wisdom.

Regarding the unwholesome dharmas of previously committed sinful karma that have already arisen, one should, with such modes of conduct and deep mental attention, desire to eliminate and sever them, and arouse a mind of diligence to embrace right aspirations.
These unwholesome dharmas should be shielded by the mind and not disclosed; all wholesome dharmas should be constantly gathered and practiced by the mind.

Regarding the afflictions to be countered, such as greed, hatred, and delusion, one should fully understand that they arise from objective conditions (*ālambana*): counteract greed with the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), counteract hatred with the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*), and counteract the darkness of delusion with the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*). Purifying all afflictions in this way constitutes liberation.
Furthermore, regarding all those things that should not be universally abandoned, one generates observation toward all phenomena.
This is called the first and second right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Moreover, it is said: "In order to give rise to wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one arouses the mind of diligence and embraces the right vow."
These are immeasurable. Why is this so?
It is because all bodhisattvas plant roots of goodness, apply themselves with diligence and aspiration to embrace superior practices, and thus accumulate immeasurable wholesome dharmas.
This is called the third right abandonment (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding right abandonment: for the sake of causing already arisen wholesome dharmas to endure long, remain undamaged, and not be forgotten, one arouses a mind of diligence and embraces right aspiration.
If one dedicates these roots of goodness toward enlightenment, this is merely a figurative expression. Why is that?
Because there is no enlightenment toward which one can dedicate; thus, these roots of goodness remain undestroyed.
Why is this? Because such a resolve does not emerge from the triple world.
If it were to emerge from the triple world, these roots of goodness would then be utterly exhausted.

Why is this? Because such a resolve issues forth from the triple world; if one can dedicate [merit] toward omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*) without having emerged from the triple world, then these roots of goodness will never be exhausted.
This is called the fourth right abandonment. Śāriputra,
this is how a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains skillfulness in the fourfold path regarding the practice of the perfection of superior wisdom.
"Furthermore, there are five characteristics of bodhisattvas' skillfulness regarding the right path.
What are these five? First, the faculty of faith; second, the faculty of diligence; third, the faculty of mindfulness; fourth, the faculty of samādhi; and fifth, the faculty of supreme wisdom."
What is the faculty of faith?
There are four dharmas in which one has faith. What are these four?
This means giving rise to right view, believing in the existence of the world and the activities of saṃsāra, and obtaining the karmic results thereof as an antidote.

By virtue of that life-force, one refrains from committing sinful deeds; one believes in the bodhisattva practices and practices accordingly; one does not give rise to attachment toward the requisites for sustaining the body; and one generates correct understanding regarding the profound ultimate truth and all definitive teachings.

Regarding the conduct toward sentient beings, they believe that all phenomena are characterized by emptiness and signlessness; they take no pleasure in or resolve upon the fabrications of various views.
Having heard of the powers and fearlessnesses of the Buddha-dharmas, they become free from all attachment.
Furthermore, all other verbal expressions concerning those Buddha-dharmas are entirely accumulated.
This is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
What is the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*)?
This means that having faith in this Dharma, one initiates diligence; this is called the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*).
Through this diligence, one accumulates all dharmas without causing any impairment to the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*); this is called the faculty of mindfulness.
Because this faculty of mindfulness is indestructible, it possesses one-pointedness regarding the samādhi-faculty among all phenomena; this is called the samādhi-faculty.
Because of this one-pointedness of the samādhi-faculty, one is able to observe all phenomena with the wisdom-faculty and thereby achieve thorough understanding; this is called the wisdom-faculty.
Thus, by accumulating and binding oneself to these five faculties, one attains the perfection of all Buddha-dharmas up to the stage of receiving the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*).

For example, just as those with the five external supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) do not undergo gestation in a womb, and even attain liberation from the male and female faculties and so forth, so too do the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the Bodhisattvas achieve accomplishment through these five faculties.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness in the five kinds of right paths regarding the perfection of superior wisdom. “Śāriputra!
Furthermore, the right path of a bodhisattva has five characteristics.
What are these five? First is the power of faith; second is the power of diligence; third is the power of mindfulness; fourth is the power of samādhi; and fifth is the power of superior wisdom.
What is the power of faith?
It refers to having faith and understanding in the Dharma.

Even if Māra Pāpīyas were to manifest in the form of a Buddha and approach one to preach a divergent teaching, by virtue of the power of faith, not even a particle of dust’s worth of this True Dharma could be destroyed; through the investigation of wisdom, one completely eliminates and severs it.
Furthermore, that which is spoken by Māra is not the Buddha-dharma; it is a perverted accumulation regarding the four great elements and the retributions of karma.
Yet, through the power of faith and understanding, Bodhisattvas investigate with a profound mind and do not accept it at all. This is called the Bodhisattva’s power of faith.
What is the bodhisattva’s power of diligence?

It refers to being able to initiate courageous diligence to enter into and understand wholesome dharmas, attaining firm strength wherever one may be. Whether among devas or humans, no such power can cause the bodhisattva to waver or be shaken from their station; this is called the bodhisattva’s power of diligence.
What is the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*) of a bodhisattva?

It refers to the mind abiding securely in the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding phenomena; such that various afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot disturb it, and by the power of mindfulness, one destroys all afflictions and further attains this pure right mindfulness—this is called the power of mindfulness of a bodhisattva.
What is the bodhisattva’s power of samādhi?

It refers to dwelling alone in a secluded and quiet place, far removed from all bustle and clamor, completely detached from all speech and sounds, and free from any攀缘 (pān-yuan) or counteractive application; this is called the first dhyāna-concentration.
Attaining unimpeded mastery over wholesome vitarka and vicāra is called the second dhyāna.
Attaining unimpeded mastery over the practice of joy and bliss is called the third dhyāna.
To embrace the True Dharma and transform sentient beings without ever abandoning them or encountering obstacles is called the fourth dhyāna-concentration.

To be unable to be destroyed by the counteractive factors within the practice of the four dhyānas, to remain undetached from the state of that concentration, and to give rise to no craving or attachment toward samādhi—this is called the bodhisattva’s power of samādhi.
What is the bodhisattva’s power of superior wisdom?

It is the ability to comprehend mundane and supramundane phenomena in a single instant; such wisdom cannot be destroyed by anything. Furthermore, regarding all crafts and various worldly arts, whether near or far, he is able to accomplish that which is difficult to perform.

Furthermore, these bodhisattvas manifest the attainment of supramundane dharmas; that is to say, their wisdom is lofty and eminent, surpassing all mundane things, and cannot be destroyed by any devas, humans, asuras, or others. This is called the bodhisattva’s power of superior wisdom.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva attains these five kinds of skillfulness in the right path regarding the perfection of superior wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The Mahāyāna Sūtra of the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, Scroll Thirty-Seven.
