Translated by the Imperial Edict by the Śramaṇa Dharma-pāla, a Subject and Master of the Transmission of the *Fan* (Sanskrit) Language, who was conferred the rank of Purple-Robed Monk and the title of Director of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Shiguangluqing), together with others. Chapter Eleven: The Perfection of Superior Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā), Part Six. "Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."

To speak briefly of the single type of noble path of a bodhisattva: it is that a bodhisattva, regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment as solitary and peerless, receives it with a profound mind through the power of their own courageous and great diligence; without relying on external conditions or the instruction of others, they personally accomplish a most powerful efficacy and are thus able to don such firm armor.

Furthermore, those sentient beings who find it difficult to attain have now attained; those who have newly resolved to abide in the Bodhisattva vehicle have now attained what they had not previously attained.
Moreover, they are able to practice all that is difficult to give, and the same applies to their observance of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and supreme wisdom.
Furthermore, while there is no one capable of establishing the *pāramitās*, this bodhisattva is able to establish all the *pāramitās*.

To speak briefly, no one can equal him in planting roots of goodness for the sake of vast awakening; thus, in the practice of this Dharma, he is solitary and peerless. Proceeding to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), he sits upon the diamond throne (*vajrāsana*) and subdues the power of Māra. In a single instant, through the union with transcendent wisdom (*jñāna*), he becomes certain and equanimous regarding the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, never again to regress.
Śāriputra! This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillfulness regarding the noble path of a bodhisattva attained within the perfection of superior wisdom.
"What is the bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding dependent origination?"

It means that this bodhisattva, dwelling alone in seclusion during the day and night, gives rise to wholesome investigation and reflection: "From what do the aggregates arise? By what power do they come to be? He reflects:

"Through such improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), ignorance (*avidyā*) arises; conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); conditioned by volitional formations is consciousness (*vijñāna*); conditioned by consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); conditioned by the six sense bases is contact (*sparśa*); conditioned by contact is feeling (*vedanā*); conditioned by feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); conditioned by craving is grasping (*upādāna*); conditioned by grasping is becoming (*bhava*); conditioned by becoming is birth (*jāti*); and conditioned by birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair, as well as the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), arise through their accumulation."
Furthermore, because these phenomena lack intrinsic nature, lack agency, and lack a sovereign controller, all causes—whether virtuous, non-virtuous, or indeterminate—are dependently originated.

Furthermore, all sentient beings have their respective measures; that is to say, he fully understands all the causes for their arising and gathering—namely, the cause of the faculties, the dominant cause of the faculties, the cause of karma, the cause of results, and the causes such as the finite or infinite limits of existence.
This is called skillfulness regarding dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Furthermore, as for the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*), how do they cease? It is said:

through the cessation of improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), ignorance (*avidyā*) ceases; with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness (*vijñāna*) ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact (*sparśa*) ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling (*vedanā*) ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging (*upādāna*) ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence (*bhava*) ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth (*jāti*) ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. One attains such wisdom regarding this process.

Furthermore, skill in the dependent origination [of phenomena] means that all dharmas are bound to the conjunction of causes and conditions; thus, one is able to sustain the absence of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span, and thereby attains non-conceptualization regarding such things.

Furthermore, regarding this dependent origination, bodhisattvas are able to establish all the Buddha-dharmas and the characteristics of enlightenment; they should skillfully contemplate the cessation of that which is finite, while gathering and transforming sentient beings through the cessation of that which is infinite.
Śāriputra! A bodhisattva mahāsattva, regarding the perfection of superior wisdom,
attains such skillfulness in dependent origination.
“What is a bodhisattva’s skillfulness regarding all phenomena?
‘All phenomena’ refers to the conditioned and the unconditioned.
A bodhisattva should understand that they are skillful regarding both the conditioned and the unconditioned in this way.”

Skillfulness regarding the conditioned refers to all virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind that observes the conditioned awakening directed toward omniscience; this is called skillfulness regarding the conditioned.

Furthermore, there is skillfulness regarding the conditioned, which refers to the accumulation of the five perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration;

and if one further attains unconditioned wisdom within the perfection of superior insight (*prajñāpāramitā*), yet does not abandon the other five perfections, skillfully seeking all perfections, and with faith and understanding in untainted awakening (*anāsrava-bodhi*) directed toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), this is called skillfulness regarding the unconditioned.

Furthermore, there is skillfulness regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This refers to practicing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) toward sentient beings without any sense of rejection; although one gathers in sentient beings, in reality there is no gathering, for there is neither self nor person.

One is also without grasping toward skillfulness in these means of attraction, and with faith and understanding directed toward unconditioned enlightenment and all-knowledge—this is called skillfulness regarding the unconditioned.

Furthermore, skill in the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-kauśalya*) refers to severing the continuity of the bonds of all formations (*saṃskāra*). That is to say, it is the severing of saṃsāra and the bonds of afflictions (*kleśa*); it is the non-accumulation of the subtle portions of continuity and bondage that would otherwise maintain the characteristics of enlightenment (*bodhi*). This is called skill in the conditioned.

Furthermore, if one uses wisdom to investigate emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, thoroughly understands the causal conditions of all phenomena, and practices the conduct of enlightenment without realizing the unconditioned, this is called skillfulness regarding the unconditioned.
Furthermore, although one acts within the three realms, one is not bound or attached by the afflictions of the three realms; this is called skillfulness regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-kuśala*).

If, through wisdom, one understands the transcendence of the three realms, yet does not depart from them nor fall into them, this is called skillfulness regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-kuśala*).
If one speaks of skillfulness regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma-kuśala*), this is merely a designation for omniscience (*sarvajñā*).

If one thoroughly penetrates and perfects omniscience without any diminution, and speaks of this as skillfulness in supreme wisdom, this is precisely what is called skillfulness regarding all phenomena.

Śāriputra! When bodhisattva-mahāsattvas abide in the practice of the perfection of superior wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they attain these ten kinds of skillfulness within the category of superior wisdom.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“What is superior wisdom?
What is the pāramitā?”
Exalted wisdom refers to the observation and thorough knowledge of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; this is called exalted wisdom.
To differentiate immeasurable gateways of reality as they truly are, this is called exalted wisdom.
To penetrate all views and attain the dharma of non-obstruction is called supreme wisdom.
To abide securely in all right vows while truly relinquishing all seeking through those vows is called supreme wisdom.
To be free from all feverish afflictions and attain pliancy is called supreme wisdom.
To sever all objects of attachment and attain the great dharma-joy is called supreme wisdom.
To observe according to the meaning is called supreme wisdom.
To abide in all factors of enlightenment is called supreme wisdom.
To understand, as they truly are, both signs and signlessness is called supreme wisdom.
To illuminate and comprehend the essential nature of all phenomena through gnosis is called supreme wisdom.
To transcend all perils and difficulties and attain non-obstruction is called supreme wisdom.
To embrace correct realization is called supreme wisdom.
To bring all wholesome dharmas to purity is called supreme wisdom.
To sever the habitual tendencies of afflictions is called supreme wisdom.
To have previously cultivated and realized all wholesome dharmas is called supreme wisdom.
To give rise to awakening regarding that which arises spontaneously and so forth, thereby guiding others toward detachment, is called supreme wisdom.
Non-attachment to the three realms is called supreme wisdom.
The uninterrupted continuity of all noble vows is called supreme wisdom.
Subduing and eliminating pervasive conceptualization through signlessness, thereby attaining the purity of the antidote, is called supreme wisdom.
To be free from all dullness and to accomplish all stages of corresponding practice is called supreme wisdom.
To abide in the path of light within the knowledge of all modes of knowledge is called supreme wisdom.
To act as a clear eye for those obscured by the darkness of ignorance is called supreme wisdom.
To attain the faculty of the untainted eye through such faith and understanding is called supreme wisdom.
That which transcends all ultimate meanings within the path of the eye’s objects is called supreme wisdom.
True renunciation, immovability, and self-mastery are called supreme wisdom.
Illuminating the gateway of wisdom without end is called supreme wisdom.
That which is non-contradictory throughout all places is called supreme wisdom.
That which is ever exalted within the path of liberation is called supreme wisdom.
That which dwells nowhere with any afflictions or obstructive dharmas is called supreme wisdom.

Śāriputra! By means of such supreme wisdom, bodhisattvas are able to penetrate and understand the inclinations of the minds of all sentient beings, the distinctions among their karmic actions, and the various gateways of worldly afflictions; even by means of such wisdom regarding the gateway of grasping, they are able to fully know all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and samyaksaṃbuddhas. This is what is called supreme wisdom.
Furthermore, all bodhisattvas should train in the meaning of these phrases.
Moreover, Śāriputra, as for "pāramitā," it refers to supreme wisdom that thoroughly understands all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas; this is called pāramitā.
In brief, all that is to be studied regarding the meaning of these phrases is called *pāramitā*.
Furthermore, the supreme perfection of the bodhisattva’s conduct is called *pāramitā*.
The perfection of the knowledge of all modes is called *pāramitā*.
Being entirely without attachment to conditioned and unconditioned phenomena is called *pāramitā*.
That which brings about awakening to the faults of saṃsāra is called a pāramitā.
That which can universally manifest the inexhaustible treasury of Dharma is called a pāramitā.
That which is free from all objective referents and possesses the perfection of liberation is called a *pāramitā*.
That which universally awakens others to generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and superior wisdom is called a *pāramitā*.

Ultimate skillfulness that guides all within the realm of sentient beings, in order to bring them to the fulfillment of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena and the stage of non-retrogression, is called a *pāramitā*.

To fully perfect the buddha-field and transform sentient beings, to reach the site of enlightenment and eliminate all demonic adversaries, and to attain the perfection of all buddha-dharmas—this is called *pāramitā*.
Furthermore, that which can thus establish the sublime Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva-piṭaka is called the *pāramitā*.
Śāriputra, because all bodhisattvas,
having trained in this treasury of the sublime Dharma in such a manner, attain the further shore (*pāra*), they should train accordingly in all these *pāramitās* of the Mahāyāna.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!

If a son of good family or a daughter of good family receives, maintains, reads, recites, extensively expounds, and explains to others this True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, they shall obtain ten kinds of praiseworthy merits."

What are these ten? First, having passed beyond this life, one attains mastery over all undertakings; second, one is born into a noble lineage; third, one possesses great renown; fourth, the words one speaks are joyfully accepted with faith by others; fifth, one attains great wealth and abundance; sixth, one is loved and respected by humans and devas; seventh, one becomes a universal monarch (*cakravartin*); eighth, one is born in the Brahma world; ninth, [the original Sanskrit text is missing]; tenth, in all places, one’s bodhicitta remains without decline or loss.
Furthermore, one attains ten kinds of praiseworthy merits. What are these ten? First, not dwelling together with the Nirgranthas and others;

second, not giving rise to the view of a self (*ātman*); third, not giving rise to the view of a person (*pudgala*); fourth, not giving rise to the view of a sentient being (*sattva*); fifth, not giving rise to the view of a life-force (*jīva*); sixth, not giving rise to the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*); seventh, not giving rise to the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*); eighth, relinquishing all worldly amusements and pleasures; ninth, generating pure faith and constantly delighting in renunciation; and tenth, swiftly attaining realization and entry into names, phrases, and syllables.
Furthermore, one attains ten kinds of praiseworthy qualities.

What are these ten? First, right mindfulness; second, keen intelligence; third, dhāraṇī-retention; fourth, superior wisdom; fifth, perfection in every moment; sixth, attainment of the recollection of past lives; seventh, a nature with little desire; eighth, a nature with little anger; ninth, a nature with little delusion; and tenth, not being scorched or boiled by the blazing three poisons.
Furthermore, they attain ten kinds of praiseworthy qualities.

What are these ten? First, rare and superior wisdom; second, swift and nimble superior wisdom; third, fierce and sharp superior wisdom; fourth, extremely rapid superior wisdom; fifth, vast and expansive superior wisdom; sixth, profoundly deep superior wisdom; seventh, discerning superior wisdom; eighth, unimpeded superior wisdom; ninth, the ability to behold the Tathāgata face-to-face and praise him with verses and songs; and tenth, engaging in profound dialogue with the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, one attains ten kinds of praiseworthy merits. What are these ten?

First, being able to guard against and protect oneself from evil associates; second, understanding and releasing the bonds of Māra; third, destroying the armies of Māra; fourth, severing all defilements and delusions; fifth, eliminating and subduing arrogance within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); sixth, proceeding toward the various wholesome paths; seventh, heading toward the gate of Nirvāṇa; eighth, through giving and receiving gifts, transcending all cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); ninth, following and learning from everything in the Bodhisattva path; and tenth, acceding to and complying with all the instructions and commands of the Buddhas.

Śāriputra! Regarding the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, you should receive, uphold, read, and recite it; you should extensively reveal it and explain it to others, thereby fully attaining such praised merits as these.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more,
spoke in verse: “Those who possess great wisdom, Who thoroughly understand the meaning of words and phrases,
And uphold this king of sutras, Shall attain immeasurable, supreme insight.”
That bhikṣu, a Dharma teacher, constantly practices this gift of Dharma;
upholding this king of sūtras, he gives rise to supreme joy and proclaims such a Dharma for all who listen.
By upholding this King of Sūtras, one obtains praiseworthy merit;
having attained this supreme wisdom, there shall be no diminution of the Dharma.
Furthermore, through the power of superior mindfulness, one is able to expound the unsurpassed words.
One who skillfully expounds the essential teachings always praises the instructions of the Buddha.
Holding this king of sutras, they possess abundant learning at all times;
having heard it, those who receive and uphold it do not cling to the mere words.
Constantly observing according to the meaning, one increases the Buddha’s wisdom;
through that boundless wisdom, one deeply penetrates the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Proclaiming it throughout the ten directions, those who hear it receive praise.
Furthermore, greed, anger, and delusion—through this, all shall gradually diminish.
With the most supreme and pure mind, one who hears this receives praise;
amidst the enjoyment of requisites, they weigh them according to their true meaning.
Thoroughly understanding that which is not real, he left home to seek liberation;
delighting in dwelling in secluded places, he never grew weary of hearing the Dharma.
He inquired at the place of the World-Honored One, and in bestowing the gift of Dharma, he was without stinginess.
"May wisdom increase, Pure and without diminution.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

"These bodhisattvas, regarding the practice of the perfection of supreme wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), should with vigor employ the four means of attraction (saṃgrahavastu) to gather in sentient beings throughout the long night."
What are the four?
They are giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation; these are called the four kinds.
What is giving?
These are the gift of material wealth, the gift of Dharma, and the gift of fearlessness.
What is kind speech?
It refers to uttering gentle and compliant words toward those who listen to the Dharma.
What is beneficial conduct?
It refers to the perfection of the intention toward oneself and others.
What is collaborative action?
That is to say, regarding this wisdom, one conceives of it as a merit, thereby gathering in sentient beings and causing them to dwell securely in this Dharma.
Furthermore, "generosity" refers to having an extremely pure intention toward all who come seeking alms.
Loving speech means severing all attachments.
Beneficial action means ensuring there is no retreat or discouragement.
Shared purpose means dedicating [merit] toward the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, as for generosity, it is to act in accordance with great compassion, without any sense of regret or stinginess.
As for pleasant speech, it is to give with a joyful heart.
As for beneficial conduct, it is to don the great armor of physical and mental fortitude for the sake of all sentient beings.
Regarding "common practice" (samānārthatā): it is the mind relinquishing all notions of high and low and directing itself toward omniscience (sarvajñatā).
Furthermore, regarding "generosity" (dāna): it is seeking in accordance with the Dharma and relinquishing all material requisites.
Regarding "loving speech" (priyavāditā): it is guiding others by means of the True Dharma.
Regarding beneficial conduct, one gives rise to equanimity toward both self-benefit and the benefit of others.
Regarding collaborative conduct, one causes all sentient beings to collectively give rise to the mind of omniscience.
Furthermore, generosity consists of personally relinquishing all things, whether internal or external.
Kind speech consists of praising the practice of all dharmas, as well as merit, wisdom, and skillful means.
Regarding beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), one abandons one’s own benefit to follow through with the benefit of others.

Regarding collaborative conduct (*samānārthatā*), one brings enlightenment to maturity; it is like an *āmala* fruit held in the palm of one’s hand, which one bestows universally upon all without any timidity.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra,
the gift of Dharma refers to explaining to others exactly as one has heard it.
Loving speech refers to providing correct instruction without any expectation of reward."
As for beneficial conduct, one expounds the Dharma for others without becoming weary or fatigued.
As for concordant conduct, one never abandons the mind that delights in the profound Dharma of omniscience.
Furthermore, the gift of Dharma consists of teaching without distraction to those who come to listen to the Dharma.
Kind speech consists of traveling even to distant lands to expound the various teachings.

Beneficial conduct consists of providing for and attending to all Dharma masters—supplying them with food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and even protecting them with one’s own body—for the sake of the meaning of the Dharma.
"Concordant conduct" means causing the seeds of the lineage to be perfumed and stabilized.
Furthermore, among all forms of giving, the gift of Dharma is unsurpassed.
"Loving speech" means discerning what is meaningful and beneficial.
Beneficial conduct means following the meaning rather than the literal words and phrases.
Common purpose means acting so as to bring all Buddha-dharmas to fulfillment.
Furthermore, giving is precisely the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā).
Loving speech is the perfection of ethical discipline and patience;
beneficial action is the perfection of diligence;
and collaborative conduct is the perfections of meditative concentration and superior wisdom.
Furthermore, the one who practices giving is the bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [upon enlightenment].
The one who practices kind speech is the bodhisattva practicing with superior conviction.
The one who practices beneficial conduct is the bodhisattva on the stage of non-retrogression.
Cooperative conduct is the Bodhisattva in his last birth before Buddhahood.
Furthermore, generosity is that which abides in the root of bodhi;
kind speech is that which nurtures the sprout of bodhi.
Beneficial conduct is that which opens the flower of bodhi;
shared conduct is that which binds the fruit of bodhi. "Śāriputra!

Therefore, throughout the long night, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas gather sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), enabling them to follow along with the practices of awakening and the various perfections (*pāramitā*). Furthermore, there are immeasurable and boundless other such means of attraction.
At that time, the Buddha said to Śāriputra:

"That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha has fully and correctly revealed the path to enlightenment for Prince Vīryaprabha, and he is praised by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the past, future, and present."

At that time, Prince Vīryaprabha, having heard such a true path to enlightenment from that Buddha and having heard the praises of the World-Honored Buddhas of the three periods of time, attained great benefit and felt immense joy. Furthermore, for ninety-nine *koṭi* years, he made offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine to that Buddha and the assembly of great *śrāvakas*, honoring, respecting, and praising them.
Śāriputra! That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mahāskandha immediately bestowed upon him the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Thirty-Eight;
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha,
Volume Thirty-Nine.

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperial Preceptor of the Western Heaven, Silver Light Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, Great Master of the Transmission of Sanskrit, Purple-Robed Śramaṇa Subject [Dharmapāla], by Imperial Decree. Chapter Eleven: The Perfection of Supreme Wisdom (VII). At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra:
"You must not, upon hearing that Prince Vīryacaryā has received his prediction, give rise to divergent views or harbor doubts."

Why is this so? This Prince Viśeṣacintin, during ninety-nine koṭis of past years, personally attended upon, made offerings to, honored, and praised the Tathāgata Mahāskandha and his assembly of śrāvakas; he also diligently served them with food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine, providing for all their needs until they were fully satisfied.

By virtue of his original vow, that Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestowed upon him the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, declaring that in a future age, after incalculable kalpas have passed, he shall attain Buddhahood under the name of Ratnakāya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

That Buddha had a community of eighty nayutas of great śrāvakas, all of whom were arhats; their outflows were exhausted, they were free from further afflictions, their minds attained mastery, and they had reached the other shore.

Śāriputra! Furthermore, at that time there appeared in the world a king named Suprabha. That king governed his people solely through the Dharma; he turned the wheel of the true Dharma and practiced diligent conduct. He was protected by a fourfold army and possessed the seven treasures, namely: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the mani-jewel treasure, the woman-treasure, the military commander treasure, and the steward treasure. These seven treasures were thus preeminent and beyond compare.
Furthermore, there is a great city named Jāmbūnada-gold; that city is twelve yojanas in length from east to west, and likewise seven yojanas in breadth from south to north.

The people of that land are free from all hardships and sufferings; their needs are fulfilled according to their wishes, and possessing great supernormal powers, they experience supreme and wondrous bliss—such sentient beings fill its midst.

There was a great elder named Śubhamati, who possessed an abundance of precious jewels and enjoyed them without lack; his treasuries were all completely filled, and having planted many roots of goodness under various Buddhas, he was certified and approved by those Buddhas.

Śāriputra! At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Ratnakāya observed the elder Suprajña and thoroughly knew that he was a vessel capable of upholding the True Dharma of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka, and was a vessel for the teachings of all Buddhas.

Having understood this, he immediately went to that place and manifested great supernatural power, sitting cross-legged in mid-air. He then expounded the Dharma of the Bodhisattva path according to their needs and further praised the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Śāriputra! At that time, having heard the Dharma, that elder felt deep affection and joy, his faith and understanding became pure, and he was filled with great rapture.

For a thousand years, he provided food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and all other necessities, while prostrating, making offerings, honoring, and praising the Tathāgata Ratnakāya and his assembly of śrāvakas.
Having completed a thousand years without weariness or indolence, he made this vow:
"May I attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When that Tathāgata heard this vow, he immediately bestowed upon him a prediction of enlightenment.
Śāriputra! Do not think that after the householder Suprajña received his prophecy, he gave rise to divergent views or fell into doubt.

At that time, I too aspired for bodhi, and for a thousand years I made offerings of food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine, while honoring, respecting, revering, and praising the Tathāgata Ratnakāya and his assembly of śrāvakas.
That Buddha, the World-Honored One, did not bestow upon me the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnakāya addressed Suvijña, saying:

"In a future age, after incalculable kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Dīpaṃkara Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣa-damya-sārathi, Śāstā deva-manuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."

In that Buddha-field there was a king named Ajātaśatru; his city was named Padmasamṛddha. The people of that country were free from all suffering and hardship, and they enjoyed great peace and security, accomplishing all their wishes as they desired.

"Śāriputra! Furthermore, at that time there was a king named Mahāsāla. That king had a son named Pradīpasaṃpanna, who possessed sovereign majesty and virtue, was handsome of countenance, endowed with all the marks of excellence, beloved by all people, and whose treasuries were so full that he lacked for nothing in his enjoyments."
At that time, King Ajātaśatru entrusted half of his kingdom to him for governance.
Once Pradīpasaṃpanna had ascended the throne, he likewise ruled and transformed the people through wholesome dharmas.

Śāriputra! This Lamp-Endowed One then gave birth to a crown prince whose physical marks were dignified, most excellent, and perfectly complete; who was pure and translucent like a pond; who possessed the thirty-two marks of a great man; and whose majestic radiance shone brilliantly like the orb of the sun.
The king immediately felt joy arise in his heart and bestowed upon him the name Dīpaṃkara (Lamp-Maker).
At that time, the king summoned a brahmin to examine the physiognomy of his son.
Then the brahmin addressed the king, saying:

"This crown prince has planted roots of goodness in past lives; he shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), and before long he will certainly attain great supernormal powers."

At that time, a devaputra of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven suddenly vanished from the Akaniṣṭha heaven and went to where the Prince was. He prostrated with his head at the Prince’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and spoke these verses for the Prince:
“In former times, while amidst the causes, You accumulated all manner of merit;
You have awakened to unsurpassed Bodhi, Just like the banner of a supreme rishi.”
In the prime of life one possesses power and majesty, yet decline comes as swift as the wind;
the vigor of youth is assailed by old age—this world is not a place for delight.
Pressed by aging and decay, one grows weary of suffering and seeks liberation.
One should reflect well that this splendor does not endure for long.
Excellent, O one of great wisdom! Swiftly seek liberation;
upon this path to enlightenment, firmly uphold the pure precepts.

At that time, after the Śuddhāvāsa devaputra had spoken these verses, during the first watch of the night, he immediately awakened and instructed the Prince, causing him to give rise to faith and understanding, renounce his home and leave the household life, so that he would attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and possess great majestic virtue with a reputation heard afar.

At that time, having received those instructions, the prince applied himself with diligence to faith and understanding within the Buddha-dharma, practicing and training in accordance with the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Śāriputra! At that time, when King Prabhūtaratna heard that the prince had left his home to renounce the world and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, he immediately dispatched a messenger to the abode of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, conveying this instruction in full:
"I pray only that you, out of great compassion, will take pity on me and return at once."
"If he does not come at the appointed time, I shall immediately array the fourfold army and go there myself. Śāriputra,
King Pradīpasaṃpanna then summoned his ministers to deliberate on this matter, and immediately prepared his carriage to welcome the World-Honored One.

Beholding the Buddha’s physical marks, so majestic and extraordinary, they marveled at such an unprecedented sight; each arose with reverence, prostrated themselves at his feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One..."
"He has deep compassion for King Ajātaśatru and brings us great benefit.
Śāriputra, at that time,

after the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara had accepted the king's invitation, the king, together with twenty koṭis of royal kinsmen and the fourfold army, followed and surrounded the Buddha, the World-Honored One, as they proceeded to the royal palace.

The king then provided him with robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and all manner of articles of pleasure, ensuring they were fully supplied and offering them for his enjoyment according to his every desire.
At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, expounded the essentials of the Dharma for them, delivering many from suffering.
They prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and wept with tears of sorrow, harboring deep feelings of longing and veneration.
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, together with twenty koṭis of great arhats, immediately proceeded to the great city of Aśoka-rāja, named Padmasampanna.

"Śāriputra! At that time, when King Ajātaśatru heard that the Buddha, having lit the lamp, had arrived at his city, he immediately issued an edict to the people. He commanded that all the crossroads, streets, and lanes within the city be made pure; all broken tiles, rubble, thorns, and briars were to be cleared away. Fragrant water was sprinkled upon the ground so that there was no dust or dirt, and various famous flowers were scattered until they reached the height of the knees. Precious vases and incense burners spread their smoke everywhere, and various precious garments hung down in every place. Drums, horns, and conch shells were struck in continuous succession, and ointments, incense, and flower garlands filled the space—a magnificent adornment such as had never existed before."
The people of that land provided offerings according to their own means; there was no commerce, and all beheld it with joy. Śāriputra!

At that time, King Ajātaśatru further welcomed the Tathāgata by presenting various flowers, incense, necklaces, burning incense, powdered incense, robes, silken canopies, banners, pennants, music, songs, and hymns of praise, and he paid homage and made offerings to him within his own palace.

At that time, the king immediately attained a mind of supreme joy, a mind of wondrous auspiciousness, an unobstructed mind, and a mind free from feverish affliction, and he dwelt in peace and security. Śāriputra!

Furthermore, there were elder householders, lay devotees, brahmins, and others who also approached the Buddha with the various kinds of offerings mentioned above; they prostrated themselves at his feet, gazing up in reverence at the World-Honored One.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Ratnaka who, together with a retinue of five hundred people, lived on the banks of the Himavat River; he constantly maintained three types of maṇḍala rites, namely: the Nigraṇṭha rite, the Gāthāpāda rite, and the Akṣarapada rite.
At that time, his entire assembly was able to master these three kinds of teachings, and he himself declared:
"One who recites these phrases is most excellent in the world; such a person is a great man and a preceptor."
"Śāriputra! At that time, there was also a brahmin named Ratnamegha, who, together with a retinue of five hundred people, studied under him and claimed to have reached the ultimate realization."
At that time, Ratnamegha addressed his teacher, saying:
"I have already attained thorough mastery of this Dharma. Now I wish to return to my place of birth; I shall seek five hundred gold coins to repay your instruction."

At that time, the Jewel Cloud gradually traveled through kingdoms, cities, and villages until he reached the great city of Lotus-Abundance. Seeing that the city was magnificently adorned, he immediately went to inquire:
"What extraordinary event is taking place in this city?"
They spoke together, saying:

"Virtuous one, you should know that the present Buddha, the World-Honored One, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, together with eighty koṭis of great arhats and an assembly of eighty-four thousand great bodhisattvas, is currently residing within the royal palace, expounding the True Dharma to deliver all beings."
"The people of that land are adorned in such a manner.
At that time, having heard these words, Jewel Cloud gave rise to a pure mind and felt great joy, reflecting:
"The appearance of a Buddha in the world is as difficult to encounter as the blooming of the udumbara flower, which appears but once in an age."
"I shall now take the gold coins I have sought and use them to buy flowers to scatter upon the Buddha.
As he proceeded gradually on his way, he saw a young girl holding seven stalks of *utpala* lotuses in her hand.
At that time, Ratnamegha said to the young woman:
"These flowers are most exquisite; from where were they obtained?
I now wish to trade five hundred gold coins for these flowers so as to fashion a wonderful floral garland, which I shall offer to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara."
At that time, having heard the name of the Buddha, the young girl, through the power of her roots of goodness from past lives, spoke these words:
"Now that this body of mine has fallen into the midst of birth and death, I ought to awaken to myself."
Having heard this, Ratnamegha immediately asked the young girl,
"What did you just say?
The young girl replied:

"In the past, during incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I accumulated roots of merit within the Buddha-dharma. Whether it was by means of pearls, lapis lazuli, gold, silver, conch shells, elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, palanquins, carriages, retinues of maidens and attendants, or my own head, eyes, marrow, brain, flesh, hands, and feet—giving away all internal and external wealth with profound and pure faith and understanding—I abandoned the household life to go forth and practice the bodhisattva path. Regarding all dharmas, I remained free from all obstacles, not sparing even a single grain of mustard seed’s worth of my body or life."
"Why do you treat me with such contempt?
At that time, the young girl took an *utpala* flower and went to where the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was; she offered it to the Buddha, and the Buddha accepted it.

“At that time, the World-Honored One was again surrounded by a multitude of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas who paid him reverent homage; amidst them, the Buddha’s majestic virtue was towering, vast, and pure.”
The maiden marveled at this unprecedented occurrence; she immediately gave rise to the most supreme and excellent resolve, and her devotion and joy increased. Śāriputra!

At that time, the brahmin Ratnamegha also went to where the Buddha was, and having developed pure faith, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and gazed upon his venerable countenance without averting his eyes for even a moment.
Seeing that multitude of people all offering exquisite and sublime Dharma-robes to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara,
the Jewel Cloud then thought to himself:
"What exquisite Dharma-robes do I now possess with which to make an offering?"
He then took the deer-skin garment he was wearing and offered it to the Buddha.
When the assembly of people witnessed this, they immediately began to revile him.
As they spoke these words, that deer-skin garment suddenly transformed into something made of the seven precious jewels.
At that time, Ratnamegha was filled with immense joy and leaped for joy beyond measure; he immediately offered it to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and spoke these words:
"I pray you look upon me with compassion and deign to accept it."
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately accepted them.
He further took five stalks of *utpala* flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, extending the offering to the entire assembly.

At that moment, there were also countless devaputras who held celestial *mandārava*, *mahāmandārava*, *mañjūṣaka*, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers and scattered them over the Buddha. In the midst of the void, they performed celestial music and sang hymns of praise. By means of their supernormal powers (*ṛddhibala*), they further manifested countless *utpala* flowers; these flowers had a thousand petals and were suffused with extraordinary fragrances. They swirled and covered the sky, transforming into flower canopies as an act of worship.
"Śāriputra!

At that time, the brahmin Ratnamegha served the Buddha Dīpaṃkara with a pure mind for twelve years. By the power of his superior progress and through the force of his original vow, he obtained a golden topknot and spoke these words:
'I only pray that the World-Honored One will comfort me and make me firm, so that I may soon receive the prediction of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.'"

Translated by the Tripitaka Master Dharmapāla and others, Imperial Preceptor for the Propagation of the Sanskrit Canon, Silver Light Grandee, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments, and Great Master of Compassionate Enlightenment, bestowed with the purple robe, by imperial decree. Chapter Eleven: The Perfection of Supreme Wisdom (8). "Furthermore, Śāriputra!"
That Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara was able to know all things throughout the three periods of time with his universal eye of wisdom.

When the brahmin Ratnamegha had thus understood this, he spread his golden locks upon the ground and requested the Buddha, the śrāvakas, and the other bhikṣus to walk over them, circling to the right.
Why is this? The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The brahmin Ratnamegha shall, after the passing of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, attain Buddhahood, being named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat."

"Śāriputra! At that time, having heard the Buddha’s prophecy, that brahmin leaped for joy and manifested great supernormal powers; instantaneously, within the midst of space, he realized immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of unspeakable samādhi-doors."

By the power of his supernormal knowledge, he transcended worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction, where all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, bestowed upon him this prophecy:
"In a future age, after immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni."
"In this same way, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir did likewise. Śāriputra!

Having heard that all the Buddhas had conferred the prediction upon him in unison, the brahmin Ratnamegha attained great consolation. Descending from mid-air, he immediately went to the place where Dīpaṃkara Buddha was, gave rise to pure faith, left the home life for homelessness, and constantly cultivated the holy life."
Śāriputra! Do not conceive a divergent view regarding the brahmin Ratnamegha, nor give rise to doubt. Why is this?
That brahmin was none other than myself.

At that time, I scattered five-stalked *utpala* flowers upon the crown of the Buddha’s head; furthermore, regarding the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, I delighted in hearing it, receiving and upholding it, reciting and chanting it, and extensively revealing and expounding it for others. I was fully endowed with right practice, namely the practice of signlessness (*animitta*). For these reasons, I swiftly obtained the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Śāriputra! If I had not accomplished various deeds through those pure practices of the Dharma by means of the power of my supernormal knowledges and wisdom, that Buddha, the World-Honored One, would not have bestowed upon me the prediction of enlightenment.
At that time, regarding the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka as I had heard it, I established correct practice— namely, the practice of signlessness and the practice of non-apprehension—
and upon seeing that Buddha, I attained the equal transcendence of all practices.

Under that Buddha, I realized that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is unborn; by acceding to all phenomena, I gave rise to the view of equality and was able to attain the supreme dharma-patience.
What is it that one who has attained this patience endures?

It is what is called patience toward form, patience toward sensation, patience toward perception, patience toward formations, and patience toward consciousness; and so on, up to patience toward the various phenomena of the aggregates, sense bases, and elements.
Although one has attained this dharma-patience, it is like that aforementioned designation. Why is this?

Because it is not an accumulation of worldly dharmas; because it is not an accumulation of the dharmas of ordinary beings, nor of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), nor of pratyekabuddhas, nor of bodhisattvas, nor of the Buddhas; because all dharmas are unobtainable and there is nothing to be accumulated, this is called the attainment of patience regarding all dharmas.

Furthermore, that patience is such that, regarding all marks and all objects of attachment, one attains this patience even in a single kṣaṇa; that is to say, it is not the exhaustion of the eye-element nor the eye-object, and so on up to the exhaustion of the objects of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and even toward that object of patience, there is no arrival.
Śāriputra!

Because I have desired to hear, receive, uphold, read, and recite this true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, and because I have extensively revealed it for others and expounded it, and because I have been fully endowed with right practice—namely, the practice of signlessness and the practice of non-apprehension—I swiftly received the prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.

When these words were spoken, there was in the assembly a son of a householder named Viśvantara. Having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, the merits of the Buddhas, and the practices of the bodhisattvas, he immediately rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

In the past, I followed and studied under the Venerable Ānanda, entering into the realization of the Dharma of Arhatship and dwelling in the abode of emptiness and stillness until the end of old age and death.

Now, suddenly hearing the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, the merits of all Buddhas, and the practices of Bodhisattvas—namely, that the Mahāyāna is the supreme vehicle, the foremost, most profound, and unsurpassed, being the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi—I am filled with wonder.
I have personally heard this taught by the Buddha and have personally received it; regarding this true Dharma, I have given rise to immeasurable, profound, and sublime resolve.
Furthermore, regarding this Dharma, I do not engage in measurement or evaluation, nor do I harbor any attachment or form a conceptual resolve.
If one were to say that this Dharma is the foremost, most profound, and most subtle, beyond which nothing superior exists, that person would be regressing from the accumulation [of merit] therein.
World-Honored One!

This True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is the supreme and foremost revelation among all Buddha-vehicles and indeed all vehicles; it is characterized by great compassion and great benefit, bringing peace and happiness to devas and humans, and delivering all beings.
"For those in training and those beyond training who have attained their respective goals up to the stage of a Bodhisattva, who would not resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
At that time, the elder’s son Viśvantara addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is it difficult to accomplish *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* through the concentration on suffering?
The Buddha said,
"Ren-shou!"
"So it is, so it is. World-Honored One, according to that mode of practice, one accumulates diligence without regressing from the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."

Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, gave rise to the bodhicitta in the presence of each and every Buddha as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and was further able to dwell with equanimity in such diligence to realize the fruit of enlightenment, he was also able to bring peace and security to the path of all bodhisattvas.
Why is this so? Because the wisdom of all Buddhas is immeasurable and boundless.

O World-Honored One, it is inconceivable and incalculable; if one does not skillfully cultivate and practice this Dharma, remaining obstructed by conceptual discrimination, then even after hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of kalpas, the fruit of Bodhi will be extremely difficult to attain.
At that time, the elder’s son Viśvantara spoke these verses before the Buddha:
“Throughout thousands of koṭis of eons, I have resolved upon bodhicitta;
yet I see sentient beings who are indolent, sinking and wallowing in manifold sufferings.”
Even if one were to give away one's head and eyes, their accumulated measure exceeding Mount Sumeru,
with such a single-mindedness, one would practice with diligence,
never flagging or retreating. If I abide in the Buddha-way, I shall bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
By relying upon the Tathāgata, one attains this power of diligence.
This vehicle is called the Mahāyāna; it is the supreme teaching of the Buddha.
Those who desire bodhi will ultimately be free from views and grasping.
"Protecting against all suffering and distress, Liberating one from the evil realms— This is the benefit of perfect awakening, Spoken by the Tathāgata alone.

When the elder’s son Viśvantara had spoken this verse, he gave rise to great faith and understanding within the Buddha-dharma; he no longer clung to worldly pleasures, nor to his wife, children, or kinsmen.

Having prostrated with his head at the feet of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and circumambulated him three times to the right, he returned to his own residence in an instant. Together with his retinue of seven wives, seven sons, seven daughters, seven male servants, and seven female servants—each holding exquisite fine cotton cloth worth ten million—and accompanied by five hundred musicians, he departed from the great city of Rājagṛha, intending to go to where the Buddha was.
When the crowd of people saw this, they immediately went to inquire.
The son of the elder addressed them, saying:

"Virtuous ones, you should know that the Tathāgata is currently at Vulture Peak Mountain, surrounded with reverence by an immeasurable and incalculable multitude of hundreds of thousands of followers, extensively revealing and teaching immeasurable wholesome dharmas."

The wisdom of the Buddha is inconceivable and immeasurable; I and my retinue wish to go there to joyfully hear the profound and wondrous meaning of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, to resolve all nets of doubt through the power of our roots of goodness, and to embrace *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"You virtuous ones should also draw near to that Buddha and plant the roots of all manner of goodness.
When those people heard these words, they were filled with great joy and followed him in unison.

At that time, the son of the elder, together with his own retinue of five hundred musicians and a thousand followers, arrived at the place where the Buddha was. He immediately made various offerings of flowers, incense, necklaces, ointments, powdered incense, silk canopies, banners, and streamers, as well as music and song; he also scattered upon the Buddha exquisite, fine cotton cloths worth hundreds of thousands.
Then, before the Buddha, he spoke these verses:
“Throughout many kalpas in the past, You diligently cultivated the practices for enlightenment;
Having attained mastery over all phenomena, You bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.”
Thus, I shall now extend this offering;
seeing the World-Honored One of Two Legs, who always dwells in pure conduct and has realized the unsurpassed path, I therefore extend this offering.
"My retinue and the thousand followers I have brought all draw near to the Tathāgata;
we all take refuge in him and pay him homage.
Having spoken this verse of praise, the son of the elder addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I and my retinue, along with the multitude of people we have brought with us to the Buddha’s presence, have all established themselves in the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and planted the roots of various wholesome deeds; we vow never to regress from the Unsurpassed Way.”
Having spoken these words, they all cried out with one voice:
“World-Honored One!
We lay followers take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; may you graciously accept us.”
For as long as our lives last, we shall remain far removed from killing and enter the gate of purity; at this very moment, we all resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment.

We pray that the World-Honored One, for our sake, will preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma; do not abandon such a multitude, and we pray that you will deliver and save the suffering sentient beings of future ages.
Thus he requested twice.
At that time, out of extreme compassion, the World-Honored One manifested a great supernormal power and ascended into the air, where he sat cross-legged.
When the son of the elder and the others saw this, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
By the majestic spiritual power of that Buddha, World-Honored One, he sustained the entire great assembly so that they all remained suspended in mid-air.

At that time, the son of the elder, together with his own retinue of five hundred musicians and others, gave rise to great joy. Standing upright in the air with palms joined, he circumambulated [the Buddha] three times to the right, prostrated himself at his feet, and performed various musical offerings while singing praises of the Buddha’s virtues. This extended throughout the entire assembly, pervading immeasurable hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*.

By the spiritual power of the Buddha, there suddenly appeared in the air another great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, together with their retinue of sixty thousand people, coming from the east, desiring to hear the Dharma with joy.

At that time, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, beholding that great assembly, immediately employed his supernormal powers to manifest five multi-storied pavilions, adorned with myriad wonders and most rare. From each and every pavilion issued forth Brahma-sounds, expounding the sublime Dharma.
Furthermore, there were hundreds of thousands of koṭis of devaputras who took celestial māndārava flowers and scattered them over the Buddha, completely covering the air;
through the Buddha’s supernatural power, these became a pavilion of flowers.
At that time, the son of the elder and the great assembly, beholding such vast and divine transformations of pure adornment, gave rise to immeasurable feelings of intimacy and affection.
The Buddha, having known this, immediately withdrew his supernormal power, and the eastern direction returned to its original appearance as before.
At that time, Ānanda, having witnessed this event, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"For what cause and condition has this miraculous transformation been manifested?
We pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for us.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"I shall now bestow upon you, the son of the householder Ren-shou, along with your retinue and your musical ensemble, so that you may make offerings to me; this person shall not fall into the evil realms for a thousand koṭis of kalpas, but shall always be born among humans and devas, experiencing supreme and wondrous bliss."

After this kalpa has passed, he will likewise honor and make offerings to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Mārgacaryā, and for twenty-five koṭis of kalpas he will no longer undergo saṃsāric rebirth.

After these seven wives and the others have cast off this body, they shall transform their female bodies into male forms and, together with the Bodhisattva Ren-shou, cultivate the bodhisattva practices for one kalpa.

Ānanda! That Bodhisattva Renśou shall attain Buddhahood, with the title Tathāgata Equal-Mind, fully endowed with the ten epithets; together with his own retinue, they shall all receive successive predictions of their own attainment of Buddhahood.

At that time, those five hundred musicians, by virtue of making offerings to the Buddha, did not fall into the evil realms for incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, and for a thousand *koṭi* kalpas they constantly served as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*).
After this number has passed, they shall honor and revere ten thousand Tathāgatas, all of whom will become Buddhas within a single kalpa, sharing the same name.

Furthermore, the remaining thousand followers, after the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Maitreya, shall pass through as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, honoring and making offerings to a thousand koṭis of Buddhas; they shall then attain Buddhahood, with the name Tathāgata Viśeṣa, fully endowed with the ten titles.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

"That King Ajātaśatru, together with the brahmin Pradīpadatta and his thousand followers, after the True Dharma has perished and the kalpa of weapons has passed, will, in a future age, encounter a Buddha appearing in the world named Maitreya."

At that time, those sentient beings will have a long lifespan of eighty thousand years; furthermore, one thousand pratyekabuddhas will appear in the world, whom they will approach, make offerings to, revere, and praise, and they will likewise revere, make offerings to, and honor the Tathāgata Maitreya.
For twenty-five koṭi-nayuta kalpas, he will never again regress as he plants various roots of goodness, leaves the household life for homelessness, and attains the fruit of Bodhi.

Furthermore, seeing those one thousand people simultaneously resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, sixty nayutas of devas and humans at that time become free from dust and defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As for those foolish commoners, they are unable to give rise toward the Buddha to affectionate joy, pure faith and understanding, respect, and praise."
"Why is this? Because these people cannot even attain a small root of virtue, let alone realize the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke in verse:
"Because of honoring all Buddhas, one attains this supreme auspiciousness;
by making offerings to the Teachers who tame others, one obtains the most excellent great fruit.
After the Buddhas have entered parinirvāṇa, one is able to behold their relics."
Just as with a measure of mustard seeds, one should perform extensive and sublime offerings.
Furthermore, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, those who make offerings to the śarīra relics should give rise to a mind of equanimity, as if the Tathāgata were still dwelling in the world.
Because of giving rise to this mind, one makes offerings to the Unsurpassed Honored One,
awakens to equal enlightenment, and the karmic fruit is likewise so.
Being taken into the care of the Sugata, one remains far removed from the evil realms.
Such a person proceeds toward nirvāṇa, And does not consider it difficult to attain.
They are able to demonstrate the Buddha’s prohibitions and precepts, The supreme samādhi,
and pure resolute conviction, Thereby attaining the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood.
Having performed such offerings, one swiftly proceeds to practice well and attains unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, proclaiming the supreme Dharma.
If a person wishes to fully understand and draw near to the teachings of all Buddhas, [they should do so].
Desiring to attain great learning, with a profound mind free from weariness or indolence,
one becomes a sovereign wheel-turning monarch or born into a noble family of pure conduct;
adorned with the marks of merit, one attains liberation at the opportune moment.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the World-Honored One addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:

“If sons or daughters of good family who abide in the Mahāyāna wish to swiftly attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they should delight in hearing much, receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting the sublime meaning and benefit of the true Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, even to the point of extensively explaining and teaching it to others. By doing so, they will succeed in perpetuating the Three Jewels so that they are never interrupted; they will attain non-retrogression in the four immeasurables, the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni*), and so forth, because they will be fully in accord with benefiting sentient beings.”
Furthermore, Śāriputra!
This True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka is the path to enlightenment. Why is this so?
This True Dharma of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka encompasses Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
it is the very provision for all bodhisattvas, and you should train in it accordingly so that it is never interrupted.
Śāriputra! This refers to the attainment of all pāramitās of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, which enables one to skillfully achieve transcendence through all the pāramitās of the Tathāgata.
In immeasurable stages, one successively attains all the pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) of a Tathāgata, up to the attainment of the stage of a Tathāgata itself.
If one abides in such a perfection (*pāramitā*), one thereby dwells in all perfections.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to clarify this meaning once more, spoke these verses:
"When wisdom arises, one speaks of all conditioned phenomena;
Because of wisdom and ignorance, there are the various sufferings of the conditioned."
"Regarding karma and its retribution, one should understand it thus:
that which is neither karma nor retribution is liberation attained in the present.

When the World-Honored One had spoken these verses, the Venerable Śāriputra, the great Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, the assembly of bhikṣus, and all the world—including devas, humans, asuras, and gandharvas—having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced; they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Piṭaka Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll Forty.
